Initially created: 2025-11-27T21:41:42.058+09:00 by dsehnal Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into $lang.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.
5. The target language is $lang.
Input text:

p.seg: I, your servant, have heard:
“To speak without knowing is
unwise;
to know and not speak is
disloyal.”
To be disloyal as a subject
deserves death;
to speak improperly
also deserves death.
However,
I wish to fully speak of what I have heard,
and leave it to Your Majesty to decide my punishment.
I have heard:
The world secretly aligns Yān 燕 and Wèi 魏,
connects Jīng 荊 and secures Qí 齊,
and gathers Hán 韓 to form a vertical alliance,
intending to face west and cause trouble for the powerful Qín 秦.
I secretly laugh at this.
The world embodies three ways to perish,
and the world has them all.
Is this what is meant by that?
I have heard it said:
"To attack order with chaos leads to ruin,
to attack righteousness with evil leads to ruin,
to attack obedience with rebellion leads to ruin."
Now, the treasuries of the world are not full,
and the granaries are empty.
They exhaust their soldiers and people,
and deploy armies of several hundred thousand,
yet those who kowtow and wear feathers as generals
die in front
but do not reach a thousand,
and all die talking.
With white blades in front
and axes and chopping blocks behind,
they retreat and cannot die.
It is not that their soldiers and people cannot die,
but that their superiors are incapable.
If they speak of rewards, they are not given;
if they speak of punishments, they are not carried out.
Rewards and punishments lack credibility,
therefore the soldiers and people do not die.
Now, Qín 秦 issues decrees and carries out rewards and punishments,
and the deserving and undeserving all serve.
They come straight from their parents' embrace,
and have never seen a bandit before.
Upon hearing of battle,
they stamp their feet, strip off their clothes,
charge against white blades,
and step on burning coals.
Those who die in front
are all like this.
The resolve to die and the resolve to live are different,
but the people do it because
they value fighting to the death.
One person fighting to the death can face ten,
ten can face a hundred,
a hundred can face a thousand,
a thousand can face ten thousand,
and ten thousand can conquer the world.
Now, the territory of Qín 秦, leveling the long and supplementing the short,
is several thousand square *lǐ*,
and its renowned soldiers number several hundred thousand.
The decrees and punishments of Qín 秦,
the advantages and disadvantages of its terrain,
are things that the world cannot match.
With this, taking on the world,
the world is not enough to possess entirely.
Therefore, Qín 秦 has never failed to win in battle,
has never failed to conquer in attack,
has never failed to break through what it faces,
and has opened up thousands of *lǐ* of land.
This is its great achievement.
However, its armor is worn out,
its soldiers and people are weary,
its accumulated resources are exhausted,
its fields are barren,
its granaries are empty,
the lords of the surrounding states do not submit,
and the name of a hegemon king is not achieved.
There is no other reason for this
than that its strategists do not fully devote their loyalty.
I dare to speak of it.
In the past, Qí 齊 broke Jīng 荊 to the south,
broke Sòng 宋 to the east,
subdued Qín 秦 to the west,
broke Yān 燕 to the north,
and used Hán 韓
and Wèi 魏 in the center.
Its land was vast and its army strong,
it won battles and seized territories,
and it issued commands to the world.
The clear Jì 濟 River and the muddy Hé 河 River of Qí 齊
were enough to serve as borders;
the Great Wall and massive defenses
were enough to serve as fortresses.
Qí 齊
is a state of five battles;
one battle lost and there would be no Qí 齊.
From this perspective,
battle is a matter of survival or destruction for a state of ten thousand chariots.
Furthermore, I have heard it said:
"Cut off the stump without leaving a root,
do not associate with a neighboring calamity,
and calamity will not exist."
Qín 秦 fought with the people of Jīng 荊,
greatly defeating Jīng 荊,
attacking Yǐng 郢,
and taking Dòngtíng 洞庭,
Wǔzhǔ 五渚,
and the land south of the Jiāng 江 River.
The king and ministers of Jīng 荊 fled,
seeking refuge in Chén 陳 to the east.
At this time,
if we had followed Jīng 荊 with our troops,
then Jīng 荊 could have been taken;
if Jīng 荊 could have been taken,
then its people would have been greedy,
and its land would have been profitable,
weakening Qí 齊 and Yān 燕 in the east,
and dominating the Three Jìn 晉 in the center.
In that case, with one move,
the name of a hegemon king could have been achieved,
and the lords of the surrounding states could have paid tribute.
But the strategists did not do this,
withdrawing their troops
and making peace with the people of Jīng 荊 again.
This allowed the people of Jīng 荊 to recover their lost state,
gather their scattered people,
establish a sovereign,
and set up ancestral temples;
causing them to lead the world in facing west
to cause trouble for Qín 秦.
This is the first way in which we lost the path to becoming a hegemon.
The world then formed alliances and massed troops below Huá 華,
and Your Majesty used decrees to break them,
with the troops reaching below the walls of Liáng 梁.
Besieging Liáng 梁 for several weeks,
Liáng 梁 could have been captured;
capturing Liáng 梁,
Wèi 魏 could have been taken;
taking Wèi 魏,
the intentions of Jīng 荊
and Zhào 趙 would have been cut off;
with the intentions of Jīng 荊 and Zhào 趙 cut off,
Zhào 趙 would have been in danger;
with Zhào 趙 in danger, Jīng 荊 would have been suspicious;
weakening Qí 齊
and Yān 燕 in the east,
and dominating the Three Jìn 晉 in the center.
In that case, with one move, the name of a hegemon king could have been achieved,
and the lords of the surrounding states could have paid tribute.
But the strategists did not do this,
withdrawing their troops
and making peace with the Wèi 魏 again.
This allowed the Wèi 魏 to recover their lost state,
gather their scattered people,
establish a sovereign,
and set up ancestral temples,
causing them to lead the world in facing west to cause trouble for Qín 秦.
This is the second way in which we lost the path to becoming a hegemon.
Previously, when Rǎng Hóu 穰侯 governed Qín 秦,
he used the troops of one state
to try to achieve the achievements of two states,
therefore the troops were constantly exposed abroad,
the soldiers and people were weary and sick at home,
and the name of a hegemon king was not achieved.
This is the third way in which we lost the path to becoming a hegemon.
The Zhào 趙 are
a state in the center,
inhabited by mixed peoples,
whose people are fickle and difficult to use.
Orders are not well enforced,
rewards and punishments lack credibility,
the terrain is unfavorable,
and the rulers below cannot fully utilize the strength of their people.
That was certainly the shape of a state doomed to perish,
yet you did not worry about the common people,
but mobilized all your soldiers and people for battle below Chángpíng,
to contend for Hán's Shàngdǎng.
Your Majesty used an edict to defeat them,
and captured Wǔ'ān.
At that time,
the Zhào family, from top to bottom, were not close to each other,
the noble and the base did not trust each other.
In that case, Hándān would not hold.
Capture Hándān,
control the lands east of the mountains and Héjiān,
withdraw the army,
attack Xiūwǔ to the west,
cross Yángcháng,
and subdue Dài
and Shàngdǎng.
Dài, with thirty-six counties,
and Shàngdǎng, with seventeen counties,
without using a single suit of armor,
without distressing a single soldier or citizen,
all this would belong to Qín.
Dài and Shàngdǎng would have completely become Qín's without a fight;
Dōngyáng
and the lands outside the Hé would have completely turned against you to Qí without a fight;
Zhōngshān
and the lands north of Hūtuó would have completely become Yān's without a fight.
If that were the case, Zhào would be conquered,
and if Zhào were conquered, then Hán would perish;
if Hán perished, then Jīng
and Wèi would not be able to stand alone;
if Jīng and Wèi could not stand alone,
then it would be one move that would destroy Hán,
undermine Wèi,
coerce Jīng,
and weaken Qí and Yān in the east,
breaching the mouth of the Báimǎ to flood the Wèi territory—
it would be one move that would bring about the downfall of the Three Jìn states,
and the alliance would be defeated.
Your Majesty could fold your hands and wait for it,
and the world would fall into line and submit;
the name of Hegemon-King could be achieved.
Yet your strategists did not do this,
but withdrew the army and retreated,
and instead made peace with the Zhào family.
Indeed, with Your Majesty's brilliance
and the strength of the Qín army,
to abandon the enterprise of Hegemon-King,
when territory could have been gained,
but instead to accept deceit from a state on the verge of collapse,
this is the clumsiness of your strategists.
Moreover, that Zhào should have perished but did not,
and Qín should have become hegemon but did not,
the world certainly judged the strategists of Qín to be one-dimensional in their planning.
Then you mobilized all the soldiers again to attack Hándān,
but could not capture it,
discarding armor and weapons,
fighting fearfully and retreating;
the world certainly judged the strength of Qín to be two-dimensional in its capacity.
Then the army was withdrawn and returned,
joining at Lǐxià,
and Your Majesty also joined the army and arrived,
but in battle could not overcome them,
nor could you reverse the situation,
so the army was dismissed and departed;
the world certainly judged the strength of Qín to be three-dimensional in its capacity.
Internally, they assessed our strategists;
externally, they exhausted our military strength.
Judging from this,
I believe that the alliance against us in the world
will hardly be difficult.
Internally,
our armor and weapons are worn out,
the soldiers and people are weary,
our stores are exhausted,
the fields are barren,
and the granaries are empty.
Externally,
the world is united in purpose and very steadfast.
I hope that Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
Moreover, I have heard it said,
"Be ever cautious and apprehensive,
be more careful each day.
If you are careful in your conduct,
the world can be yours."
How do I know this is true?
In the past, Zhòu was the Son of Heaven,
commanding a million soldiers in the world,
drinking on the left at the Qí Stream
and drinking on the right at the Huán Stream,
so that the Qí River was exhausted and the Huán River did not flow,
using this strength to make trouble with King Wǔ of Zhōu.
King Wǔ led three thousand soldiers in plain armor,
and in one day of battle
destroyed the state of Zhòu,
captured his person,
seized his land and possessed his people,
and the world suffered no harm.
Zhì Bó led the armies of the Three States
to attack Lord Xiāng of Zhào at Jìnyáng,
diverting water to flood the city for three months,
and the city was about to fall;
Lord Xiāng consulted the tortoise shell and divining stalks to determine the omens,
in order to see what was advantageous or disadvantageous,
and which state he could surrender to.
Then he sent his minister Zhāng Mèngtán,
who secretly slipped out,
reversed the agreement of Zhì Bó,
obtained the armies of two states,
and attacked Zhì Bó,
capturing his person,
in order to restore Lord Xiāng's original position.
Now the territory of Qín, adding to its length and breadth,
is several thousand square *lǐ*,
and its renowned armies number in the hundreds of thousands.
The commands, decrees, rewards, and punishments of the state of Qín,
the advantages and disadvantages of its terrain,
are unmatched in the world.
With this strength, to engage the world,
you could annex and possess it.
I, at the risk of death, wish to have an audience with Your Majesty,
to speak of the means by which to break the alliance in the world,
conquer Zhào
and destroy Hán,
subject Jīng
and Wèi,
befriend Qí
and Yān,
to achieve the name of Hegemon-King,
and bring the surrounding lords to court.
If Your Majesty truly listens to my words,
but in one move the alliance in the world is not broken,
Zhào is not conquered,
Hán is not destroyed,
Jīng and Wèi do not become subjects,
Qí and Yān do not become friends,
the name of Hegemon-King is not achieved,
and the surrounding lords do not come to court,
Your Majesty should execute me and display my head in the country,
as a warning to those who devise disloyal plans for the king.
Hán has served Qín for more than thirty years,
serving as a shield and barrier when you go out,
and as a mat and cushion when you come in.
Qín simply sends out crack troops to seize territory,
and Hán follows along,
accumulating resentment throughout the world,
while the credit goes to the powerful Qín.
Moreover, Hán's submission of tribute
is no different from that of a commandery or county.
Now I have secretly heard of the plan of your noble ministers,
to raise troops and attack Hán.
The Zhào family gathers soldiers,
supports followers,
intending to burden the world with troops;
making it clear that Qín is not weak,
otherwise the lords would surely destroy their ancestral temples,
wishing to face west and carry out their intentions;
this is not a plan of one day.
Now, if you release the worries about Zhào
and instead reject Hán, an internal subject,
then the world will understand the Zhào family's plan.
Hán
is a small state,
yet it must respond to attacks from all sides in the world;
the ruler is disgraced and the ministers suffer,
and those above and below have shared the same worries for a long time.
They cultivate defenses,
are wary of powerful enemies,
have accumulated stores,
and have built walls and moats
to defend their fortifications.
Now, attacking Hán,
it cannot be destroyed in a year.
Retreating after capturing a single city
would diminish our authority in the world,
and the world would then attack our armies.
If Hán rebels,
then Wèi will respond.
Zhào, relying on Qí as a resource,
would, in this case,
use Hán and
Wèi to supply Zhào and lend to Qí,
to strengthen their alliance
and compete with us for power.
This would be a blessing for Zhào but a disaster for Qín.
If we advance to attack Zhào but cannot capture it,
and retreat to attack Hán but cannot conquer it,
then our elite troops will be exhausted in field battles,
and the supply train will be weary from internal assaults.
Uniting the weak and suffering to oppose
and share the burden of two ten-thousand-chariot states
is not a way to extinguish the will of Hán.
If we follow the plan of the esteemed ministers,
then Qín will certainly become a hostage to the world.
Even if Your Majesty exhausts gold and stone
, the day of unifying the world will not arrive.
Now, according to my humble and foolish plan,
send someone to Chǔ,
offer heavy bribes to influential ministers,
and reveal how Zhào deceives Qín;
exchange hostages with Wèi to reassure them,
follow Hán and attack Zhào.
Even if Zhào is allied with Qí,
it is not a cause for concern.
Once the affairs of these two states are concluded,
then Hán can be settled with a written decree.
In this way, with one move, two states will show signs of demise,
then Chǔ
and Wèi will surely submit of their own accord.
Therefore, it is said:
"War is an inauspicious instrument."
It must be used with caution.
Considering Qín and Zhào as equal
in strength,
adding Qí,
and now turning against Hán,
without a way to secure the loyalty of Chǔ
and Wèi,
if we lose a single battle,
then disaster will ensue.
Planning
is for determining affairs,
and must be carefully examined.
The strength and weakness of Zhào and Qín
lie in this year alone.
Moreover, Zhào has been plotting with the other lords for a long time.
If one move weakens us in relation to the other lords,
it is a dangerous matter;
if a plan causes the lords to harbor suspicions about us,
it is extremely perilous.
Showing alienation to two states
is not the way to strengthen ourselves among the lords.
I humbly hope that Your Majesty will carefully consider this!
If an attack causes our allies to become estranged,
it will be too late to regret.
The edict ordered me, Sī,
to consider the memorial submitted by the Hán envoy,
which stated that Hán could not be attacked.
I, Sī, strongly disagree.
Qín's relationship with Hán
is like a person with a disease in their heart and stomach.
When the area is empty it is feverish,
like living in a damp place.
It clings without leaving,
and breaking into a sprint,
then it erupts.
Although Hán is a subject of Qín,
it has never ceased to be a source of trouble for Qín.
Now, if there is a sudden emergency,
Hán cannot be trusted.
With Qín and Zhào in conflict,
Jīng Sū is sent as an envoy to Qí;
it is unknown what the outcome will be.
In my opinion,
the relationship between Qí
and Zhào
will not necessarily be severed by Jīng Sū.
If it is not severed,
it means pitting all of Qín against two ten-thousand-chariot states.
Hán does not submit to Qín because of righteousness
but because of strength.
If they now focus on Qí
and Zhào,
then Hán will certainly become a disease in the heart and stomach
and erupt.
If Hán conspires with Chǔ,
and the other lords respond,
then Qín will surely face the troubles of the Xiáo Pass again.
Fēi's coming
is perhaps not without the intent to preserve Hán
and give it more weight than it deserves.
Using eloquent arguments
to embellish deceitful schemes,
he seeks to gain advantage from Qín
and exploit Your Majesty for Hán's benefit.
If the relationship between Qín
and Hán is close,
then Fēi gains importance;
this is a plan that benefits him.
I see Fēi's words
as ornate, licentious, and persuasive arguments,
very talented.
I fear that Your Majesty will be swayed by Fēi's eloquence
and listen to his deceptive intentions,
thereby failing to thoroughly investigate the situation.
Now, according to my foolish opinion,
if Qín sends troops without declaring where they will attack,
then those in power in Hán will consider serving Qín as their best option.
I, Sī, request to go and meet the King of Hán
and make him come to have an audience;
when Your Majesty sees him,
detain him and do not let him leave,
gradually summon his ministers of state,
and negotiate with the people of Hán,
then Hán can be deeply divided.
Then order Xiàng Wǔ to mobilize the troops of the Eastern Commandery,
display troops on the border
without declaring where they are going,
then the people of Qí will be afraid
and follow Sū's plan.
In this way, before our troops are even sent out,
strong Hán will be captured through prestige,
and powerful Qí will submit through righteousness.
When this is heard by the other lords,
the Zhào clan will be frightened,
the Chǔ people will be hesitant,
and will surely have loyal plans.
If the Chǔ people do not move,
Wèi is not a cause for concern,
then the other lords can be gradually devoured,
and the Zhào clan can be confronted.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider my foolish plan,
do not neglect it."
Qín then sent Sī as an envoy to Hán.
Lǐ Sī went to inform the King of Hán,
but could not get an audience,
so he submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, Qín and Hán worked together with one heart
not to invade each other,
and no one in the world dared to offend them.
This was the case for several generations.
Previously, five lords once joined forces to attack Hán,
and Qín sent troops to save them.
Hán is located in the central states,
its territory not even a thousand *lǐ* in extent,
yet it has been able to rank among the lords in the world,
and its ruler and ministers have been able to protect themselves,
because they have taught each other for generations
to exert effort in serving Qín.
In the past, five lords joined forces to attack Qín,
and Hán instead took the lead with the other lords,
to face the Qín army below the pass.
The lords' troops were exhausted,
and there was nothing they could do,
so the lords' troops were dismissed.
Dù Cāng, serving as chancellor of Qín,
raised troops and dispatched generals to avenge the resentment of the world
and attacked Chǔ first.
The chief minister of Chǔ was worried about this,
and said:
'Hán considers Qín to be unrighteous,
and considers it brotherly with Qín,
sharing the suffering of the world.
Having already turned its back on Qín,
it took the lead to attack the pass.
Hán is located in the central states,
and its intentions are constantly shifting.'
The world then jointly ceded ten cities of Hán's territory
to apologize to Qín,
and Qín released its troops.
Hán once rebelled against Qín,
and its state was pressed and its land invaded,
its army weak to this day.
The reason for this
is that it listened to the specious words of treacherous ministers,
and did not weigh the actual facts.
Therefore, even though it executed the treacherous ministers,
it could not make Hán strong again."
"Now Zhào desires to gather soldiers and
treat Qín as an enemy.
It has sent a man to borrow a road,
saying it wishes to attack Qín.
Its intent is certainly to attack Hán before Qín.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
'When the lips are gone,
the teeth will be cold.'
Qín and
Hán cannot but share the same anxieties;
the situation is clear.
Wèi desired to send troops to attack Hán,
and Qín sent a man to escort the envoy to Hán.
Now, the King of Qín sent me, Sī,
but I cannot gain an audience.
I fear that those around the King will resort to the schemes of the treacherous ministers of the past,
causing Hán to once again suffer the calamity of lost territory.
If I, Sī, cannot gain an audience,
I request to return and report back;
the relationship between Qín and Hán will surely be severed.
My coming as an envoy
is to please the heart of the King of Qín,
desiring to offer a convenient plan.
Is it possible that Your Majesty would oppose and disdain a humble subject like me?
I, Sī, wish to gain an audience
to present my foolish plan and,
if it fails, to be minced into meat paste.
I hope Your Majesty will give this some thought.
Now, killing me in Hán
will not be enough to strengthen the Great King.
If you do not listen to my plan,
then disaster will surely arise.
If Qín sends troops without delay,
then the altars of Hán will be in peril.
If I, Sī, expose my body in the markets of Hán,
then even if you wish to examine the foolish and loyal plan of a humble subject,
it will be impossible.
If the borders are devastated
and the state is forced to defend itself,
the sound of drums and bells will be in your ears,
and then you use my, Sī's, plan,
it will be too late.
Moreover, the military strength of Hán is known to all under Heaven,
and now it is turning its back on the strong Qín.
If it abandons its cities and its army is defeated,
then the bandits in the rear will surely attack the cities.
If the cities are lost, then the people will scatter;
if the people scatter, then there will be no army.
If the cities are strongly defended,
then Qín will surely raise troops and besiege the capital of the King.
If the roads are blocked
then difficulties will be unavoidable and a new plan will be needed,
and the situation will be beyond saving.
If those around you do not use my plan,
I hope Your Majesty will consider it carefully.
If what I, Sī, have said does not correspond to the facts,
I hope that the Great King will allow me to finish my argument before you,
and then hand me over to the officials for punishment.
It will not be too late.
The King of Qín does not find his food sweet,
nor his travels and sights enjoyable.
His mind is focused on planning against Zhào.
He sent me, Sī, to speak,
hoping to see you in person,
so that we can urgently devise a plan together.
If I am not allowed to pass through now,
then the trustworthiness of Hán will be in doubt.
Qín will surely release Zhào from its worries
and move its troops to Hán.
I hope Your Majesty will reconsider and carefully consider this,
and grant me a reply to report back."
It is not that I, Fēi, find it difficult to speak,
but the reason I find it difficult to speak is this:
If the words are smooth and slippery,
flowing and elaborate,
then they are seen as flowery and insubstantial.
If the words are sincere, respectful,
straightforward, firm, cautious, and complete,
then they are seen as clumsy and inappropriate.
If the words are verbose, with many descriptions,
connecting and comparing things,
then they are seen as empty and useless.
If the words summarize the subtle and explain the essential,
directly and concisely without embellishment,
then they are seen as cutting and unclear.
If the words are urgent, aggressive, and intimate,
probing and understanding human nature,
then they are seen as slanderous and unyielding.
If the words are grand, broad,
profound, distant, and unfathomable,
then they are seen as boastful and useless.
If the words discuss household matters in petty terms,
detailing specific numbers,
then they are seen as vulgar.
If the words are about contemporary affairs,
and the language is not rebellious,
then they are seen as greedy for life and flattering superiors.
If the words are distant from common customs,
and agitate the people,
then they are seen as absurd.
If the words are quick, sharp, and eloquent,
abundant in literary embellishments,
then they are seen as mere historical records.
If the words abandon literary expression
and speak with sincerity,
then they are seen as crude.
If one constantly quotes the *Shī* and *Shū*,
and speaks of the laws of the past,
then they are seen as reciting.
This is why I, Fēi, find it difficult to speak
and why I fear trouble.
Therefore, even if the standards are correct,
they may not be listened to;
even if the principles are complete,
they may not be used.
If the Great King does not believe this,
then the small will see it as disparagement, criticism, and slander,
and the great will suffer calamity, disaster, death, and misfortune to their person.
Therefore, Zǐ Xū was good at planning, but Wú killed him;
Zhòng Ní was good at persuading, but Kuàng besieged him;
Guǎn Yíwú was truly wise, but Lǔ imprisoned him.
Therefore, were these three grandees
not wise?
It was that their three lords were unenlightened.
In ancient times, there was Tāng,
a supremely sage;
Yī Yǐn,
a supremely wise.
That the supremely wise persuaded the supremely sage,
yet he was not accepted after seventy attempts.
Yī Yǐn personally held the tripods and cutting boards as a cook.
He was close and intimate,
and only then did Tāng finally recognize his worth and employ him.
Therefore, it is said:
"That the supremely wise persuade the supremely sage
does not necessarily mean they will be received.
Yī Yǐn persuading Tāng is an example of this.
That the wise persuade the foolish
will certainly not be listened to.
Wén Wáng persuading Zhòu is an example of this."
Therefore, Wén Wáng persuaded Zhòu, and Zhòu imprisoned him;
Hóu of Yì was barbecued;
Hóu of Guǐ was pickled;
Bǐ Gān had his heart cut out;
Méi Bó was minced;
Yíwú was bound and imprisoned;
and Cáo Jī fled to Chén;
Bólǐ Zǐ begged on the road;
Fù Yuè was sold and resold;
Sūn Zǐ had his kneecaps removed in Wèi;
Wú Qǐ wiped away tears at Ànmén,
lamenting that Xī Hé had become Qín's,
and was eventually dismembered in Chǔ;
Gōngshū Cuò's words on state affairs
were turned into treachery, and Gōngsūn Yāng fled to Qín;
Guān Lóngpáng was beheaded;
Cháng Hóng was torn limb from limb;
Yǐn Zǐ was trapped in thorns;
Sīmǎ Zǐqī died and floated in the river;
Tián Míng was shot to death;
Mìzǐ Jiàn and
Xīmén Bào died by human hands without a fight;
Dǒng Ānyú died and was displayed in the market;
Zǎiyǔ could not escape from Tián Cháng;
and Fàn Jū had his ribs broken in Wèi.
These dozen or so people
were all rén xián 仁賢, zhōng liáng 忠良, virtuous, and skilled men of the world,
but unfortunately met with rebellious, chaotic, and benighted rulers and died.
In that case, why is it that even the wise and sage cannot escape death
or avoid being killed and disgraced?
It is because it is difficult to reason with the foolish.
Therefore, a jūnzǐ 君子 finds it difficult to speak.
Moreover, words of utmost sincerity grate on the ear and are contrary to the heart.
None but the wise and sage are able to listen to them.
I hope that Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
If a beloved minister is too close,
he will surely endanger his own life.
If a subject is too highly esteemed,
he will surely usurp the ruler's position.
If there is no distinction between the primary consort and concubines,
the heir apparent will surely be endangered.
If brothers do not submit,
the state will surely be endangered.
Your subject has heard that if the ruler of a state of a thousand chariots is unprepared,
there will surely be a minister with a hundred chariots at his side,
who will move his people and overthrow his state.
If the ruler of a state of ten thousand chariots is unprepared,
there will surely be a family with a thousand chariots at his side,
who will transfer his power and overthrow his state.
Therefore, treacherous ministers thrive,
and the Way of the ruler declines and perishes.
Therefore, the greater the power of the feudal lords,
the greater the harm to the Son of Heaven.
The richer the ministers,
the greater the ruin to the sovereign.
When generals and ministers control the ruler and enrich their own families,
this is what a ruler should be wary of.
Nothing is more precious than one's own person,
more supreme than one's position,
more weighty than a ruler's authority,
or more flourishing than a ruler's power.
These four excellent things
should not be sought from external sources
or requested from others,
but can be obtained through deliberation.
Therefore, it is said:
If a ruler cannot use his wealth,
he will end up dependent on external forces.
This is what a ruler must understand.
In the past, the downfall of Zhòu 紂
and the decline of Zhōu 周
both resulted from the great power of the feudal lords.
The division of Jìn 晉
and the usurpation in Qí 齊
both resulted from the great wealth of the ministers.
The assassinations of their rulers in Yān 燕
and Sòng 宋
were all of this kind.
Therefore, comparing them to the cases of Yīn 殷 and Zhōu 周 above
, and comparing them to the cases of Yān 燕 and Sòng 宋 in the middle,
none of them failed to follow this path.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler governs his ministers
by exhausting them with the law
and verifying them with precautions.
Therefore, he does not pardon death
or excuse punishment.
Pardoning death and excusing punishment
is called unrestrained authority.
The state will be in danger,
and the country will be weakened.
Therefore, even if the salaries of high ministers are large,
they must not use their authority to control cities.
Even if their factions are numerous,
they must not enlist soldiers.
Therefore, ministers in the state should not have private audiences,
and those in the army should not have private alliances.
Their treasuries must not privately lend to their families.
This is how an enlightened ruler prevents wickedness.
Therefore, they must not be allowed to follow the ruler's retinue freely,
or carry unusual weapons.
Without a warrant or urgent matter,
carrying unusual weapons will be punished with death without pardon.
This is how an enlightened ruler prepares for unforeseen events.
The Way (dào 道)
is the beginning of all things
and the standard of right and wrong.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler guards the beginning to know the source of all things
and governs the standard to know the origins of good and bad.
Therefore, he remains empty and still to await orders.
Reputations come from self-declaration,
and affairs are settled by self-determination.
Emptiness allows him to know the truth of reality,
and stillness allows him to know the correctness of movement.
Those who speak do so to make a name for themselves,
and those who act do so to make a shape for themselves.
When shapes and names are aligned,
the ruler has nothing to do
and returns to the truth of the matter.
Therefore, it is said:
If the ruler does not reveal his desires,
but reveals his desires,
then his ministers will naturally carve and polish to suit him.
If the ruler does not reveal his intentions,
but reveals his intentions,
then his ministers will naturally distinguish themselves to please him.
Therefore, it is said:
Discard likes and dislikes,
and ministers will reveal their true nature.
Discard wisdom
and tradition,
and ministers will naturally prepare themselves.
Therefore, if one is wise but does not use it for deliberation,
all things will know their place.
If one is virtuous but does not use it for action,
he can observe the actions of his subordinates.
If one is courageous but does not use it for anger,
he can allow his ministers to fully exert their martial prowess.
Therefore, by discarding wisdom, one gains clarity.
By discarding virtue, one gains achievement.
By discarding courage, one gains strength.
When ministers guard their posts,
and all officials have their duties,
they can be employed according to their abilities.
This is called practicing constancy.
Therefore, it is said:
Silent, as if without position.
Still, as if no one can find him.
When the enlightened ruler is non-interfering above,
his ministers are respectful and fearful below.
The way of the enlightened ruler
is to make the wise exhaust their deliberations,
and the ruler uses this to make decisions.
Therefore, the ruler is not limited in wisdom.
The virtuous are tasked with their talents,
and the ruler employs them accordingly.
Therefore, the ruler is not limited in ability.
If there is merit, the ruler has the virtue.
If there is fault, the ministers bear the blame.
Therefore, the ruler is not limited in reputation.
Therefore, the unwise can be the teacher of the wise,
and the unintelligent can correct the intelligent.
The ministers bear the labor,
and the ruler enjoys the success.
This is called the model of an enlightened ruler.
The Way is invisible,
and its use is unknowable.
Being empty, still, and doing nothing allows
one to perceive flaws in the dark.
See as if not seeing,
hear as if not hearing,
know as if not knowing.
Know the words spoken in the past,
do not change or alter them,
and use them to examine and compare.
If there is only one person in a position,
do not allow them to communicate,
and all things will be exhausted.
Conceal their tracks,
hide their beginnings,
and subordinates will not be able to trace them back.
Remove their wisdom,
sever their abilities,
and subordinates will not be able to guess their intentions.
Preserve the path by which I go and verify their accordance,
carefully hold their handles and firmly grasp them.
Cut off their hopes,
break their intentions,
and do not allow them to desire anything.
If one is not careful about closing,
and does not secure the gate,
the tiger will then exist.
If one is not cautious in one's affairs,
and does not conceal one's feelings,
the thief will then be born.
Slaying one's lord,
taking his place,
everyone participates in it,
therefore it is called a tiger.
Dwelling at the side of the lord
to practice insidious concealment,
hearing of the lord's faults,
therefore it is called a thief.
Disperse their faction,
collect their remnants,
close their gates,
seize their supports,
and then the state will be without tigers.
Being so great as to be immeasurable,
so deep as to be unfathomable,
unifying the coordination of punishment and designation,
carefully examining and verifying legal models,
punishing those who act presumptuously,
and then the state will be without thieves.
Therefore, the ruler of men has five blockages:
when ministers obstruct their ruler, it is called a blockage;
when ministers control wealth and profit, it is called a blockage;
when ministers arbitrarily issue commands, it is called a blockage;
when ministers are able to practice righteousness, it is called a blockage;
when ministers are able to establish people, it is called a blockage.
When ministers obstruct their ruler,
then the ruler loses his position;
when ministers control wealth and profit,
then the ruler loses his virtue;
when ministers arbitrarily issue commands,
then the ruler loses his control;
when ministers are able to practice righteousness,
then the ruler loses his clarity;
when ministers are able to establish people,
then the ruler loses his party.
These are what the ruler of men should possess exclusively,
not what the ministers should be allowed to manipulate.
The way of the ruler of men
is to value stillness and retreat.
Without personally handling affairs,
one knows skill and clumsiness;
without personally calculating,
one knows fortune and misfortune.
Therefore, without speaking, one responds well;
without making agreements, one is good at increasing.
When words have been responded to,
then seize their contract;
when affairs have been increased,
then grasp their tally.
Where tallies and contracts meet,
there rewards and punishments arise.
Therefore, when the assembled ministers present their words,
the ruler assigns tasks based on their words,
and uses the tasks to demand their achievements.
If the achievement matches the task,
and the task matches the words,
then reward;
if the achievement does not match the task,
and the task does not match the words,
then punish.
The way of the enlightened ruler is that
ministers cannot present words that are not fitting.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler's dispensing of rewards
is gentle like timely rain,
and the people benefit from its grace;
his dispensing of punishments
is fearful like thunder and lightning,
and even the divine and sage cannot resolve it.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler has no stolen rewards
and no pardoned punishments.
If rewards are stolen,
then meritorious ministers will abandon their tasks;
if punishments are pardoned,
then treacherous ministers will easily commit wrongdoings.
Therefore, if there is indeed merit,
then even if one is distant and lowly, one must be rewarded;
if there is indeed fault,
then even if one is close and beloved, one must be punished.
Rewarding the distant and lowly,
punishing the close and beloved,
then the distant and lowly will not be negligent,
and the close and beloved will not be arrogant.
A state is not always strong
nor always weak.
If those who uphold the law are strong,
then the state is strong;
if those who uphold the law are weak,
then the state is weak.
Wáng Zhuāng of Jīng annexed twenty-six states,
opened up three thousand *lǐ* of land;
when Wáng Zhuāng abandoned the altars of soil and grain,
Jīng perished because of it.
Gōng Huán of Qí annexed thirty states,
opened up three thousand *lǐ* of land;
when Gōng Huán abandoned the altars of soil and grain,
Qí perished because of it.
Wáng Xiāng of Yān took the Hé River as a boundary,
took Jì as the capital,
attacked Zhuō,
Fāngchéng,
devastated Qí,
pacified Zhōngshān;
those who had Yān were valued,
those who did not have Yān were devalued;
when Wáng Xiāng abandoned the altars of soil and grain,
Yān perished because of it.
Wáng Ānxī of Wèi attacked Yān to rescue Zhào,
seized land east of the Hé River;
attacked and exhausted the lands of Táo and
Wèi;
added troops to Qí,
privately leveled the capital of Pínglù;
attacked Hán and captured Guǎn,
winning below Qí;
in the events of Suīyáng,
the Jīng army aged and fled;
in the events of Cài and Shàolíng,
the Jīng army was defeated;
troops were deployed throughout the world,
and his prestige was exerted among the civilized states;
Wáng Ānxī died, and Wèi perished because of it.
Therefore, having Zhuāng of Jīng
and Huán of Qí,
Jīng
and Qí could become hegemons;
having Xiāng of Yān
and Ānxī of Wèi,
Yān
and Wèi could become strong.
Now, the reason they all perished as states is that
their ministers and officials
all strived for what would cause disorder
and did not strive for what would cause order.
Their states were disordered and weak,
and they all abandoned the state laws
and favored their own outside connections;
this is like carrying firewood to put out a fire,
the disorder and weakness is extreme!
Therefore, in this present time,
those who can abandon selfish biases
and adhere to public law,
the people will be secure and the state will be governed;
those who can abandon private conduct
and practice public law,
then the army will be strong and the enemy will be weak.
Therefore, carefully evaluating gains and losses
with a system of laws and measures,
and applying it above the assembled ministers,
then the ruler cannot be deceived by fraud and falsehood;
carefully evaluating gains and losses
with the standards of a scale,
in order to hear of distant matters,
then the ruler cannot be deceived about the gravity of the world.
Now, if one advances the able through praise,
then the ministers will distance themselves from the ruler
and collude with those below;
if one promotes officials through factions,
then the people will strive for connections
and not seek to be employed through the law.
Therefore, when officials lose their ability,
the state is disordered;
using praise as reward,
and using slander as punishment,
then those who like reward and dislike punishment
will abandon public conduct,
practice private arts,
and collude to help each other.
To forget one’s lord in foreign diplomacy
in order to advance one’s own allies,
then the respect of subordinates for their superiors will be diminished.
To have many diplomatic contacts and numerous allies,
to form cliques both inside and outside the court,
even if one commits great transgressions,
they will be greatly concealed.
Therefore, loyal ministers risk death unjustly,
while treacherous and wicked ministers enjoy ease and profit without merit.
When loyal ministers risk death
without deserving such punishment,
then good ministers will retreat into obscurity;
when treacherous and wicked ministers enjoy ease and profit
without merit,
then wicked ministers will advance;
this is the foundation of ruin.
If this is the case,
then the assembled ministers will abandon the law
and pursue private gains,
slighting the public law.
They frequently visit the homes of capable individuals,
but rarely attend the sovereign's court;
they ponder the convenience of their private families a hundred times,
but never once plan for the good of the sovereign's state.
Although the number of dependents is large,
this is not a way to honor the sovereign;
although the hundred officials are complete,
this is not a way to govern the state.
In that case, the sovereign has the name of a ruler,
but in reality relies on the households of the assembled ministers.
Therefore, I, your minister, say:
in the court of a state heading for ruin, there are no [loyal] men.
When the court has no [loyal] men,
it is not the decline of the imperial court.
Families strive to enrich each other,
not to enrich the state;
great ministers strive to honor each other,
not to honor the sovereign;
petty ministers receive their salaries and cultivate their connections,
not treating their official duties as their work.
The reason why this is so
is because the sovereign does not make decisions based on the law,
but trusts his subordinates to do it for him.
Therefore, an enlightened sovereign uses the law to select people,
not promoting them himself;
he uses the law to measure merit,
not judging it himself.
The capable cannot be suppressed,
the failures cannot be embellished,
those who praise cannot be advanced,
those who criticize cannot be demoted,
then the distinction between sovereign and minister will be clear
and easy to govern,
therefore a sovereign who relies on the law is acceptable.
When a worthy man serves as a minister,
he turns north and submits himself completely,
without any divided loyalties;
in the court, he dares not refuse lowly tasks;
in the military, he dares not refuse difficult missions;
he complies with the actions of his superior,
follows the sovereign’s laws,
and awaits orders with an open mind,
without passing judgment on right or wrong.
Therefore, he has a mouth but does not speak for private gain,
he has eyes but does not see for private purposes,
and the sovereign completely controls him.
One who serves as a minister
is like a hand,
which is used by the superior to groom the head
and by the inferior to groom the feet;
regardless of whether it is cool, warm, or cold,
it must respond;
even if the Mòyé (莫邪) sword is pressed against the body,
it dares not refuse to fend it off.
He has no private worthy or wise ministers,
and no private capable officials.
Therefore, the people do not cross their villages to associate with others,
and there is no cause for worry within a hundred *lǐ*.
The noble and the base do not overstep each other,
and the foolish and the wise stand on equal footing;
this is the epitome of good governance.
Now, to despise high rank and generous emoluments,
to easily leave and abandon one's state,
in order to choose one's sovereign,
I, your minister, do not call that integrity.
To use deceptive words and defy the law,
to contradict one’s sovereign and forcefully remonstrate,
I, your minister, do not call that loyalty.
To practice generosity and bestow benefits,
to gain the support of subordinates in order to build a reputation,
I, your minister, do not call that benevolence.
To isolate oneself from society and live in seclusion,
and to falsely criticize one’s superior,
I, your minister, do not call that righteousness.
To serve the feudal lords externally,
while draining the resources of one's own state internally,
to observe the dangerous and precarious situations,
in order to intimidate one’s sovereign by saying:
"If I am not involved, diplomacy will not be intimate,
and if I am not involved, grievances will not be resolved,"
and if the sovereign then believes him,
and listens to him on matters of state,
demeaning the sovereign's name to elevate his own position,
damaging the state's wealth to benefit his own family,
I, your minister, do not call that wisdom.
These several things
are the sayings of a dangerous age,
and are what the laws of the former kings rejected.
The laws of the former kings said:
"Ministers must not act with their own authority,
nor create their own benefits,
but follow the sovereign's instructions;
do not engage in wrongdoing,
but follow the sovereign's path."
The people of ancient times who were well-governed
upheld public law,
abandoned private arts,
focused on one course of action,
and prepared themselves for their responsibilities.
Now, for a ruler to personally examine all the officials,
the day would not be long enough,
and his strength would not suffice.
Moreover, if the ruler uses his eyes,
then the subordinates will adorn their appearances;
if the ruler uses his ears,
then the subordinates will embellish their words;
if the ruler uses his thoughts,
then the subordinates will complicate their rhetoric.
The former kings considered these three things insufficient,
therefore they abandoned their own abilities and relied on the law and numerical standards,
and carefully examined rewards and punishments.
The former kings held to what was essential,
therefore the law was simple and not violated.
Ruling alone within the four seas,
the clever and wise could not use their deception,
the treacherous and rash could not peddle their flattery,
and the treacherous and wicked had nothing to rely on.
Even those far away, thousands of *lǐ* distant,
dared not change their words;
even those in positions close to the emperor
dared not conceal the good and embellish the wrong.
The assembled officials in the court
directly addressed even minor issues,
and dared not overstep their bounds.
Therefore, good governance is not lacking, and there is plenty of time;
this is because the sovereign relies on the power of his position.
When a minister encroaches upon his sovereign,
it is like the terrain:
advancing gradually,
causing the ruler to lose his bearings,
turning east and west without realizing it.
Therefore, the former kings established the sī nán (司南, south-pointing chariot)
to determine direction at all times.
Therefore, an enlightened sovereign ensures that his ministers do not stray outside the law,
and do not bestow favors within the law,
and that their actions are never unlawful.
Strict laws
are used to prevent excessive private behavior,
and severe punishments
are used to enforce orders and punish subordinates.
Authority must not be shared,
and control must not come from multiple sources.
When authority and control are shared,
then numerous evils will be revealed;
when the law is not trusted,
then the sovereign's actions will be perilous;
when punishments are not decisive,
then wickedness will not be overcome.
Therefore, it is said:
even though a skilled craftsman can envision a straight line,
he must first use a compass and square as his standards;
even though a superior mind can quickly handle affairs,
it must use the laws of the former kings as its comparison.
Therefore, with a straight line, crooked wood is planed;
with a level, high places are shaved;
when scales are hung, heavy things become light;
when measures are set, large quantities become small.
Therefore, governing a state by law
is simply a matter of application.
The law does not favor the noble;
the plumb line does not bend for the crooked.
Where the law is applied,
the wise cannot evade it,
the brave dare not contend with it.
Punishment does not spare great ministers for their transgressions,
rewards do not overlook commoners for their merits.
Therefore, to correct the errors of superiors,
to investigate the wickedness of subordinates,
to resolve chaos and correct mistakes,
to eliminate excess and standardize the irregular,
and to unify the people's standards,
nothing is better than law.
To make officials strict and the people respectful,
to eliminate licentiousness and indolence,
to stop deceit and falsehood,
nothing is better than punishment.
When punishments are severe,
people will not dare to exchange the noble for the lowly;
when the laws are clear,
superiors will be respected and not infringed upon.
When superiors are respected and not infringed upon,
the ruler will be strong and maintain control.
Therefore, the former kings valued it and passed it down.
If a ruler abandons the law and uses personal preferences,
then superiors and subordinates will not be distinguished.
What an enlightened ruler uses to control his ministers
are merely the two handles.
The two handles
are punishment and virtue.
What are punishment and virtue?
I say:
Killing is called punishment,
granting rewards is called virtue.
As ministers, they fear punishment
and desire rewards.
Therefore, if the ruler uses punishment and virtue himself,
then the ministers will fear his power
and turn to him for their benefit.
Therefore, treacherous ministers in the world are not like this;
those they hate
they can persuade their lord to punish,
those they love
they can persuade their lord to reward.
Now, if a ruler does not let the power and benefit of rewards and punishments come from himself,
but listens to his ministers and carries out their rewards and punishments,
then all the people of the state will fear his ministers and disrespect their ruler,
turning to his ministers and abandoning their ruler.
This is the danger of a ruler losing control of punishment and virtue.
That the tiger can subdue the dog
is because of its claws and teeth.
If the tiger releases its claws and teeth
and lets the dog use them,
then the tiger will be subdued by the dog instead.
A ruler
uses punishment and virtue to control ministers.
Now, if a ruler releases his punishment and virtue
and lets his ministers use them,
then the ruler will be controlled by his ministers instead.
Therefore, Tián Cháng 田常 requested titles and stipends
and distributed them among the ministers;
he lowered the standard measures
and applied them to the people.
This was because Jiǎn Gōng 簡公 lost control of virtue
and Tián Cháng 田常 used it,
so Jiǎn Gōng 簡公 was assassinated.
Zǐ Hǎn 子罕 said to the Sòng 宋 ruler:
"Rewards and gifts
are what the people like;
Your Lordship should do them yourself.
Killing and punishment
are what the people hate;
allow your minister to undertake them."
Therefore, the Sòng 宋 ruler lost control of punishment
and Zǐ Hǎn 子罕 used it,
so the Sòng 宋 ruler was coerced.
Tián Cháng 田常 only used virtue
and Jiǎn Gōng 簡公 was assassinated;
Zǐ Hǎn 子罕 only used punishment
and the Sòng 宋 ruler was coerced.
Therefore, ministers in the world today
who combine punishment and virtue and use them
are more dangerous to their rulers than Jiǎn Gōng 簡公 and the Sòng 宋 ruler.
Therefore, a ruler who is coerced, killed, or controlled,
who loses control of punishment and virtue
and allows his ministers to use them,
and yet does not face danger and destruction,
has never existed.
If a ruler wants to prevent treachery,
then he must carefully match punishments to names.
Punishments and names
are words and deeds.
Ministers present their words,
and the ruler assigns them tasks according to their words,
holding them accountable for their accomplishments based solely on their tasks.
If the accomplishment matches the task,
and the task matches the words,
then reward them;
if the accomplishment does not match the task,
and the task does not match the words,
then punish them.
Therefore, if a minister's words are grand but his accomplishments are small,
then punish him.
This is not punishing small accomplishments,
but punishing accomplishments that do not match the reputation.
If a minister's words are small but his accomplishments are great,
he is also punished.
This is not because one is displeased with great accomplishments,
but because the harm of not matching the reputation is greater than having great accomplishments,
therefore he is punished.
In the past, Hán Zhāo Hóu 韓昭侯 fell asleep drunk,
and the cap attendant saw that the ruler was cold,
so he put a robe on the ruler.
Awakening from his sleep, the ruler was pleased
and asked those around him,
"Who put the robe on me?"
Those around him replied,
"The cap attendant."
The ruler then punished both the robe attendant and the cap attendant.
He punished the robe attendant
for neglecting his duty;
he punished the cap attendant
for overstepping his position.
It was not that he did not dislike being cold,
but that he thought the harm of infringing upon one's office was greater than being cold.
Therefore, in the way an enlightened ruler employs his ministers,
ministers must not overstep their positions to achieve merit,
nor should they make statements that do not correspond to reality.
Overstepping one's position results in death,
not corresponding to reality results in punishment.
If they guard their offices and
what they say is truthful,
then the ministers will not be able to form factions and help each other.
A ruler has two worries:
employing the worthy,
then the ministers will take advantage of their worthiness to coerce their ruler;
reckless promotion,
then affairs will be ruined and cannot be accomplished.
Therefore, if a ruler likes the worthy,
then the ministers will adorn their behavior
to cater to the ruler's desires.
In that case, the ministers' true feelings will not be revealed;
if the ministers' true feelings are not revealed,
then the ruler will have no way to distinguish his ministers.
Therefore, the Yuè 越 ruler liked bravery,
and the people were prone to disregard death;
King Líng of Chǔ 楚靈王 liked slender waists,
and there were many starving people in the state;
Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓公 was jealous and liked to be surrounded by inner court officials,
so Shù Diāo 豎刁 castrated himself to manage the inner court;
Duke Huán 桓公 liked flavors,
so Yì Yá 易牙 steamed his son's head and presented it to him;
Lord Kuài of Yān 燕子噲 liked the worthy,
so Zǐ Zhī 子之 clearly did not accept the state.
Therefore, if a ruler shows what he dislikes,
then the ministers will hide their shortcomings;
if a ruler shows what he likes,
then the ministers will falsely claim abilities.
If a ruler wants to see [something],
then the ministers' true intentions and behaviors will have a means to achieve their goals.
Therefore, Zǐ Kuài's trusting in a worthy
to usurp his lord,
and Shù Diāo's and
Yì Yá's catering to the ruler's desires
to encroach upon their lord,
resulted in Zǐ Kuài's dying in rebellion
and Duke Huán's maggots crawling out the door
without burial.
What is the reason for this?
It is the calamity of rulers entrusting ministers with their emotions.
The feelings of ministers do not necessarily extend to loving their ruler;
they are for the sake of great profit.
Now, if rulers do not conceal their emotions,
do not hide their intentions,
and allow ministers an opportunity
to encroach upon their lord,
then ministers will find it easy to become another Zǐ Zhī
or Tián Cháng.
Therefore, it is said:
"Discard likes and dislikes,
and the ministers will reveal their true nature."
When ministers reveal their true nature,
then the great ruler will not be deceived.
Heaven has its great mandate,
and man has his great destiny.
Fragrant and delicious flavors,
strong wine and fatty meat,
please the mouth but harm the body;
slender waists and white teeth
please the emotions but drain the essence.
Therefore, discard excess and extravagance,
and the body will be unharmed.
Authority should not be displayed;
simplicity means non-action.
Affairs are dispersed in all directions,
but the key lies in the center.
The sage grasps the key,
and all directions come to offer their services.
Be empty and await them,
and they will bring themselves to you.
When the whole world is contained,
the Dao emerges from the shadows into the light.
Once the left and right are established,
open the door and meet them head-on.
Do not change or alter,
but proceed with both;
continue to proceed,
and this is called following principle.
Things have their proper places,
talents have their proper uses;
each being in its proper place,
the ruler is therefore without action.
Let the rooster crow at night,
and let the cat catch mice;
each using its ability,
the ruler will then have nothing to do.
If the ruler has personal strengths,
affairs will not be well-rounded.
If one is arrogant and fond of displaying ability,
one will be deceived by subordinates;
if one is clever and fond of creating,
subordinates will exploit one's talents.
If superiors and inferiors misuse their positions,
the state will not be well-governed.
The way to employ the One,
is to take names as the head.
When names are correct,
things are settled;
when names are relied upon,
things shift.
Therefore, the sage grasps the One and remains still,
allowing names to name themselves,
and allowing affairs to settle themselves.
If one does not reveal one's talents,
subordinates will be naturally upright.
Rely on them and entrust them,
allowing them to manage their own affairs;
grant to them accordingly,
and they will promote themselves;
deal with them justly,
and allow them all to settle their own affairs.
If the ruler raises them by name,
but does not know their true names,
he will repeatedly correct their forms.
When form and name correspond,
use what is produced from them.
When these two are genuine and trustworthy,
subordinates will then offer their true feelings.
Carefully cultivate one's duties,
and await the mandate of Heaven.
Do not lose its key,
and one will then be a sage.
The way of the sage,
is to discard wisdom and skill;
if wisdom and skill are not discarded,
it will be difficult to establish constancy.
If the common people use them,
their bodies will suffer many calamities;
if the ruler uses them,
his state will be in danger of ruin.
Follow the Way of Heaven,
revert to the principles of form,
supervise, examine, and scrutinize them;
when it ends, there is a beginning.
Be empty, still, and patient,
never using oneself.
All the troubles of rulers
must have the same source;
trust but do not become the same,
and all the people will follow as one.
The Dao
is vast and without form;
Virtue
is to investigate principle and universally reach.
As for living beings,
gauge and use them,
and all things will flourish,
without disturbing their peace.
The Dao
universally attends to affairs,
investigates and assigns tasks,
and lives and dies with the times.
Examine different names and different affairs,
and connect them with the same underlying principle.
Therefore, it is said:
The Dao is different from all things,
Virtue is different from yin and yang,
the balance is different from light and heavy,
the plumb line is different from going out and coming in,
harmony is different from dryness and wetness,
and the ruler is different from the ministers.
All these six,
are the expressions of the Dao.
The Dao is without parallel,
therefore it is called One.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler values the appearance of adhering to the Dao alone.
If ruler and ministers do not follow the same Dao,
subordinates will petition with names,
the ruler will grasp the names,
and the ministers will offer their forms.
When form and name correspond,
superiors and inferiors will be in harmony.
The way of listening
is to take what comes out,
and reverse it to make it go back in.
Therefore, examine names to determine positions,
and clarify distinctions to differentiate categories.
The way of listening to words,
is to be as if very drunk.
Are they lips or are they teeth?
Should I not begin?
Are they teeth or are they lips?
It becomes more and more confusing.
They separate themselves,
and I use this to understand them;
when right and wrong converge,
the ruler does not participate in the construction.
Emptiness and stillness without action
are the essence of the Dao;
comparison and categorization
are the forms of affairs.
Compare them by categorizing things,
and categorize them by combining with emptiness.
If the roots and trunk are not changed,
then movements will not leak or fail.
Move them and dissolve them,
attack them with non-action.
If one rejoices,
there will be many affairs;
if one dislikes,
resentment will arise.
Therefore, discard joy and dislike,
and empty the heart to make it a dwelling for the Dao.
If the ruler does not share with them,
the people will favor them;
if the ruler does not share righteousness with them,
he causes them to act alone.
If the ruler firmly closes the inner gate,
observing the courtyard from the room,
everything within a few feet is known,
everyone will be in their place.
Use rewards to reward,
use punishments to punish,
according to their actions,
each will achieve their own.
Good and evil will surely reach them,
who would dare not believe?
Once the compass and square are set,
the three sides will be aligned.
If the ruler is not discerning,
the subordinates will have a reason;
if matters are not appropriate,
the subordinates will examine their regularity.
Like Heaven and Earth,
this is called untangling accumulation.
Like Earth and Heaven,
who is distant, who is close?
To be able to imitate Heaven and Earth,
this is called a sage.
If you want to govern the interior,
appoint and do not be close;
if you want to govern the exterior,
appoint one official,
do not allow them to be arbitrary,
how could they move or merge?
At the gates of great ministers,
only fear that there are many people.
The extreme of all governance
is that inferiors cannot gain.
Completely unite xíng míng,
the people will then guard their duties;
to abandon this and seek elsewhere,
this is called great confusion.
Cunning people will become more numerous,
treachery and evil will fill the sides.
Therefore it is said:
Do not enrich the rich and lend to them,
do not ennoble the noble and oppress them,
do not exclusively trust one person and lose your capital and state.
If the calf is larger than the thigh,
it will be difficult to run quickly.
If the ruler loses his discernment,
a tiger will follow behind him.
If the ruler does not know,
the tiger will become a dog.
If the ruler does not stop it early,
the dog will become even more unrestrained.
The tiger will form its pack,
to kill its mother.
To be a ruler without subjects,
what state is there?
If the ruler enacts his laws,
the great tiger will be timid;
if the ruler enacts his punishments,
the great tiger will be at peace.
If law and punishment are truly trusted,
the tiger will transform into a person,
and return to its true nature.
If you want to establish your state,
you must cut down its gatherings;
if you do not cut down its gatherings,
they will gather a crowd.
If you want to manage its land,
you must properly allocate its rewards;
if you do not properly allocate its rewards,
disorderly people will seek gain.
If they seek and I give,
it is like lending an axe to an enemy,
if lending is not allowed,
they will use it to attack me.
Huángdì 有言曰:
"Above and below fight a hundred battles a day."
Inferiors hide their private interests,
to test their superiors;
superiors hold the standards,
to cut down their inferiors.
Therefore, the establishment of standards
is the ruler's treasure;
the tools of factions
are the minister's treasure.
The reason why ministers do not assassinate their rulers
is that factions are not complete.
Therefore, if the superior loses a fū cùn,
the inferior gains a xún cháng.
A ruler who has a state
should not enlarge his capital;
a minister who has the Dao
should not enrich his family.
A ruler who has the Dao
should not ennoble his ministers.
If you ennoble and enrich them,
they will replace you.
Prepare for danger and fear peril,
quickly establish a crown prince,
and disaster will have no way to arise.
Inwardly search for outward defenses,
you must personally hold the standards.
For the thick, reduce it;
for the thin, supplement it.
Reducing and supplementing have measures,
do not allow the people to form factions,
and deceive their superiors together.
Reduce it like the moon,
supplement it like heat.
Simplify orders and be careful in executions,
be sure to exhaust their penalties.
Do not relax your bow,
one perch, two heroes.
One perch, two heroes,
their fight will be fierce.
If jackals and wolves are in the pen,
the sheep will not thrive.
If there are two nobles in one family,
affairs will have no success.
If husband and wife hold power,
the son will have no one to follow.
For those who are rulers,
frequently prune their trees,
do not allow the branches to be sparse.
If the branches are sparse,
they will block the public gate,
private doors will be filled,
public courts will be empty,
and the ruler will be blocked and surrounded.
Frequently prune their trees,
do not allow the branches to resist outward;
if the branches resist outward,
they will force the ruler's residence.
Frequently prune their trees,
do not allow the branches to be large and the trunk small;
if the branches are large and the trunk is small,
it will not withstand the spring wind;
if it does not withstand the spring wind,
the branches will harm the heartwood.
If the dukes are numerous,
the imperial family will worry and groan.
The way to stop them
is to frequently prune their trees,
do not allow the branches to be lush.
If the trees are frequently pruned,
factions will then separate.
Dig up their roots,
the trunk,
and the trees will lose their power.
Fill their surging abyss,
do not allow the water to be clear.
Probe their hearts,
and seize their power.
If the ruler uses these,
it will be like lightning and thunder.
In general, there are eight techniques by which subjects achieve treachery:
There are eight arts:
The first is being in the same bed.
What is meant by "same bed"?
It means:
to value the lady,
love the young son,
be fond of flattery and lust,
these are what confuse the ruler.
Entrusting to times of leisurely ease,
taking advantage of times of drunkenness and satiety,
and seeking what they desire,
this is a technique that will surely be listened to.
For subjects to serve internally with gold and jade,
to confuse their ruler,
this is what is called "same bed."
The second is being at the side.
What does it mean to be at the side?
It means:
court jesters and dwarfs,
close attendants on the left and right.
These are the ones who say "yes, yes" before the ruler has given an order,
and who reply "of course, of course" before being commanded.
They anticipate his intentions and comply with his wishes,
observing his appearance and noting his expressions
to understand what is on the ruler’s mind.
These all advance and retreat together,
all respond and reply together,
with unified words and same direction
to sway the ruler's mind.
Those who act as subjects serve
internally with gold, jade, and trinkets,
and externally act illegally,
causing them to transform their ruler.
This is what is meant by "being at the side."
The third is paternal elders and elder brothers.
What are paternal elders and elder brothers?
It means:
concubines, lateral sons,
those whom the ruler cherishes;
high ministers and court officials,
with whom the ruler deliberates and plans.
These are the ones who exert their strength and fully discuss matters,
and the ruler invariably listens to them.
Those who act as subjects serve the lateral sons and concubines with music, women, and children;
they win over high ministers and court officials with rhetoric;
they handle matters in secret,
and if things succeed, they advance in rank and increase their stipends
to encourage their loyalty,
causing them to offend their ruler.
This is what is meant by "paternal elders and elder brothers."
The fourth is nurturing disaster.
What is nurturing disaster?
It means:
the ruler delights in beautiful palaces, terraces, and ponds,
and loves to adorn his daughters, sons, dogs, and horses to please his heart.
This is a disaster for the ruler.
Those who act as subjects exhaust the people's strength
to beautify palaces, terraces, and ponds,
increase taxes and levies
to adorn his daughters, sons, dogs, and horses,
to please their ruler and disrupt his mind,
following his desires,
and planting their private interests in between.
This is called "nurturing disaster."
The fifth is the common people.
What is the common people?
It means:
those who act as subjects distribute public wealth to please the people,
and perform small favors to win over the common folk,
causing the court and the marketplace to praise them,
in order to block their ruler and accomplish their desires.
This is called "the common people."
The sixth is spreading trends.
What is spreading trends?
It means:
the ruler
invariably obstructs his words
and rarely listens to discussions and deliberations,
being easily swayed by eloquent arguments.
Those who act as subjects
seek out persuasive speakers from the feudal lords
and support skilled orators within the state,
causing them to speak on their behalf.
Creating clever and ornate words,
popular and trending rhetoric,
showing them the benefits of power,
and frightening them with calamities and harms,
spreading deceptive words to ruin their ruler.
This is called "spreading trends."
The seventh is imposing strength.
What is imposing strength?
It means:
those who rule
use the assembled ministers and the common people
as their imposing strength.
What the assembled ministers and the common people approve of,
the ruler approves of;
what the assembled ministers and the common people do not approve of,
the ruler does not approve of.
Those who act as subjects
gather swordsmen as retainers,
and support soldiers willing to die,
to display their power,
making it clear that those who work for them will surely benefit,
and those who do not work for them will surely die,
in order to frighten their assembled ministers and the common people
and carry out their private schemes.
This is called "imposing strength."
The eighth is the four directions.
What is the four directions?
It means:
those who rule,
if the state is small,
serve the large state;
if the army is weak,
fear the strong army.
What the large state demands,
the small state invariably listens to;
what the strong army imposes,
the weak army invariably submits to.
Those who act as subjects
increase taxes and levies,
deplete the treasuries,
and empty their state to serve the large state,
and use its power to seek to entice their ruler.
In severe cases, they raise troops to gather at the border
and impose levies internally;
in minor cases, they frequently send great emissaries to intimidate their ruler,
causing him to be fearful.
This is called "the four directions."
All these eight things
are the ways in which subjects achieve treachery,
and the ways in which rulers are obstructed and seized,
losing all that they possess.
These cannot but be examined.
A wise ruler, internally,
enjoys his consorts but does not allow their requests to be carried out,
and does not allow private solicitations.
With regard to those on his left and right,
he makes their persons responsible and demands responsibility for their words,
and does not allow them to add words.
With regard to his paternal elders, elder brothers, and high ministers,
he listens to their words but invariably makes them responsible with punishments
based on the results,
and does not allow reckless actions.
With regard to viewing amusements and enjoying hobbies,
he invariably makes it so that they have a source,
and does not allow unauthorized advances or withdrawals,
and does not allow the assembled ministers to anticipate his intentions.
With regard to bestowing virtue and granting favors,
if he releases forbidden wealth,
opens tombs for grain storage,
anything beneficial to the people
must come from the ruler,
and he does not allow his subjects to privately offer their virtue.
With regard to speeches and discussions,
he invariably substantiates the abilities of those who praise and commend,
and examines the faults of those who criticize and disparage,
he ascertains their abilities,
and investigates their mistakes,
and does not allow the assembled ministers to speak for each other.
With regard to courageous and strong warriors,
the merits of military expeditions must not exceed rewards,
and the valor of village brawls must not be pardoned,
and he does not allow the assembled ministers to act upon private interests.
With regard to the demands of the feudal lords,
if they are in accordance with the law, he listens to them;
if they are not in accordance with the law, he rejects them.
What is meant by a "lost ruler"
is not that he no longer possesses his state,
but that those who possess it
do not belong to him.
If ministers externally
make decisions internally,
then the ruler is lost.
Listening to the great states in order to save the state is the same as listening without saving,
and to be lost is more urgent than not listening,
therefore do not listen.
If the assembled ministers know that he will not listen,
then they will not seek help from the feudal lords;
if the feudal lords know that he will not listen,
then they will not accept the ministers' false accusations against their ruler.
The reason why an enlightened ruler establishes official positions, ranks, and emoluments is
to promote worthy men and encourage those with meritorious service.
Therefore, it is said:
Worthy men hold high ranks,
and are entrusted with important offices;
Those with great merit receive honorable titles
and are richly rewarded.
The official positions of the worthy are measured by their abilities,
and the emoluments granted are commensurate with their merits.
Therefore, the worthy do not falsely claim abilities
in serving their ruler,
and those with merit are happy to advance their careers,
so that achievements are accomplished and reputations established.
Now it is not so;
the worthy and unworthy are not assessed,
and meritorious service is not considered.
The influence of the feudal lords is used,
and the requests of those close at hand are heeded.
Fathers, elder brothers, and senior ministers request titles and emoluments from above,
and sell them below to collect wealth and profit,
and to establish private factions.
Therefore, those with much wealth buy official positions to become noble,
and those with connections to those close at hand
make requests to gain influence.
Ministers with meritorious service are not considered,
and the promotions of official positions are mistaken and erroneous.
Therefore, officials steal office
and engage in foreign affairs,
abandoning their duties and becoming intimate with wealth.
Therefore, the worthy become lax and are not encouraged,
and those with merit neglect and simplify their work.
This is the way of a country's ruin.
Ten transgressions:
First, practicing petty loyalty
is the bane of great loyalty.
Second, being concerned with small gains
is the ruin of great benefits.
Third, acting obstinately and self-importantly,
and being discourteous to the feudal lords,
is the path to one's own destruction.
Fourth, not striving to listen to governance
but indulging in music,
is a matter that will impoverish one's life.
Fifth, being greedy, stubborn, and fond of profit
is the root of national destruction and personal death.
Sixth, indulging in female entertainment
and not attending to state affairs
is the calamity of national ruin.
Seventh, traveling far away from the inner court
and neglecting remonstrating scholars
is the way to endanger oneself.
Eighth, not listening to loyal ministers when one errs
and acting solely on one's own ideas
is the beginning of destroying one's high reputation
and becoming a laughingstock.
Ninth, not assessing one's own strength internally
and relying on the feudal lords externally
is the misfortune of diminishing the state.
Tenth, if a small state is without propriety
and does not employ remonstrating ministers,
then its succession will be cut off.
What is meant by petty loyalty?
In the past, Chǔ Gòng Wáng 楚共王 and Jìn Lì Gōng 晉厲公 fought
at Yānlíng 鄢陵.
The Chǔ 楚 army was defeated,
and Gòng Wáng 楚共王 was wounded in the eye.
During the heat of battle,
Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn 司馬子反 was thirsty and asked for a drink.
The attendant Gǔyáng 穀陽 held a cup of wine and offered it to him.
Zǐfǎn 司馬子反 said:
"Alas,
take it away!
It is wine."
Gǔyáng 穀陽 said:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn 司馬子反 accepted it and drank it.
Zǐfǎn's 司馬子反 character was such that he
loved wine
and found it sweet.
He could not resist it,
and became drunk.
After the battle had ended,
Gòng Wáng 楚共王 wanted to fight again,
and sent someone to summon Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn 司馬子反.
Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn 司馬子反 declined, claiming a heart ailment.
Gòng Wáng 楚共王 drove there himself,
entered his tent,
smelled the odor of wine, and returned,
saying:
"In today's battle,
I myself was wounded.
The one I relied on
was the Sīmǎ 司馬.
But the Sīmǎ 司馬 is so drunk,
that he abandons the state and altars of Chǔ 楚
and does not care for our troops.
I will not fight again."
Thereupon he withdrew his troops and left,
and executed Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn 司馬子反 as a great punishment.
Therefore, Gǔyáng's 穀陽 offering of wine
was not because he hated Zǐfǎn 司馬子反.
His heart was loyal and loved him,
but it was precisely enough to kill him.
Therefore, it is said:
Practicing petty loyalty
is the bane of great loyalty.
What is meant by being concerned with small gains?
In the past, Jìn Xiàn Gōng 晉獻公 wanted to borrow a road from Yú 虞
to attack Guó 虢.
Xún Xī 荀息 said:
"Your Lordship should use the Chuíjí Jade 垂棘之璧 and the Qūchǎn Team 屈產之乘
to bribe the Lord of Yú 虞,
and request to borrow a road from him.
He will surely lend us the road."
The ruler said:
"The Chuíjí Jade 垂棘之璧 is a treasure of my late lord;
