the Qūchǎn Team 屈產之乘
is my excellent horse.
If he receives our gifts but does not lend us the road,
what shall we do?"
Xún Xī 荀息 said:
"If he does not lend us the road,
he will certainly not dare to accept our gifts.
If he accepts our gifts and lends us the road,
then it is like taking the treasure from the inner treasury
and storing it in the outer treasury,
and like taking the horse from the inner stable
and placing it in the outer stable.
Your Lordship should not worry."
The ruler said:
"Very well."
Thereupon, he sent Xún Xī 荀息 to bribe the Lord of Yú 虞 with the Chuíjí Jade 垂棘之璧 and the Qūchǎn Team 屈產之乘
and to request to borrow a road.
The Lord of Yú 虞 was greedy for the jade and the horses and wanted to agree to it.
Gōng Zhīqí 宮之奇 remonstrated, saying:
"It is not permissible to agree.
That Yú 虞 has Guó 虢
is like a carriage having a side rail.
The side rail depends on the carriage,
and the carriage also depends on the side rail.
The situation of Yú 虞 and Guó 虢 is precisely so.
If you lend them the road,
then Guó 虢 will perish in the morning, and Yú 虞 will follow it in the evening.
It is not permissible;
I wish you would not agree."
The Lord of Yú 虞 did not listen,
and thus lent them the road.
Xún Xī 荀息 attacked Guó 虢 and conquered it.
After returning and staying for three years,
he raised troops to attack Yú 虞
and conquered it as well.
Xún Xī 荀息 led the horse and held the jade
and reported to Xiàn Gōng 獻公.
Xiàn Gōng 獻公 was pleased and said:
"The jade is still the same.
However,
the horse's teeth have grown longer."
Therefore, why were the troops of the Lord of Yú 虞 endangered
and his territory diminished?
Why?
He loved small gains and did not consider the harm they would cause.
Therefore, it is said:
Being concerned with small gains
is the ruin of great benefits.
What is meant by acting obstinately?
In the past, when Chǔ Líng Wáng 楚靈王 held the meeting at Shēn 申,
the Crown Prince of Sòng 宋 arrived late,
and he was seized and imprisoned;
he treated the Lord of Xú 徐 intimately
and detained Qí Qìng Fēng 齊慶封.
The *zhōng shè shì* advised,
"It is unacceptable to lack propriety when gathering the feudal lords;
this is the key to survival or destruction.
In the past, *Jié* held a gathering at *Yǒu Róng*,
and *Yǒu Mín* rebelled against him.
*Zhòu* held a hunt at *Líqiū*,
and the *Róng*
and *Dí* rebelled against him,
because of a lack of propriety.
Your Majesty should consider this."
The ruler did not listen
and persisted in his intentions.
Before a full year had passed,
Líng Wáng traveled south,
and his ministers followed and kidnapped him.
Líng Wáng starved to death on the banks of the Qiánxī River.
Therefore, it is said,
"To act perversely and according to one's own ideas,
and to treat the feudal lords without propriety,
is the path to self-destruction."
What is meant by being fond of music?
In the past, Wèi Línggōng was about to go to Jìn.
When he arrived at the banks of the Pú River,
he stopped the carriages and released the horses,
setting up lodgings to stay overnight.
In the middle of the night,
he heard a new musical sound and was delighted by it.
He sent someone to ask those around him,
but everyone reported that they had not heard it.
So he summoned Shī Juān and told him,
"There is a new musical sound,
I sent someone to ask those around me,
but everyone reported that they had not heard it.
Its form resembles that of ghosts and spirits,
you must listen and transcribe it for me."
Shī Juān said,
"Yes."
So he sat quietly, caressed his zither, and transcribed it.
The next day, Shī Juān reported,
"I have obtained it,
but I am not yet familiar with it,
please allow me to stay another night to practice it."
Línggōng said,
"Yes."
So he stayed another night.
The next day,
having mastered it,
they departed for Jìn.
Jìn Pínggōng feasted him at the Terrace of Shīyí.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Línggōng rose.
The Duke said,
"There is a new melody,
I would like to present it."
Pínggōng said,
"Good."
So he summoned Shī Juān,
and ordered him to sit next to Shī Kuàng,
take up the zither, and play it.
Before he had finished,
Shī Kuàng stopped him,
saying,
"This is the music of a state's downfall;
it must not be continued."
Pínggōng said,
"Where did this melody come from?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"This was composed by Shī Yán,
who created decadent music for *Zhòu*.
When Wǔ Wáng attacked *Zhòu*,
Shī Yán fled east,
and threw himself into the Pú River.
Therefore, whoever hears this sound
must be on the banks of the Pú River.
Whoever first hears this sound,
their state will surely be diminished;
it must not be continued."
Pínggōng said,
"What I love
is music;
please, let him finish it."
Shī Juān finished playing.
Pínggōng asked Shī Kuàng,
"What is this melody called?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"This is called *Qīng Shāng*."
The Duke said,
"Is *Qīng Shāng* truly the most sorrowful?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"It is not as sorrowful as *Qīng Zhǐ*."
The Duke said,
"Can *Qīng Zhǐ* be heard?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"No.
In ancient times, those who listened to *Qīng Zhǐ*
were all rulers of virtue and righteousness.
Now, our lord's virtue is thin,
not sufficient to hear it."
Pínggōng said,
"What I love
is music;
I wish to try to hear it."
Shī Kuàng had no choice,
so he took up the zither and played it.
At the first playing,
sixteen black cranes
came from the south,
gathering on the ruined gate of the Láng Gate.
At the second playing,
they lined up.
At the third playing,
they stretched their necks and sang,
spreading their wings and dancing.
The sound matched the tones of the palace and the *shāng* mode,
and the sound was heard in the heavens.
Pínggōng was greatly pleased,
and all those seated were delighted.
Pínggōng raised his wine cup
and stood up to offer a toast to Shī Kuàng,
then sat back down and asked,
"Is there no music more sorrowful than *Qīng Zhǐ*?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"It is not as sorrowful as *Qīng Jiǎo*."
Pínggōng said,
"Can *Qīng Jiǎo* be heard?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"No.
In the past, Huángdì gathered the ghosts and spirits
on Mount Tài,
driving an elephant cart with six *jiāo* dragons,
*Bìfāng* accompanying the axles,
*Chīyóu* in the front,
the wind master sweeping ahead,
the rain master sprinkling the road,
tigers and wolves in front,
ghosts and spirits behind,
*Téngshé* prostrate on the ground,
phoenixes covering above,
a grand gathering of ghosts and spirits,
to create *Qīng Jiǎo*.
Now, our lord's virtue is thin,
not sufficient to hear it.
If you hear it,
I fear there will be ruin."
Pínggōng said,
"I am old,
and what I love is music,
I wish to hear it."
Shī Kuàng had no choice but to play it.
At the first playing,
black clouds arose from the northwest;
at the second playing,
a great wind arrived,
and great rain followed,
tearing the curtains,
breaking the *zǔdòu*,
and destroying the tiles of the corridors.
Those seated scattered and fled,
Pínggōng was frightened,
and hid in the corridor chamber.
The state of Jìn suffered a great drought,
and the land was barren for three years.
Pínggōng himself became crippled and ill.
Therefore, it is said,
"If one does not attend to governance
but indulges in the five tones without ceasing,
it will lead to a life of impoverishment."
What is meant by "greedy and obstinate"?
In the past, Zhì Bó Yáo 智伯瑤 led the armies of Zhào 赵,
Hán 韩, and Wèi 魏
to attack Fàn 范 and
Zhōng Háng 中行,
and destroyed them.
Upon returning,
after resting the troops for several years,
he then sent someone to request land from Hán 韩.
Hán Kāngzǐ 韩康子 wanted to refuse,
but Duàn Guī 段规 advised,
"You must not refuse.
Zhì Bó's 智伯 character is that he
loves profit and is arrogant and obstinate.
If he requests land and you refuse,
he will certainly move his troops to attack Hán 韩.
Your lord should give it to him.
If he becomes complacent by giving it to him,
he will then request land from other states,
and those other states will not listen.
If they do not listen,
then Zhì Bó 智伯 will certainly add his troops against them.
If this is the case,
Hán 韩 can avoid the trouble
and await the change in events."
Kāngzǐ 康子 said,
"Agreed."
He then ordered an envoy to give a county of ten thousand households
to Zhì Bó 智伯.
Zhì Bó 智伯 was pleased and again sent someone to request land from Wèi 魏.
Xuānzǐ 宣子 wanted to refuse,
but Zhào Jiā 赵葭 advised,
"He requested land from Hán 韩,
and Hán 韩 gave it to him.
Now he requests land from Wèi 魏,
and if Wèi 魏 does not give it to him,
then this means Wèi 魏 strengthens itself internally
and angers Zhì Bó 智伯 externally.
If you don't give it,
he will certainly move his troops against Wèi 魏.
It is better to give it to him."
Xuānzǐ 宣子 said,
"Agreed."
He then ordered an envoy to give a county of ten thousand households
to Zhì Bó 智伯.
Zhì Bó 智伯 again sent someone to Zhào 赵 to request the lands of Cài 蔡 and Gāo Láng 皋狼.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ 赵襄子 refused.
Zhì Bó 智伯 then secretly allied with Hán 韩 and Wèi 魏
to attack Zhào 赵.
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 summoned Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 and told him,
"Zhì Bó's 智伯 character is that he
is outwardly friendly but inwardly distant.
He has sent three envoys to Hán 韩 and Wèi 魏,
but I alone have not given him anything,
he will certainly move his troops against me.
Where can I live safely?"
Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 said,
"In the past, Dǒng Èyú 董閼于,
who was a talented minister of Lord Jiǎn 简,
governed Jìnyáng 晋阳,
and Yǐn Duó 尹鐸 followed his ways.
His remaining teachings still exist,
Your Lordship should settle in Jìnyáng 晋阳."
The lord said,
"Agreed."
He then summoned Yánlíng Shēng 延陵生,
ordering him to lead the chariots and cavalry
to Jìnyáng 晋阳 first,
and the lord followed him.
When the lord arrived,
he inspected the city walls and the storage of the five offices.
The city walls were not fortified,
the granaries had no stored grain,
the treasuries had no stored money,
the armories had no armor or weapons,
and the town had no defensive equipment.
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 was afraid
and summoned Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈, saying,
"I have inspected the city walls
and the storage of the five offices,
and they are all unprepared.
How will I respond to the enemy?"
Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 said,
"I have heard that the sage's governance
is stored among the people,
not in the treasuries and armories.
Focus on cultivating education,
not fortifying city walls.
Your Lordship should issue an order
ordering the people to contribute three years' worth of food.
Those with surplus grain should put it into the granaries.
Contribute three years' worth of expenses.
Those with surplus money should put it into the treasuries;
those with extraordinary talents
should use them to repair the city walls."
The lord issued the order in the evening,
and the next day,
the granaries could not hold all the grain,
the treasuries were full of money,
and the armories could not accept all the armor and weapons.
Within five days, the city walls were fortified,
and the defenses were complete.
The lord summoned Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 and asked him,
"My city walls are fortified,
the defenses are complete,
the money and grain are sufficient,
and the armor and weapons are plentiful,
but what can I do about the lack of arrows?"
Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 said,
"I have heard that when Dǒngzǐ 董子 governed Jìnyáng 晋阳,
the walls of the public palace
were all walled with dì 荻, hāo 蒿, hǔ 楛, and chǔ 楚,
with the hǔ 楛 reaching a height of ten feet.
Your Lordship should take them and use them."
So he took them and tested them,
and their strength was even greater than that of the strongest jūn lù 菌簏.
The lord said,
"My arrows are sufficient, but what can I do about the lack of metal?"
Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 said,
"I have heard that when Dǒngzǐ 董子 governed Jìnyáng 晋阳,
the halls of the public palace and offices
all had pillars and foundations made of refined copper.
Your Lordship should take them and use them."
So he took them and used them,
and there was surplus metal.
The orders were established,
and the defenses were complete.
The troops of the three states indeed arrived.
Upon arriving, they attacked the city of Jìnyáng 晋阳
and engaged in battle.
For three months, they were unable to capture it.
They then spread out their troops and surrounded it,
controlling the waters of Jìnyáng 晋阳 to flood it,
surrounding Jìnyáng 晋阳 for three years.
The people in the city lived in nests and dwelled there,
hanging their pots to cook,
the wealth and food were about to run out,
and the officials and gentlemen were weak and ill.
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 said to Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈,
"The grain is exhausted,
the wealth and strength are depleted,
and the officials and gentlemen are weak and ill.
I fear we cannot defend any longer!
I want to surrender the city.
To which state should I surrender?"
Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 said,
"I have heard that
if you cannot preserve what is about to be lost,
and you cannot secure what is in danger,
then there is no point in valuing wisdom.
If Your Lordship dismisses this plan,
I ask to try secretly going out
to see the lords of Hán 韩 and Wèi 魏."
Zhāng Mèngtán 张孟谈 met with the lords of Hán 韩 and Wèi 魏, saying,
"I have heard that if the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold.
Now, Zhì Bó 智伯 is leading you two lords to attack Zhào 赵,
and Zhào 赵 is about to be destroyed.
If Zhào 赵 is destroyed,
then you two lords will be next."
The two lords said,
"We know this to be true.
However,
Zhì Bó's 智伯 character is
rough in his dealings and lacks intimacy.
If we plot and he finds out,
then disaster will certainly come.
What can be done about it?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said,
"The plan comes from the mouths of the two lords,
and enters the ears of your servant,
so that no one will know it."
The two lords then made a pact with Zhāng Mèngtán
regarding the rebellion of the three armies,
and set a date with him.
That night, they sent Mèngtán to enter Jìnyáng,
to inform him of the rebellion of the two lords.
Xiāngzǐ welcomed Mèngtán and bowed to him twice,
both fearful and joyful.
The two lords sent Zhāng Mèngtán after making the agreement,
and then went to court Zhī Bó and exited,
encountering Zhì Guò outside the gate of the barracks.
Zhì Guò found his expression strange,
and so he went to see Zhī Bó and said,
"The appearance of the two lords suggests something is about to change."
The lord said,
"How so?"
He said,
"Their conduct is arrogant and their intentions are high,
not like their usual behavior.
It would be better for you, my lord, to act first."
The lord said,
"My agreement with the two lords is very solid,
to conquer Zhào and divide its territory into three parts.
The reason I am close to them
is that they will certainly not encroach or deceive me.
The army has been stationed at Jìnyáng for three years,
and we will soon take it,
so they are leaning towards their own interests.
Why would they have other intentions?
That must not be the case.
Put your mind at ease, don't worry,
and don't say anything about it."
The next morning,
the two lords again went to court and exited,
again seeing Zhì Guò at the gate of the barracks.
Zhì Guò went to see him and said,
"Did you, my lord, tell the two lords what I said?"
The lord said,
"How did you know?"
He said,
"Today, when the two lords went to court and exited,
they saw me and their expressions changed,
and they kept looking at me.
This certainly means something is about to change.
It would be better for you, my lord, to kill them."
The lord said,
"Set aside this matter and speak no more of it."
Zhì Guò said,
"That is not acceptable.
You must kill them.
If you cannot kill them,
then you should become close to them."
The lord said,
"How can I become close to them?"
Zhì Guò said,
"Wèi Xuānzǐ's strategist is named Zhào Jiā,
and Hán Kāngzǐ's strategist is named Duàn Guī.
These men are both capable of changing their lords' plans.
You, my lord, should make an agreement with the two lords
to conquer the state of Zhào,
and then enfeoff each of these two men
with a county of ten thousand households.
If you do so,
then the hearts of the two lords will not change."
Zhī Bó said,
"If we conquer Zhào and divide its territory into three parts,
and also enfeoff each of these two men
with a county of ten thousand households,
then what I obtain will be little.
That is unacceptable."
Zhì Guò, seeing that his words were not heeded,
left,
and consequently changed his clan to Fǔshì.
On the night of the appointed date,
the Zhào clan killed the official guarding the dyke
and breached it to flood Zhī Bó's army.
Zhī Bó's army was in chaos as it tried to control the flood,
and Hán and Wèi attacked from the flanks.
Xiāngzǐ led his troops to attack from the front,
greatly defeating Zhī Bó's army
and capturing Zhī Bó.
Zhī Bó died and his army was destroyed,
his state was divided into three,
and he became a laughingstock in the world.
Therefore it is said:
"Greed and stubbornness lead to a fondness for profit,
which is the root of destroying the state and killing oneself."
What is meant by being addicted to female entertainment?
Formerly, the Róng king sent Yóu Yú
as an envoy to Qín.
Mù Gōng asked him, saying,
"I have heard of the Dao
but have not been able to see it firsthand.
I would like to hear how the wise rulers of old gained and lost their states."
Yóu Yú replied,
"I have heard it said:
one always gains it through frugality
and loses it through extravagance."
Mù Gōng said,
"I do not disgrace myself by asking you about the Dao,
but you respond to me with frugality.
Why is that?"
Yóu Yú replied,
"I have heard that in the past, when Yáo possessed the world,
he ate from earthenware bowls
and drank from earthenware kettles.
His territory stretched south to Jiāozhǐ,
north to Yōudū,
and east and west to where the sun rises and sets.
All submitted to him.
When Yáo abdicated the world,
Yú Shùn received it.
He made wooden eating utensils,
cutting down mountain trees and working them,
planing and sawing to smooth the surfaces,
and applying black lacquer to them,
sending them to the palace to be used as eating utensils.
The feudal lords considered this increasingly extravagant,
and thirteen states did not submit.
When Shùn abdicated the world and passed it on to Yǔ,
Yǔ made sacrificial vessels,
black lacquering the outside
and painting the inside red,
using silk cloths as cushions,
and bordering rush mats,
with colored wine cups,
and decorated goblets and stands.
This was even more extravagant,
and thirty-three states did not submit.
After the Xià dynasty ended,
the Yīn people received it.
They made grand carriages
and erected nine-streamer banners,
carved eating utensils,
and engraved wine cups,
whitewashed walls,
and embroidered cushions and mats.
This was even more extravagant,
and fifty-three states did not submit.
The nobles all knew of elaborate ornamentation,
but fewer and fewer wanted to submit.
Therefore I say:
frugality is the way."
After Yóu Yú left,
the Duke then summoned the Chamberlain Liào and informed him, saying,
"I have heard that a neighboring state has a sage,
which is a worry for an enemy state.
Now, Yóu Yú
is a sage,
and I am worried about him.
What should I do?"
Chamberlain Liào said,
"I have heard that the Róng king's residence
is remote and the road is long,
and he has not heard the sounds of the Central States.
You, my lord, should send him female entertainers
to disrupt his government,
and then ask Yóu Yú for a meeting,
in order to alienate his advice.
When there is a rift between the ruler and his ministers,
then he can be dealt with."
The Duke said,
"Agreed."
Thereupon he sent Chamberlain Liào
with sixteen female entertainers as a gift to the Róng king,
and asked Yóu Yú for a meeting.
The Róng King agreed,
saw his female musicians and was pleased with them,
set up wine and began to drink,
listening to music day after day,
not moving for a whole year,
and half of his cattle and horses died.
Yóu Yú returned
and therefore admonished the Róng King,
but the Róng King did not listen.
Yóu Yú then left him for Qín.
Qín Mù Gōng welcomed him and appointed him as a senior minister,
asking him about military strategies and the terrain.
Having learned from him,
he raised troops and attacked them,
annexing twelve states
and expanding the territory by a thousand *lǐ*.
Therefore, it is said:
Being absorbed in female musicians
and not caring about state affairs
is the disaster of a ruined country.
What is meant by "leaving the interior and traveling far"?
In the past, Qí Jǐng Gōng traveled to the sea
and enjoyed it.
He issued an order to the senior officials, saying:
"Anyone who suggests returning will die."
Yán Zhuōjù said:
"If the ruler travels to the sea and enjoys it,
what if your ministers plot against the state?
Even if the ruler enjoys it,
how will it be secured?"
Qí Jǐng Gōng said:
"I issued an order saying
'Anyone who suggests returning will die.'
Now you are violating my order."
He raised his spear to strike him.
Yán Zhuōjù said:
"In the past, Jié killed Guān Lóngféng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
Even if the ruler kills me,
it would be worth it three times over.
I speak for the sake of the state,
not for my own sake."
He stretched his neck forward and said:
"Strike me!"
The ruler then released the spear
and hurried back in his carriage.
Three days later,
he heard that the people of the state were plotting
not to let Qí Jǐng Gōng enter.
The reason why Qí Jǐng Gōng was able to maintain the state of Qí
was due to the effort of Yán Zhuōjù.
Therefore, it is said:
Leaving the interior and traveling far
is the way to endanger oneself.
What is meant by
"disregarding the advice of loyal ministers"?
In the past, Qí Huán Gōng united the feudal lords nine times,
rectified the world,
and became the leader of the Five Hegemons,
with Guǎn Zhòng assisting him.
When Guǎn Zhòng grew old
and could no longer handle affairs,
he retired to his home.
Huán Gōng went to him and asked:
"If Zhòng Fù is at home with an illness,
and unfortunately does not recover from this illness,
to whom should the government be transferred?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am old
and should not be asked.
However,
I have heard that
no one knows a minister better than the ruler,
and no one knows a son better than the father.
Your Highness should try to decide with your heart."
The ruler said:
"What about Bào Shūyá?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"He is not suitable.
Bào Shūyá's character is
obstinate and disrespectful to his superiors.
If he is obstinate, he will offend the people with violence;
if he is stubborn, he will not gain the people's hearts;
if he is disrespectful, his subordinates will not be useful to him;
his heart is without fear,
and he is not a helper of a hegemon."
The duke said:
"Then what about Shù Diāo?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"He is not suitable.
Everyone cherishes their own body.
The duke is jealous and fond of the inner palace,
and Shù Diāo castrated himself to manage the inner palace.
If he does not cherish his own body,
how can he love the ruler?"
The duke said:
"Then what about Wèi Gōngzǐ Kāifāng?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"He is not suitable.
The distance between Qí and Wèi is no more than ten days' journey.
Kāifāng, in order to serve the ruler,
and wanting to please the ruler,
has not returned to see his parents for fifteen years.
This is not human nature.
If he is not close to his parents,
how can he be close to the ruler?"
The duke said:
"Then what about Yìyá?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"He is not suitable.
Yìyá manages the ruler's taste.
The only thing the ruler has not tasted is human flesh.
Yìyá steamed his son's head and presented it to the ruler,
as Your Highness knows.
Everyone cherishes their own children.
Now he steams his son to make a dish for the ruler.
If he does not love his own son,
how can he love the ruler?"
The duke said:
"Then who is suitable?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Xí Péng is suitable.
His character is
firm in his heart and honest in his dealings,
with few desires and much trustworthiness.
Being firm in his heart
is enough to be a model,
being honest in his dealings
allows him to handle great responsibilities,
having few desires
allows him to govern his people,
and being trustworthy
allows him to befriend neighboring states.
He is a helper of a hegemon,
Your Highness should employ him."
The duke said:
"Agreed."
More than a year later,
Guǎn Zhòng died.
The duke then did not employ Xí Péng
but instead relied on Shù Diāo.
After Diāo took charge for three years,
Huán Gōng traveled south to Tángfù,
and Shù Diāo led Yìyá,
Wèi Gōngzǐ Kāifāng, and other ministers in a rebellion.
Huán Gōng died of thirst and starvation in the southern gate chamber.
His chamberlains guarded the room,
but his body was not collected for three months,
and worms crawled out of the door.
Therefore, Huán Gōng's army marched across the world,
and he became the leader of the Five Hegemons,
but in the end, he was murdered by his ministers
and lost his great reputation,
becoming a laughingstock to the world.
Why?
It was because he did not listen to Guǎn Zhòng's advice.
Therefore, it is said:
Disregarding the advice of loyal ministers
and acting solely on one's own ideas
will destroy one's great reputation
and be the beginning of becoming a laughingstock.
What is meant by "not measuring one's strength internally"?
In the past, when Qín attacked Yíyáng,
the Hán were anxious.
Gōngzhòng Péng said to the ruler of Hán:
"Other states cannot be relied upon.
Why not use Zhāng Yí to make peace with Qín?
Bribe him with a famous city
and join them in attacking Chǔ to the south.
This will resolve the trouble with Qín
and create enmity with Chǔ."
The Duke said,
"Good."
Thereupon, he alerted Gōngzhòng's journey,
intending to make peace with Qín in the west.
The King of Chǔ heard of it,
and, fearing,
summoned Chén Zhěn and told him,
"Hán Péng is about to go west to make peace with Qín,
what shall we do now?"
Chén Zhěn said,
"If Qín obtains a capital from Hán,
and mobilizes its well-trained soldiers,
Qín and Hán becoming one to one another in marching south towards Chǔ,
this is what the King of Qín would pray for in his ancestral temple,
it will certainly be harmful to Chǔ.
Your Majesty should quickly dispatch a trusted minister,
increase the number of his carriages,
and increase the value of his gifts,
to present to Hán, saying:
'Although the state of the unworthy one is small,
all the soldiers have already been mobilized,
I hope your great state will be sincere in its intentions towards Qín.
Furthermore, I wish your great state would order its envoy to enter our borders
to observe Chǔ's mobilized troops.'"
The Hán envoy went to Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ accordingly dispatched chariots and cavalry,
lining them up along the road,
and said to the Hán envoy,
"Report to the Lord of Hán,
saying that our state's troops are now about to enter the border."
The envoy returned and reported to the Lord of Hán,
who was greatly pleased,
and stopped Gōngzhòng.
Gōngzhòng said,
"That won't do.
For the one who harms us in reality
is Qín,
while the one who saves us in name
is Chǔ.
To listen to the empty words of Chǔ
and disregard the real disaster of the powerful Qín,
is the foundation of a state in danger."
The Lord of Hán did not listen to him.
Gōngzhòng became angry and returned home,
not attending court for ten days.
Yíyáng became even more urgent,
the Lord of Hán ordered his envoy to urge troops from Chǔ,
with officials' carriages following one after another,
but no troops arrived.
Yíyáng was indeed captured,
and became the laughingstock of the feudal lords.
Therefore, it is said:
"One who does not measure his own strength internally,
and relies on the feudal lords externally,
is bound to suffer the affliction of a weakened state."
What does it mean for a small state to be without propriety?
In the past, when Duke Chóng'ěr of Jìn was in exile,
he passed through Cáo,
and the Lord of Cáo bared his chest to watch him.
Lí Fùjī and Shū Zhān stood in attendance before him.
Shū Zhān said to the Lord of Cáo,
"I observe the Duke of Jìn,
and he is no ordinary man.
If Your Lordship treats him without propriety,
and if he has a chance to return to his state and raise troops,
I fear it will cause harm to Cáo.
Your Lordship would be better off killing him."
The Lord of Cáo did not listen.
Lí Fùjī returned home unhappy,
and his wife asked him,
"You have come home from outside with an unhappy expression,
what is the matter?"
Fùjī said,
"I have heard that if good fortune does not reach us,
misfortune will come and involve us.
Today, our lord summoned the Duke of Jìn,
and treated him without propriety.
I was in attendance before him,
that is why I am unhappy."
His wife said,
"I observe the Duke of Jìn,
and he is a ruler of ten thousand chariots;
those who follow him on the left and right,
are ministers of ten thousand chariots.
Now that he is in dire straits and in exile passing through Cáo,
Cáo treats him without propriety.
If he returns to his state,
he will certainly punish those without propriety,
and Cáo will be the first to suffer.
Why don't you first distance yourself from it?"
Fùjī said,
"Agreed."
He filled a pot with yellow gold,
filling it with food,
added a jade disc on top,
and had someone secretly deliver it to the Duke at night.
The Duke saw the envoy,
bowed twice,
accepted the food and declined the jade disc.
The Duke went from Cáo to Chǔ,
and from Chǔ to Qín.
Three years after entering Qín,
Duke Mù of Qín summoned his ministers
and consulted them, saying:
"In the past, Duke Xiàn of Jìn had relations with me,
which none of the feudal lords have not heard of.
Unfortunately, Duke Xiàn has departed from his ministers,
and has been gone for ten years.
His successor is not good,
and I fear that this will cause
his ancestral temples to not be swept and cleaned
and his altars of the soil and grain to not be blood-fed.
If this is not settled,
then it is not the way to have relations with others.
I want to assist Chóng'ěr in entering Jìn,
what do you think?"
The ministers all said,
"Good."
The Duke then raised troops,
five hundred war chariots,
two thousand cavalry,
and fifty thousand infantry,
to assist Chóng'ěr in entering Jìn,
and established him as the Lord of Jìn.
Three years after Chóng'ěr ascended the throne,
he raised troops and attacked Cáo.
He then sent someone to inform the Lord of Cáo, saying:
"Hang Shū Zhān and bring him out,
and I will kill him as a great punishment."
He also sent someone to inform Lí Fùjī, saying:
"Our army is approaching the city,
I know that you will not go against us.
Mark the gate of your alley,
and I will make it an order,
ordering the army not to dare to violate it."
When the people of Cáo heard of this,
more than seven hundred families gathered their relatives
to protect the gate of Lí Fùjī's alley,
this is where propriety is used.
Therefore, Cáo
was a small state,
and was situated between Jìn and Chǔ,
its lord's danger was like stacked eggs,
yet he governed it without propriety,
this is why it was cut off from the world.
Therefore, it is said:
"If a small state lacks propriety
and does not listen to remonstrating ministers,
then it is in a position to be cut off from the world."
Scholars with intelligence and skill
must have far-sightedness and clear discernment,
without clear discernment,
they cannot illuminate private matters;
scholars who are capable of enforcing the law
must be strong, resolute, and upright,
without being upright,
they cannot correct wrongdoing.
For ministers to follow orders and carry out tasks,
and manage their offices according to the law,
is not what is meant by important officials.
Important officials
are those who act on their own without orders,
violate the law to benefit themselves,
deplete the state to benefit their families,
and have the power to sway their lord,
this is what is meant by important officials.
If scholars with intelligence and skill are clear-sighted
and listened to,
they can illuminate the secret affairs of important officials;
if scholars capable of enforcing the law are firm and upright
and listened to,
they can correct the corrupt actions of important officials.
Therefore, if men of wisdom, skill, and law are employed,
then highly regarded ministers must be outside the reach of the law.
Thus, men of wisdom and law, and those in power,
are enemies who cannot coexist.
If those in power monopolize important affairs,
then both the outer and inner circles will be at their disposal.
Therefore, if the feudal lords do not rely on them,
then affairs will not be responded to,
so enemy states will speak on their behalf;
if the hundred officials do not rely on them,
then their careers will not advance,
so the many ministers will work for them;
if the court gentlemen do not rely on them,
then they will not be able to get close to the ruler,
so those on the left and right will conceal them;
if scholars do not rely on them,
then their salaries will be meager and their gifts mean,
so the scholars will speak on their behalf.
These four aids
are how wicked ministers adorn themselves.
If important people cannot be loyal to the ruler
and instead promote their enemies,
and if the ruler cannot bypass these four aids
to clearly observe his ministers,
then the ruler will become more confused
and the ministers more powerful.
In general, those in power in relation to the ruler
are rarely not trusted and loved,
and are also familiar figures.
As for conforming to the ruler's mind
and agreeing with his likes and dislikes,
that is certainly how they advance themselves.
Their official positions and ranks are high and respected,
their factions are numerous,
and the whole country speaks on their behalf.
Therefore, if men of law and skill
wish to influence the ruler,
they do not have the intimacy of trusted and loved ones,
nor the favor of familiar figures;
moreover, they will use the language of law and skill
to correct the ruler's biased mind,
which is to oppose the ruler.
They are in a low and humble position,
without allies and isolated.
If they use alienation to compete with intimacy and trust,
they will certainly not win;
if they use new arrivals to compete with familiar figures,
they will certainly not win;
if they use opposing the ruler's intentions
to compete with agreeing with his likes and dislikes,
they will certainly not win;
if they use lowliness and humbleness to compete with high rank and respect,
they will certainly not win;
if they use one mouth to compete with the entire country,
they will certainly not win.
Men of law and skill
wield the power of these five certain losses,
and still may not be seen even after many years;
those in power, relying on the resources of these five certain wins,
exclusively speak to the ruler day and night.
Therefore, how can men of law and skill
find a way to advance,
and when will the ruler be enlightened?
Therefore, since resources will certainly not prevail
and these two positions cannot coexist,
how can men of law and skill
not be in danger?
Those who can be falsely accused of crimes
will be punished by public law;
those who cannot be accused of crimes
will be cornered with private swords.
Thus, those who clarify the law and oppose the ruler
will not only be killed by officials,
but will certainly die by private swords.
Those who form factions and collude to mislead the ruler,
and whose words are twisted to benefit their own interests,
will certainly be trusted by those in power.
Therefore, those whose achievements can be borrowed
will be honored with official positions and ranks;
those whose good names cannot be borrowed
will be given power outside the court to increase their importance.
Thus, those who mislead the ruler and flock to private interests
will not only be prominent in official positions and ranks,
but will certainly be important due to external power.
Now, if the ruler does not combine verification and examination when carrying out punishments,
and does not grant ranks and salaries after seeing merit,
then how can men of law and skill
risk death to advance their theories?
How would treacherous and wicked ministers be willing to relinquish their positions when taking advantage of benefits?
Therefore, the ruler becomes increasingly humble,
and private interests become more respected.
Even though the state of Yuè 越 is rich and its army is strong,
the rulers of the central states all know that it is of no benefit to them,
saying,
"It is not something I can control."
Now, if a ruler has a state
with a vast territory and a large population,
but the ruler is obstructed and misled,
and the ministers monopolize power,
then this state is like Yuè 越.
To know but not be like Yuè 越,
and not knowing not be like one's own state,
is to not examine their similarities.
The reason why people say that Qí 齊 was destroyed
is not because its land and cities were lost.
The Lǚ 呂 family did not control it,
and the Tián 田 family used it;
the reason why people say that Jìn 晉 was destroyed
is also not because its land and cities were lost,
but because the Jī 姬 family did not control it,
and the six ministers monopolized it.
Now, if the ministers hold the reins and make decisions independently,
and the ruler does not know to take them back,
then the ruler is not enlightened.
Those who have the same illness as the dead
cannot be brought back to life;
those who do the same things as those who destroyed states
cannot survive.
Now, if one follows the paths of Qí 齊 and Jìn 晉,
wishing for the state to be safe and secure,
it cannot be achieved.
The difficulty of implementing law and skill
is not limited to states with ten thousand chariots,
but is also true for states with a thousand chariots.
Those around the ruler do not necessarily need to be wise;
if the ruler considers someone wise and listens to him,
and then discusses his words with those around him,
it is like discussing wisdom with fools.
Those around the ruler do not necessarily need to be virtuous;
if the ruler considers someone virtuous and treats him with respect,
and then discusses his actions with those around him,
it is like discussing virtue with the unworthy.
If the wise make decisions based on the opinions of fools,
and virtuous men have their actions judged by the unworthy,
then wise and virtuous men will be ashamed and the ruler's judgments will be flawed.
Ministers who wish to obtain office,
if they are cultivated scholars, will preserve their integrity and purity,
and if they are wise scholars, will advance their careers through governance and eloquence.
If cultivated scholars cannot serve people through bribery,
relying on their integrity,
and furthermore cannot govern by bending the law,
then cultivated and wise men will not serve those around the ruler
and will not listen to requests and solicitations.
Those around the ruler
do not act like Bó Yí 伯夷;
if they cannot obtain what they seek
and bribes do not arrive,
then the benefits of cultivated eloquence will cease,
and slanderous words will arise.
If the benefits of governance and eloquence
are controlled by those close to the ruler,
and the actions of integrity and purity
are determined by slander and praise,
then cultivated and wise officials will be abandoned,
and the ruler's clarity will be obstructed.
If one does not decide on wisdom and action based on merit and achievement,
does not examine crimes and transgressions through comprehensive assessment,
and instead listens to the words of those close to the ruler,
then incompetent men will be in court
and foolish and corrupt officials will hold office.
The problem for a state with ten thousand chariots
is that its ministers are too powerful;
the problem for a state with a thousand chariots
is that its ruler trusts those around him too much:
this is a common problem for rulers.
Furthermore, when ministers commit great crimes
and rulers make great mistakes,
the interests of the ministers and the ruler are different.
How can this be made clear?
It is said:
The ruler's benefit lies in having the able and appointing them to office,
the minister's benefit lies in being incompetent and yet obtaining employment;
the ruler's benefit lies in having meritorious service and bestowing rank and emolument,
the minister's benefit lies in having no accomplishment and yet becoming rich and noble;
the ruler's benefit lies in heroes and outstanding individuals being put to use,
the minister's benefit lies in cliques and partisan factions using private interests.
Therefore, the state's territory is diminished while private families grow rich,
the ruler above is demeaned while the great ministers become powerful.
Thus, the ruler loses power while the ministers gain the state,
the ruler is further addressed as a vassal,
and the chief minister divides the symbols of authority.
This is how ministers deceive their rulers for their own private benefit.
Therefore, among the important ministers of the present age
who maintain their position
and secure lasting favor when the ruler's power changes,
there are scarcely two or three.
What is the reason for this?
The crimes of ministers are great.
Ministers who commit great crimes
deceive their rulers,
and their crimes deserve death.
Wise men, with foresight
and fearing death,
will certainly not follow powerful men;
virtuous men, cultivating integrity
and ashamed to deceive their ruler with treacherous ministers,
will certainly not follow powerful men.
Therefore, the followers of the powerful ministers
are either foolish and unaware of the danger,
or certainly corrupt and unconcerned about committing treacherous acts.
Great ministers, embracing the foolish and corrupt,
together with them deceive the ruler above,
and together with them collect profits and encroach upon the people below,
forming cliques and engaging in mutual protection,
speaking with one voice together,
misleading the ruler and undermining the laws,
to throw the scholar-officials and common people into chaos,
causing the state to become endangered and weakened,
and the ruler above to be burdened and humiliated.
This is a great crime.
If a minister commits a great crime and the ruler does not prevent it,
this is a great mistake.
If the ruler makes a great mistake above,
and the minister commits a great crime below,
to search for a state that will not perish
is impossible.
Generally speaking, the difficulty in persuasion
is not just in the difficulty of knowing how to persuade,
nor is it merely the difficulty of being able to clearly express one's meaning with eloquence,
nor is it simply the difficulty of daring to be unrestrained and fully expressing oneself.
Generally speaking, the difficulty in persuasion
lies in understanding the mind of the person being persuaded,
so that one's words may be appropriate.
If the person being persuaded values high reputation,
and one persuades him with substantial profit,
then he will be seen as having low principles and meeting with baseness and meanness,
and will certainly reject and distance himself.
If the person being persuaded values substantial profit,
and one persuades him with high reputation,
then he will be seen as lacking ambition and distancing himself from practical matters,
and will certainly not accept it.
If the person being persuaded secretly seeks substantial profit
but openly seeks high reputation,
and one persuades him with high reputation,
then he will outwardly accept your person
but in reality distance himself from you;
if one persuades him with substantial profit,
then he will secretly use your words but openly reject your person.
This is something that cannot but be observed.
Affairs are accomplished through secrecy,
and ruined through divulgence.
It is not necessarily that one divulges it oneself,
but if the conversation touches upon concealed matters,
in this case, one's person is in danger.
If he openly brings forth an affair,
but actually uses it to accomplish another purpose,
the persuader must not only know what is brought forth,
but also know the reason why it is done;
in this case, one's person is in danger.
If one proposes an unusual plan and it succeeds,
and a knowing person infers it from the outside and obtains it,
and the affair is divulged externally,
he will certainly think it was oneself;
in this case, one's person is in danger.
If the kindness of the ruler is not yet deep,
and one speaks with extreme knowledge,
if the persuasion is successful and there is merit,
then the virtue will be forgotten;
if the persuasion is unsuccessful and there is failure,
then one will be viewed with suspicion;
in this case, one's person is in danger.
If a noble person has a transgression,
and the persuader clearly speaks of ritual propriety to provoke his wickedness,
in this case, one's person is in danger.
If a noble person perhaps obtains a plan and wants to regard it as his own accomplishment,
and the persuader participates in the knowledge of it,
in this case, one's person is in danger.
To force him to do what he is incapable of doing,
to stop him from doing what he is unable to stop,
in this case, one's person is in danger.
Therefore, if one discusses great men with him,
he will think one is sowing discord;
if one discusses small men with him,
he will think one is selling weight.
If one discusses what he loves,
he will think one is seeking to borrow resources;
if one discusses what he hates,
he will think one is testing him.
If one's words are direct and concise,
he will think one is unwise and clumsy;
if one debates extensively on petty matters,
he will think one is verbose and long-winded.
If one states one's intentions briefly,
he will say one is timid and does not fully express oneself;
if one deliberates broadly and unrestrainedly,
he will say one is rustic and arrogant.
These difficulties in persuasion
cannot but be known.
Generally speaking, the task of persuasion
lies in knowing how to embellish what the person being persuaded takes pride in
and suppressing what he is ashamed of.
If he has a private urgency,
one must certainly use public righteousness to show
and reinforce it.
If his intention is low,
but he cannot stop,
the persuader should then embellish its beauty
and lessen what is not done.
If his heart is high,
but in reality he cannot reach it,
the persuader should then point out his faults
and show his wickedness,
and increase what is not done.
If he wants to take pride in his intelligence and ability,
then cite different affairs of the same kind for him,
create more opportunities for him,
so that he relies on me for his arguments,
and pretend not to know
in order to assist his intelligence.
If one wants to speak words that mutually preserve each other internally,
then one must certainly clarify it with beautiful names,
and subtly show its agreement with private benefit.
If one wants to present matters of harm and danger,
then openly show its destruction and defamation
and subtly show its agreement with private troubles.
Praise different men who are doing the same thing,
plan different affairs with the same plan.
If there are those who share the same corruption,
then one must certainly greatly embellish its harmlessness;
if there are those who share the same failure,
then one must certainly clearly embellish its lack of error.
If he himself overestimates his strength,
then do not generalize about its difficulty;
if he is confident in his decisiveness,
then do not anger him with blame;
if he trusts in his plans,
then do not exhaust him with his failures.
If the main idea does not encounter opposition,
and the words and language are not restrained,
then one can fully display one's intelligence and eloquence.
If this way is obtained,
one will be close and not doubted
and be able to fully express one's words.
Yī Yǐn became a cook,
Bǎilǐ Xī became a captive;
both used these means to approach their rulers.
These two men
were both sages.
Yet they still could not avoid debasing themselves to advance,
so base was it.
Now, if my words are used as those of a cook or captive,
and can be listened to and used to revitalize the world,
this is not something that a capable official should be ashamed of.
If days are prolonged and separation lasts long,
and the royal favor is already abundant,
deeply consider but do not doubt,
advance arguments without being punished,
then clearly delineate profits and harms to achieve success,
and directly point out right and wrong to cultivate oneself.
Holding onto each other in this way,
this is the way to make one's persuasion successful.
In the past, Zhèng Wǔgōng wanted to attack the Hú state,
so he first married his daughter to the Hú ruler to please him.
Then he asked his assembled ministers:
"I want to use troops,
who can be attacked?"
The grandee Guān Qísī replied:
"Hú can be attacked."
Wǔgōng became angry and executed him,
saying:
"Hú
is a brother state.
You say to attack it,
why?"
The Hú ruler heard of this,
and considered Zhèng to be friendly to him,
and thus did not prepare for Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng ambushed Hú
and took it.
There was a rich man in Sòng;
when it rained, his wall collapsed.
His son said:
"If you don't rebuild it,
there will surely be a thief."
The father of his neighbor also said this.
That evening, he indeed lost a great deal of his wealth.
His family considered his son very wise,
but suspected the neighbor's father.
Both of these persuaders were correct;
the one who spoke frankly was executed,
the one who spoke cautiously was suspected.
Thus, it is not difficult to know,
but it is difficult to know how to apply knowledge.
Therefore, the words of Rào Cháo were correct;
he was a sage in Jìn,
but was executed in Qín;
this must be carefully considered.
In the past, Mí Zixiá was favored by the ruler of Wèi.
The law of the state of Wèi was:
Whoever steals and drives the ruler's chariot will have his feet amputated.
Mí Zixiá’s mother was ill,
and someone went at night to tell Mí Zǐ,
so Mí Zǐ falsely drove the ruler’s chariot to go out.
The ruler heard of this and considered him virtuous,
saying:
"How filial!
For the sake of his mother,
he forgot about the punishment of foot amputation."
Another day,
he was with the ruler, traveling in the orchard,
eating a peach that was sweet,
not finishing it,
using half of it to feed the ruler.
The ruler said:
"How he loves me!
He forgot the taste to feed me, the寡人."
When Mí Zǐ's appearance faded and love waned,
he offended the ruler.
The ruler said:
"This person once falsely drove my chariot,
and also once fed me the remaining peach."
Thus, Mí Zǐ's actions did not change from the beginning,
but the reason why he was seen as virtuous before and later received punishment
was because of the change in love and hate.
Therefore, if one is loved by the ruler,
then wisdom is considered appropriate and closeness is increased;
if one is hated by the ruler,
then wisdom is considered inappropriate, one is seen as guilty, and alienation is increased.
Therefore, those who advise, persuade, and debate
must carefully observe the ruler's love and hate before speaking.
Now, the dragon as an animal
is gentle, and can be tamed and ridden.
However, under its throat, there are reverse scales, a foot in diameter.
If someone touches them,
it will surely kill that person.
The ruler also has reverse scales.
If the persuader can avoid touching the ruler's reverse scales,
then he is close to succeeding.
A man from Chǔ, Héshì, found a jade in Mount Chǔ,
presented it to King Lì.
King Lì ordered a jade expert to examine it.
The jade expert said:
"It is a stone."
The king considered Hé a liar
and cut off his left foot.
When King Lì died,
King Wǔ ascended the throne.
Hé again presented his jade to King Wǔ.
King Wǔ ordered a jade expert to examine it.
Again, he said:
"It is a stone."
The king again considered Hé a liar
and cut off his right foot.
When King Wǔ died,
King Wén ascended the throne.
Hé then held his jade and cried at the foot of Mount Chǔ,
for three days and three nights,
until his tears were exhausted and followed by blood.
The king heard of this
and sent someone to ask him the reason,
saying:
"There are many who have had their feet cut off in the world;
why do you cry so sadly?"
Hé said:
"I am not saddened by the amputation,
but saddened that a precious jade is labeled as a stone,
and a righteous man is called a liar;
this is why I am sad."
The king then ordered a jade expert to process the jade
and obtained a treasure,
and then named it
"Héshì's Bi."
Now, pearls and jade
are what rulers urgently need.
Although Hé presented a jade that was not yet beautiful,
it did no harm to the ruler.
Yet still, both his feet were cut off
before the treasure was recognized;
recognizing a treasure is so difficult.
Now, the ruler's attitude towards law and technique
is not necessarily as urgent as with Hé's jade,
and they forbid the private evils of ministers, officials, and the common people.
In that case, the reason why those who possess the Dao are not punished
is simply that the ruler's jade has not yet been presented.
If the ruler uses technique,
then great ministers cannot arbitrarily make decisions,
and close attendants dare not sell their influence;
if officials execute the law,
then those who are opportunistic will flock to farming,
and wandering scholars will be endangered by warfare;
then law and technique
are what ministers, officials, and common people consider a calamity.
If the ruler cannot defy the opinions of great ministers,
surpass the slander of the common people,
and exclusively adhere to the words of the Dao,
then even if those who advocate law and technique
face death,
the Dao will surely not be recognized.
In the past, Wú Qǐ taught King Dàowáng of Chǔ, according to the customs of the state of Chǔ, saying:
"The great ministers are too powerful,
the enfeoffed lords are too numerous.
If this is the case,
then those above will pressure the ruler
and those below will oppress the people;
this is the way to impoverish the state and weaken the army.
It is better to make the sons and grandsons of the enfeoffed lords
have their ranks and stipends taken away after three generations,
reduce the stipends of hundreds of officials,
cut back on unnecessary branch offices,
and use the savings to support selected and trained soldiers."
When Dào Wáng's conduct reached the one-year mourning period, he died.
Wú Qǐ was torn apart in Chǔ.
Shāng Jūn taught Qín Xiào Gōng to organize people into groups of ten and five,
to establish a system for reporting wrongdoing,
to burn books and
clarify laws and decrees,
to block private requests
and thus accomplish public tasks,
to prohibit wandering scholars
and promote those who cultivated the land and fought in battles.
Xiào Gōng implemented these policies,
and the ruler was honored and secure,
the state became wealthy and powerful.
After eight years, Xiào Gōng died,
and Shāng Jūn was torn apart by chariots in Qín.
Chǔ, without using Wú Qǐ, became weakened and chaotic;
Qín, implementing Shāng Jūn's laws, became wealthy and powerful.
These two men's words were indeed appropriate,
yet Wú Qǐ was torn apart
and Shāng Jūn was torn apart by chariots.
Why?
Because great ministers fear the law,
while the common people hate governance.
In the present age,
great ministers are excessively greedy,
and the common people are content with chaos,
even more so than the customs of Qín
and Chǔ,
and rulers do not have Dào Wáng's
or Xiào Gōng's willingness to listen.
Then how can legalist scholars
endure the dangers faced by those two men
and clarify their laws and techniques?
This is why the world is chaotic and without a hegemon or king.
All treacherous ministers want to comply with the ruler's desires
in order to gain favor and influence.
Therefore, if the ruler favors something,
the ministers follow and praise it;
if the ruler hates something,
the ministers then disparage it.
In general,
people who have the same preferences and rejections agree with each other,
while those who have different preferences and rejections disagree with each other.
Now, what ministers praise
is what the ruler approves of;
this is called sharing preferences.
What ministers disparage
is what the ruler disapproves of;
this is called sharing rejections.
It has never been heard of
that those who share preferences and rejections
would contradict each other.
This is how ministers gain trust and favor.
If treacherous ministers
gain the power of trust and favor
to slander or praise, promote or demote other ministers,
and the ruler does not have methods to control them,
nor does he cross-reference and examine them carefully,
he will inevitably rely on past agreements
and trust present words.
This is how favored ministers are able to deceive the ruler
and achieve their private gains.
Therefore, the ruler is inevitably deceived from above,
and the ministers inevitably become powerful below.
This is what is called a minister who dominates the ruler.
If a state has a minister who dominates the ruler,
then the many below cannot fully use their wisdom and strength
to express their loyalty,
and the officials of the various departments cannot uphold the law
to achieve their merit.
How can this be made clear?
People go to what is safe and profitable
and avoid what is dangerous and harmful;
this is human nature.
Now, if ministers exert their strength to achieve merit
and exhaust their wisdom to express loyalty,
their own bodies will be troubled and their families will be poor,
and their fathers and sons will suffer harm.
If they pursue treacherous gains to harm the ruler,
and use wealth and goods to serve influential ministers,
they themselves will be honored and their families will be rich,
and their fathers and sons will enjoy the benefits.
How can people abandon the path of safety and profit
and go to the place of danger and harm?
If governing the state is so flawed,
yet the ruler wants those below to have no treachery
and the officials to uphold the law,
it is clear that this is impossible to achieve.
Therefore, those close to the ruler
know that honesty and trustworthiness cannot bring safety and profit,
and will certainly say:
"If I serve the ruler with loyalty and trustworthiness,
accumulate merit and effort to seek safety,
it is like a blind man
wanting to know the nature of black and white;
it will certainly not be close to the truth.
If I transform people with the Way and practice proper principles,
not pursuing wealth and honor,
and serve the ruler to seek safety,
it is like a deaf man
wanting to discern the sounds of clear and turbid;
it will be even further from the truth.
Since these two cannot bring safety,
how can I not collude with others,
deceive the ruler,
and engage in treachery and private dealings
to please influential people?"
They will certainly disregard the righteousness of the ruler.
The officials of the various departments also know that integrity and uprightness cannot bring safety,
and will certainly say:
"If I serve the ruler with purity and honesty to seek safety,
it is like wanting to create squares and circles
without using compasses and set squares;
it will certainly not be close to the truth.
If I uphold the law and govern without forming factions
to seek safety,
it is like scratching the top of my head with my foot;
it will be even further from the truth.
Since these two cannot bring safety,
how can I not abandon the law and engage in private dealings
to please influential people?"
They will certainly disregard the laws of the ruler.
Therefore, there are many who prioritize private connections,
and few who serve the ruler with the law.
This is why the ruler is isolated above
and the ministers form factions below.
This is how Tián Chéng assassinated Jiǎn Gōng.
Now, a minister who possesses methods
is able to present words of measurement and calculation,
so that the ruler understands the law,
the treacherous ministers are constrained,
and the ruler is honored and the state is secure.
Therefore, if words of measurement and calculation are effective in advance,
then rewards and punishments will certainly be applied afterward.
If the ruler truly understands the techniques of the sages,
and does not blindly follow the words of the common people,
follows names and realities to determine right and wrong,
and relies on cross-referencing to examine words and arguments,
then the close and intimate ministers
will know that deceit and falsehood cannot bring safety,
and will certainly say:
"If I do not abandon treacherous and private conduct,
exhaust my strength and wisdom to serve the ruler,
but instead collude with others and recklessly slander and praise
to seek safety,
it is like carrying a thousand钧 weight
and falling into an unfathomable abyss
and seeking to survive;
it will certainly not be close to the truth."
The officials of the various departments will also know
that engaging in treachery and profit cannot bring safety,
and will certainly say:
"If I do not serve with purity, honesty, uprightness, and upholding the law,
but instead use greed to distort the law
to obtain private gain,
it is like climbing to the top of a high hill
and falling into a steep ravine below
and seeking to survive;
it will certainly not be close to the truth."
Since the path of safety and danger is so clear,
how can those close to the ruler deceive the ruler with empty words,
and how dare the officials of the various departments exploit those below with greed?
Therefore, ministers are able to express their loyalty without being harmed,
and those below are able to maintain their positions without resentment.
This is how Guǎn Zhòng governed Qí
and how Shāng Jūn strengthened Qín.
From this perspective,
the sage's governance of the state
certainly has a way to make people have no choice but to love me,
and does not rely on people loving me of their own accord.
Relying on people loving me of their own accord
is dangerous,
relying on me being indispensable
is safe.
Now, the relationship between ruler and subject is not based on kinship;
if the way of integrity can bring benefit,
then the subject will exert his strength to serve the ruler.
If the way of integrity cannot bring security,
then the subject will act privately
to influence his superior.
An enlightened ruler knows this,
therefore he establishes the way of benefit and harm
to show the world.
Thus, even if the ruler
does not verbally instruct the officials,
nor personally seek out the treacherous and wicked,
the state is already well-governed.
A ruler
does not need eyes like Lí Lóu
to be considered perceptive, nor
ears like Shī Kuàng
to be considered discerning.
If the eyes must not rely on their own capacity,
but rely on other eyes to see clearly,
what is seen will be little,
and it is not a method to prevent being deceived.
If the ears must not depend on their own ability,
but rely on other ears to hear clearly,
what is heard will be scant,
and it is not a way to prevent being deceived.
An enlightened ruler
makes the world have no choice but to see for him,
makes the world have no choice but to listen for him.
Therefore, though he dwells deep within the palace,
his insight illuminates all within the four seas,
and the world cannot conceal anything from him nor deceive him.
Why is this?
The path of darkness and disorder is abandoned,
and the power of discernment flourishes.
Therefore, those who are good at leveraging power,
their states are secure;
those who do not know how to leverage power,
their states are in danger.
In the customs of ancient Qín,
rulers and subjects abandoned the law and indulged in private interests,
therefore the state was chaotic, the army weak,
and the ruler was demeaned.
Shāng​ Jūn persuaded Duke Xiào of Qín to transform the laws
and change the customs, making public justice clear,
rewarding those who reported wrongdoing,
suppressing those who engaged in secondary occupations,
and favoring those who devoted themselves to fundamental tasks.
At that time,
the people of Qín were accustomed to old customs where having committed a crime
could be avoided,
and where one could gain honor and prominence without merit;
therefore, they lightly violated the new law.
Consequently, those who violated it were punished severely and certainly,
and those who reported it were rewarded generously and reliably.
Therefore, no wrongdoing could escape detection,
and those who were punished were numerous,
the people were resentful
and reports of misdeeds were heard daily.
Duke Xiào did not listen,
and proceeded to implement the laws of Shāng​ Jūn.
After the people realized that committing a crime would certainly be punished,
and that those who reported private wrongdoing were many,
therefore the people did not commit crimes,
and there was nowhere to apply punishment.
Therefore, the state was well-governed, the army was strong,
the territory was expanded, and the ruler was respected.
The reason why this was so
was that the penalty for concealing crimes was severe,
and the reward for reporting wrongdoing was generous.
This was also a way to make the world inevitably
see and hear for oneself.
The methods of perfect governance are already clear,
but the scholars of the world do not understand them.
Moreover, the foolish scholars of the world
all do not understand the reality of order and chaos,
they chatter and volubly recite ancient books,
using them to disrupt the governance of the present day;
their wisdom and deliberation are insufficient to avoid falling into traps and pitfalls,
and they presumptuously criticize men skilled in statecraft.
To listen to their words is dangerous,
to use their plans is chaotic;
this is the greatest folly
and the most severe calamity.
They both share the reputation of discussing matters
with men skilled in statecraft,
but in reality, they are separated by a distance of thousands upon thousands of miles;
this is a case of names being the same
but realities being different.
For the foolish scholars of the world
to be compared to men skilled in statecraft
is like comparing mounds to great mountains;
the distance between them is vast.
Therefore, the sage
discerns the reality of right and wrong,
and observes the truth of order and chaos.
Therefore, in governing his state,
he rectifies and clarifies the laws,
and establishes strict punishments,
intending to save the multitude from chaos,
remove calamity from the world,
so that the strong do not oppress the weak,
the many do not tyrannize the few,
the elderly can live out their years,
orphans can grow up,
borders are not invaded,
rulers and subjects are kind to each other,
fathers and sons protect each other,
and there is no worry of death or captivity;
this is the greatest of merits.
The foolish do not understand,
and instead consider it tyrannical.
The foolish indeed desire order but resent the means to achieve it,
and they all hate danger but delight in the causes of it.
How do we know this?
For strict punishments and heavy penalties
are what the people hate,
but are the means by which the state is governed;
compassionately pitying the people and lightly applying penalties
are what the people love,
but are the means by which the state is endangered.
The sage who creates laws
must go against the world
but be in accordance with morality.
Those who understand it
agree with righteousness but differ from custom;
those who do not understand it
differ from righteousness but agree with custom.
If few in the world understand it,
then righteousness is undermined.
To occupy a position of injustice,
to be subjected to the slander of the masses,
to be immersed in the words of the current era,
and yet to desire to stand up to a stern Son of Heaven and seek security,
is it not exceedingly difficult?
This is why wise men die without achieving fame in the world.
Chūnshēn Jūn, the younger brother of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
had a beloved concubine named Yú,
and Chūnshēn Jūn’s legal wife was named Jiǎ.
Yú wanted the lord to abandon his wife,
so she deliberately injured herself
to show the lord while weeping,
saying:
"To be able to be the lord's concubine
is very fortunate.
However,
it is not appropriate for a proper lady to serve the lord,
nor is it appropriate for the lord to serve the proper lady.
Because I am unworthy
and my strength is insufficient to serve two masters,
it is impossible to serve both.
Rather than dying at the hands of the proper lady,
it would be better to be granted death before the lord.
If I am granted death
and I am fortunate enough to be favored by those around you again,
I hope the lord will observe carefully
and not be laughed at by others."
The lord then believed the deceit of concubine Yú
and abandoned his proper wife.
Yú also wanted to kill Jiǎ
and have her son become the heir,
so she deliberately tore the lining of her own clothes,
to show the lord while weeping,
saying:
"It has been a long time since I was favored by the lord,
and Jiǎ surely knows this,
but now she wants to forcefully mock me.
When I argued with her,
she even tore my clothes,
and the unfilial behavior of this son
is greater than this."
The lord was angered
and killed Jiǎ.
Therefore, the wife thought she had been fraudulently abandoned by her husband for a concubine,
and the son died because of it.
Judging from this,
a father's love for his son
can still be destroyed and harmful.
The relationship between ruler and ministers
is not one of parental affection.
The slanderous words of the assembled ministers
are not just the talk of one concubine.
How can one be surprised that the wise and sagacious are put to death?
This is why Shāng Jūn was torn apart by chariots in Qín,
and Wú Qǐ was dismembered in Chǔ.
Generally, ministers
who are guilty certainly do not want to be punished,
and those without merit all desire to be honored and elevated.
But a sage's way of governing a state
is to not bestow rewards on those without merit,
and to ensure that punishment is carried out on the guilty.
Therefore, those with skills and methods,
are certainly harmed by treacherous ministers on all sides.
Only a discerning ruler can listen to them.
Scholars of the world, when advising rulers,
do not say,
"Use the power of awe and authority
to subdue treacherous and deceitful ministers,"
but all say,
"Only practice benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and love."
Rulers of the world admire the name of benevolence and righteousness
but do not examine its reality.
Therefore, in great matters, the state is lost and the ruler dies;
in small matters, territory is diminished and the ruler is debased.
How can this be made clear?
Giving to the poor and needy
is what the world calls benevolence and righteousness;
having pity on the common people
and being unwilling to punish them
is what the world calls kindness and love.
If there is giving to the poor and needy,
then those without merit receive rewards;
if one is unwilling to punish,
then violence and disorder will not cease.
If a state has those without merit receiving rewards,
then the people will not focus on fighting the enemy and cutting off heads,
nor will they diligently cultivate the fields and work hard.
They will all seek to traffic in wealth and pursue riches and honor,
performing private good deeds and establishing reputations
in order to obtain high office and generous stipends.
Thus, treacherous and self-serving ministers become more numerous,
and violent and rebellious elements become more victorious.
What else is there to wait for but ruin?
Severe penalties
are what the people fear;
heavy punishments
are what the people hate.
Therefore, the sage
displays what they fear
to prohibit their deceit,
and establishes what they hate
to prevent their treachery.
Thus, the state is secure and violence and rebellion do not arise.
From this, I show that benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and love are insufficient to use,
but that severe penalties and heavy punishments can govern a state.
Without the power of the whip and the spur,
and the preparation of the bit and bridle,
even Zào Fù cannot subdue a horse;
without the laws of the compass and square,
and the standard of the plumb line and ink marker,
even Wáng Ěr cannot make squares and circles;
without the power of awe and authority,
and the laws of rewards and punishments,
even Yáo and Shùn cannot govern.
If present-day rulers all lightly release those who deserve heavy punishment and severe execution,
and practice love and kindness,
but desire the achievements of hegemony and kingship,
it is also impossible to expect them.
Therefore, one who is good at being a ruler
clearly establishes rewards and sets up benefits to encourage the people,
causing the people to be rewarded based on merit
and not granted favors based on benevolence and righteousness;
strictly enforces penalties and heavy punishments to prohibit them,
causing the people to be punished based on crimes
and not exempted based on love and kindness.
Thus, those without merit do not hope for rewards,
and those who are guilty will not escape misfortune.
Relying on a rhinoceros-hide chariot and good horses,
one can overcome the difficulties of traversing hills and obstacles on land;
taking advantage of the security of a boat,
and holding the benefit of oars,
one can cross the difficulties of rivers and streams on water;
wielding the methods of law and technique,
and practicing heavy punishments and severe executions,
one can achieve the accomplishments of hegemony and kingship.
Governing a state with law, technique, rewards, and punishments
is like having a rhinoceros-hide chariot and good horses for traveling on land,
or a light boat and convenient oars for traveling on water;
those who use them accordingly achieve their goals.
Yī Yǐn obtained them,
and Tāng became king because of it;
Guǎn Zhòng obtained them,
and Qí achieved hegemony because of it;
Shāng Jūn obtained them,
and Qín became strong because of it.
These three men
were all clear on the methods of hegemony and kingship,
insightful about the techniques of governance and strengthening the state,
and were not constrained by the words of worldly custom.
Appropriately meeting the intentions of enlightened rulers of their time,
even a commoner with integrity and directness
could immediately be appointed to the position of high minister;
by occupying the position and governing the state,
they could achieve the reality of honoring the ruler and expanding the territory;
these are what are called truly valuable ministers.
Tāng obtained Yī Yǐn,
and with a territory of a hundred *lǐ* established himself as the Son of Heaven;
Duke Huán obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
and established himself as the chief among the Five Hegemons,
assembled the lords nine times,
and brought order to the world in one stroke;
Duke Xiào obtained Shāng Jūn,
and the territory was expanded,
and the military was strengthened.
Therefore, having loyal ministers
means that there are no external threats from enemy states,
and no internal worries about rebellious ministers,
ensuring long-lasting peace in the world,
and a name that is passed down to later generations;
this is what is meant by a loyal minister.
As for Yù Ràng being a minister of Zhì Bó,
he was unable to persuade his ruler to
understand the principles of law, technique, measurement, and calculation
in order to avoid the calamity of misfortune;
and he was unable to lead and govern his people
to secure his state.
When Xiāng Zǐ killed Zhì Bó,
Yù Ràng then tattooed his face and cut off his nose,
ruining his appearance,
in order to avenge Zhì Bó against Xiāng Zǐ.
Although he inflicted mutilation and death on himself
to create a reputation for his ruler,
in reality he was of no benefit to Zhì Bó,
not even the tip of an autumn hair.
This is what I disparage,
but the rulers of the world consider it loyalty and praise it highly.
In ancient times, there were Bó Yí and Shū Qí;
King Wǔ offered them the empire, but they did not accept it.
The two starved to death on the hill of Shǒuyáng.
As for ministers like these,
not fearing heavy punishment
nor benefiting from generous rewards,
they cannot be restrained by punishment,
nor can they be employed by rewards.
These are what are called useless ministers.
I decrease and reject them,
but the rulers of the world increase and seek them.
The proverb says:
"Have pity on Lì."
These are disrespectful words.
However,
ancient proverbs are never empty,
and cannot but be examined.
This refers to rulers who are robbed, killed, and die.
If a ruler does not have law and technique
to control his ministers,
even if he lives long and possesses great talent,
the high ministers will still seize power
and decide matters on their own authority,
each acting for their own selfish interests.
And fearing that fathers, elder brothers, heroes, and outstanding men
might borrow the ruler's power
to prohibit and punish them,
they therefore assassinate wise elders and establish young and weak rulers,
and depose the rightful heir and establish the unrighteous.
Therefore, the *Chūn Qiū* records it, saying:
"Crown Prince Wéi of Chǔ was about to go as envoy to Zhèng;
before leaving the border,
he heard that the king was ill and returned.
He then entered to inquire about the illness,
and strangled the king with the tassel of his hat,
and thus established himself."
In Qí, Cuī Zhù's wife was beautiful,
and Duke Zhuāng had illicit relations with her,
frequently going to the Cuī family's residence.
When the duke went,
Jiǎ Jǔ, a follower of Cuī Zǐ, led Cuī Zǐ's followers to attack the duke.
The duke entered a room,
requesting to divide the state with them,
but Cuī Zǐ did not allow it;
the duke requested to kill himself in the ancestral temple,
but Cuī Zǐ still did not listen.
The duke then fled,
climbing over the north wall.
Jiǎ Jǔ shot the duke,
hitting his thigh,
and the duke fell.
Cuī Zǐ's followers hacked the duke to death with halberds,
and established his younger brother, Duke Jǐng."
In recent times:
when Lǐ Duì was employed in Zhào,
he starved Lord Father for a hundred days until he died;
when Nào Chǐ was employed in Qí,
he drew out King Mǐn's tendons,
hanging him from a beam in the temple,
and he died overnight.
Therefore, though Lì may have had boils, swellings, and sores,
compared to the *Chūn Qiū*,
it did not reach the point of strangling the neck and shooting the thigh;
compared to recent times,
it did not reach the point of starvation and tendon extraction.
Therefore, the anxieties and fears in the hearts,
and the suffering and pain in the bodies,
of rulers who are robbed, killed, or die,
must be much greater than those of Lì.
From this perspective,
it can even be said that "Lì pitied the king."
In general, when a ruler's state is small while his family is large,
and his power is weak while his ministers are strong,
it is liable to perish.
Simplifying laws and prohibitions
while focusing on scheming and strategizing,
neglecting the interior
while relying on external support,
it is liable to perish.
When ministers pursue learning,
disciples enjoy debate,
merchants accumulate wealth abroad,
and the common people value weapons,
it is liable to perish.
Being fond of palaces, terraces, pavilions, and ponds,
indulging in carriages, clothing, vessels, and toys,
enjoying exhausting the common people,
and squandering wealth,
it is liable to perish.
Using oracles,
serving ghosts and spirits,
believing in divination,
and being fond of sacrifices,
it is liable to perish.
Accepting recommendations without investigation,
and relying on one person as a gatekeeper,
it is liable to perish.
When official positions can be heavily sought,
and titles and stipends can be obtained with money,
it is liable to perish.
Being lax and accomplishing nothing,
being soft and indecisive,
having no resolution in likes and dislikes,
and establishing nothing definite,
it is liable to perish.
Being greedy and insatiable,
pursuing immediate gains and being fond of acquisitions,
it is liable to perish.
Delighting in extravagant language that does not adhere to the law,
enjoying debate that does not seek practical application,
and indulging in ornate writing without regard for its function,
it is liable to perish.
Being shallow and easily seen through,
leaking secrets and concealing nothing,
unable to be thorough and discreet,
and divulging the words of all the ministers,
it is liable to perish.
Being stubbornly inflexible and not harmonious,
