rejecting advice and enjoying victory,
not considering the state and
lightly trusting oneself,
it is liable to perish.
Relying on external support
while neglecting nearby neighbors,
depending on the assistance of the powerful,
while insulting the states being coerced,
it is liable to perish.
When wandering travelers
hold heavy positions abroad,
the ruler is excluded from planning,
and the inferiors are involved in the people's affairs,
it is liable to perish.
When the people trust their ministers,
the inferiors are unable to control their superiors,
and the ruler loves and trusts them but cannot dismiss them,
it is liable to perish.
When the outstanding talents within the borders are not employed,
but officials are sought from beyond the borders,
when accomplishments are not assessed,
but appointments are based on reputation,
and wandering travelers rise to prominence and surpass the old guard,
it is liable to perish.
Devaluing the legitimate heir,
allowing the illegitimate son to assume power,
and the crown prince is not yet decided when the ruler passes away,
it is liable to perish.
Being arrogant and unrepentant,
rejoicing in the chaos of the state,
not assessing the resources within the borders
and underestimating neighboring enemies,
it is liable to perish.
When a state is small but does not act humbly,
its strength is weak but it does not fear the strong,
lacking in propriety and insulting large neighbors,
being greedy, stubborn, and clumsy in diplomacy,
it is liable to perish.
When a crown prince has already been established,
but a wife from a powerful enemy is taken as the queen,
the crown prince is in danger,
and in such a case, the ministers will easily change their plans;
when the ministers easily change their plans,
it is liable to perish.
Being fearful and weak in defense,
seeing dangers early but being soft and weak-willed,
knowing what can be said,
but hesitating to act decisively,
it is liable to perish.
When the ruler is abroad and the state is replaced,
when the hostage crown prince has not returned
but the ruler changes his heir,
in such cases, the state will be alienated;
when the state is alienated,
it is liable to perish.
Humiliating and insulting great ministers while being intimate with their persons,
punishing and executing the common people while defying their envoys,
harboring anger and dwelling on shame
while focusing on rebellion,
and when rebellion arises,
it is liable to perish.
When great ministers have overlapping authority,
fathers and elder brothers are numerous and powerful,
forming internal factions and external alliances to contend for power,
it is liable to perish.
Listening to the words of concubines,
employing the wisdom of loved ones,
with inner and outer lamentations,
and frequently engaging in unlawful conduct,
it is liable to perish.
Treating great ministers with contempt,
lacking propriety towards fathers and elder brothers,
oppressing the common people with hard labor,
and killing the innocent,
it is liable to perish.
Enjoying using intelligence to evade the law,
constantly mixing private actions with public affairs,
constantly changing laws and prohibitions,
and frequently issuing orders,
it is liable to perish.
A state that has no firm borders,
evil city walls,
no stored provisions,
scant wealth and goods,
no preparations for defense and warfare,
and lightly engages in attacks and conquests,
is liable to perish.
If the line of succession is short-lived,
the ruler frequently dies,
an infant becomes the sovereign,
high ministers monopolize power,
factions are formed by harboring travelers,
and territory is often ceded to curry favor with other states,
it is liable to perish.
If the crown prince is honored and prominent,
his followers are numerous and powerful,
he has many connections with major states,
and his influence has been established early,
it is liable to perish.
Someone who is narrow-minded and impatient,
frivolous and easily moved to anger,
whose heart is consumed by resentment and who does not consider the consequences,
is liable to perish.
A ruler who is often angry and fond of using military force,
who neglects fundamental instruction and values war and aggression,
is liable to perish.
If noble ministers are mutually jealous,
high ministers are flourishing,
they rely on enemy states from the outside,
oppress the common people from within,
attack to avenge grudges,
and the ruler does not punish them,
it is liable to perish.
If the ruler is unworthy while his concubine is virtuous,
the crown prince is regarded lightly while the sons of concubines are respected,
officials are weak while the people are unruly,
the state will be agitated;
a state that is agitated
is liable to perish.
To harbor resentment without expressing it,
to suspend punishment without executing it,
causing the ministers to secretly hate
and become increasingly fearful,
and for a long time it remains unknown,
it is liable to perish.
If the authority to issue military commands and appoint generals is too great,
the power of the border officials and governors is too honored,
they act with exclusive authority and make decisions on their own,
acting directly without seeking approval,
it is liable to perish.
If the queen is promiscuous and immoral,
the ruling mother keeps filth,
the outer and inner realms are mixed,
and there is no distinction between men and women,
this is called two rulers.
Having two rulers
is liable to perish.
If the queen is base while the concubines are honored,
the crown prince is lowly while the sons of concubines are respected,
the chancellor's office is insignificant while the eunuch's office is important,
then the inner and outer realms will be at odds.
When the inner and outer realms are at odds,
it is liable to perish.
If high ministers are extremely honored,
partisan groups are numerous and powerful,
they block the ruler's decisions
and heavily monopolize the state's power,
it is liable to perish.
If officials from private households are employed,
those from the state stables are dismissed,
good people from the villages are promoted,
and those who labor in official posts are abandoned,
valuing private conduct while devaluing public achievements,
it is liable to perish.
If the public treasury is empty while the ministers are wealthy,
the registered households are poor while the immigrants are rich,
those who farm and fight are impoverished,
while those who engage in non-essential occupations profit,
it is liable to perish.
To see great profit but not pursue it,
to hear of the beginning of disaster but not prepare for it,
to be shallow in matters of defense and protection,
while striving to adorn oneself with benevolence and righteousness,
it is liable to perish.
Not practicing the filial piety of a ruler,
but admiring the filial piety of a commoner,
not considering the benefit of the state,
but listening to the orders of the ruling mother,
women using the state,
and eunuchs handling affairs,
it is liable to perish.
Eloquence without law,
intelligence without tactics,
a ruler who is multi-talented
but does not act according to laws and standards,
is liable to perish.
If close ministers are advanced while old acquaintances are退,
unworthy people are employed while virtuous and good people are hidden,
the powerless are honored while the laborious are base,
then those below will resent it.
Those below who resent it
are liable to perish.
If fathers, elder brothers, and high ministers receive salaries and ranks beyond their merit,
their attire and insignia infringe on the proper distinctions,
their palaces and provisions are extravagantly lavish,
and the ruler does not prohibit it,
then the ministers' hearts will have no limit.
Ministers whose hearts have no limit
are liable to perish.
If the sons-in-law and grandsons of the royal family live among the common people
and are violently arrogant toward their neighbors,
it is liable to perish.
Signs of ruin
do not necessarily mean certain ruin,
but they indicate the possibility of ruin.
Two Yáos cannot both be kings,
two Jiés cannot both be ruined.
The opportunity for ruin or kingship
necessarily lies in whether there is order or chaos, 〓#
whether there is strength or weakness.
A tree that breaks must have a wormhole,
a wall that collapses must have a crack.
However, even if the tree has a wormhole,
without a strong wind it will not break;
even if the wall has a crack,
without heavy rain it will not collapse.
If the ruler of a ten-thousand-chariot state
can practice techniques and implement laws,
and treat these signs of ruin as wind and rain,
conquering the world will not be difficult.
A ruler has three guards.
If the three guards are complete,
then the state is secure and the ruler's person is honored;
if the three guards are incomplete,
then the state is in danger and the ruler's person is imperiled.
What are the three guards?
If ministers criticize the errors of those in power,
the mistakes of those in office,
and the true nature of the ministers,
and the ruler does not keep this to himself
but leaks it to his close attendants and capable men,
so that ministers who want to speak out
do not dare to not first cater to the minds of the close attendants and capable men,
before reporting it to the ruler,
then honest and upright men
will not be seen,
and loyalty and integrity will become increasingly alienated.
To love a man
is not solely for profit;
one waits for praise before benefiting him.
To hate a man
is not solely for harm;
one waits for criticism before harming him.
Then the ruler will have no authority
and the power will reside in those around him.
To dislike the labor and dread the effort of governing oneself,
allowing the ministers to change things and gather power,
transferring authority and shifting responsibilities,
allowing the power of life and death
and the essentials of granting and taking
to lie with the ministers,
such a state is being encroached upon.
This is what is meant by the three guards being incomplete.
If the three guards are incomplete,
then it is a sign of assassination.
There are three types of assassination:
obvious assassination,
assassination through events,
and assassination through punishment.
When a subject is of the status of a great minister,
outwardly wielding the important affairs of the state to enrich his followers,
making it so that external and internal affairs
cannot be carried out without him,
even if there are worthy and virtuous men,
those who oppose him will certainly suffer disaster,
while those who comply will certainly receive blessings.
In that case, the assembled ministers will directly not dare to be loyal to the ruler and worry about the state,
or contend for the benefits and harms of the state.
Even if the ruler is virtuous,
he cannot make decisions alone,
and if his subjects do not dare to be loyal,
then the state will become a ruined state.
This is called a state without ministers.
A state without ministers,
is it merely that the *lángzhōng* are empty
and the court ministers are few?
The assembled ministers hold their emoluments and cultivate relationships,
pursuing private gains without demonstrating public loyalty,
this is called open coercion.
Selling favors and monopolizing power,
using external influence to overcome internal authority,
deceitfully speaking of the forms of fortune, misfortune, gain, and loss,
in order to cater to the ruler’s likes and dislikes.
The ruler listens to them,
humbles himself and diminishes the state to enrich them,
when things fail, he shares the blame with the ruler,
but when things succeed, the minister alone takes the credit.
All those who are employed in affairs
are of one mind and speak with one voice to praise his merits,
then the ruler will certainly not believe those who speak ill of him,
this is called coercion through affairs.
As for those who guard the prisons
and control punishments,
if the ministers monopolize these,
this is called coercion through punishment.
If the three safeguards are not complete,
then the three coercions arise;
if the three safeguards are complete,
then the three coercions cease.
When the three coercions are stopped and blocked,
then the ruler will be a true king.
The ruler's trouble lies in trusting people;
if he trusts people,
then he is controlled by them.
The relationship between a minister and his ruler
is not one of blood relation;
it is being bound by power that makes them have to serve.
Therefore, those who are ministers
spy on their ruler’s mind without a moment’s rest,
while the ruler is lazy and arrogant above them;
this is why the world has cases of coercing the ruler
and assassinating the sovereign.
If a ruler greatly trusts his son,
then treacherous ministers can take advantage of the son
to accomplish their private gains,
therefore Lǐ Duì 李兌 served as tutor to the King of Zhào 趙
and starved the Lord Father.
If a ruler greatly trusts his wife,
then treacherous ministers can take advantage of the wife
to accomplish their private gains,
therefore Yōu Shī 優施 served as tutor to Lì Jī 麗姬,
killed Shēn Shēng 申生, and established Xī Qí 奚齊.
Even with the closeness of a wife and the intimacy of a son,
they still cannot be trusted,
then there is nothing else that can be trusted.
Moreover, the ruler of ten thousand chariots
and the lord of a thousand chariots,
the empresses, consorts, and the legitimate son who is the heir apparent,
some may wish for their ruler to die early.
How do we know this is so?
Husbands and wives
do not have the kindness of blood relations;
they are close if they love each other,
but distant if they do not.
The saying goes,
“The son is held by the mother who loves him.”
Then, if the mother hates him,
the son is rejected.
A husband at fifty
still has not lost his fondness for beauty,
but a woman at thirty has already seen her beauty decline.
When a woman of declining beauty serves a husband who is fond of beauty,
then she will find herself neglected and despised,
and the son will suspect that he will not be the successor;
this is why empresses and
consorts hope for their ruler's death.
Only when the mother is the empress and the son is the ruler
will orders be carried out without fail
and prohibitions be stopped without exception.
The pleasures of men and women will not be less than those of the former ruler,
and monopolizing ten thousand chariots will not be doubted;
this is how poison and smothering are used.
Therefore, the *Táo Zuǒ Chūnqiū* 《桃左春秋》 says,
“Rulers who die of illness account for less than half.”
If the ruler does not know this,
then disorder will have many sources.
Therefore, it is said,
“If there are many who benefit from the ruler’s death,
then the ruler is in danger.”
Therefore, Wáng Liáng 王良 loved horses,
and Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn 越王勾踐 loved people,
for fighting and racing.
A doctor is good at sucking the wounds of others
and holding the blood of others,
not because of blood relations,
but because of the benefits involved.
Therefore, a cartwright who makes carts
wants people to be rich and noble;
a carpenter who makes coffins
wants people to die young.
It is not that the cartwright is benevolent while the carpenter is wicked;
if people are not wealthy,
then carts will not sell;
if people do not die,
then coffins will not be bought.
The feeling is not hatred of people,
but the benefit lies in people's death.
Therefore, when the parties of the empresses,
consorts, and crown prince are formed
they want the ruler's death;
if the ruler does not die,
their power will not be significant.
The feeling is not hatred of the ruler,
but the benefit lies in the ruler's death.
Therefore, the ruler cannot but pay attention to those who benefit from his death.
Therefore, when there are halos around the sun and moon on the outside,
the treachery is on the inside;
be prepared for those you hate,
disaster lies in those you love.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler
does not undertake affairs without investigation,
nor does he eat food that is not ordinary;
he listens from afar and observes closely
to examine the faults within and without;
he examines words of agreement and difference
to know the divisions of factions;
he uses the verification of paired comparisons
to demand the truth of presented words;
he holds on to what comes later to respond to what came before,
he relies on laws to govern the masses,
and observes all aspects for comparison.
If gentlemen receive no rewards by chance
and do not overstep their bounds,
if executions are certainly appropriate
and crimes are not pardoned,
then the treacherous will have no place to harbor their private gains.
If corvée labor is excessive, then the people will suffer;
if the people suffer, then power and influence will arise;
if power and influence arise, then double taxes and levies will increase;
if double taxes and levies increase, then the nobles will become rich.
To make the people suffer in order to enrich the nobles,
to raise power and influence in order to depend on the ministers,
is not a long-term benefit for the realm.
Therefore, it is said,
“If corvée labor is little, then the people will be at peace;
if the people are at peace, then there will be no great power below;
if there is no great power below,
then power and influence will be extinguished;
if power and influence are extinguished, then virtue will be above.”
Now, it is clear that water overcomes fire,
but if a pot or cauldron separates them,
the water will boil and be exhausted above,
and the fire will be able to burn fiercely below;
the water has lost what it used to overcome with.
Now, the prohibition of treachery in governance is even clearer than this,
but if the ministers who uphold the law act like pots and cauldrons,
then the law will be clear only in their minds,
and they will have lost what they used to prohibit treachery with.
According to ancient traditions and
records in the *Chūn Qiū* (春秋),
those who commit illegal acts and engage in great treachery
have invariably come from among esteemed and powerful ministers.
However, the provisions of laws and statutes
and the executions of punishments
are always directed at the lowly and base.
Consequently, the common people are filled with despair
and have nowhere to lodge their complaints.
Great ministers form factions,
uniting to deceive the ruler,
secretly favoring each other while outwardly feigning animosity
to appear impartial.
They act as each other's eyes and ears
to watch for the ruler's vulnerabilities.
The ruler is obscured and misled,
unable to hear the truth,
possessing the title of ruler but lacking the substance,
while ministers monopolize the law and execute it themselves,
as was the case with the Zhōu (周) Son of Heaven.
If the ministers are partially granted authority and power,
then the positions of superiors and inferiors will be reversed.
This speaks to the inadvisability of granting ministers authority and power.
The ruler's errors
lie in relying solely on appointed ministers,
and inevitably turning to those who are not appointed
to keep them in check.
This approach necessarily creates enmity between those he relies on and those he doesn't,
and the ruler is instead controlled by those he does not rely on.
Those who are now used as checks
were previously the ones who were being checked.
If the ruler cannot clarify the laws
to control the power of great ministers,
he will unintentionally gain the trust of petty individuals.
If the ruler abandons the law and uses ministers to control other ministers,
then those who love each other will form factions and praise one another,
while those who hate each other will form cliques and slander one another.
With praise and slander constantly clashing,
the ruler will be confused and misled.
Ministers,
without seeking advancement through fame, praise, and requests,
have no means of progressing;
without defying the law and acting despotically,
they have no way to establish their authority;
without feigning loyalty and trustworthiness,
they have no means to prohibit wrongdoing.
These three things
are the resources for a muddled ruler to ruin the law.
When a ruler employs ministers,
even if they possess intelligence and ability,
they must not be allowed to defy the law and act despotically;
even if they possess virtuous conduct,
they must not be allowed to overstep their merits and take precedence in labor;
even if they possess loyalty and trustworthiness,
they must not be allowed to abandon the law and fail to prohibit wrongdoing.
This is what is meant by clarifying the law.
A ruler can be either deceived by events
or blocked by words.
These two possibilities must be examined carefully.
Ministers who readily speak of affairs
demand little resources
to deceive the ruler with their proposals.
If the ruler is tempted but does not examine closely
and consequently increases such activities,
then the ministers will in turn use these affairs to control the ruler.
Such a situation is called being deceived.
One who is deceived by events will be plagued by troubles.
If their advancement is small,
but their expenditures are large,
even if they have merit,
their words will not be believed.
If those whose words are not believed are punished,
and those whose actions have merit are not rewarded,
then no minister will dare to embellish their words
to muddle the ruler.
The way of the ruler
is to ensure that a minister's previous words do not align with their later words,
and their later words do not align with their previous words.
Even if their actions have merit,
they must be held accountable for their offenses.
This is called employing subordinates.
When ministers propose actions for the ruler
but fear that they might be wrong,
they will first issue theories and set forth arguments, saying,
"Those who oppose this matter
are jealous of those who propose it."
If the ruler hides these words
and no longer listens to the other ministers,
and the ministers fear these words
and dare not discuss the matter,
when these two tactics are used,
loyal ministers will not be heard
and only those who offer praise will be entrusted with responsibility.
Such a situation is called being blocked by words.
One who is blocked by words is controlled by ministers.
The way of the ruler
is to ensure that ministers have a responsibility to speak
and also a responsibility not to speak.
Those who speak without clear evidence or verifiable arguments
are held responsible for their words;
those who avoid responsibility by not speaking
and hold high positions
are held responsible for their silence.
When the ruler has ministers speak,
he must know the source of their words
in order to demand the truth from them.
When ministers remain silent, he must inquire about their choices
in order to hold them accountable.
In this way, no minister will dare to speak recklessly,
nor will they dare to remain silent.
Whether speaking or remaining silent, they will all be held responsible.
If the ruler wants to undertake an action
without understanding its beginning and end,
but makes his desires clear,
then those who act on it,
if their actions do not bring benefit,
will inevitably cause harm in return.
Those who understand this
will prioritize reason and discard desire.
There is a way to undertake actions:
calculate that the income will be greater
and the expenditure less;
only then can it be done.
A deluded ruler is not like this;
he calculates the income
but does not calculate the expenditure.
Even if the expenditure is double the income,
he does not realize the harm.
This is called gaining the name but losing the substance.
In such cases, the achievement is small
and the harm is great.
All achievements
should have greater income
than expenditure;
only then can it be called an achievement.
If now large expenditures are not punished
while small gains are considered achievements,
then ministers will incur large expenditures
to achieve small gains.
Once small gains are achieved,
the ruler will also suffer harm.
Those who do not understand governance
will invariably say,
"Do not change the old ways;
do not alter the constants."
Change and no-change are not matters for the sage to heed;
only proper governance is.
Thus, whether to have no change in the old ways
and to have no alteration in the constants
depends on what in the old and constant is permissible or not.
If Yī Yǐn (伊尹) had not changed the Yīn (殷) dynasty,
and Tài Gōng (太公) had not changed the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
then Tāng (湯) and
Wǔ (武) would not have become kings.
If Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) had not changed the Qí (齊) state,
and Guō Yǎn (郭偃) had not reformed the Jìn (晉) state,
then Huán (桓) and Wén (文) would not have become hegemons.
The reason why people find it difficult to change the old ways
is that they fear disrupting the people's stability.
But not changing the old ways
means perpetuating the traces of chaos;
catering to the people's desires
means indulging in the actions of the wicked.
If the people are foolish and do not know chaos,
and the ruler is weak and cannot reform,
this is a failure of governance.
The ruler
must be intelligent enough to know governance
and strict enough to carry it out.
Therefore, even if it goes against the people's wishes,
he must establish his governance.
The *Shāng Jūn*'s (商君) regulations, both internal and external, included iron spears
and heavy shields, and he took precautions in advance.
Thus, when *Guō Yǎn* (郭偃) first governed,
Duke *Wén* (文公) had official soldiers;
when *Guǎn Zhòng* (管仲) first governed,
Duke *Huán* (桓公) had military chariots,
preparing the people for defense.
Therefore, foolish, stubborn, lazy, and slothful people
begrudge small expenses and forget great benefits.
Therefore, *Yín Hǔ* (夤虎) received slander and disparagement.
Because they were unwilling to change small things, they lost long-term advantages.
Therefore, *Zōu Jiǎ* (鄒賈) did not travel with merchants.
Those accustomed to disorder accommodate themselves to order,
so the people of *Zhèng* (鄭) could not return to simplicity.
Chiseling tortoise shells and counting yarrow stalks,
the divination said "Great Auspiciousness,"
and using this to attack *Yān* (燕) was *Zhào* (趙).
Chiseling tortoise shells and counting yarrow stalks,
the divination said "Great Auspiciousness,"
and using this to attack *Zhào* (趙) was *Yān* (燕).
*Jù Xīn*'s (劇辛) service to *Yān* (燕) was without merit, and the state was endangered;
*Zōu Yǎn*'s (鄒衍) service to *Yān* (燕) was without merit, and the state's path was cut off.
*Zhào Dài* (趙代) first rejoiced over *Yān* (燕),
then rejoiced over *Qí* (齊),
the state was in chaos, but its integrity was high.
It thought it could compete with *Qín* (秦),
but it was not that *Zhào*'s (趙) tortoises were divine
and *Yān*'s (燕) tortoises were deceptive.
*Zhào* (趙) once chiseled tortoise shells and counted yarrow stalks
and launched a northern attack on *Yān* (燕),
intending to coerce *Yān* (燕) to resist *Qín* (秦).
The divination said "Great Auspiciousness."
It first attacked *Dàliáng* (大梁),
and *Qín* (秦) came out from *Shàngdǎng* (上黨).
When the army reached *Lí* (釐), six cities were captured.
Reaching *Yángchéng* (陽城),
*Qín* (秦) captured *Yè* (鄴).
When *Páng Yuán* (龐援) moved his troops south,
*Zhāng* (鄣) was completely lost.
Therefore, your servant says:
*Zhào*'s (趙) tortoise, though lacking distant vision regarding *Yān* (燕),
should at least have had near vision regarding *Qín* (秦).
*Qín* (秦) used its "Great Auspiciousness"
to effectively expand its territory
and to have a good reason to rescue *Yān* (燕).
*Zhào* (趙) used its
"Great Auspiciousness"
to have its territory reduced and its army disgraced,
and its ruler died in disappointment.
Again, it was not that *Qín*'s (秦) tortoises were divine
and *Zhào*'s (趙) tortoises were deceptive.
Initially, *Wèi* (魏) for several years eastwardly attacked and seized all of *Táo* (陶) and *Wèi* (衛).
For several years westwardly it lost its state.
This was not because *Fēng Lóng* (豐隆), the Five Elements, *Tài Yī* (太一), the King's Auxiliary,
*Shè Tí* (攝提), the Six Gods, the Five Encompassers, the Heavenly River, *Yīn Qiǎng* (殷搶), and the Year Star
were for several years in the west.
Nor was it because the Heavenly Defect, the Reverse Arc, the Punishing Star,
*Yínghuò* (熒惑), and *Kuí Tái* (奎台) were for several years in the east.
Therefore, it is said:
Tortoise shells and yarrow stalks and ghosts and spirits are insufficient to ensure victory,
and aligning to the left or turning the back is
insufficient to ensure exclusive victory in battle.
Yet relying on them is
the height of foolishness.
In ancient times, the former kings devoted their efforts to cherishing the people
and emphasizing clear laws.
When the laws are clear, loyal officials are encouraged;
when punishments are certain, wicked officials are deterred.
Encouraging loyalty and deterring wickedness
to expand territory and honor the ruler is what *Qín* (秦) did.
Groups of officials forming factions and cliques
to obscure the correct path,
acting with selfish bias
to shrink territory and debase the ruler is what the states east of *Hán* (函) did.
The weak perishing is the nature of things.
The strong ruling is the ancient way.
King *Gōujiàn* (勾踐) of *Yuè* (越) relied on the great *Péng* (朋) tortoise
to fight *Wú* (吳) and was not victorious,
becoming a servant and entering the service of *Wú* (吳);
returning to his state, he abandoned the tortoise,
clarified the laws, and cherished the people
to avenge himself on *Wú* (吳),
and so *Fūchāi* (夫差) was captured.
Therefore, those who rely on ghosts and spirits are negligent of the law,
and those who rely on the feudal lords endanger their state.
*Cáo* (曹) relied on *Qí* (齊) and did not listen to *Sòng* (宋);
*Qí* (齊) attacked *Jīng* (荊), and *Sòng* (宋) destroyed *Cáo* (曹).
*Xíng* (邢) relied on *Wú* (吳) and did not listen to *Qí* (齊);
*Yuè* (越) attacked *Wú* (吳), and *Qí* (齊) destroyed *Xíng* (邢).
*Xǔ* (許) relied on *Jīng* (荊) and did not listen to *Wèi* (魏);
*Jīng* (荊) attacked *Sòng* (宋), and *Wèi* (魏) destroyed *Xǔ* (許).
*Zhèng* (鄭) relied on *Wèi* (魏) and did not listen to *Hán* (韓);
*Wèi* (魏) attacked *Jīng* (荊), and *Hán* (韓) destroyed *Zhèng* (鄭).
Now *Hán* (韓國) is small and relies on a large state;
the ruler is negligent and listens to *Qín* (秦)
and *Wèi* (魏), relying on *Qí* (齊) and *Jīng* (荊) for aid,
but the small state increasingly perishes.
Therefore, relying on others is insufficient to expand territory,
but *Hán* (韓國) does not see this.
*Jīng* (荊) attacked *Wèi* (魏) and reinforced its troops in *Xǔ* (許) and *Yān* (鄢);
*Qí* (齊) attacked *Rèn* (任) and *Hù* (扈) and weakened *Wèi* (魏),
but this was insufficient to preserve *Zhèng* (鄭),
and *Hán* (韓) does not know this.
All of these states did not clarify their laws
to govern their states,
relying on outside forces
to destroy their states.
Therefore, your servant says:
If one is clear about the methods of governance,
then the state, though small,
will be wealthy;
if rewards and punishments are respected and trusted,
then the people, though few,
will be strong.
If rewards and punishments are without measure,
then the state, though large,
will have a weak army,
its land will not be its own,
and its people will not be its own.
Without land or people,
even *Yáo* (堯) and *Shùn* (舜) could not rule as kings,
and the Three Dynasties could not be strong.
If the ruler bestows favors excessively,
and the ministers take profits without merit,
abandoning the laws
to speak of the accomplishments of former kings and enlightened rulers is to
entrust the state to them.
Therefore, your servant says:
It is to desire the accomplishments of the past
to reward the people of the present with the rewards of the past.
The ruler excessively bestows favors in this way,
and the ministers take profits without merit in this way.
When the ruler excessively bestows favors,
then the ministers become opportunistic;
when the ministers take profits without merit,
then merit is not respected.
When those without merit receive rewards,
then the treasury is depleted and the people resentful;
when the treasury is depleted and the people resentful,
then the people will not exert their full effort.
Therefore, using rewards excessively leads to losing the people,
and using punishments excessively
leads to the people not fearing them.
When rewards are insufficient to encourage
and punishments are insufficient to deter,
then the state, though large,
will certainly be in danger.
Therefore, it is said:
Those of small wisdom cannot be entrusted to plan affairs,
and those of small loyalty cannot be entrusted to uphold the law.
The King *Gōng* (恭王) of *Jīng* (荊) fought Duke *Lì* (厲公) of *Jìn* (晉) at *Yānlíng* (鄢陵).
The *Jīng* (荊) army was defeated,
and King *Gōng* (恭王) was wounded.
In the midst of fierce fighting,
the *Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn* (司馬子反) was thirsty and asked for a drink.
His friend Shù Gǔyáng presented him with a cup of wine.
Zǐ Fǎn said,
"Take it away,
this is wine."
Shù Gǔyáng said,
"It is not."
Zǐ Fǎn received it and drank it.
Zǐ Fǎn was a man who loved wine,
he enjoyed it,
and could not keep it from his mouth,
and became drunk and slept.
Gōng Wáng wanted to resume the battle and planned matters,
and sent someone to summon Zǐ Fǎn,
Zǐ Fǎn declined on the grounds of illness.
Gōng Wáng drove to visit him,
entered the tent,
smelled the odor of wine, and returned,
saying,
"In today's battle,
I, myself, was wounded,
and relied on the Sīmǎ,
but the Sīmǎ is like this,
he is destroying the state of Jīng
and does not care for our people.
I have no one to resume the battle with."
He withdrew the army and left,
executing Zǐ Fǎn as a great punishment.
Therefore, it is said:
Shù Gǔyáng's offering of wine,
was not to deliberately harm Zǐ Fǎn,
but truly out of loyalty and love for him,
yet it was precisely enough to kill him.
This is acting with small loyalty
and harming great loyalty.
Therefore, it is said:
Small loyalty
is the enemy of great loyalty.
If small loyalty were to govern the law,
then it would certainly pardon sins out of mutual affection,
this would bring peace to subordinates,
but it would hinder the governance of the people.
When Wèi was clearly establishing laws
and following constitutional decrees,
those with merit were certainly rewarded,
and those with sins were certainly punished,
strongly correcting the world,
and its power extended to the four neighbors;
but when the laws became lax,
and favors were bestowed indiscriminately,
the state declined daily.
When Zhào was clearly establishing state laws
and following the laws of the army,
the people were numerous and the soldiers strong,
expanding its territory to Qí and Yān;
but when the state laws became lax,
and the weak were employed,
the state declined daily.
When Yān was clearly upholding the law
and carefully adjudicating officials,
it extended eastward to the state of Qí,
and southward to the land of Zhōngshān;
but when upholding the law was abandoned,
and official adjudication was not used,
the left and right factions contended,
and arguments followed those below,
then the soldiers became weak, the land diminished,
and the state was controlled by its neighbors and enemies.
Therefore, it is said:
Those who clarify the law are strong,
those who neglect the law are weak.
The strength and weakness are as clear as this,
but the rulers of the world do not do it,
it is fitting that the state should perish.
The saying goes:
"A family with a constant occupation,
though hungry, will not starve;
a state with constant laws,
though in danger, will not perish."
To abandon constant laws and follow private intentions
will cause ministers and subordinates to embellish their intelligence and abilities;
when ministers and subordinates embellish their intelligence and abilities,
then laws and prohibitions will not be established.
This is the path of reckless intentions being practiced,
and the path of governing the state being abandoned.
The way to govern a state
is to eliminate those who harm the law,
then one will not be deluded by intelligence and abilities,
nor falsely led by fame and reputation.
In the past, Shùn sent officials to control the great flood,
he first ordered Yǒu Gōng
and then Shùn killed him;
Yǔ held a court of the lords of the various states at the meeting on Kuàijī,
and the lord of Fángfēng arrived late and Yǔ beheaded him.
From this perspective,
those who preceded the decree were killed,
and those who followed the decree were beheaded,
then in ancient times, prioritizing the decree was highly valued.
Therefore, a mirror held clear is without effort,
and good and evil are accordingly compared;
a balance held straight is without effort,
and lightness and heaviness are accordingly measured.
To shake the mirror
will prevent it from being clear,
to shake the balance
will prevent it from being straight,
this is what is meant by law.
Therefore, the former kings took the Dào as constant
and the law as fundamental.
Those who base their governance on it are respected,
those who base their chaos on it have their names cut off.
All intelligence and understanding,
with a way, it can be carried out,
without a way, it stops.
Therefore, intelligence is a singular path,
it cannot be transmitted to others.
But the Dào and law are complete in every way,
while intelligence often fails.
To suspend a balance and know the level,
to set a compass and know the circle,
this is the way of complete perfection.
An enlightened ruler causes the people to adorn themselves with the reason of the Dào,
therefore they are at ease and have merit.
To abandon the compass and rely on skill,
to abandon the law and rely on wisdom,
is the way to confusion and chaos.
A chaotic ruler causes the people to adorn themselves with wisdom,
not knowing the reason of the Dào,
therefore they labor and have no merit.
To abandon laws and prohibitions and listen to requests and solicitations,
will cause ministers to sell official positions to their superiors,
and seek rewards from their subordinates,
thus profit will be in private hands
and power will be in the hands of the ministers.
Therefore, the people will not have the heart to exert themselves to serve the ruler,
but will strive to establish relationships with those above.
When the people like to interact with those above,
then wealth will flow upwards,
and those with clever words will be employed.
If this is the case,
then those with merit will become fewer and fewer.
Treacherous ministers will advance further
and talented ministers will retreat,
then the ruler will be confused and not know what to do,
and the people will gather but not know what path to take.
This is the error of abandoning laws and prohibitions, delaying rewards for merit, promoting fame and reputation, and listening to requests and solicitations.
All those who corrupt the law
will certainly set up fraudulent pretexts
to gain intimacy,
and will also like to talk about what is rarely found in the world.
This is how tyrannical and chaotic rulers are deluded,
and how wise and capable ministers are encroached upon.
Therefore, if ministers praise the merits of Yī Yǐn and
Guǎn Zhòng,
then they will have the means to defy the law and embellish their wisdom;
if they praise the loyalty of Bǐgān and Zǐ Xū and are killed,
then they will have an excuse to criticize strongly.
If the superiors praise virtue and intelligence,
and the subordinates praise tyranny and chaos,
they cannot be compared,
those like this should be prohibited.
The ruler's establishment of the law is considered correct,
but now many ministers establish their private intelligence
to consider the law as wrong,
they are crooked with their intelligence,
and surpassing the law to establish their intelligence.
Those like this should be prohibited,
this is the way of the ruler.
The way of the enlightened ruler
must be clear about the distinction between public and private,
clarify the legal system,
and eliminate private favors.
That orders must be carried out and
prohibitions must be stopped is the impartiality of the ruler;
to ensure his private matters are executed
and keep faith with friends
so that one cannot be encouraged by reward
or deterred by punishment
is the personal righteousness of a minister.
If personal righteousness is practiced, there will be chaos;
if public righteousness is practiced, there will be order.
Therefore, there is a distinction between public and private.
Ministers have private desires
and public righteousness.
Cultivating oneself to be pure and upright
and acting publicly and correctly,
holding office without personal bias,
is the public righteousness of a minister;
corrupt conduct, indulging desires,
ensuring personal safety and benefiting one's family
are the private desires of a minister.
When an enlightened ruler is above,
then ministers discard private desires
and practice public righteousness;
when a chaotic ruler is above,
then ministers discard public righteousness
and practice private desires.
Therefore, ruler and ministers have different intentions;
the ruler uses schemes to control ministers,
and ministers use schemes to serve the ruler.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is based on calculation.
To harm oneself for the benefit of the state
is not what a minister will do;
to harm the state for the benefit of a minister
is not what a ruler will do.
A minister's concern
is that harming oneself is of no benefit;
a ruler's concern
is that harming the state gains no support.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is one of agreement based on calculation.
As for facing difficulties and being willing to die,
exhausting wisdom and expending effort,
it is done for the sake of the law.
Therefore, the former kings clearly used rewards to encourage it
and severe punishments to deter it.
If rewards and punishments are clear,
the people will give their all;
if the people give their all,
the army will be strong and the ruler respected.
If rewards and punishments are not carefully considered,
the people will seek gain without merit
and hope to escape punishment even when guilty,
and the army will be weak and the ruler humbled.
Therefore, the former kings and wise advisors
exhausted their efforts and expended their wisdom.
Thus it is said:
Public and private must be clearly distinguished,
and laws and prohibitions must be carefully examined;
the former kings knew this.
Virtue (*dé*) is
internal;
gain (*dé*) is
external.
"Superior virtue is not virtue,"
meaning its spirit does not dissipate outwards.
If the spirit does not dissipate outwards,
the body is preserved;
preserving the body is called virtue (*dé*).
Virtue (*dé*) is
gaining oneself.
All virtue (*dé*) is
accumulated through non-action,
and achieved through non-desire;
it is secured through non-thinking
and solidified through non-use.
If one acts and desires,
virtue (*dé*) has no abode;
if virtue (*dé*) has no abode,
it will not be complete.
If one uses and thinks,
it will not be solid;
if it is not solid,
it will have no merit;
if it has no merit,
it departs from virtue (*dé*).
Virtue (*dé*) then becomes non-virtue,
and non-virtue becomes virtue (*dé*).
Therefore, it is said:
"Superior virtue is not virtue;
therefore, it has virtue (*dé*)."
The reason for valuing non-action, non-thinking, and emptiness
is that their intention is unrestrained.
Those without method,
ah!
Therefore, they take non-action, non-thinking, as emptiness.
Those who take non-action, non-thinking, as emptiness
constantly remember emptiness in their intentions,
and are thus constrained by the pursuit of emptiness.
Emptiness
means that one's intention is unrestrained.
To be constrained by the pursuit of emptiness
is not emptiness.
The non-action of emptiness
does not treat non-action as a constant.
Not treating non-action as a constant
is emptiness;
emptiness
results in flourishing virtue (*dé*);
flourishing virtue (*dé*) is called superior virtue.
Therefore, it is said:
"Superior virtue does nothing
and yet there is nothing it does not do."
Benevolence (*rén*)
means that from the center of one's heart, one gladly loves others;
rejoicing in the blessings of others
and hating the misfortunes of others;
it is what the heart cannot help but do,
not seeking reward for it.
Therefore, it is said:
"Superior benevolence does things without a purpose."
Righteousness (*yì*)
refers to the affairs between ruler and ministers,
the differences between father and son, noble and base,
the interactions between intimate friends,
and the distinctions between close and distant, internal and external.
Ministers serving the ruler appropriately,
inferiors cherishing superiors appropriately,
sons serving fathers appropriately,
the base respecting the noble appropriately,
intimate friends assisting each other appropriately,
the close being internal and the distant being external appropriately.
Righteousness (*yì*)
means what is appropriate;
doing what is appropriate.
Therefore, it is said:
"Superior righteousness does things with a purpose."
Ritual (*lǐ*)
is the means of expressing feelings,
the patterned expression of righteousness,
the interaction between ruler and ministers, father and son,
and the means of distinguishing noble and base, virtuous and unworthy.
When the heart harbors something unexpressed,
one hurries forward and bows humbly to make it clear;
when one truly loves but lacks understanding,
one uses eloquent and elaborate words to convey it.
Ritual (*lǐ*)
is the outward adornment used to express what is within.
Therefore, it is said:
Ritual (*lǐ*) is used to express feelings.
When people are moved by external things,
they do not know that they are performing rituals for themselves.
When most people perform rituals (*lǐ*),
it is to honor others,
so it sometimes encourages and sometimes declines.
When a *jūnzǐ* performs rituals (*lǐ*),
it is for his own sake;
because it is for his own sake,
his spirit is considered the highest ritual (*lǐ*);
if the highest ritual (*lǐ*) is spiritual,
the multitude is divided,
and therefore cannot respond;
because they cannot respond,
it is said:
"Superior ritual (*lǐ*) is performed, but no one responds."
Even though the multitude is divided,
the sage's repeated reverence
and exhaustive physical performance of ritual
do not decline.
Therefore, it is said:
"He rolls up his sleeves and continues to practice it."
The Dào accumulates, and accumulation leads to merit;
Dé,
is the merit of the Dào.
Merit has substance, and substance has radiance;
Rén,
is the radiance of Dé.
Radiance has beneficence, and beneficence has actions;
Yì,
is the actions of Rén.
Actions have Lǐ
and Lǐ has adornment;
Lǐ,
is the adornment of Yì.
Therefore, it is said:
"Losing the Dào leads to losing Dé,
losing Dé leads to losing Rén,
losing Rén leads to losing Yì,
losing Yì leads to losing Lǐ."
Lǐ is the outward appearance of emotion,
adornment is the decoration of substance.
The Jūnzǐ values emotion and rejects outward appearance,
loves substance and despises decoration.
Those who rely on outward appearance to judge emotion,
their emotions are evil;
those who need adornment to discuss substance,
their substance is declining.
How can this be argued?
The Héshì Jade
is not adorned with five colors,
the Zhōu Hóu Pearl
is not adorned with silver and yellow.
Their substance is supremely beautiful,
things are not enough to adorn them.
Things that rely on adornment to be valued,
their substance is not beautiful.
Therefore, between father and son,
their Lǐ is simple and not explicit,
therefore it is said
that Lǐ is weak.
All things do not prosper together,
Yīn and Yáng are like this;
principles compete and yield,
authority and virtue are like this,
those with deep substance have shallow appearances,
the Lǐ between father and son is like this.
From this perspective,
abundant Lǐ,
shows a decline of genuine heart.
Therefore, those who perform Lǐ,
deal with the genuine hearts of all people,
the way common people perform Lǐ,
if people respond, they are lightly joyful,
if they do not respond, they blame and resent.
Now, those who perform Lǐ
deal with the genuine hearts of all people,
and add to it the division of mutual blame,
how can there be no strife?
With strife comes chaos,
therefore, it is said:
"Lǐ,
is the weakening of loyalty and trust,
and the beginning of chaos."
To act before things, to move before principles, is called foresight.
Foresight,
is to forget intention and measure without cause.
How can this be argued?
Zhān Hé was sitting,
his disciples attending,
a cow bellowed outside the door.
A disciple said:
"It is a black cow with a white forehead."
Zhān Hé said:
"Yes,
it is a black cow,
but the white is on its horns."
He sent someone to look,
and indeed it was a black cow with its horns wrapped in cloth.
Using Master Zhān's skill,
to indulge the hearts of the multitude,
is utterly flowery.
Therefore, it is said:
"It is the flower of the Dào."
Try releasing Master Zhān's discernment,
and let a five-foot-tall foolish child look at it,
they would also know it is a black cow
with its horns wrapped in cloth.
Therefore, with Master Zhān's discernment,
tormenting the heart and injuring the spirit,
and then achieving the same result as a five-foot-tall foolish child,
therefore, it is said
"It is the beginning of foolishness."
Therefore, it is said:
"Foresight,
is the flower of the Dào,
and the beginning of foolishness."
That which is called
"Dà Zhàngfū"
refers to the greatness of his wisdom.
That which is called
"abiding in substance, not in appearance"
is valuing reality
and rejecting outward courtesy.
That which is called
"abiding in reality, not in flourish"
is necessarily following principles and not taking shortcuts.
That which is called
"rejecting that and taking this"
is rejecting shortcuts based on appearances,
and taking following principles and valuing reality.
Therefore, it is said:
"Rejecting that and taking this."
When people have misfortune,
their hearts fear,
when hearts fear,
actions become upright,
when actions are upright,
thoughts become mature,
when thoughts are mature,
they grasp the principles of things,
when actions are upright,
there are no disasters,
when there are no disasters,
they exhaust their natural lifespan;
when they grasp the principles of things,
they are bound to succeed.
Exhausting the natural lifespan
leads to wholeness and longevity;
bound to succeed
leads to wealth and honor.
Wholeness, longevity, wealth, and honor are called fortune.
And fortune originates from having misfortune,
therefore, it is said:
"Misfortune is what fortune leans upon."
To complete its merit.
When people have fortune,
wealth and honor arrive,
when wealth and honor arrive,
clothing and food become luxurious,
when clothing and food are luxurious,
a proud heart arises,
when a proud heart arises,
actions become perverse and movements abandon principles.
When actions are perverse,
the body dies young,
when movements abandon principles,
there is no success.
Having the difficulty of death and premature death internally,
and lacking the name of success externally,
is a great disaster.
And disaster originates from having fortune,
therefore, it is said:
"Fortune is where disaster lies hidden."
Those who follow principles in their endeavors,
there is nothing they cannot accomplish.
Those who can accomplish everything,
can achieve the supreme position of the Son of Heaven,
and can easily obtain the rewards and stipends of ministers and generals.
Those who abandon principles and act recklessly,
even if they have the position and honor of the Son of Heaven and lords above,
and have the wealth of Ǐ Dùn,
Táo Zhū,
and Bǔ Zhù below,
will still lose their people
and lose their wealth.
Common people lightly abandon principles
and easily act recklessly,
not knowing the depth and magnitude of their misfortune and fortune
and that the Dào is as broad and distant as this,
therefore, instruct people, saying:
"Who knows its limit?"
Everyone desires wealth, honor, and a full lifespan,
yet no one can escape the misfortune of poverty, lowliness, death, and premature demise.
If one desires wealth, honor, and a full lifespan,
but is now in poverty, lowliness, death, and premature demise,
it means they cannot reach their desired destination.
To lose the way to one's desired destination and wander aimlessly is called being lost.
If lost, one cannot reach their desired destination.
That the masses cannot reach their desired destination,
therefore it is said:
"They are lost."
That the masses cannot reach their desired destination
has been the case since the separation of Heaven and Earth until now.
Therefore it is said:
"The people's bewilderment
has indeed been long-standing."
What is meant by *fāng* (方, square, upright) is
that the inside and outside correspond,
and that words and actions match.
What is meant by *lián* (廉, incorruptible, virtuous) is
regarding life and death as destiny,
and valuing material possessions lightly.
What is meant by *zhí* (直, straight, honest) is
that righteousness must be just and fair,
and the public mind must be impartial and unbiased.
What is meant by *guāng* (光, bright, glorious) is
having high official rank and noble status,
and wearing magnificent clothing and furs.
Now, a virtuous person,
even if trusted and obeyed internally and externally,
will not be ruined by slander and defamation;
even if they value integrity over life and treat wealth lightly,
they will not be insulted for dismissing greed and ashamed of being greedy;
even if their righteousness is upright and impartial,
they will not abandon the wicked or condone private wrongdoing;
even if they possess high status and beautiful clothes,
they will not boast to the lowly or deceive the poor.
Why is this so?
If those who have lost their way
are willing to listen, learn, inquire, and understand,
they will not become lost.
That the masses desire success
but instead fail
is because they do not know the principles of Dao (道, the Way) and *lǐ* (理, principle),
and are unwilling to inquire and learn and listen to the capable.
The masses are unwilling to inquire, learn,
and listen to the capable,
and when the sages forcibly impose their misfortunes and failures upon them,
they resent it.
The masses are many, and the sages are few.
That the few cannot overcome the many
is a matter of numbers.
Now, to act in a way that makes oneself an enemy of the world
is not the way to preserve oneself and live long.
Therefore, one must act in accordance with established principles
and conduct oneself accordingly.
Therefore, it is said:
"Be *fāng* (方, square, upright) but not cutting,
be *lián* (廉, incorruptible, virtuous) but not sharp,
be *zhí* (直, straight, honest) but not unrestrained,
be *guāng* (光, bright, glorious) but not dazzling."
Intelligence and wisdom
are from Heaven;
movement, stillness, thought, and deliberation
are from humans.
Humans
rely on the brightness of Heaven to see,
depend on the hearing of Heaven to listen,
and entrust themselves to the wisdom of Heaven to think and deliberate.
Therefore, if one strains their vision,
their eyes will become dim;
if one strains their hearing,
their ears will become deaf;
if one thinks and deliberates excessively,
their knowledge and understanding will be disordered.
If the eyes are dim,
one cannot distinguish between black and white;
if the ears are deaf,
one cannot distinguish between clear and turbid sounds;
if knowledge and understanding are disordered,
one cannot discern the place of gain and loss.
If the eyes cannot distinguish between black and white colors,
it is called blindness;
if the ears cannot distinguish between clear and turbid sounds,
it is called deafness;
if the mind cannot discern the place of gain and loss,
it is called madness.
The blind
cannot avoid dangers in broad daylight;
the deaf
cannot know the harm of thunder and lightning;
the mad
cannot escape the calamities of human laws.
What the *shū* (書, book) calls "governing people"
regulating the rhythm of movement and stillness
and economizing on the expenditure of thought and deliberation.
What it calls
"serving Heaven"
is not exhausting the power of intelligence
and not fully utilizing the function of knowledge.
If one exhausts and fully utilizes them,
one expends too much spirit.
If one expends too much spirit,
the calamities of blindness, deafness, perversity, and madness will arrive.
Therefore, one must be frugal with them.
To be frugal with them
is to cherish one's spirit
and be frugal with one's knowledge.
Therefore, it is said:
"In governing people and serving Heaven, nothing is better than frugality."
The masses use their spirit restlessly,
and if restless, they expend much;
expending much is called extravagance.
The sages use their spirit calmly,
and if calm, they expend little;
expending little is called frugality.
Frugality is called a skill,
born from Dao (道, the Way) and *lǐ* (理, principle).
To be able to be frugal
is to follow Dao (道, the Way)
and submit to *lǐ* (理, principle).
The masses, departing from misfortune
and falling into calamity,
still do not know to retreat
and do not submit to Dao (道, the Way) and *lǐ* (理, principle).
The sages, even without seeing the form of misfortune,
empty themselves and submit to Dao (道, the Way) and *lǐ* (理, principle),
which is called early submission.
Therefore, it is said:
"That which is called frugality
is to submit early."
Those who know how to govern people
have quiet thoughts;
those who know how to serve Heaven
have empty apertures.
If thoughts are quiet,
virtue does not depart;
if the apertures are empty,
harmonious qi (氣, vital energy) enters daily.
Therefore, it is said:
"Accumulate virtue repeatedly."
To be able to cause old virtue not to depart
and new harmonious qi (氣, vital energy) to arrive daily
is to submit early.
Therefore, it is said:
"Early submission
is called repeatedly accumulating virtue."
After accumulating virtue, the spirit is quiet;
after the spirit is quiet, harmony is abundant;
after harmony is abundant, plans succeed;
after plans succeed, one can control all things.
Being able to control all things
means battles are easily won;
battles being easily won
means discussions will certainly surpass the world.
Discussions will certainly surpass the world;
therefore, it is said:
"There is nothing that cannot be overcome."
Being invincible originates from repeatedly accumulating virtue;
therefore, it is said:
"Repeatedly accumulating virtue
leads to invincibility."
Winning battles easily allows one to annex the world;
discussions certainly surpassing the world allow one to gain the support of the people.
Advancing to annex the world
and retreating to gain the support of the people,
the method is so far-reaching
that the masses cannot see its origin and end.
Since the masses cannot see its origin and end,
they do not know its limit.
Therefore, it is said:
"Being invincible
means that no one knows its limit."
Anyone who possesses a state and then loses it,
or possesses a body and then brings calamity upon it,
cannot be said to be capable of possessing their state,
or capable of preserving their body.
If one is capable of possessing their state,
they must be capable of securing their altars of soil and grain;
if one is capable of preserving their body,
they must be capable of completing their natural lifespan.
Only then can they be said to be capable of possessing their state,
and capable of preserving their body.
One who is capable of possessing their state
and preserving their body
must embody the Dào.
Embodying the Dào
leads to profound wisdom;
profound wisdom
leads to far-reaching understanding;
and far-reaching understanding
means that the multitude cannot see its limit.
Only one who can make others unable to see the limit of their actions,
one whose actions have no perceivable limit,
can preserve their body
and possess their state.
Therefore, it is said:
"No one knows its limit.
No one knows its limit,
and therefore one can possess the state."
This is what is meant by
"the mother of the state."
"Mother"
refers to the Dào.
The Dào
gives rise to the methods by which the state is possessed;
these methods of possessing the state
are why it is called "the mother of the state."
If the Dào
is used to engage with the world,
its establishment of life will be long-lasting,
and its maintenance of position will be enduring.
Therefore, it is said:
"The mother of the state
can bring longevity."
Trees have both spreading roots
and straight roots.
Straight roots
are what books call "dǐ."
"Dǐ"
is what allows the tree to establish life.
Spreading roots
are what allow the tree to sustain life.
Virtue is what allows a person to establish life;
Lù
is what allows a person to sustain life.
Now, if one is established upon principle,
the maintenance of their Lù
will be long-lasting.
Therefore, it is said:
"Deepen its roots."
If one embodies the Dào,
their daily growth will be long-lasting.
Therefore, it is said:
"Strengthen its dǐ."
If the dǐ is strong,
growth will be sustained;
if the roots are deep,
vision will be enduring.
Therefore, it is said:
"Deepen its roots,
strengthen its dǐ:
this is the way to long life and enduring vision."
If artisans frequently change their trades,
they will lose their skill;
if craftsmen frequently relocate,
they will lose their work.
If one person's work is reduced by half a day,
the loss after ten days is equivalent to five people's labor.
If ten thousand people's work is reduced by half a day,
the loss after ten days is equivalent to the labor of fifty thousand people.
Therefore, if those who frequently change their trades
are numerous,
the loss will be even greater.
Whenever laws and decrees are changed,
benefits and harms are altered;
when benefits and harms are altered,
the people's occupations change.
Changing occupations is what is meant by changing trades.
Therefore, viewed through the lens of principle,
managing a large group of people with frequent changes
results in little success;
storing a large vessel with frequent relocations
results in much damage;
cooking a small fish with frequent stirring
spoils its flavor;
and governing a large state with frequent changes in laws
causes the people suffering.
Therefore, enlightened rulers value tranquility
and do not frequently change laws.
Therefore, it is said:
"Governing a large state is like cooking a small fish."
When people are ill, they value doctors;
when they encounter misfortune, they fear ghosts.
If a sage is above,
the people will have few desires;
if the people have few desires,
their Qi and blood will be regulated, and their actions will be orderly;
orderly actions will lead to few disasters.
If one has no internal ailments such as boils, sores, or hemorrhoids,
and no external calamities such as criminal punishments or executions,
they will lightly regard ghosts.
Therefore, it is said:
"If the world is governed by the Dào,
the spirits will not be divine."
The people of a well-governed world
do not harm each other with ghosts and spirits.
Therefore, it is said:
"It is not that the spirits are not divine,
but that the spirits do not harm people."
Ghosts harming people
means that ghosts cause people to fall ill;
people expelling and eliminating ghosts
means that people harm ghosts.
People violating laws and decrees
means that the people harm their superiors;
superiors punishing the people with executions
means that superiors harm the people.
If the people do not violate the law,
then superiors will not carry out punishments;
superiors not carrying out punishments
means that superiors do not harm the people.
Therefore, it is said:
"Sages also do not harm the people."
Superiors do not harm the people,
and the people do not harm the spirits,
therefore it is said:
"Neither harms the other."
If the people do not dare to violate the law,
then superiors will not need to use internal punishments,
and will not be concerned with profiting from their industries externally.
If superiors do not need to use internal punishments,
and are not concerned with profiting from their industries externally,
then the people will flourish.
If the people flourish and their savings are abundant,
this flourishing and abundant saving
is called having virtue.
All that is called "suì"
is when the soul and spirit depart, and the mental spirit is disordered;
if the mental spirit is disordered, there is no virtue.
If ghosts do not "suì" people,
then the soul and spirit do not depart;
if the soul and spirit do not depart,
then the mental spirit is not disordered;
a mental spirit that is not disordered is called having virtue.
If superiors have abundant savings,
and ghosts do not disorder their mental spirit,
then all virtue resides in the people.
Therefore, it is said:
"If neither harms the other,
then virtue will mutually return."
This means that virtue above and below is mutually abundant
and both return to the people.
An enlightened ruler
has no external grievances or hostilities with neighboring enemies,
and internally bestows virtuous favor upon the people.
To have no external grievances or hostilities with neighboring enemies
means that in dealings with the feudal lords, they outwardly maintain propriety and righteousness.
To internally bestow virtuous favor upon the people
means that in governing the people, they strive for the essentials.
To treat the feudal lords with propriety and righteousness
means that wars rarely arise;
to govern the people by striving for the essentials
means that extravagance and waste cease.
In general, horses are greatly used because
externally they supply armor and weapons
and internally they provide for excessive extravagance.
Now, a ruler who possesses the Dao
rarely uses armor and weapons externally,
and internally forbids excessive extravagance.
The ruler does not employ horses in battles to pursue fleeing enemies,
and the people do not use horses to travel far for licentious activities
or to exchange goods.
All strength is focused on agriculture,
and focusing strength on agriculture
necessarily leads to fertilization and irrigation.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the world possesses the Dao,
horses are turned back to fertilize the fields."
When the ruler of men lacks the Dao,
he is tyrannical to his people internally
and externally aggresses against his neighboring countries.
Internal tyranny
leads to the destruction of the people's livelihood,
and external aggression
leads to frequent wars.
The destruction of the people's livelihood
leads to a decrease in livestock,
and frequent wars
lead to the depletion of soldiers.
A decrease in livestock
leads to a shortage of warhorses,
and the depletion of soldiers
leads to a perilous military situation.
A shortage of warhorses
leads to the use of female horses,
and a perilous military situation
leads to the enslavement of close officials.
Horses
are of great importance to the military;
the "suburbs"
are referred to because they are nearby.
Now, the means to supply the military are derived from female horses and close officials.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the world lacks the Dao,
warhorses are born in the suburbs."
When people have desires,
their plans become chaotic;
when their plans become chaotic,
their desires intensify;
when their desires intensify,
evil intentions prevail;
when evil intentions prevail,
the principles of affairs are abandoned;
when the principles of affairs are abandoned,
disasters arise.
From this perspective,
disasters arise from evil intentions,
and evil intentions are induced by that which is desirable.
Things that are desirable,
if pursued, teach good people to be treacherous,
and if abandoned, cause good people to suffer misfortune.
When treachery arises,
it encroaches upon the weak ruler;
when misfortune arrives,
the people suffer great harm.
Thus, that which is desirable
encroaches upon the weak ruler above and harms the people below.
To encroach upon the weak ruler above and harm the people below
is a great crime.
Therefore, it is said:
"No disaster is greater than that which is desirable."
Therefore, the sage does not indulge in the five colors
nor become excessive in sounds and music;
an enlightened ruler despises playthings and rejects extravagance and beauty.
Humans lack fur or feathers;
if they do not wear clothes, they cannot withstand the cold.
They do not belong to the heavens above
nor are they attached to the earth below;
they depend on their stomach and intestines as their foundation,
and if they do not eat, they cannot live.
Therefore, they cannot avoid having a desire for gain.
If the desire for gain is not eliminated,
it becomes a source of worry for the self.
Therefore, the sage has enough clothing to withstand the cold
and enough food to fill his emptiness,
and thus he has no worries.
The common people are not like this;
even if they are great as feudal lords
or possess the remaining wealth of a thousand gold coins,
their worries about acquiring more are not eliminated.
Convicts in penal servitude can be released,
those sentenced to death can sometimes be spared,
but the worries of those who do not know contentment are never resolved in their lifetime.
Therefore, it is said:
"No disaster is greater than not knowing contentment."
Therefore, the desire for gain is greater than worry;
worry causes illness to arise;
when illness arises, wisdom declines;
when wisdom declines,
one loses measure and judgment;
when one loses measure and judgment,
one acts recklessly;
when one acts recklessly,
disasters and harm arrive.
When disasters and harm arrive
and illness afflicts one internally,
when illness afflicts one internally,
pain and disaster press upon one externally;
when pain and disaster press upon one externally,
bitter pain is mixed within the stomach and intestines.
When bitter pain is mixed within the stomach and intestines,
the harm to the person is severe.
When it is severe, one retreats and blames oneself,
and the retreat and self-blame arises from the desire for gain.
Therefore, it is said:
"No blame is more severe than that arising from the desire for gain."
The Dao is
the inherent nature of all things
and the basis for understanding all principles.
Principle is
the pattern by which things are formed;
the Dao is
that by which all things are brought into being.
Therefore, it is said:
"The Dao
is that which governs principle."
Things have principles
that cannot be violated;
things have principles
that cannot be violated,
therefore principle is the means to regulate things.
All things have different principles,
but the Dao exhaustively examines the principles of all things,
therefore it cannot but transform;
since it cannot but transform,
it has no constant operation.
Because it has no constant operation,
life and death, qi and nature depend on it;
all wisdom is weighed by it;
all affairs rise and fall because of it.
Heaven obtains it and becomes high,
Earth obtains it and becomes sheltering,
the Wéi Dǒu obtains it and completes its majesty,
the sun and moon obtain it and maintain their light,
the Five Constants obtain it and maintain their positions,
the constellations obtain it and regulate their movements,
the four seasons obtain it and control their changing qi,
Xuānyuán obtains it and dominates the four directions,
Chìsōng obtains it and unites with Heaven and Earth,
and sages obtain it and complete their writings.
The Dao
is wise with Yáo and Shùn,
mad with Jiē Yú,
destroyed with Jié and Zhòu,
and prospered with Tāng and Wǔ.
If one thinks it is near,
it roams to the four poles;
if one thinks it is far,
it is always at our side;
if one thinks it is dark,
its light is brilliant;
if one thinks it is bright,
its substance is dim.
Yet it completes the achievements of Heaven and Earth,
harmonizes and transforms thunder and lightning,
and the things within the universe
rely on it to be completed.
In general, the nature of the Dao
is that it is neither constrained nor shaped;
it is gentle and yielding with the times
and corresponds with principle.
All things obtain it and die,
and obtain it and live;
all affairs obtain it and fail,
and obtain it and succeed.
The Dào is like water:
those who are drowning drink too much of it and die,
while those who are thirsty drink just the right amount and live.
It is like swords and halberds:
fools use them to indulge their anger and bring disaster upon themselves,
while sages use them to punish violence and achieve success.
Therefore, one can gain it and die,
gain it and live,
gain it and fail,
gain it and succeed.
People rarely see a living elephant,
but they obtain the bones of a dead elephant,
and based on a drawing, they imagine its living form.
Therefore, what people imagine
is all called "xiàng" (象, image).
Now, although the Dào cannot be heard or seen,
the sage grasps its visible effects
to infer its form,
therefore it is said:
"A shape without shape,
an image without substance."
All principles ("lǐ" 理) are
divisions of square and round, short and long,
coarse and fine, hard and brittle.
Therefore, only after principles are defined can the Dào be attained.
Thus, defined principles have existence and extinction,
have life and death,
have flourishing and decline.
That a thing exists and then ceases to exist,
now dies, now lives,
first flourishes and then declines,
cannot be called constant.
Only that which is born together with the separation of Heaven and Earth,
and does not die or decline until the dissolution of Heaven and Earth, is called "constant."
And that which is constant
is unchangeable,
without fixed principles.
Being without fixed principles,
it is not located in a constant place,
therefore it cannot be spoken of.
The sage observes its profound emptiness,
and utilizes its all-encompassing movement,
forcefully naming it
"Dào,"
and thus it can be discussed.
Therefore it is said:
"The Dào that can be spoken of
is not the constant Dào."
People begin with birth and end with death.
Beginning is called exiting,
ending is called entering.
Therefore it is said:
"Exiting birth, entering death."
The human body has three hundred and sixty joints,
four limbs and nine orifices,
these are its major components.
The four limbs and nine orifices, these thirteen,
the movements and stillness of these thirteen
all belong to life.
Belonging is called a retinue,
therefore it is said:
"The retinue of life consists of thirteen."
Upon death,
these thirteen components all return
and belong to death,
the retinue of death also consists of thirteen.
Therefore it is said:
"The retinue of life is thirteen,
the retinue of death is thirteen."
All people live their lives,
and the living are naturally active,
when activity is exhausted, there is loss;
but activity does not cease,
so loss is unceasing.
Unceasing loss
results in the exhaustion of life,
the exhaustion of life is called death,
then these thirteen components
all go to the realm of death.
Therefore it is said:
"The people's living,
living and moving,
all move towards the realm of death,
towards thirteen."
Therefore, the sage cherishes essence and spirit
and values dwelling in stillness.
Not cherishing essence and spirit
and not valuing dwelling in stillness,
this is a greater harm than the rhinoceros and tiger.
The rhinoceros and tiger have territories,
activity and stillness have times.
Avoid their territories,
be mindful of their times,
then one can avoid the harm of the rhinoceros and tiger.
People only know that the rhinoceros and tiger have claws and horns,
but do not know that all things have claws and horns,
and thus cannot avoid the harm of all things.
How can we discuss this?
When seasonal rains fall,
and the open wilderness is calm,
yet one invades the mountains and rivers in the dusk and dawn,
then the claws and horns of wind and dew will harm them.
Serving superiors disloyally,
lightly violating prohibitions and orders,
then the claws and horns of punishments and laws will harm them.
Living in a community without restraint,
having boundless likes and dislikes,
then the claws and horns of disputes and fights will harm them.
Having unlimited desires,
and immoderate activity and stillness,
then the claws and horns of carbuncles and sores will harm them.
Liking to use one's private wisdom and abandoning reason,
then the claws and horns of nets and snares will harm them.
The rhinoceros and tiger have territories,
and the myriad harms have origins.
Avoid their territories,
block their origins,
then one can avoid all harms.
All weapons and armor
are for preparing against harm.
Those who value life
even if they enter the army,
have no mind of anger and contention.
Having no mind of anger and contention,
then there is no use for preparing against harm.
This does not only refer to armies in the wilderness.
The sage's wandering in the world
has no intention to harm others,
then certainly no one will harm them.
If no one harms them,
then there is no need to prepare against others.
Therefore it is said:
"Traveling on land, one does not encounter rhinoceroses or tigers."
Entering the mountains,
one does not rely on preparations to guard against harm,
therefore it is said:
"Entering the army, one does not prepare armor and weapons."
Being far from all harms,
therefore it is said:
"The rhinoceros has nowhere to thrust its horn,
the tiger has nowhere to place its claws,
the weapon has nowhere to accommodate its blade."
Not preparing defenses and yet certainly having no harm,
this is the principle of Heaven and Earth.
Embodying the Dào of Heaven and Earth,
therefore it is said:
"There is no place of death."
Moving without a place of death,
this is called "skillful nurturing of life."
One who loves a child is kind to the child,
one who values life is kind to the body,
one who values achievement is kind to the task.
A kind mother towards her weak child
strives to bring about its good fortune;
striving to bring about its good fortune,
then she removes its misfortunes;
removing its misfortunes,
then her thoughts and considerations are thorough;
when her thoughts and considerations are thorough,
then she grasps the principles of things;
grasping the principles of things,
then she will surely succeed;
surely succeeding,
then her actions are without doubt,
being without doubt is called courage.
The sage's approach to all matters
is entirely like a kind mother's concern for her weak child,
therefore he sees the path that must be followed.
Seeing the path that must be followed is called clarity,
his engagement in affairs is also without doubt,
being without doubt is called courage.
Kindness arises from apprehension,
therefore it is said:
"Kindness,
therefore enables courage."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"If the freezing in winter is not firm,
then the growth of grasses and trees in spring and summer
will not be lush."
Heaven and Earth cannot always be extravagant and wasteful,
how much less so can humans?
Therefore, all things must have periods of flourishing and decline,
all affairs must have periods of tension and relaxation,
a state must have both civil and military aspects,
and official governance must have both rewards and punishments.
Therefore, a wise person uses their wealth sparingly,
and their family becomes rich;
a sage cherishes their spirit,
and their essence becomes abundant;
a ruler values their soldiers in battle,
and the population becomes numerous;
with a numerous population,
the state expands.
Therefore, it is said:
"Frugality,
therefore enables expansion."
All things that have form are easy to measure,
easy to cut.
How can we discuss this?
Having form
implies having short and long,
having short and long
implies having small and large,
having small and large
implies having square and round;
having square and round
implies having hard and brittle;
having hard and brittle
implies having light and heavy;
having light and heavy
implies having white and black.
Short and long, small and large, square and round, hard and brittle,
light and heavy, white and black are called principles;
when the principles are established, things are easy to cut.
Therefore, discussing in the public court before speaking
establishes truth, 〓#
