and a clumsy craftsman follow compasses, rulers, and measurements,
then nothing will be missed.
The ruler of men
is able to abandon what the wise and clever cannot do,
and uphold what the mediocre and clumsy cannot lose,
then human effort is exhausted
and achievements are established.
An enlightened ruler establishes rewards that can be achieved
and sets up punishments that can be avoided.
Therefore, the wise are encouraged by rewards
and do not see the disaster of Zǐ Xū 子胥,
the unworthy commit minor crimes
and do not see Ǒu 傴 having his back cut open,
the blind stay on level ground
and do not encounter deep ravines,
the foolish remain quiet
and do not fall into danger and peril.
In this way,
the kindness between those above and those below is solidified.
The ancients said:
"Their hearts are difficult to know,
and their joys and angers are difficult to hit."
Therefore, signals are used to guide the eyes,
drums are used to speak to the ears,
and laws are used to teach the heart.
If the ruler of men abandons these three easy methods
and acts according to his own inscrutable heart,
then
anger will accumulate above
and resentment will accumulate below.
To use accumulated anger to control accumulated resentment
is to be in double danger.
The signals of an enlightened ruler are easy to see,
so regulations are established;
their teachings are easy to understand,
so words are used;
their laws are easy to follow,
so orders are carried out.
When these three are established
and those above have no selfish intentions,
then those below can follow the law and govern,
moving according to signals,
cutting according to the plumb line,
and sewing according to the awl.
In this way,
those above have no venom of personal authority,
and those below have no punishment for foolishness or clumsiness.
Therefore, those above reside in clarity and have little anger,
and those below are loyal and have few crimes.
It is said:
"To undertake affairs without worry
is something even Yáo 堯 could not do."
Yet the world has never been without affairs.
A ruler of men does not lightly grant titles and stipends,
nor easily give wealth and honor,
for this cannot save a state in danger.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler encourages integrity and shame
and recruits benevolence and righteousness.
In the past, Jiè Zǐtuī 介子推 had no title or stipend,
yet righteously followed Duke Wén 文公,
unwilling to indulge his appetite
and benevolently cutting off his own flesh;
therefore, the ruler cherished his virtue
and recorded his name in books and pictures.
A ruler delights in making people exert their strength publicly,
and suffers from having his authority usurped privately.
A subject feels secure in receiving office based on ability,
and suffers from being burdened with conflicting responsibilities.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler removes what subjects suffer from
and establishes what the ruler delights in.
No benefit for those above and those below
is greater than this.
Failing to investigate matters within one's private affairs,
lightly considering important matters,
severely punishing minor offenses,
holding grudges over trivial faults for a long time,
promoting deceitful and opportunistic pleasures,
and frequently pursuing misfortune with virtue,
is like cutting off a hand and replacing it with jade;
therefore, the world has troubles of changing one's person.
If a ruler establishes difficult tasks
and is not held accountable for failures,
then private resentments arise;
if a subject loses their strengths
and is given tasks difficult to fulfill,
then hidden resentments accumulate.
Labor and hardship are not consoled,
and worry and grief are not pitied;
when happy, one praises petty people,
and both the virtuous and unworthy are rewarded;
when angry, one destroys gentlemen,
causing Bó Yí 伯夷 and Dào Zhí 盜跖 to be disgraced together;
therefore, subjects rebel against their rulers.
If one makes the King of Yān 燕 inwardly hate his own people
and outwardly love the people of Lǔ 魯,
then Yān 燕 will not be utilized and Lǔ 魯 will not be attached.
If the people see hatred,
they will not exert their full strength and devote themselves to their duties;
if Lǔ 魯 sees affection,
they will not abandon their lives
and be close to another ruler.
In this way,
subjects become sources of internal strife,
and the ruler stands alone.
To use subjects who are sources of internal strife
to serve a ruler who stands alone
is called danger.
If one abandons the target and shoots wildly,
even if one hits the target, it is not skillful;
if one abandons the laws and regulations and rages wildly,
even if one kills
treacherous people, they will not be afraid.
If a crime is born from A,
and misfortune is attributed to B,
then hidden resentment will accumulate.
Therefore, in a supremely well-governed state,
there are rewards and punishments but no joy or anger.
Therefore, the sage is extremely strict with punishments,
yet his death is without sting or poison,
and thus treacherous people submit.
If an arrow hits the target,
and rewards and punishments are appropriate,
then Yáo 堯 will be reborn,
and Yì 羿 will be re-established.
In this way,
those above will not have the troubles of Yīn 殷 and Xià 夏,
and those below will not have the disasters of Bǐ Gān 比干,
the ruler will sleep soundly
and the subjects will enjoy their work,
the Way will cover heaven and earth,
and virtue will reach myriad generations.
If a ruler does not seal the cracks of internal strife
but labors on painting and plastering,
heavy rain and strong winds will surely destroy it.
Not removing the troubles close to the eyebrows,
but admiring the deaths of Bēn 賁 and Yù 育,
not being careful about troubles within the walls,
but fortifying the golden city in distant borders,
not using the plans of wise men nearby,
but forming alliances with states of ten thousand chariots from a thousand miles away,
once a whirlwind arises,
then Bēn 賁 and Yù 育 will not be able to save,
and foreign alliances will not be able to arrive;
no disaster is greater than this.
In the present age,
those who faithfully plan for the ruler
will certainly not make the King of Yān 燕 love the people of Lǔ 魯,
not make the present age admire the wise men of the past,
not think of using the people of Yuè 越
to save those drowning in the Central States.
In this way,
those above and those below will be close,
internal achievements will be established,
and external reputation will be accomplished.
The reasons why enlightened rulers establish merit
and achieve fame are fourfold:
first, opportune timing (tiānshí);
second, the will of the people (rénxīn);
third, skills and abilities (jìnéng);
fourth, power and position (shìwèi).
Without opportune timing (tiānshí),
even ten Yáos could not produce a single ear of grain in winter;
against the will of the people (rénxīn),
even Bēn and Yù could not fully exert human effort.
Therefore, having opportune timing (tiānshí),
things grow naturally without effort;
having the will of the people (rénxīn),
people encourage each other without urging;
relying on skills and abilities (jìnéng),
things become fast without rushing;
having power and position (shìwèi),
fame is achieved without pushing forward.
It is like the flow of water,
like the floating of a boat.
Adhering to the way of nature,
implementing limitless orders,
hence the saying of an enlightened ruler.
If one has talent but lacks power,
even the wise cannot control the unworthy.
Therefore, placing a foot-long timber on a high mountain,
it overlooks a thousand-fathom ravine;
it is not that the timber is long,
but that its position is high.
Jié, as the Son of Heaven,
could control the world;
it was not because he was wise,
but because his power was great.
Yáo, as a commoner,
could not correct three households;
it was not because he was unworthy,
but because his position was low.
A thousand *jūn* float with a boat,
a *zīzhū* sinks without a boat;
it is not that a thousand *jūn* are light or a *zīzhū* is heavy,
but the presence or absence of power (shì).
Therefore, the short overlook the tall by position,
and the unworthy control the worthy by power (shì).
The ruler of men
has the world united to support him,
so he is secure;
has the multitude of minds united to establish him,
so he is revered.
The subjects guard their strengths
and exhaust their abilities,
so they are loyal.
When a revered ruler governs loyal subjects,
lasting joy is produced
and fame is achieved.
Fame and reality support each other to succeed,
form and shadow correspond to stand;
therefore, subjects and rulers share the same desires but have different responsibilities.
The trouble of the ruler lies in having no response
hence the saying:
"One hand clapping alone,
though fast, makes no sound."
The worry of the subjects lies in not being unified;
hence the saying:
"The right hand draws a circle,
the left hand draws a square,
neither can be accomplished."
Therefore it is said:
"In a well-governed state,
the ruler is like a drumstick (fú),
the ministers are like a drum (gǔ),
skills are like a cart (chē),
affairs are like a horse (mǎ)."
Therefore, when people have surplus energy, they respond easily,
and when skills have surplus dexterity, they are convenient for affairs.
Those who establish merit lack strength,
those who are close lack trust,
those who achieve fame lack power (shì).
If those who are near are not intimate,
and those who are far are not allied,
then the name does not match the reality.
If a sage has the virtue of Yáo and Shùn,
and the conduct of Bó Yí,
but his position is not recorded in the world,
then his merit will not be established
and his fame will not be achieved.
Therefore, those of old who could achieve merit and fame
had the multitude assist them with strength,
the near allied with them to succeed,
the distant praised them with fame,
and the honored supported them with power (shì).
Because of this,
the merit of Tài Shān
stands long in the state,
and the fame of the sun and moon
lasts long in heaven and earth.
This is why Yáo faced south and guarded his fame,
and Shùn faced north and devoted himself to his achievements.
Those of old who fully grasped the grand scheme
looked to the heavens and the earth,
observed the rivers and seas,
followed the mountains and valleys,
where the sun and moon shine,
where the four seasons proceed,
where clouds spread and wind moves;
they did not burden their hearts with wisdom,
nor burden themselves with selfishness;
they entrusted order and chaos to laws and techniques (fǎshù),
they entrusted right and wrong to rewards and punishments,
they attributed lightness and weight to weights and measures (quánhéng);
they did not go against the principles of heaven,
nor harm emotions and nature;
they did not blow the hair to find small flaws,
nor wash away grime to observe the difficult to know;
they did not pull outside the string,
nor push inside the string;
they were not hasty outside the law,
nor were they lenient inside the law;
they guarded established principles,
and followed nature;
misfortune and fortune arise from the Dao and the law,
and do not come from love and hate;
responsibility for honor and disgrace lies with oneself,
and not with others.
Therefore, in an era of utmost peace,
the law is like morning dew,
pure and unscattered,
hearts have no resentment,
mouths have no troublesome words.
Therefore, carriages and horses are not weary on long roads,
banners and flags are not disordered in the great marshes,
the myriad people do not lose their lives to bandits and soldiers,
and heroes do not shorten their lives at the banner staff;
heroes are not named in books and records,
nor are merits recorded on basins and tripods,
and the records of years are empty.
Therefore, it is said:
"No benefit is greater than simplicity,
no fortune is longer than peace."
Suppose we made the craftsman Shǐ using his thousand years of life, holding a hook,
watching the compass and square,
raising the plumb line and ink marker,
to correct Tài Shān;
and had Bēn and
Yù carry the Gānjiàng
to regulate the myriad people;
even if they exhausted their skill and ingenuity,
and reached the height of their lifespan,
Tài Shān would not be straight,
and the people could not be regulated.
Therefore it is said:
"Those of old who governed the world
did not have the craftsman Shǐ exhaust his skill
to ruin the form of Tài Shān,
nor did they have Bēn and Yù exhaust their might
to harm the nature of the myriad people,
following the Dao to complete the law,
the gentlemen are happy and the great villains stop."
Being detached and quiet,
following the mandate of heaven,
holding the grand scheme.
Therefore, people are made to have no crime of deviating from the law,
and fish have no disaster of losing water.
Because of this,
the world lacks little that is not permissible.
If the top does not follow heaven, then the bottom will not be universally covered;
if the heart does not follow earth, then things will not necessarily be carried.
Tài Shān does not establish likes and dislikes,
therefore it can achieve its height;
rivers and seas do not reject small assistance,
therefore they can achieve their richness.
Therefore, a great man entrusts his form to Heaven and Earth
and finds all things complete;
he exercises his mind on mountains and seas
and makes the state wealthy.
Above, there is no poison of resentment;
below, there is no trouble of concealed grievances.
Those above and those below interact with simplicity,
taking the Dào as their dwelling.
Thus, lasting benefits accumulate,
great achievements are established,
fame is achieved in the present,
and virtue is passed on to posterity—
this is the ultimate in governance.
The ruler employs seven arts,
and observes six subtleties.
The seven arts are:
First, comprehensive observation of all affairs;
Second, certain punishment to manifest authority;
Third, trustworthy reward to exhaust capabilities;
Fourth, listen only once and hold subordinates responsible;
Fifth, issue ambiguous orders and employ deceptive envoys;
Sixth, obtain knowledge through questioning;
Seventh, contradict words and reverse actions.
These seven are what the ruler employs.
Chapter One: Comprehensive Observation.
If observation and listening are not comprehensive,
then the truth will not be heard;
if listening has its own channels,
then the ministers will obstruct.
The explanation lies in the dwarf's dream of the stove
and Āi Gōng's saying, "None are so lost as the many."
Thus, it is like the man of Qí seeing the Hé Bó
and the words of Huìzi, "losing half of it."
The trouble lies in Shù Niú starving Shū Sūn
and Jiāng Yǐ's description of the customs of Jīng.
Sì Gōng wanted to govern, but did not know how,
so he created opposition.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler examines things like accumulated iron
and observes the troubles of a single market.
Chapter Two: Certain Punishment. 〓#
If love is excessive,
then the law will not be established;
if authority is weak,
then subordinates will encroach upon superiors.
Therefore, if punishments are not certain,
then prohibitions and orders will not be carried out.
The explanation lies in Dǒngzi's governance of Shíyì
and Zǐchǎn's teaching of Yóu Jí.
Thus, Zhòng Ní spoke of falling frost,
and the laws of Yīn punished those who discarded ashes.
Jiāng Háng removed the pleasure pond,
and Gōngsūn Yāng made light crimes heavily punishable.
Therefore, the gold of Líshuǐ was not guarded,
and the fire of Jízé was not rescued.
Chéng Huān weakened the state of Qí with excessive benevolence,
and Bǔ Pí caused the King of Wèi to perish with kindness and grace.
Guǎn Zhòng knew this,
therefore he executed the dead man.
Sì Gōng knew this, therefore he bought the convicts.
Chapter Three: Awards and Praise. 〓#
If awards and praise are meager and false,
then subordinates will not serve;
if awards and praise are generous and trustworthy,
then subordinates will lightly risk death.
The explanation lies in Wénzi's saying,
“Like a deer or elk.”
Therefore, the King of Yuè burned down palaces and houses,
and Wú Qǐ leaned on the carriage shaft;
Lǐ Kuī judged lawsuits by archery,
and Sòng Chóng died by destroying the gate.
Gōujiàn knew this,
therefore he paid homage to the angry frog.
Zhāo Hóu knew this,
therefore he hid his worn trousers.
Generous rewards cause men to act like Bēn and Zhū;
the woman picking silk worms,
the fisherman grasping the sturgeon,
are examples of this effect.
Chapter Four: Listen Only Once. 〓#
If you listen only once, then the foolish and wise will not be confused;
if you hold subordinates responsible, then ministers will not collude.
The explanation lies in searching for Zhèng and playing the yú.
The trouble lies in Shēnzi's use of Zhào Shào and Hán Tà as tests.
Therefore, Gōngzǐ Fàn discussed ceding Hédōng,
and Yìng Hóu plotted to abandon Shàngdǎng.
Chapter Five: Deceptive Envoys. 〓#
If seen frequently and waited upon for a long time, but not entrusted with tasks,
the deceitful will scatter.
If envoys are sent to inquire about other matters,
then they will not sell private favors.
Therefore, Páng Jìng returned the high officials,
and Dài Huān ordered that the carriages be inspected;
the Zhōu ruler lost a jade hairpin,
and the Grand Steward of Shāng discussed cow dung.
Chapter Six: Obtain Knowledge. 〓#
If you obtain knowledge through questioning,
then even the ignorant will become wise;
if you deeply understand one thing,
then all hidden matters will be revealed.
The explanation lies in Zhāo Hóu holding one claw.
Therefore, Bì Nánmén and the three townships were obtained.
The Zhōu ruler searched for a crooked staff and the ministers were afraid,
Bǔ Pí used a servant,
and Xīmén Bào pretended to lose a linchpin.
Chapter Seven: Contradictory Words. 〓#
Contradictory words and reversed actions
are used to test suspected matters,
then the truth can be obtained.
Therefore, Yáng Shān deceived Jiū Shù,
Nào Chǐ acted as an envoy for Qín,
a man of Qí wanted to cause trouble,
Zǐzhī used white horses,
Zǐchǎn separated the litigants,
and Sì Gōng crossed the border market.
Explanation One: 〓#
During the time of Wèi Líng Gōng,
Mí Zixia was favored
and had a monopoly in the state of Wèi.
A dwarf who had an audience with the duke said,
“My dream has come true.”
The duke said,
“What dream?”
He replied,
“I dreamed of seeing a stove,
which means seeing the duke.”
The duke angrily said,
“I have heard that those who see a ruler dream of the sun.
Why is it that seeing me, you dream of a stove?”
He replied,
“The sun shines on all under heaven,
and no one thing can obstruct it.
The ruler shines on the people of a state,
and no one person can obstruct him.
Therefore, those who are about to see a ruler dream of the sun.
Now, the stove,
if one person warms himself at it,
then those behind him have no way to see it.
Now, is it that someone is monopolizing the ruler?
Then, though I dreamed of seeing a stove,
is it not appropriate?”
Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying,
“The proverb says,
‘None are so lost as the many.’
Now, when I undertake affairs,
I deliberate with the ministers,
but the state becomes even more chaotic.
What is the reason for this?”
Kǒngzǐ replied,
“When an enlightened ruler asks his ministers,
one person knows and
one person does not know.
In such a case,
an enlightened ruler is above,
and the ministers offer straightforward advice below.
Now, all the ministers without exception echo Jì Sūn,
and the entire state of Lǔ is transformed into one.
Even if you ask the people within the borders,
you will still not avoid chaos.”
First:
Yànzi was sent to Lǔ,
and Āi Gōng asked, saying,
“The saying goes,
‘No three are so lost as the many.’
Now, I deliberate with the entire state,
but Lǔ cannot avoid chaos.
Why is this?”
Yànzi said,
“The ancient saying, ‘No three are so lost as the many,’
means that if one person loses,
and two people gain,
three people are enough to form a crowd,
therefore it is said
‘No three are so lost as the many.’
Now, the ministers of Lǔ number in the thousands,
all speaking to Jìshì's private interests.
The number of people is not small,
but what they say is the same as one person.
How can there be three?”
A man of Qí told the King of Qí, saying,
"The Hé Bó
is a great god.
Why does Your Majesty not try to meet with him?
I request to enable Your Majesty to meet him."
So he built an altar on a great body of water,
and stood there with the king.
After a while,
a large fish moved,
and he said,
"This is the Hé Bó."
Zhāng Yí wanted to use the power of Qín, Hán, and Wèi
to attack Qí and Jīng,
while Huì Shī wanted to have Qí and Jīng cease military actions.
The two men argued,
and the assembled ministers and attendants all spoke on behalf of Zhāng Zǐ,
considering attacking Qí and Jīng to be advantageous,
but no one spoke on behalf of Huì Zǐ.
The king indeed listened to Zhāng Zǐ,
and considered Huì Zǐ's words to be unacceptable.
The matter of attacking Qí and Jīng having been decided,
Huì Zǐ entered to have an audience.
The king said,
"Sir, there is no need to speak!
The matter of attacking Qí and Jīng is truly advantageous,
the entire country thinks so."
Huì Zǐ then argued:
"It cannot but be examined.
If the matter of Qí and Jīng is truly advantageous,
and the entire country considers it advantageous,
then what a crowd of wise men there is!
If the matter of attacking Qí and Jīng were truly not advantageous,
and the entire country considered it advantageous,
what a crowd of fools there is!
All plans
involve doubt.
Doubt
is genuine doubt:
half believe it is possible,
half believe it is not possible.
Now, if the entire country believes it is possible,
then Your Majesty has lost half.
One who coerces the ruler
is certainly one who has lost half."
Shū Sūn was the prime minister of Lǔ,
noble and held authority.
His favorite was named Shù Niú,
who also presumptuously used Shū Sūn's authority.
Shū Sūn had a son named Rén,
and Shù Niú was jealous and wanted to kill him,
so he went with Rén to visit the ruler of Lǔ.
The ruler of Lǔ granted him a jade ring,
Rén bowed to receive it, but dared not wear it,
and had Shù Niú request permission from Shū Sūn.
Shù Niú deceived him, saying,
"I have already requested it for you,
so you may wear it."
Rén then wore it.
Shù Niú then said to Shū Sūn,
"Why have you not seen Rén in the presence of the ruler?"
Shū Sūn said, 〓#
"Why is such a child worth seeing?" 〓#
Shù Niú said,
"Rén has already been seen by the ruler many times.
The ruler granted him a jade ring,
and Rén has already worn it."
Shū Sūn summoned Rén to see him,
and he was indeed wearing it,
Shū Sūn was angry and killed Rén.
Rén's elder brother was named Bǐng,
and Shù Niú was again jealous and wanted to kill him.
Shū Sūn had a bell cast for Bǐng,
and when the bell was completed,
Bǐng did not dare to strike it,
and had Shù Niú request permission from Shū Sūn.
Shù Niú did not request permission,
and again deceived him, saying,
"I have already requested it for you,
so you may strike it."
Bǐng then struck it.
Shū Sūn heard it and said,
"Bǐng struck the bell without permission."
He was angry and drove him away.
Bǐng fled to Qí.
After a year,
Shù Niú apologized for Bǐng to Shū Sūn,
Shū Sūn had Shù Niú summon him,
but he did not summon him and reported, saying,
"I have already summoned him,
but Bǐng is very angry
and refuses to come."
Shū Sūn was greatly angered
and had someone kill him.
His two sons having died,
Shū Sūn became ill,
and Shù Niú then cared for him alone,
removing those around him,
not letting anyone in,
saying,
"Shū Sūn does not want to hear people's voices."
He did not feed him, and he starved to death.
Shū Sūn having died,
Shù Niú then did not announce the funeral,
but moved his storehouses and precious treasures,
emptying them, and fled to Qí.
To listen to the words of those you trust,
and for father and son to be killed by others,
this is the calamity of not consulting widely.
Jiāng Yǐ was sent as an envoy by the King of Wèi to Jīng,
and said to the King of Jīng,
"When your servant entered the territory of Your Majesty,
I heard that the custom of Your Majesty's country is:
'A gentleman does not conceal the good in others,
nor does he speak of the evil in others.'
Is there truly such a thing?"
The king said,
"There is such a thing."
"In that case, concerning the rebellion of Bái Gōng,
could there be no danger?
If it were truly so,
your servant would be spared the death penalty."
Wèi Sìjūn valued Rú Ěr highly,
and loved Shì Jī,
but feared that they would both use his love and high regard to block him.
He therefore valued Bó Yí to counter Rú Ěr,
and honored Wèi Jī to match Shì Jī,
saying,
"I use these to cross-check each other."
Sìjūn knew that he wanted to avoid being blocked,
but had not found the method.
If you do not allow the lowly to discuss the noble,
those below will certainly sit on those above,
and only when their power is equally heavy
will they dare to discuss each other,
which is to further establish ministers who obstruct and block.
Sìjūn's blockage has only just begun.
If arrows come from a known direction,
then stockpile iron to prepare for that one direction;
if arrows come from no known direction,
then build an iron room to prepare for all directions.
If you prepare for them, then the body will not be harmed.
Therefore, the latter does not suffer harm by preparing for all possibilities,
and the former does not have deceit by countering all enemies.
Páng Gōng accompanied the Crown Prince as a hostage in Hándān,
and said to the King of Wèi,
"Now, if one person says there is a tiger in the market,
will Your Majesty believe it?"
He said,
"I will not believe it."
"If two people say there is a tiger in the market,
will Your Majesty believe it?"
He said,
"I will not believe it."
"If three people say there is a tiger in the market,
will Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"I will believe it."
Páng Gōng said,
"That there are no tigers in the market is clear,
yet three people saying so make it seem like there is a tiger.
Now, Hándān is further from Wèi than the market is,
and those who speak ill of your servant exceed three people,
I hope Your Majesty will investigate this."
Páng Gōng returned from Hándān,
and ultimately was not granted an audience.
Sayings Two: 〓#
Dǒng Èyú was the governor of Zhaò's territory.
Traveling in the Shíyì mountains,
the ravines were deep,
as steep as walls,
hundreds of *rèn* deep,
so he asked the people on the sides of the surrounding villages, saying,
"Have people ever fallen into this before?"
He replied,
"None."
He said,
"Have infants,
the mentally impaired, the deaf, or the deranged
ever entered this place?"
He replied,
"None."
"Have oxen, horses, dogs, or pigs
ever entered this place?"
He replied,
"None."
Dǒng Èyú sighed deeply and said,
"I can govern it.
If I governed it without pardon,
so that entering the ravine was certain death,
then no one would dare to trespass,
why could it not be governed?"
Zǐchǎn, as the minister of Zhèng,
being ill and near death,
said to Yóují,
"After my death,
you will surely be employed by Zhèng,
and you must preside over the people with strictness.
For the form of fire is severe,
therefore people are seldom burned;
the form of water is weak,
and people often drown.
You must be strict in your form,
and do not let people drown in your weakness."
Zǐchǎn died,
and Yóují was unwilling to be strict in form.
The young men of Zhèng banded together as robbers,
dwelling in the reed marshes,
and were about to become a disaster for Zhèng.
Yóují led chariots and cavalry to battle them,
and after a day and a night,
barely managed to defeat them.
Yóují sighed and lamented,
"If I had followed Master's teaching earlier,
I surely would not have regretted reaching this point!"
Lǔ Āigōng asked Zhòngní,
"The records of the *Chūnqiū* state:
'In the twelfth month of winter, fallen frost did not kill the beans.'
Why is this recorded?"
Zhòngní replied,
"This speaks of something that could have been killed but was not.
If what should be killed is not killed,
then peaches and plums will bear fruit in winter.
If Heaven loses its way,
even grass and trees will dare to transgress it,
how much more so a ruler of men!"
The law of Yīn punished
those who discarded ashes on the street.
Zǐgòng thought this was excessive
and asked Zhòngní about it.
Zhòngní said,
"It is knowing the way to govern.
Discarding ashes on the street will surely cover people,
and if it covers people,
people will surely be angry,
and if they are angry, they will fight,
and if they fight, the three families will surely be destroyed.
This is the way to destroy three families,
so even punishing it is justifiable.
Moreover, heavy punishments
are what people dislike;
not discarding ashes
is what people find easy.
To make people do what is easy,
and not stray from what they dislike,
this is the way to govern."
It is said:
The law of Yīn was that
those who discarded ashes on public roads had their hands cut off.
Zǐgòng said,
"The crime of discarding ashes is light,
the punishment of cutting off hands is heavy,
why were the ancients so resolute?"
He said,
"Not discarding ashes
is what is easy;
cutting off hands
is what is disliked.
Doing what is easy
does not involve what is disliked;
the ancients considered it easy,
therefore they did it."
The minister of Zhōngshān, Lè Chí,
sent an envoy to Zhào with a hundred chariots,
choosing from his retainers those with intelligence
to serve as generals for the journey,
but chaos ensued midway.
Lè Chí said,
"I considered you to be intelligent
and appointed you as generals for the journey,
but now chaos has ensued midway,
why is this?"
The retainer then resigned and left,
saying,
"You do not know how to govern.
Having sufficient authority to subdue people,
and sufficient benefit to encourage them,
is how one can govern them.
Now, your servant
is but a minor retainer of yours.
To follow the inferior to correct the superior,
to use the lowly to govern the noble,
and not be able to grasp the handle of their benefits and harms
to control them,
this is why there is chaos.
Try appointing me:
those among them who are good, I can make ministers and chancellors,
those who are not good, I can cut off their heads,
why then would there not be order!"
Gōngsūn Yāng's laws punished light offenses severely.
Heavy crimes
are what people find difficult to commit;
minor offenses
are what people find easy to avoid.
To make people avoid what is easy,
and not stray from what is difficult,
this is the way to govern.
If minor offenses do not arise,
then major crimes will not occur,
thus people will be without crime and disorder will not arise.
It is said:
Gōngsūn Yāng said,
"In administering punishments, weigh them heavily on the light offenses.
If light offenses do not occur,
then heavy offenses will not come,
this is called using punishments to eliminate punishments."
In the land south of Jīng,
gold is produced in the waters of the Lí River,
and many people secretly mine gold.
The prohibition against mining gold
is that those caught are immediately dismembered and displayed in the market.
Many were executed,
and the water was blocked by their bodies,
yet people did not stop secretly mining gold.
Dismemberment and display in the market is the heaviest of punishments,
yet people still do not stop because
it is not certain they will be caught.
Suppose now that there is someone here who says,
"I will give you the world but kill your body."
Even an ordinary person would not do it.
To possess the world
is a great benefit,
yet they still would not do it because
they know they will certainly die.
Therefore, if it is not certain they will be caught,
then even though they face dismemberment,
they will not stop secretly mining gold;
if they know they will certainly die,
then they will not take possession of the world.
The people of Lǔ were burning a marsh.
The north wind was blowing,
and the fire leaned south,
threatening to burn the state.
Āigōng was afraid
and personally led the people to rush to extinguish the fire.
There was no one on either side of him,
everyone was chasing animals
and not saving the fire,
so he summoned and asked Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said,
"Chasing animals is enjoyable
and without punishment,
while saving the fire is laborious
and without reward,
this is why the fire is not being saved."
Āi Gōng said:
"Good."
Zhòng Ní said:
"The matter is urgent,
there is no time to give rewards.
If those who extinguish the fire are all rewarded,
then the state will not have enough to reward people,
please only administer punishments."
Āi Gōng said:
"Good."
Thereupon Zhòng Ní issued an order, saying:
"Those who do not extinguish the fire
will be punished the same as those who surrender in battle;
those who chase animals
will be punished the same as those who enter forbidden areas."
Before the order was fully circulated,
the fire was already extinguished.
Chéng Huān said to the King of Qí:
"Your Majesty is too kind,
too unwilling to be hard on people."
The King said:
"Being too kind,
too unwilling to be hard on people,
is this not a good reputation?"
He replied:
"This is a good quality for subjects,
but not what a ruler should do.
Subjects must be kind
before they can be consulted,
and unwilling to be hard on people
before they can be approached;
if they are not kind, they cannot be consulted,
and if they are willing to be hard on people, they cannot be approached."
The King said:
"In what way is this Qín too kind,
in what way unwilling to be hard on people?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty is too kind to Xuē Gōng,
and too unwilling to be hard on the various Tián.
Being too kind to Xuē Gōng
causes the great ministers to have no weight;
being too unwilling to be hard on the various Tián
causes fathers and elder brothers to break the law.
If the great ministers have no weight,
then the military will be weak externally;
if fathers and elder brothers break the law,
then the government will be in turmoil internally.
If the military is weak externally
and the government is in turmoil internally,
this is the root of national destruction."
Wèi Huì Wáng said to Bǔ Pí:
"What do you hear about my reputation?
What is it like?"
He replied:
"I hear that Your Majesty is benevolent and kind."
The King happily said:
"Then to what will my accomplishments lead?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty's accomplishments will lead to ruin."
The King said:
"Benevolence and kindness
are good deeds.
To practice them and yet be ruined,
how can this be?"
Bǔ Pí replied:
"Benevolence means not being able to bear,
and kindness means being fond of giving.
Not being able to bear
means not punishing those who have done wrong,
and being fond of giving
means rewarding without waiting for merit.
If those who have done wrong are not punished,
and those without merit receive rewards,
even if one is ruined,
is it not fitting?"
The state of Qí favored lavish burials,
cloth and silk were exhausted in burial shrouds,
wood and timber were exhausted in coffins and outer coffins.
Huán Gōng was worried about this
and told Guǎn Zhòng, saying:
"If cloth and silk are exhausted, there will be nothing to cover ourselves with;
if wood and timber are exhausted, there will be nothing for defense;
yet people do not stop lavish burials,
what can be done to prohibit it?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"All that people do
is either for fame
or for profit."
Thereupon, he issued an order, saying:
"Those whose coffins and outer coffins exceed the limits
will have their corpses mutilated,
and the one in charge of the funeral will be punished."
Mutilating the dead
brings no fame,
and punishing the one in charge of the funeral
brings no profit,
why would people do it?
During the time of Wèi Sì Jūn,
there was a convict who escaped to Wèi,
and ended up treating the illness of the Queen of Xiāng Wáng.
Wèi Sì Jūn heard of this
and sent someone to request to buy him for fifty gold pieces,
but after five attempts, the King of Wèi would not give him up,
so he exchanged him for Zuǒ Shì.
The assembled ministers and attendants remonstrated, saying:
"To buy a convict for a city,
is this acceptable?"
The King said:
"This is not something you understand.
Order has no small beginnings,
and chaos has no large beginnings.
If the laws are not established and punishments are not certain,
even having ten Zuǒ Shì will be of no benefit;
if the laws are established and punishments are certain,
even losing ten Zuǒ Shì will do no harm."
The King of Wèi heard of this and said:
"If a ruler wants to govern well but is not listened to,
it is inauspicious."
Therefore, he loaded up the convict and sent him back,
presenting him as a gift.
Sayings Three: 〓
The King of Qí asked Wén Zǐ, saying:
"How should a state be governed?"
He replied:
"Rewards and punishments as a means
are sharp weapons.
The ruler should firmly grasp them
and not show them to others.
Those like me
are like deer and elk,
who only follow where there is good grass."
The King of Yuè asked the grand master Wén Zhǒng, saying:
"I want to attack Wú,
is it possible?"
He replied:
"It is possible.
Our rewards are generous and trustworthy,
and our punishments are severe and certain.
If Your Majesty wants to know,
why not try burning down the palace?"
Thereupon, he burned down the palace,
and no one saved it.
Then he issued an order, saying:
"Those who save the fire will be rewarded as if they died fighting the enemy;
those who save the fire and do not die will be rewarded as if they defeated the enemy;
those who do not save the fire
will be punished as if they surrendered in battle."
People smeared their bodies,
wore wet clothing, and ran into the fire;
three thousand on the left,
and three thousand on the right.
This is knowing the situation of certain victory.
Wú Qǐ was appointed the Western River Administrator for Wèi Wǔ Hóu.
Qín had a small outpost bordering the territory,
and Wú Qǐ wanted to attack it.
Not removing it
would greatly harm the fields,
but removing it
would not be enough to justify mobilizing the armor and soldiers.
Thereupon, he leaned a cart shaft outside the north gate
and issued an order, saying:
"Whoever can move this to outside the south gate
will be rewarded with the best fields and the best houses."
No one moved it.
When someone finally moved it,
he rewarded him as promised.
Soon after, he placed a stone of red beans outside the east gate
and issued an order, saying:
"Whoever can move this to outside the west gate
will be rewarded as before."
People rushed to move it.
Then he issued an order, saying:
"Tomorrow we will attack the fort.
Whoever is the first to scale the walls
will be made a senior minister of the state
and granted superior fields and houses."
People rushed to compete for this,
and so they attacked the fort
and captured it in a single morning.
Lǐ Kuī 李悝, serving as the governor of the lands bordering Wèi 文侯,
desired the people to be skilled in archery.
Thus he issued an order, saying:
"For those who have lawsuits involving doubt,
have them shoot at a target.
Whoever hits it wins,
and whoever misses loses."
After the order was issued, the people all diligently practiced archery,
day and night without rest.
When they fought against the people of Qín 秦,
they greatly defeated them,
because the people were skilled in battle and archery.
A man in the alley of the Chóngmén 崇門 gate in Sòng 宋 mourned
and wasted away severely.
The ruler thought he was filial and loving towards his parents
and appointed him as an official and teacher.
The next year,
the number of people who wasted away in mourning
exceeded ten per year.
A son who mourns for his parents
does so out of love,
and yet this can be rewarded and encouraged.
How much more so the ruler towards his people!
The King of Yuè 越, considering attacking Wú 吳,
desired the people to not fear death.
He went out and saw an angry frog and saluted it.
His attendants said:
"Why do you respect it so?"
The King said:
"Because it has such spirit."
The next year, more than ten people
offered their heads to the king.
From this, it can be seen that
praise is enough to kill people.
It is said:
King Gōujiàn 勾踐 of Yuè 越 saw an angry frog and saluted it.
The charioteer said:
"Why do you salute it?"
The King said:
"The frog has so much spirit,
how could I not salute it?"
The gentlemen heard this and said:
"The frog has spirit,
and the King salutes it.
How much more so those gentlemen who are brave!"
That year,
there were people who cut their own throats and offered their heads.
Therefore, the King of Yuè 越 was about to avenge himself on Wú 吳
and test his teachings.
He set fire to a platform and beat a drum,
and those who rushed into the fire
were rewarded in the fire.
He stood by the river and beat a drum,
and those who rushed into the water
were rewarded in the water.
He stood by the battlefield and had people cut off heads
and disembowel themselves without hesitation;
the reward was on the battlefield.
How much more so if one promotes the worthy according to the law;
the encouragement would be much greater than this!
Hán Zhāo Hóu 韓昭侯 had someone store away worn-out trousers.
An attendant said:
"My lord, you are not benevolent!
You do not give the worn-out trousers to those around you
but store them away."
Zhāo Hóu 昭侯 said:
"This is not something you understand.
I have heard that a wise ruler cherishes every frown and smile.
Frowning has a reason for frowning,
and smiling has a reason for smiling.
Now, these trousers,
how could they be like a frown or a smile!
Trousers are far removed from frowns and smiles.
I must wait for someone who has achieved merit,
and so I have stored them away, not yet given them out."
The sturgeon resembles a snake,
and the silkworm resembles a caterpillar.
People are startled and frightened when they see a snake,
and their hair stands on end when they see a caterpillar.
However, women gather silkworms,
and fishermen grasp sturgeon.
Where there is profit,
they forget what they dislike
and all become like Mèng Bēn 孟賁.
Speeches Four: 〓#
The King of Wèi 魏 said to the King of Zhèng 鄭:
"Originally, Zhèng 鄭 and Liáng 梁 were one state.
Later, they separated.
Now, I wish to regain Zhèng 鄭 and unite it with Liáng 梁."
The King of Zhèng 鄭 was troubled by this
and summoned his ministers
to discuss with him how to respond to Wèi 魏.
A prince said to the King of Zhèng 鄭:
"This is very easy to answer.
You should respond to Wèi 魏:
'If Zhèng 鄭 can be considered old Wèi 魏 and can be united,
then our humble state also wishes to regain Liáng 梁
and unite it with Zhèng 鄭.'"
The King of Wèi 魏 then stopped.
King Xuān 宣 of Qí 齊 had people play the yú,
always with three hundred people.
Nánguō 南郭 Chǔshì 處士 requested to play the yú for the king.
King Xuān 宣 was pleased with him
and provided food for several hundred people.
King Xuān 宣 died,
and King Mǐn 湣 ascended the throne.
He liked to listen to each person individually,
and Chǔshì 處士 fled.
It is said:
Hán Zhāo Hóu 韓昭侯 said:
"There are many yú players,
and I have no way to know who is good."
Tián Yán 田嚴 replied:
"Listen to them one by one."
Zhào 趙 sent a person to ask Shēn Zǐ 申子 in Hán 韓 for troops
to attack Wèi 魏.
Shēn Zǐ 申子 wanted to tell the ruler
but feared that the ruler would suspect him of colluding with outsiders.
Otherwise, he feared offending Zhào 趙.
Therefore, he had Zhào Shào 趙紹 and Hán Tà 韓沓
test the ruler's attitude
before speaking to him.
Internally, he would know the intention of Zhāo Hóu 昭侯,
and externally, he would gain merit from Zhào 趙.
When the armies of the Three Kingdoms arrived at Hán 韓,
the King of Qín 秦 said to Lóu Huǎn 樓緩:
"The armies of the Three Kingdoms are deep!
I want to cede Hédōng 河東 and negotiate.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"To cede Hédōng 河東
is a great expense.
To save the state from calamity
is a great achievement.
This is the responsibility of fathers and elder brothers.
Why does Your Majesty not summon Prince Fàn 氾
and ask him?"
The king summoned Prince Fàn 氾 and told him about it.
He replied:
"Negotiating will bring regret,
and not negotiating will also bring regret.
If Your Majesty now cedes Hédōng 河東 and negotiates,
and the Three Kingdoms withdraw,
Your Majesty will surely say:
'The Three Kingdoms were going to leave anyway;
I just sent them off with three cities.'
If you do not negotiate,
and the Three Kingdoms enter Hán 韓,
then the state will surely be greatly disrupted,
and Your Majesty will greatly regret it.
Your Majesty will say:
'I should not have offered the three cities.'
Therefore, I say:
'Negotiating will bring regret,
and not negotiating will also bring regret.'"
The King said:
"For my sake, let there be regret.
I would rather lose three cities and regret it
than face danger and regret it. 〓#
I have decided to negotiate."
Yīng Hóu 應侯 said to the King of Qín 秦:
"Your Majesty has obtained Wǎn 宛, Yè 葉, Lántián 藍田, and Yángxià 陽夏,
cut off Hénèi 河內,
and troubled Liáng 梁 and Zhèng 鄭.
The reason why you have not become king
is that Zhào 趙 has not been subdued.
Relinquishing Shàngdǎng 上黨 is the only way,
in order to approach Dōngyáng 東陽.
Then Hándān 邯鄲 is like a louse in one's mouth."
Wáng Gǒng'ér held court over the world,
and the latecomers attacked him with weapons.
However, Ānlè of Shàngdǎng,
its location is extremely critical.
I fear that if we dismiss him, he will not listen.
What should we do?"
The king said,
"We must dismiss him and replace him easily."
Discourses Five: 〓#
Páng Jìng was
a county magistrate.
He sent the market inspectors out,
then summoned the officials and grandees back.
After a while,
he had nothing to instruct them with,
so he finally sent the inspectors out.
The market inspectors thought the magistrate and officials had something to say,
and did not trust each other,
so that no treachery occurred.
Dài Huān,
the Tài Zǎi of Sòng,
sent a man at night, saying:
"I heard that for several nights a covered carriage has been coming to the gate of Lǐ Shǐ.
Be sure to watch it for me."
The messenger reported:
"I didn't see a covered carriage,
but I saw someone holding a box and talking to Lǐ Shǐ.
After a while,
Lǐ Shǐ received the box."
The Zhōu ruler lost a jade hairpin,
and ordered the officials to find it,
but they could not find it for three days.
The Zhōu ruler ordered someone to search,
and it was found in the space between the houses of a family.
The Zhōu ruler said:
"My officials are not diligent!
Searching for a hairpin,
they could not find it in three days;
when I ordered someone to search for it,
it was found in less than a day."
Thereupon the officials were all terrified,
thinking the ruler was divine.
The Tài Zǎi of Shāng sent a junior steward to the market,
and when he returned, asked him:
"What did you see in the market?"
He replied:
"Nothing."
The Tài Zǎi said:
"Even so,
what did you see?"
He replied:
"Outside the south gate of the market, there were many oxcarts,
barely enough room to pass."
The Tài Zǎi then warned the messenger:
"Do not dare tell anyone what I asked you."
Then he summoned the market officials and rebuked them, saying:
"Why is there so much cow dung outside the market gate?"
The market officials were very surprised that the Tài Zǎi knew so quickly,
and were terrified of him.
Discourses Six: 〓#
Hán Zhāohóu clenched his fist,
and pretended to lose a fingernail.
He searched for it urgently,
and the attendants cut off their own fingernails and offered them.
Zhāohóu used this to observe the sincerity of his attendants.
Hán Zhāohóu sent a cavalryman to the county.
The messenger reported,
and Zhāohóu asked:
"What did you see?"
He replied:
"I saw nothing."
Zhāohóu said:
"Even so,
what did you see?"
He said:
"Outside the south gate,
there was a yellow calf eating seedlings on the left side of the road."
Zhāohóu told the messenger:
"Do not dare reveal what I asked you."
Then he issued an order, saying:
"During the seedling season,
there is already an order prohibiting cattle and horses from entering other people's fields,
but the officials do not take it seriously.
Many cattle and horses are entering other people's fields.
Quickly report the number of them;
if you do not,
I will severely punish you."
Thereupon the three townships reported them.
Zhāohóu said:
"It's not complete."
They went back to investigate,
and found the yellow calf outside the south gate.
The officials considered Zhāohóu to be insightful,
and were all terrified
and did not dare to do wrong.
The Zhōu ruler issued an order to search for a crooked staff,
and the officials searched for it for several days
but could not find it.
The Zhōu ruler privately ordered someone to search for it,
and they found it in less than a day.
Then he said to the officials:
"I know the officials are not diligent.
A crooked staff is very easy to find,
but the officials could not find it.
I ordered someone to search for it,
and they found it in less than a day.
How can you be called loyal!"
The officials were all terrified,
and considered the ruler to be divine.
Bǔ Pí was the county magistrate,
and his censor was corrupt and had a beloved concubine.
Bǔ Pí then sent a junior steward to pretend to love her,
in order to know the censor's secret affairs.
Xīmén Bào was the magistrate of Yè,
and pretended to lose his linchpin,
ordering the officials to find it, but they could not.
He ordered someone to search for it
and they found it in the space between the houses of a family.
Discourses Seven: 〓#
Yángshān Jūn was the chancellor of Wèi.
Hearing that the king suspected him,
he falsely slandered Jiū Shù in order to know it.
Nào Chǐ, hearing that the Qí king disliked him,
falsely acted as an envoy of Qín in order to know it.
There was a man of Qí who wanted to rebel,
fearing that the king would know,
so he falsely drove away his beloved,
causing her to run to the king and tell him.
Zǐ Zhī, being the chancellor of Yàn,
sat and said, pretending:
"What was that running out the door,
a white horse?"
The attendants all said they did not see it.
One person ran after it,
and reported:
"Yes."
Zǐ Zhī used this to know that his attendants were not sincere.
There were those who were suing each other,
and Zǐchǎn separated them
and did not allow them to communicate their arguments.
He reversed their words to tell them
and knew it.
Wèi Sìgōng sent a man to act as a merchant passing through the market gate.
The market gate was harsh and difficult for him,
so he bribed the market gate with gold,
and the gate official let him go.
Sìgōng said to the gate official:
"At such and such a time, there was a merchant passing through and
he gave you gold,
and you therefore let him go."
The market gate was greatly terrified,
and considered Sìgōng to be insightful.
Six Subtle Points:
First is the borrowing of power by subordinates;
second is the external borrowing of benefit;
third is entrusting to similar things;
fourth is the reversal of benefit and harm;
fifth is internal strife caused by doubt;
sixth is the discarding of enemy states.
These six things
are what the ruler should observe.
Classic One: 〓#
Borrowing Power.
Power and influence cannot be lent to others.
If the ruler loses one,
the subjects will take it as a hundred.
Therefore, if the subjects are allowed to borrow,
their strength will increase;
if their strength increases,
they will be used internally and externally;
if they are used internally and externally,
the ruler will be obstructed.
The explanation lies in Lǎo Dān's saying about losing the fish.
Therefore, when a ruler speaks for a long time,
his attendants sell favors and promote themselves.
The problem lies in Xū Tóng's remonstrance to Lì Gōng,
and the one-sided account of the Zhōu Marquis,
which led the Yàn people to bathe in excrement.
Chapter Two: 〓#
Divergent Interests.
The interests of the ruler and ministers are different,
therefore, ministers are not loyal;
thus, the minister's profit leads to
the ruler's destruction.
Therefore, treacherous ministers
summon enemy troops to eliminate internal threats,
use external affairs to deceive the ruler,
selfishly achieving their private gains,
without regard for the country's troubles.
The explanation lies in the Wèi person's wife's prayer for her husband.
Therefore, Dài Xiē plotted against his younger brother,
and the Three Huán attacked Zhāo Gōng;
Gōngshū brought in the Qí army,
and Dí Huáng summoned the Hán troops;
Tàizǎi Pǐ persuaded Dàfū Zhǒng,
Dàchéng Niú instructed Shēn Bùhài;
Sīmǎ Xǐ informed the Zhào King,
Lǚ Cāng schemed against Qín and Chǔ;
Sòng Shí left a letter for the Wèi ruler,
and Bái Guī taught about tyrannical reprimands.
Chapter Three: 〓#
Superficial Similarity.
Similar matters
are how rulers lose their judgments,
and how ministers achieve their selfish goals.
Therefore, the gatekeeper discarded water, and Yí Shè was punished;
Jìyáng falsely accused himself, and two people were punished;
Sīmǎ Xǐ killed Yuán Qiān, and Jì Xīn was punished;
Zhèng Xiù spoke of a bad odor, and the new concubine's nose was cut off;
Fèi Wújì instructed Xì Wǎn, and the Chief Minister was punished;
Chén Xū killed Zhāng Shòu, and Xīshǒu fled.
Therefore, burning straw sheds led to the punishment of Zhōngshān,
while killing an old scholar led to Jìyáng's reward.
Chapter Four: 〓#
Reversal.
If an event arises and there is a benefit,
attribute it to the ruler;
if there is harm,
be sure to investigate its origin.
Therefore, in the discussions of an enlightened ruler,
if the country is harmed, examine those who benefited;
if the minister is harmed, observe those who opposed him.
The explanation lies in Chén Xū becoming chancellor when the Chǔ army arrived,
and the granary official being overthrown when millet became expensive.
Therefore, Zhāo Xīxù seized the peddler of thatch,
and Xī Hóu questioned his motives,
Wén Gōng twisted heated meat,
and Rǎng Hóu requested to establish an emperor.
Chapter Five: 〓#
Triangulation and Doubt.
The situation of triangulation and doubt
is where chaos arises,
therefore, an enlightened ruler is cautious about it.
Therefore, Lì Jī of Jìn killed the crown prince Shēnshēng,
and the Zhèng Consort used poison;
Zhōu Xū of Wèi killed his lord Wán,
Gōngzǐ Gēn seized Dōng Zhōu,
Wángzǐ Zhí was greatly favored,
yet Shāng Chén actually rebelled,
Yán Suí and Hán Huì contended,
and Āi Hóu was indeed murdered,
Tián Cháng, Kàn Zhǐ, Dài Huān, and Huáng Xǐ were rivals,
and the Sòng ruler and Jiǎn Gōng were killed.
The explanation lies in Hú Tū's praise of two favorites,
and Zhèng Zhāo's response about being unborn.
Chapter Six: 〓#
Abolishment and Appointment. 〓#
What the enemy strives for
is to excessively scrutinize and indulge in extravagance;
if the ruler does not discern,
then the enemy will abolish and appoint at will.
Therefore, Wén Wáng patronized Fèi Zhòng,
and the Qín king worried about the Chǔ envoy,
Lí Qiě abandoned Zhòng Ní,
and Gān Xiàng frustrated Gān Mào.
Therefore, Zǐxū made proclamations, and Zǐcháng was employed,
introducing beautiful women led to the downfall of Yú and Guó,
pretending to leave a letter led to Cháng Hóng's death,
and using a rooster and castrated pig led to the extinction of Kuài Jié.
Temple Attack. 〓#
Matters of triangulation, doubt, abolishment, and appointment,
an enlightened ruler cuts them off internally
and applies them externally.
Support the weaker ones,
aid the weaker ones;
this is called temple attack.
After triangulation and comparison are used internally,
observation and listening are also carried out externally,
then the enemy's deception is exposed.
The explanation lies in the Qín dwarf's report to King Huìwén.
Therefore, Xiāng Cī spoke of attacking Yè,
and Sì Gōng bestowed an order of mats.
Explanation One: 〓#
The accumulation of power
is the abyss for the ruler;
ministers
are the fish in the abyss of power.
If the fish is lost from the abyss,
it cannot be recovered;
if the ruler loses his accumulated power to the minister,
it cannot be regained.
The ancients found it difficult to speak directly,
therefore, they entrusted it to the fish.
Rewards and punishments
are sharp weapons;
the ruler wields them to control ministers,
and ministers obtain them to control the ruler.
Therefore, if the ruler first reveals what he will reward,
then the minister sells it to gain favor;
if the ruler first reveals what he will punish,
then the minister sells it to gain authority.
Therefore, it is said:
"The sharp weapons of the state
cannot be shown to others."
When Lord Jìngguō was the chancellor of Qí,
speaking with old friends for a long time
made the old friends wealthy;
keeping attendants close and brushing them off
made the attendants influential.
Speaking for a long time and keeping attendants close,
are small favors,
yet they can lead to wealth,
how much more so in official positions?
During the time of Lì Gōng of Jìn,
the six ministers were powerful;
Xū Tóng and Chángyú Jiǎo remonstrated, saying:
"If ministers are highly valued,
they will rival the ruler in handling affairs,
establish factions in the outer markets,
disrupt the laws of the country,
and rebel against the ruler above;
there has never been a case where the country is not endangered."
The duke said:
"Good."
Then he executed three ministers.
Xū Tóng and Chángyú Jiǎo further remonstrated, saying:
"If people of the same crime
are only partially punished and not all eliminated,
it is harboring resentment and providing them with opportunities."
The duke said:
"I executed three ministers in one morning,
I could not bear to eliminate them all."
Chángyú Jiǎo replied:
"If you cannot bear to do it to them,
they will bear to do it to you."
The duke did not listen.
After three months,
the ministers started a rebellion,
and killed Lì Gōng and divided his territory.
The Zhōu Marquis was chancellor of Jīng,
powerful and with authority to decide.
The Jīng King suspected him,
and asked his attendants,
who replied:
"There is nothing."
As if speaking with one voice.
The Yàn people were not confused,
therefore, they bathed in dog excrement.
A man from Yàn,
whose wife was having an affair with a scholar,
returned home early from outside,
and the scholar had just left.
The husband said:
"Who was that guest?"
His wife said:
"There was no guest."
He asked those around him,
and those around him said "nothing there,"
as if from one mouth.
His wife said:
"Husband, you are confused by the *Yì*."
Therefore, she bathed him with dog feces.
It is said:
The *Yàn* man, *Lǐ Jì*, liked to travel far.
His wife was secretly having an affair with a scholar.
*Jì* suddenly arrived.
The scholar was inside.
The wife was worried about this.
Her chambermaid said:
"Have the young master strip naked and let down his hair.
Go straight out the door.
We will pretend not to see him."
Thereupon, the young master followed her plan
and ran quickly out the door.
*Jì* said:
"Who is this person?"
The household all said:
"No one."
*Jì* said:
"Did I see a ghost?"
The woman said:
"Yes."
"What should be done about it?"
She said:
"Take the excrement of the five domestic animals and bathe with it."
*Jì* said:
"Okay."
Then he bathed with excrement.
One account says he bathed in fragrant water.
Explanation two: 〓#
There was a couple from *Wèi* who were praying,
and the husband prayed:
"May I, without cause,
obtain one hundred bundles of cloth."
The wife said:
"Why so little?"
He replied:
"If there is more,
you will use it to buy a concubine."
The *Jīng* King wanted to send his sons as officials to the neighboring states.
*Dài Xiē* said:
"Not possible."
"To send the princes as officials to the neighboring states
will surely cause the neighboring states to value them."
He said:
"When a son goes out, he is valued;
if valued,
he will surely become partisan to the state that values him.
This is like teaching your son in the marketplace,
not beneficial."
*Lǔ Mèngsūn*, *Shūsūn*, and *Jìsūn*
joined forces to coerce Duke *Zhāo*,
then seized his state and monopolized its governance.
The Three *Huán* of *Lǔ* oppressed the Duke.
Duke *Zhāo* attacked the *Jìsūn* clan,
and the *Mèngsūn* and *Shūsūn* clans discussed together, saying:
"Should we rescue him?"
The charioteer of the *Shūsūn* clan said:
"I
am a household servant,
how would I know about the ducal family?
What is more beneficial to me, having *Jìsūn* or not having *Jìsūn*?"
They all said:
"Without *Jìsūn*, there will definitely be no *Shūsūn*."
"In that case, rescue him."
Therefore, they crashed through the northwest corner and entered.
Seeing the banner of the *Shūsūn* entering,
*Mèngsūn* also rescued him.
The Three *Huán* became as one.
Duke *Zhāo* could not defeat them,
and drove him out,
dying in *Gānhòu*.
*Gōngshū* was the chancellor of *Hán* and planned to attack *Qí*.
*Gōngzhòng* was greatly favored by the King.
*Gōngshū* feared that the King would make *Gōngzhòng* chancellor.
He had *Qí* and *Hán* make an agreement to attack *Wèi*.
*Gōngshū* then brought the *Qí* army into *Zhèng*
in order to threaten his lord,
to solidify his position,
and to strengthen the agreement between the two states.
*Dí Huáng*
was a minister of the King of *Wèi*,
and he was on good terms with *Hán*.
He then summoned the *Hán* soldiers and ordered them to attack *Wèi*,
and then asked to mediate for the King of *Wèi*
in order to enhance his own importance.
The King of *Yuè* attacked the King of *Wú*.
The King of *Wú* apologized and declared his submission.
The King of *Yuè* wanted to agree to it.
*Fàn Lǐ* and *Dàfū Zhǒng* said:
"Not possible.
In the past, Heaven gave *Wú* to *Yuè*,
but *Wú* did not accept it.
Today, *Fūchāi* has turned against Heaven;
this is also a calamity from Heaven.
To give *Wú* to *Yuè*,
bow twice and accept it.
It is not permissible to agree to it."
*Tàizǎi Pǐ* sent a letter to *Dàfū Zhǒng*, saying:
"When the cunning rabbit is exhausted, the good dog is cooked.
When the enemy state is destroyed, the strategic advisor dies.
Why doesn't the Grand Master release *Wú* and worry about *Yuè*?"
*Dàfū Zhǒng* received the letter, read it,
sighed, and lamented:
"If he is killed,
*Yuè* and *Wú* will share the same fate."
*Dàchéng Niú* spoke to *Shēn Bùhài* of *Hán* from *Zhào*, saying:
"If *Hán* values me more than *Zhào*,
I ask to make *Zhào* value you more than *Hán*.
Then you will have two *Hán*s,
and I will have two *Zhào*s."
*Sīmǎ Xǐ*
was a minister of the lord of *Zhōngshān*,
and he was on good terms with *Zhào*.
He once subtly informed the King of *Zhào* of the plans of *Zhōngshān*.
*Lǚ Cāng*,
a minister of the King of *Wèi*,
was on good terms with *Qín* and *Jīng*.
He subtly advised *Qín* and *Jīng*
to order them to attack *Wèi*,
and then asked to carry out peace negotiations to enhance his own importance.
*Sòng Shí*,
was a general of *Wèi*;
Lord *Wèi*,
was a general of *Jīng*.
The two states encountered difficulties,
and the two men were both generals.
*Sòng Shí* sent a letter to Lord *Wèi*, saying:
"The two armies are facing each other,
the two banners are within sight of each other.
Only do not engage in battle;
if you fight, both will surely not survive.
This is a matter for the two lords.
I have no personal grudges against you.
The wise avoid each other."
*Bái Guī* was the prime minister of *Wèi*,
and *Bào Qiǎn* was the prime minister of *Hán*.
*Bái Guī* said to *Bào Qiǎn*:
"If you use *Hán* to assist me in *Wèi*,
I will use *Wèi* to treat you well in *Hán*.
I will serve *Wèi* for a long time,
and you will serve *Hán* for a long time."
Explanation three: 〓#
In *Qí*, there was a grand master named *Yí Yè*
who was serving wine to the king.
He became very drunk and went out,
leaning against the gate of the palace.
The gatekeeper, a *yuè* (one-footed person), knelt down and asked:
"Would your Excellency not be willing to bestow a bit of your leftover wine?"
*Yí Yè* rebuked him, saying:
"Get out!
You are a person who has suffered punishment.
What business do you have daring to beg for wine from an elder!"
The *yuè* retreated.
After *Yí Yè* left,
the *yuè* then poured water under the eaves of the palace gate,
resembling someone drowning.
The next day,
the king went out and questioned him,
saying:
"Who urinated here?"
The *yuè* replied:
"I did not see it.
However, yesterday the grand master *Yí Yè* stood here."
The king therefore executed *Yí Yè*.
Two ministers of the Wèi King were not on good terms with Jìyáng Jūn,
so Jìyáng Jūn used someone to falsely
issue a forged royal decree to plot an attack against himself.
The King sent someone to ask Jìyáng Jūn, saying:
"Who do you have a grievance with?"
He replied:
"I dare not have a grievance with anyone.
However,
I once had a disagreement with two people,
but it is not enough to lead to this."
The King asked his attendants,
and the attendants said:
"Indeed."
Consequently, the King executed the two men.
Jì Xīn and Yuán Qiān harbored resentment against each other.
Sīmǎ Xǐxīn had a new grudge against Jì Xīn,
and secretly sent someone to kill Yuán Qiān.
The ruler of Zhōngshān thought it was Jì Xīn,
and consequently executed him.
The Jīng King had a favored concubine named Zhèng Xiù.
The Jīng King had recently acquired a beautiful woman,
and Zhèng Xiù taught her, saying:
"The King greatly likes people who cover their mouths.
To get close to the King,
you must cover your mouth."
When the beautiful woman entered to see the King,
she approached the King,
and covered her mouth.
The King asked the reason for this,
and Zhèng Xiù said:
"She is actually saying that she dislikes the King's odor."
When the King, Zhèng Xiù, and the beautiful woman were sitting together,
Xiù first cautioned the attendant, saying:
"If the King happens to say something,
you must quickly obey the King's words."
The beautiful woman approached the King closely,
and repeatedly covered her mouth.
The King became enraged and said:
"Cut off her nose!"
The attendant then drew his knife and cut off the beautiful woman's nose.
Another account says:
The Wèi King sent a beautiful woman to the Jīng King as a gift.
The Jīng King was very pleased with her.
The King's consort, Zhèng Xiù, knowing that the King was pleased and loved her,
also pleased and loved her,
even more than the King.
As for clothes and playthings,
she chose what the new beauty desired for her.
The King said:
"The consort knows that I love the new beauty,
and her pleasing and loving her is even greater than my own.
This is how a filial son should care for his parents,
and how a loyal minister should serve his ruler."
The consort, knowing that the King did not consider her jealous,
then said to the new beauty:
"The King is very pleased and loves you,
but he dislikes your nose.
When you see the King, always cover your nose,
and then the King will favor you for a long time."
Thereupon the new beauty followed her advice,
and every time she saw the King,
she would always cover her nose.
The King said to the consort:
"The new beauty always covers her nose when she sees me,
why is that?"
She replied:
"I don't know."
The King pressed her for an answer,
and she replied:
"She once said that she disliked smelling the King's odor."
The King angrily said:
"Cut off her nose!"
The consort first cautioned the attendant, saying:
"If the King happens to say something,
you must obey the order."
The attendant then drew his knife and cut off the beautiful woman's nose.
Fèi Wújí was
a close associate of the Jīng Chancellor.
Qì Wǎn had newly served the Chancellor,
and the Chancellor loved him greatly.
Wújí then said to the Chancellor:
"You love Wǎn greatly,
why not host a banquet at his home once?"
The Chancellor said:
"Good."
He then ordered preparations to be made at Qì Wǎn's home.
Wújí taught Wǎn, saying:
"The Chancellor is very arrogant and fond of military matters,
you must be respectful and cautious,
and quickly arrange soldiers below the hall and in the courtyard."
Wǎn did as he was told.
The Chancellor went and was greatly alarmed,
saying:
"What is this?"
Wújí said:
"You are in danger,
leave quickly!
The situation is unpredictable."
The Chancellor was furious,
raised his troops, and executed Qì Wǎn,
ultimately killing him.
Xī Shǒu and Zhāng Shòu had a feud.
Chén Xū had recently entered service
and did not get along with Xī Shǒu,
so he secretly sent someone to kill Zhāng Shòu.
The Wèi King thought it was Xī Shǒu,
and consequently executed him.
In Zhōngshān, there was a low-ranking noble son
whose horse was very thin
and carriage very dilapidated.
One of his attendants, who harbored a secret grudge,
then requested the King on his behalf, saying:
"The noble son is very poor,
and his horse is very thin.
Why doesn't Your Majesty increase the horse's feed?"
The King did not agree.
The attendant then secretly ordered
the hay barn to be burned down at night.
The King thought it was the low-ranking noble son,
and consequently executed him.
In Wèi, there was an old scholar
who did not get along with Jìyáng Jūn.
A guest who had a private feud with the old scholar
then attacked and killed the old scholar,
hoping to gain favor with Jìyáng Jūn,
saying:
"Because he was disrespectful to you,
I killed him for you."
Jìyáng Jūn did not investigate and rewarded him.
Another account says:
Jìyáng Jūn had a young, low-ranking son,
who, being unnoticed,
wanted to gain favor with the ruler.
The Qí envoy ordered an old scholar
to dig for medicinal herbs on Mount Mǎlí.
The Jìyáng junior son wanted to use this as a merit,
and went to see the ruler, saying:
"The Qí envoy ordered an old scholar
to dig for medicinal herbs on Mount Mǎlí.
He is ostensibly digging for medicinal herbs,
but in reality, he is spying on your state.
If you do not kill him,
he will use Jìyáng Jūn
to accuse you of crimes in Qí.
I request to assassinate him."
The ruler said:
"You may."
Thereupon, the next day, he caught him in Chéngyīn
and assassinated him,
and Jìyáng Jūn became even more intimate with him.
Persuasion Four:
Chén Xū,
a minister of the Wèi King,
was on good terms with the Jīng King,
and induced Jīng to attack Wèi.
After Jīng attacked Wèi,
Chén Xū then requested to act as an intermediary for the Wèi King to resolve the conflict,
using the power of Jīng to intimidate Wèi.
During the time of Hán Zhāo Hóu,
millet seeds were once very expensive.
Zhāo Hóu ordered people to inspect the granary,
and the officials were indeed stealing millet seeds
and selling them in great quantities.
When Zhāo Xīxù was employed by Jīng,
someone burned down the granary and cellar,
but the person was unknown.
Zhāo Xīxù ordered the officials to arrest straw merchants
and question them,
and it turned out they were the arsonists.
During the time of Zhāo Xī Hóu,
the cook presented food,
and there was raw liver in the soup.
Zhāo Hóu summoned the cook's assistant
and scolded him, saying:
"Why did you put raw liver in my soup?"
The cook kowtowed, admitting his crime and deserving death,
saying:
"I secretly wanted to replace the head cook."
First:
Xī Hóu was bathing,
and there was gravel in the water.
Xī Hóu said:
"If the bath is dispensed with,
will there be someone to replace me?"
Those nearby answered,
"There is."
Xī Hóu said:
"Summon him here."
He questioned him, saying:
"Why did you put gravel in the bath water?"
He replied:
"If the bath is dispensed with,
then your servant can replace you,
therefore I put gravel in the bath water."
During the time of Wén Gōng,
the kitchen steward served roasted meat, and hair was entangled around it.
Wén Gōng summoned the cook and questioned him, saying:
"Do you want to choke me?
Why is there hair around the roasted meat?"
The cook kowtowed and bowed repeatedly, pleading:
"Your servant has three capital offenses:
Grasping the whetstone to sharpen the knife,
the sharpness is like Gàn Jiàng's sword,
cutting meat so that the meat is severed, but the hair is not,
that is my first offense.
Grasping the skewer to pierce the meat cubes
without seeing the hair,
that is my second offense.
Holding the blazing stove,
with the charcoal fire all red-hot,
and the roasted meat is cooked
but the hair does not burn,
that is my third offense.
Could there be someone below the hall who secretly hates your servant?"
The Duke said:
"Good."
Then he summoned those below the hall and questioned them,
and indeed it was so,
so he executed him.
First:
Jìn Píng Gōng was feasting guests,
and the young steward presented roasted meat with hair entwined around it.
Píng Gōng hastily ordered the butcher to be killed,
without any reversing of the order.
The butcher cried out to heaven, saying:
"Alas!
I have three offenses,
and I die without knowing it!"
Píng Gōng said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"The sharpness of my knife
is such that it cuts through bone like the wind, but does not cut hair,
this is my first death.
Roasting it with mulberry charcoal,
the meat is white and red, but the hair does not char,
this is my second death.
After the roasting is done,
I peered at it closely with double eyelids,
the hair was wrapped around the roasted meat, but my eyes did not see it,
this is my third death.
I suspect that there is someone below the hall who harbors hatred for me?
Isn't killing me too soon!"
Rǎng Hóu was the chancellor of Qín, and Qí was strong.
Rǎng Hóu wanted to establish Qín as emperor,
but Qí did not agree,
so he requested to establish Qí as the Eastern Emperor,
but could not succeed.
Persuasions 5:
During the time of Jìn Xiàn Gōng,
Lí Jī was favored,
compared to the official wife,
and wanted to replace Crown Prince Shēn Shēng with her son Xī Qí,
therefore, she falsely accused Shēn Shēng to the ruler and killed him,
and then established Xī Qí as the Crown Prince.
The ruler of Zhèng had already established a Crown Prince,
but he had a beloved beauty
and wanted her son to be the heir.
The official wife was afraid,
so she used poison to assassinate the ruler.
Wèi Zhōu Xū was powerful in Wèi,
comparable to the ruler,
and all the ministers and people feared his power and influence.
Zhōu Xū eventually killed his ruler and seized his government.
Gōngzǐ Cháo,
was the crown prince of Zhōu,
and his younger brother Gōngzǐ Gēn was greatly favored by the ruler.
When the ruler died,
he rebelled with Eastern Zhōu,
dividing it into two states.
Chǔ Chéng Wáng made Shāng Chén the crown prince,
but then wanted to replace him with Gōngzǐ Zhí.
Shāng Chén rebelled,
and then attacked and killed Chéng Wáng.
First:
Chǔ Chéng Wáng made Shāng Chén the crown prince,
but then wanted to replace him with Gōngzǐ Zhí.
Shāng Chén heard of this,
but was not certain,
so he said to his tutor Pān Chóng:
"How can I verify it?"
Pān Chóng said:
"Feast Jiāng Mǐ but do not show respect."
The crown prince listened to him.
Jiāng Mǐ said:
"Alas,
you servant!
It is fitting that the king wants to depose you
and establish Zhí."
Shāng Chén said:
"It is true."
Pān Chóng said:
"Can you serve him?"
He said: "I cannot."
"Can you become a feudal lord for him?"
He said: "I cannot."
"Can you undertake a major event?"
He said:
"I can."
Thereupon, he raised troops who had encamped overnight and attacked Chéng Wáng.
Chéng Wáng asked to eat bear's paw before dying,
but it was not permitted,
so he committed suicide.
Hán Huī was the chancellor of Hán Āi Hóu,
and Yán Suì was powerful with the ruler,
and the two greatly harmed each other.
Yán Suì then ordered someone to assassinate Hán Huī in court.
Hán Huī ran to the ruler and embraced him,
and then Yán Suì assassinated Hán Huī and also Āi Hóu.
Tián Héng was the chancellor of Qí,
and Kàn Zhǐ was powerful with Jiǎn Gōng,
and the two hated each other and wanted to harm each other.
Tián Héng then carried out private favors
to seize his state,
and then killed Jiǎn Gōng and seized his government.
Dài Huān was the Grand Steward of Sòng,
and Huáng Xǐ was powerful with the ruler.
The two contended for power
and harmed each other.
Huáng Xǐ then killed the ruler of Sòng
and seized his government.
Hú Tū said:
"If the ruler of a state favors the inner court
then the crown prince is in danger,
if he favors the outer court
then the chancellor is in danger."
The ruler of Zhèng asked Zhèng Zhāo:
"How is the crown prince?"
He replied:
"The crown prince is not yet born."
The ruler said:
"The crown prince has already been established
and you say 'not yet born,'
what is the reason?"
He replied:
"Although the crown prince has been established,
if your fondness for beauty does not cease,
and your beloved has a son,
you will surely love him,
if you love him, you will surely want to make him the heir,
therefore, I say 'the crown prince is not yet born.'"
Persuasions 6:
Wén Wáng funded Fèi Zhòng and had him travel by Zhòu's side,
ordering him to advise Zhòu and disrupt his mind.
The king of Jīng sent a messenger to Qín,
and the king of Qín treated him with great courtesy.
The king said:
"A neighboring state having a wise man
is a worry for our state.
Now the messenger of the king of Jīng is very wise,
I am troubled by this."
The assembled ministers remonstrated, saying:
"With Your Majesty's sagacity and the state's abundant resources,
and desiring the worthy men of Jīng,
why doesn't Your Majesty deeply understand them
and secretly possess them?
If Jīng believes they are used externally,
they will surely be executed."
When Zhòng Ní governed Lǔ,
things lost on the road were not picked up,
which troubled Qí Jǐng Gōng.
Lí Qiě said to Jǐng Gōng,
"Removing Zhòng Ní is as easy as blowing away a hair.
Why doesn't Your Majesty welcome him with generous stipends and high positions,
and present Duke Āi with female entertainers to indulge and honor his desires?
If Duke Āi delights in the new music,
he will surely neglect governance,
Zhòng Ní will certainly remonstrate,
and his remonstrations will surely lead to a light severance from Lǔ."
Jǐng Gōng said,
"Good."
He then ordered Lí Qiě to present Duke Āi with six female entertainers.
Duke Āi delighted in them
and indeed neglected governance.
Zhòng Ní remonstrated but was not heeded
and left to go to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ said to Gān Xiàng,
"I wish to use Chǔ to support Gān Mào
and make him the chancellor of Qín,
is that possible?"
Gān Xiàng replied,
"It is not possible."
The King asked,
"Why?"
He said,
"Gān Mào, when young, served Shǐ Jǔ Xiānshēng,
Shǐ Jǔ,
was the gatekeeper of Shàngcài,
who greatly failed to serve his lord,
and slightly failed to care for his family,
and was known throughout the world for his harshness.
Mào served him
obediently.
King Huì's wisdom
and Zhāng Yí's eloquence
Mào served.
He obtained ten positions and avoided punishment.
This shows that Mào is worthy."
The King said,
"Choosing a chancellor for an enemy state
and choosing a worthy one,
why is that not possible?"
Gān Xiàng said,
"Previously, Your Majesty sent Shào Huá to Yuè.
In five years, he was able to destroy Yuè.
The reason for this
was that Yuè was in chaos while Chǔ was well-governed.
Previously, we knew to use him to destroy Yuè,
but now you want to destroy Qín,
wouldn't it be too quick to destroy them?"
The King said,
"If that is the case, what should be done?"
Gān Xiàng replied,
"It is better to make Gòng Lì the chancellor."
The King said,
"What can Gòng Lì do as chancellor?"
He replied,
"Gòng Lì, being young, received love and favor,
and grew to become a noble minister.
He wears the king's clothes,
holds dùruò flowers in his mouth,
and holds a jade ring,
to listen in court,
and will be useful to throw Qín into chaos."
Wú governed Jīng,
and Zǐ Xū sent someone to declare in Jīng,
"If Zǐ Qí is employed,
we will attack;
if Zǐ Cháng is employed,
we will leave."
The people of Jīng heard this
and therefore employed Zǐ Cháng and dismissed Zǐ Qí.
The people of Wú attacked them
and consequently defeated them.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn attacked Yú and Guó,
and then sent them steeds from Qūchǎn,
jade from Chuíjí,
and six female entertainers,
to indulge their desires and disrupt their governance.
Shū Xiàng slandered Cháng Hóng,
writing in a letter:
"Cháng Hóng said to Shū Xiàng,
'You should say to the ruler of Jìn for me,
that the time we agreed upon with the ruler,
the time is now right.
Why not quickly come with troops?'"
Then he pretended to leave the letter in the courtyard of the ruler of Zhōu
and hastily departed.
Zhōu thought Cháng Hóng was selling out Zhōu,
and therefore punished Cháng Hóng and killed him.
