Now, the people sing and dance for the virtue of the Tián Chéng clan,
the people's virtue turns to them.
Therefore it is said,
"It will be the Tián Chéng clan!'"
The duke wept openly, saying,
"Is this not sad!
I have the state,
but the Tián Chéng clan has it.
What can be done about this now?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"What does your lord worry about?
If your lord wishes to take it back,
then draw near to the worthy and keep distant from the unworthy,
govern its troubles,
lessen its punishments,
aid the poor and care for the orphans and widows,
practice benevolence and provide for the insufficient,
the people will return to your lord,
then even if there are ten Tián Chéng clans,
what can they do to your lord?"
Someone said,
Jǐng Gōng did not know how to use power,
and Shī Kuàng and Yàn Zǐ
did not know how to eliminate trouble.
Now, hunters
rely on the comfort of carriages,
use the speed of six horses,
and employ Wáng Liáng to assist with the reins,
then their bodies will not be tired
and they will easily catch swift beasts.
Now, abandoning the benefit of carriages,
forsaking the speed of six horses
and the skill of Wáng Liáng's driving,
and going down to chase the beasts on foot,
then even with Lóu Jì's feet, they will never catch the beasts.
Relying on good horses and sturdy carriages,
then even a slave can have plenty.
The state
is the lord's carriage;
power
is the lord's horse.
Now, not residing in power
to prohibit and punish ministers who take liberties and act on favoritism,
but necessarily being thick with kindness
and aligning with the world to compete for the people,
these are all not riding the lord's carriage,
not relying on the benefit of the horse,
abandoning the carriage and chasing on foot.
Therefore it is said,
"Jǐng Gōng was a lord who did not know how to use power,
and Shī Kuàng and
Yàn Zǐ
were ministers who did not know how to eliminate trouble."
Zǐ Xià said,
"The *Chūnqiū* records ministers killing their lords
and sons killing their fathers,
numbering in the tens.
All were not the result of a single day's accumulation,
but gradually progressed to that point."
Generally, treachery
persists for a long time and accumulates,
accumulation leads to great strength,
great strength enables killing,
therefore an enlightened lord eliminates it early.
Now, Tián Cháng's causing disorder
has shown gradual signs,
but the lord does not punish him.
Yàn Zǐ does not cause his lord to prohibit encroaching ministers,
but causes his lord to practice benevolence,
therefore Jiǎn Gōng suffered his calamity.
Therefore Zǐ Xià said,
"One who is good at holding power
eliminates the sprouts of treachery early."
Jì Sūn was minister of Lǔ,
and Zǐ Lù was the magistrate of Hòu.
Lǔ in the fifth month mobilized the people to dig a long ditch,
during this work,
Zǐ Lù used his private salary grain to make gruel and rice,
inviting those digging the ditch at the crossroads of Wǔ Fù
to eat it.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it,
and sent Zǐgòng to overturn his rice,
and smash his utensils,
saying,
"The Lord of Lǔ has people,
why do you feed them?"
Zǐlù angrily puffed up,
rolled up his sleeves and entered,
requesting,
"Does Fūzǐ dislike Yóu for being rén yì?
What I have learned from Fūzǐ
is rén yì;
rén yì
is to share what one has with the world and share its benefits.
Now, I, Yóu, am using my salary grain to feed the people,
why is that unacceptable?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Yóu is boorish!
I thought you understood this,
but you still haven't reached that level.
You are indeed so ignorant of propriety!
Your feeding them
is out of love for them.
In ritual,
the Son of Heaven loves the world,
the lords love their domains,
the grand officers love their offices,
the shì love their families.
To exceed what one loves is called encroachment.
Now the Lord of Lǔ has the people,
and you presumptuously love them,
this is your encroachment,
is it not deceitful!"
Before the words were finished,
an envoy from Jìsūn arrived,
rebuking,
"Féi also mobilizes the people and employs them,
and you, sir, have your disciples command the laborers
and feed them,
are you going to seize Féi's people?"
Kǒngzǐ harnessed his chariot and left Lǔ.
Even with Kǒngzǐ's virtue,
and Jìsūn not being the Lord of Lǔ,
using the resources of a subject,
appropriating the techniques of a ruler,
nipping things in the bud,
Zǐlù was unable to carry out his private benevolence,
and harm was prevented from arising,
how much more so with a ruler!
If with Duke Jǐng's power he had prevented Tián Cháng's encroachments,
then surely there would have been no calamity of being usurped and murdered.
Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in the east at Qí.
On the eastern seacoast of Qí, there were two hermits
named Kuáng Yù and Huáshì, brothers, who established a creed, saying:
"We do not serve the Son of Heaven,
we do not befriend the lords,
we till and eat,
we dig wells and drink,
we have no requests of others.
No supreme name,
no lord's salary,
we do not engage in officialdom but devote ourselves to labor."
Tàigōng Wàng arrived at Yíngqiū,
and ordered the officials to seize and kill them,
taking them as the first to be punished.
Zhōu Gōngdàn heard of it from Lǔ,
and sent an urgent message to inquire, saying:
"These two men
are virtuous.
Today, as you enjoy the state, you kill the virtuous,
why?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"These brothers established a creed, saying:
'We do not serve the Son of Heaven,
we do not befriend the lords,
we till and eat,
we dig wells and drink,
we have no requests of others.
No supreme name,
no lord's salary,
we do not engage in officialdom but devote ourselves to labor.'
Because they do not serve the Son of Heaven,
it means I, Wàng, cannot make them my subjects;
because they do not befriend the lords,
it means I, Wàng, cannot employ them;
they till and eat,
they dig wells and drink,
and have no requests of others,
it means I, Wàng, cannot use rewards and punishments to encourage and restrain them.
Moreover, they want no supreme name;
even if they are knowledgeable,
they will not be used by me, Wàng;
not relying on the ruler's salary; 〓#
even if they are virtuous, 〓#
they will not work for me, Wàng. 〓#
Not serving in office
means there is no governance,
not being entrusted
means there is no loyalty.
Moreover, the means by which the former kings employed their subjects and people
were through titles and salaries or through punishments.
Now these four are insufficient to employ them,
then who am I, Wàng, supposed to be ruler for?
Not submitting to arms and armor, yet being prominent;
not engaging in tilling and weeding, yet being famous;
these are not the ways to teach the country.
Now, there is a horse here,
resembling a Jì in appearance,
the finest steed in the world.
However, when driven, it does not go forward;
when reined, it does not stop;
when turned left, it does not go left;
when turned right, it does not go right;
then even a lowly servant
would not entrust his feet to it.
The reason a lowly servant is willing to entrust his feet to a Jì
is because a Jì can pursue benefits and avoid harm.
Now, if it cannot be used by people,
even a lowly servant
will not entrust his feet to it.
Having already regarded themselves as virtuous shì of the world
but not being employed by the ruler,
practicing extreme virtue but not being used by the lord,
this is not what a wise ruler can employ,
just as a Jì cannot be directed left or right,
therefore, I executed them."
Another version says:
Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in the east at Qí.
There was a virtuous man named Kuáng Yù on the seacoast.
Tàigōng Wàng heard of him and went to invite him,
but Kuáng Yù refused the gifts of horses at the door three times
and did not agree to meet with him,
so Tàigōng Wàng executed him.
At that time,
Zhōu Gōngdàn was in Lǔ,
and rushed to stop him;
by the time he arrived,
he had already been executed.
Zhōu Gōngdàn said:
"Kuáng Yù
was a virtuous man of the world,
why did you execute him?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Kuáng Yù planned not to serve the Son of Heaven,
nor to befriend the lords.
I feared that he would disrupt the laws and change the teachings,
so I took him as the first to be punished.
Now there is a horse here,
whose appearance resembles a Jì,
but when driven, it does not go forward;
when pulled, it does not advance;
even a lowly servant would not entrust his feet to its reins."
Rú Ě persuaded Duke Sìmíng of Wèi.
Duke Sìmíng of Wèi was pleased and sighed.
Those around him said:
"Why do you not appoint him as prime minister?"
The Duke said:
"The horse that resembles a deer
is valued at a thousand gold pieces.
However, there are horses worth a thousand gold pieces
but no deer worth a thousand gold pieces,
because horses are used by people,
while deer are not used by people.
Now Rú Ě
is fit to be a prime minister of a state of ten thousand chariots.
He has the interests of a great state in mind,
and his heart is not in Wèi.
Although he is articulate and wise,
he will not be used by me.
This is why I do not appoint him as prime minister."
When Lord Xuē was the prime minister of Marquis Zhāohóu of Wèi,
among those around him were Luán Zǐ,
named Yáng Hú and Pān Qí,
who were highly regarded by the king,
but did not work for Lord Xuē.
Lord Xuē worried about this,
so he summoned them to play bó with him,
giving one of them a hundred gold pieces,
and having their brothers play bó;
soon after, he added another two hundred gold pieces to each.
Fāng Bó was at leisure,
and an usher announced that the son of Zhāng Jì was at the gate.
The duke was enraged,
stroked his weapon, and instructed the usher:
"Kill him!
I have heard that Jì does not compose literary works."
After a moment,
Shí Jìyǔ was at his side
and said:
"That is not so.
I have secretly heard that Jì does much for you,
it's just that his merits have not been publicly known."
So the duke stopped the execution of the guest,
treated him with great courtesy,
and said:
"Previously, I heard that Jì did not compose literary works,
so I wanted to kill him.
Now that he truly composes literary works,
how could I forget Jì!"
He ordered the granary to present one thousand *shí* of grain,
ordered the treasury to present five hundred *jīn*,
and ordered the stable manager to present two carriages of fine horses from the private stable.
He then instructed the eunuch to send twenty beautiful concubines from the palace to Jì.
The officials of the Luán family then said to each other:
"Those who act in the duke's interest will surely benefit,
and those who do not act in the duke's interest will surely suffer harm.
Why should we begrudge acting in the duke's interest?"
So they privately competed to encourage each other
and then acted in his interest.
Duke Xuē, with the power of a subject,
employed the techniques of a ruler,
yet could not prevent harm from arising;
how much more so for a ruler who makes mistakes!
Now, those who tame birds cut off their lower flight feathers.
Cutting off their lower flight feathers
ensures they must rely on people for food;
how could they not be tame?
The way of a wise ruler raising subjects is also like this,
ensuring that subjects cannot but benefit from the lord's emoluments,
and cannot be without the reputation of serving their superiors.
Benefiting from the lord's emoluments
and having the reputation of serving one's superiors
ensures they cannot but obey.
Discourses Two:
Shēn Zǐ said:
"If the ruler is perceptive,
people will be on guard against him.
If he is not perceptive,
people will deceive him.
If his knowledge is apparent,
people will embellish for him.
If his knowledge is not apparent,
people will conceal from him.
If he has no desires that are apparent,
people will control him.
If he has desires that are apparent,
people will bait him.
Therefore, it is said:
'I have no way to know him,
only *wúwéi* can regulate him.'"
Another said:
Shēn Zǐ said:
"If you are cautious in speech,
people will know you.
If you are cautious in action,
people will follow you.
If you have knowledge that is apparent,
people will conceal you.
If you have no knowledge that is apparent,
people will guess at you.
If you have knowledge,
people will praise you.
If you have no knowledge,
people will manipulate you.
Therefore, it is said:
'Only *wúwéi* can regulate them.'"
Tián Zǐfāng asked Táng Yìjū:
"What must a hunter be cautious about?"
He replied:
"Birds watch you with hundreds of eyes,
and you control them with two eyes.
You must be cautious and watchful."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"Good.
You apply this to hunting,
and I will apply it to the state."
The Elder of Zhèng heard this and said:
"Tián Zǐfāng knows that he wants to be watchful,
but has not grasped how to be watchful.
Being empty, still, without apparent intent,
that is watchfulness."
Another said:
King Xuān of Qí asked Táng Yìzǐ about hunting:
"What is most important for a hunter?"
Táng Yìzǐ said:
"Being cautious and watchful."
The king said:
"What do you mean by being cautious and watchful?"
He replied:
"Birds watch people with dozens of eyes,
and people watch birds with two eyes.
How can one not be cautious and watchful?
Therefore, it is said
'Being cautious and watchful' is key."
The king said:
"If that is so, then for governing the world,
how does one achieve this watchfulness?
Now, the ruler observes a state with two eyes,
and a state observes the ruler with ten thousand eyes.
How will he be watchful on his own behalf?"
He replied:
"The Elder of Zhèng has said:
'Being empty, still, acting through *wúwéi*, and without apparent intent.'
This can achieve such watchfulness!"
Guó Yáng was more important than the ruler of Zhèng.
Having heard that the ruler disliked him,
he attended a drinking banquet
and first said to the ruler:
"If I should unfortunately have faults,
I hope that you will be kind enough to inform me.
If I may change,
then I can avoid the death penalty."
A guest persuaded King Xuān of Hán.
King Xuān was pleased and sighed.
His attendants recounted the king's pleasure
to the guest beforehand to show their favor.
When Lord Jìngguō was the chancellor of Qí,
the queen died,
and it was not known whom to appoint.
So he presented jade earrings to determine this.
Another said:
Duke Xuē was the chancellor of Qí.
When Lady Wēi, the wife of King Wēi of Qí, died,
there were ten palace women who were all favored by the king.
Duke Xuē wanted to know whom the king wanted to appoint,
so he requested to appoint one of them as queen.
If the king listened to him,
it meant that his suggestion was accepted by the king
and was more important than appointing a queen.
If the king did not listen,
it meant that his suggestion was not accepted,
and was less important than appointing a queen.
Wanting to know in advance whom the king wanted to appoint,
in order to encourage the king to appoint her,
he then had ten jade earrings made,
made one of them particularly beautiful,
and presented them to the king.
The king distributed them among the ten palace women.
The next day, at court,
he observed where the beautiful earrings were
and encouraged the king to make her the queen.
Gān Mào was the chancellor of King Huì of Qín.
King Huì favored Gōngsūn Yǎn.
He spoke with him privately,
saying:
"I will appoint you as chancellor."
An official of Gān Mào secretly overheard this
and told Gān Mào.
Gān Mào went to see the king
and said:
"If Your Majesty has found a worthy chancellor,
I dare to bow twice in congratulation."
The king said:
"I have entrusted the state to you;
how could I find another worthy chancellor?"
He replied:
"You are going to appoint Xīshǒu as chancellor."
The king said:
"How did you hear of this?"
He replied:
"Xīshǒu told me."
The king was angry that Xīshǒu had leaked the information
and then banished him.
First:
Xī Shǒu was a skilled general in the world,
and a minister of the King of Liáng.
The King of Qín wanted to obtain him to govern the world together.
Xī Shǒu said:
"Yǎn is merely a subject,
and dares not leave the sovereign's state."
After a year,
Xī Shǒu committed a crime against the King of Liáng,
fled and entered Qín,
and the King of Qín greatly favored him.
Chūlǐ Jí, a general of Qín,
feared that Xī Shǒu would replace him as general,
so he drilled a hole in a place where the king often spoke privately.
Soon the king indeed consulted with Xī Shǒu,
saying:
"I want to attack Hán,
what do you think?"
Xī Shǒu said:
"Autumn would be a good time."
The king said:
"I want to entrust the state to you,
you must not divulge this."
Xī Shǒu retreated, bowed twice and said:
"I accept the command."
Thereupon Chūlǐ Jí listened through the hole.
The attendants all said:
"The army will rise in autumn to attack Hán,
and Xī Shǒu will be the general."
On that day,
all the attendants knew it;
in that month,
everyone within the borders knew it.
The king summoned Chūlǐ Jí and said:
"What is all this commotion?
How did this get out?"
Chūlǐ Jí said:
"It seems to be from Xī Shǒu."
The king said:
"I said nothing to Xī Shǒu,
how could it be Xī Shǒu?"
Chūlǐ Jí said:
"Xī Shǒu is a stranger,
newly accused,
and his heart is isolated.
These words are self-inflicted upon the crowd."
The king said:
"That is so."
He sent someone to summon Xī Shǒu,
but he had already fled to the other feudal lords.
Tángxī Gōng said to Zhāo Hóu:
"Suppose there is a jade cup worth a thousand gold pieces,
open at both ends and without a bottom,
can it hold water?"
Zhāo Hóu said:
"It cannot."
"If there is a clay vessel that does not leak,
can it hold wine?"
Zhāo Hóu said:
"It can."
He replied:
"A clay vessel,
is very cheap,
but if it does not leak,
it can hold wine.
Although there is a jade cup worth a thousand gold pieces,
it is very valuable but without a bottom,
and it leaks,
so it cannot hold water,
then who would pour anything into it?"
Now, for the ruler of men,
to leak the words of his ministers,
is like a jade cup without a bottom.
Although you have sages and wisdom,
they cannot fully use their skills,
because it leaks."
Zhāo Hóu said:
"That is so."
Zhāo Hóu heard the words of Tángxī Gōng,
and from then on,
when he wanted to initiate major affairs of state,
he never failed to sleep alone,
for fear of speaking in his dreams
and letting people know his plans.
Another story:
Tángxī Gōng saw Zhāo Hóu and said:
"Suppose there is a white jade cup without a handle,
and a clay cup with a handle.
If you are thirsty,
which will you use to drink?"
The ruler said:
"I will use the clay cup."
Tángxī Gōng said:
"The white jade cup is beautiful,
but you will not use it to drink,
because it has no handle?"
The ruler said:
"That is so."
Tángxī Gōng said:
"For the ruler of men
to leak the words of his ministers,
is like a jade cup without a handle."
Every time Tángxī Gōng saw him and left,
Zhāo Hóu would sleep alone,
fearing that he would speak in his dreams
and reveal secrets to his wives and concubines.
Shēn Zǐ said:
"One who sees alone is called insightful,
one who listens alone is called discerning.
One who can decide alone,
can therefore be the ruler of the world."
Discourses 3:
There was a Sòng person who sold wine,
the measures were very fair,
he treated customers with great respect,
the wine he made was very good,
and the sign hanging was very high and visible,
yet it did not sell,
and the wine turned sour.
He wondered why,
and asked someone he knew,
he asked the elder Yáng Qiàn.
Qiàn said:
"Is your dog fierce?"
He said:
"If the dog is fierce,
then why does the wine not sell?"
He said:
"People are afraid of it.
If a child
carries money and a jug to buy wine,
and the dog comes out to bite him,
this is why the wine turns sour and does not sell."
A state also has dogs.
A man of virtue holds his skills
and wants to enlighten the lord of ten thousand chariots,
but the great ministers act as fierce dogs, welcoming and biting him,
this is why the ruler is deceived and threatened,
and why men of virtue are not employed.
Therefore, Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What is the greatest concern in governing a state?"
He replied:
"The greatest concern is shrine rats."
The Duke said:
"Why be concerned about shrine rats?"
He replied:
"Has your lordship seen those who build shrines?
They plant trees and plaster them.
Rats burrow in the gaps,
and dig holes to dwell in them.
If you smoke them out, you fear burning the trees,
if you flood them, you fear the plaster will collapse,
this is why the shrine rats cannot be caught."
Now, the people around the ruler,
when they go out, they become powerful
and extract benefits from the people,
and when they come in, they form cliques and conceal evils from the ruler.
They secretly reveal the ruler's intentions to the outside,
and the outside and inside become powerful together,
and the various ministers and officials see this as wealth.
If the officials are not punished, they will disrupt the law,
but if they are punished, the ruler will be uneasy.
They occupy and possess these positions,
and these are also the shrine rats of the state."
Therefore, if a minister holds power and monopolizes prohibitions,
and clearly benefits those who are for him,
and harms those who are not for him,
these are also fierce dogs.
If the great ministers act as fierce dogs
and bite men of virtue,
and the people around the ruler act as shrine rats, spying on the ruler's intentions,
and the ruler does not notice,
then,
how can the ruler not be obstructed,
and how can the state not perish?
First: #
In Sòng, there was a Zhuāng Shì who sold wine,
and his wine was always excellent.
Someone sent a servant to buy wine from Zhuāng Shì,
but his dog bit the person,
so the messenger didn't dare to go,
and instead bought wine from another family.
He asked:
"Why didn't you buy wine from Zhuāng Shì?"
He replied: "Today, Zhuāng Shì's wine is sour."
Therefore, it is said: "If the dog is not killed, the wine will turn sour."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng,
"What is the worry in governing a state?"
He replied:
"The most troubling are the altar rats.
The altar
is wood that has been plastered over,
and rats use it as a place to dwell.
If you smoke them out, the wood will burn;
if you flood them out, the plaster will crumble.
This is why altar rats are so troublesome.
Now, the attendants around the ruler,
when they go out, they use their influence to seize profits from the people,
and when they enter, they collude, deceive, and cover up evil
to mislead the ruler.
If they are not punished, they will disrupt the law;
if they are punished, the ruler will be in danger.
To rely on them and possess them,
this is also like having altar rats."
Therefore, when ministers hold power and monopolize prohibitions,
it is clear that those who act for their own benefit will surely profit,
and those who do not act for their own benefit will surely suffer harm;
they are like fierce dogs.
Therefore, if the attendants are altar rats,
and those in power are fierce dogs,
then strategies cannot be implemented.
Yáo wanted to pass the empire to Shùn,
but Gǔn admonished him, saying:
"This is inauspicious!
How can you pass the empire to a commoner?"
Yáo did not listen and
raised troops and executed Gǔn on the outskirts of Yǔ Shān.
Gòng Gōng again admonished him, saying:
"How can you pass the empire to a commoner?"
Yáo did not listen and
again raised troops
and executed Gòng Gōng in the capital of Yōu Zhōu.
Therefore, no one in the world dared to speak
against passing the empire to Shùn.
Zhòng Ní heard of this and said:
"Yáo's knowing of Shùn's virtue
was not the difficult part.
But to go so far as to execute those who remonstrated and then still pass the empire to Shùn
was truly the difficult part."
First:
"If you do not let what you suspect undermine what you have observed,
that is difficult."
King Zhuāng of Jīng had a law about the "thatched gate," saying:
"When ministers, high officials, and all the princes enter the court,
if a horse's hoof steps on the eaves-trough,
the court officer shall cut the shaft of the chariot
and execute the driver."
Then the crown prince entered the court,
and a horse's hoof stepped on the eaves-trough,
and the court officer cut the shaft of the chariot
and executed the driver.
The crown prince was angry
and entered and wept to the king, saying:
"Avenge me by executing the court officer."
The king said:
"The law
is that by which we revere the ancestral temples
and honor the altars of the soil and grain.
Therefore, one who can establish laws, follow orders,
and respect the altars of the soil and grain
is a minister of the altars of the soil and grain;
how can he be executed?
One who violates the law, abandons orders,
and does not respect the altars of the soil and grain
is a minister who overrides the ruler and whose subordinates surpass their superiors.
If ministers override the ruler,
then the ruler loses his authority;
if subordinates surpass
their superiors, then the position of those above is endangered.
If authority is lost and position is endangered,
the altars of the soil and grain cannot be protected;
how then shall I bequeath anything to my descendants?"
Therefore, the crown prince then turned and fled,
avoided his residence and slept in the open for three days,
and facing north, bowed twice and pleaded for the death penalty.
First:
The King of Chǔ urgently summoned the crown prince.
The law of Chǔ was that
carriages were not allowed to reach the thatched gate.
It was raining,
and there were puddles in the courtyard,
so the crown prince drove his carriage up to the thatched gate.
The court officer said:
"Carriages are not allowed to reach the thatched gate.
Reaching the thatched gate
is against the law."
The crown prince said:
"The king summoned me urgently;
I could not wait for the puddles to disappear."
He then drove on.
The court officer raised his spear and struck the horse,
destroying the carriage.
The crown prince entered and wept to the king, saying:
"There were many puddles in the courtyard,
so I drove the carriage to the thatched gate.
The court officer said:
'It is against the law.'
He raised his spear and struck my horse,
destroying my carriage.
You must punish him."
The king said:
"In the past, he did not yield to the old ruler;
in the future, he will not be subservient to the designated ruler.
How admirable!
He is truly my minister who upholds the law."
He then increased his rank by two grades
and opened the back gate to let the crown prince out.
"Do not pass this way again."
Lord Sì of Wèi said to Bó Yí:
"You consider my small state
not worth serving in,
but I am capable of employing you;
I request to advance your rank and make you a senior minister."
He then advanced him ten thousand *qǐng* of land.
Bó Yí said:
"My mother thinks that I, Yí,
am capable of being a prime minister to a state with ten thousand chariots,
which is not beyond my abilities.
However, in my family, there is a female shaman named Cài Ǒ,
whom my mother greatly loves and trusts,
and entrusts the family affairs to her.
My intelligence is sufficient to confidently manage family affairs,
and my mother completely listens to me.
However, what she has discussed with me,
she must also decide with Cài Ǒ.
Therefore, discussing my intelligence,
I am capable of being a prime minister to a state with ten thousand chariots, which is not beyond my abilities;
discussing my family relationships,
there is the relationship between mother and son;
however, she still cannot avoid consulting Cài Ǒ.
Now, my relationship with the ruler
is not as intimate as that between mother and son,
and all rulers have a Cài Ǒ.
The ruler's Cài Ǒ
must be someone important.
Someone important
is someone who can act for personal gain.
Those who act for personal gain
are outside the bounds of the plumb line;
and what I speak of
is within the law.
What is outside the plumb line and what is within the law
are enemies;
they are incompatible."
First:
The Lord of Wèi was going to Jìn
and said to Bó Yí:
"I want to travel with you."
Bó Yí said:
"My old mother is at home;
please allow me to return and discuss it with her."
The Lord of Wèi himself asked Bó's old mother.
Bó's old mother said:
"Yí is your minister;
if you intend to take him along,
that is very good."
The Lord of Wèi said:
"I have already asked you,
and you have agreed."
Bó Yí returned
and told his old mother, saying:
"How does the Lord of Wèi's love for me compare to your love for me?"
The old woman said:
"Not as good as my beloved son."
"How could Wèi Jūn's 衛君 wisdom be doubted compared to an old woman?"
She said:
"Not as good as my wise son."
"The old woman and Yí 疑 have discussed family matters,
and it has already been decided.
Yet you ask the diviner, Granny Cài 蔡嫗, for a decision.
Now Wèi Jūn 衛君 follows Yí 疑 and acts,
even if he makes decisions with Yí 疑,
he will surely have another Granny Cài 蔡嫗 overturn them.
If so,
then Yí 疑 will not be able to remain a minister for long."
To teach singing,
one must first make the student call out and then restrain the voice.
Only when the voice returns clear and sharp is the student then taught.
It is said:
To teach singing,
one must first measure with a standard.
A quick call must be centered on the *gōng* 宮 note,
and a slow call must be centered on the *zhǐ* 徵 note.
If the quick call is not centered on the *gōng* 宮,
and the slow call is not centered on the *zhǐ* 徵,
it cannot be called teaching.
Wú Qǐ 吳起,
was from the middle class of the Zuo 左 clan of Wèi 衛.
He had his wife weave silk ribbons
but the width was narrower than the standard.
Wú Zǐ 吳子 told her to redo it.
His wife said:
"Yes."
When it was finished,
he measured it again,
and indeed it was not up to standard.
Wú Zǐ 吳子 was greatly angered.
His wife replied:
"I started weaving it to the standard but it could not be redone."
Wú Zǐ 吳子 sent her away.
His wife asked her brother to intercede and seek her return.
Her brother said:
"Wú Zǐ 吳子 is a man who upholds the law.
"His purpose in upholding the law
is to use it to achieve success with a ruler of ten thousand chariots.
He will certainly first implement it on his wife and concubines,
and then carry it out.
Do not try to seek her return."
His wife's younger brother was also highly regarded by the ruler of Wèi 衛,
and thus he relied on the weight of the ruler of Wèi 衛 to plead with Wú Zǐ 吳子.
Wú Zǐ 吳子 did not listen,
and thus he left Wèi 衛 and entered Jīng 荊.
It is said:
Wú Qǐ 吳起 showed his wife a silk ribbon and said:
"Weave a silk ribbon for me,
make it like this."
The ribbon was finished and presented,
but the ribbon was exceptionally well-made.
Qǐ 起 said:
"I asked you to make the ribbon,
to make it like this,
but now it is exceptionally well-made,
why is that?"
His wife said:
"The materials used were the same,
I just put more effort into making it well."
Wú Qǐ 吳起 said:
"That is not the issue."
He sent her home in disgrace.
Her father went to plead for her return.
Wú Qǐ 吳起 said:
"The Qǐ 起 family does not retract its words."
Duke Wén of Jìn 晉文公 asked Hú Yǎn 狐偃, saying:
"I provide sweet and savory food abundantly in the hall,
goblets of wine and platters of meat fill the palace,
the wine in the flasks is pure,
the raw meat is plentiful,
and slaughtering one ox
benefits the entire country.
The accomplishments of a year
are all used to clothe the soldiers.
Is this enough to make the people fight?"
Hú Zǐ 狐子 said:
"It is not enough."
Duke Wén 文公 said:
"I have eased the taxes at the passes and markets
and relaxed the penalties,
is this enough to make the people fight?"
Hú Zǐ 狐子 said:
"It is not enough."
Duke Wén 文公 said:
"When my people have losses due to funerals,
I personally send officials to oversee the affairs,
those with crimes are pardoned,
and those who are poor and lack resources are given aid.
Is this enough to make the people fight?"
Hú Zǐ 狐子 replied:
"It is not enough.
These are all ways to protect their property,
but to have them fight is to have them killed.
The people follow you
for the sake of protecting their property,
but you then welcome their deaths,
losing the reason why they followed you."
He said:
"Then what is enough to make the people fight?"
Hú Zǐ 狐子 replied:
"Make it so that they have no choice but to fight."
The Duke said:
"How can they have no choice but to fight?"
Hú Zǐ 狐子 replied:
"Be reliable in rewarding and certain in punishing,
and that will be enough to make them fight."
The Duke said:
"How far should the severity of punishments go?"
He replied:
"Do not avoid punishing relatives or the noble,
let the law be applied to those you love."
Duke Wén 文公 said:
"Good."
The next day, he ordered the people to till in Pǔ Lù 圃陸,
setting a deadline of midday,
those who were late would be punished by military law.
Then one of the Duke's beloved, named Diān Xié 顛頡,
was late.
The officials requested his punishment,
and Duke Wén 文公 shed tears and was worried.
The officials said:
"Please allow us to carry out the law."
So they broke Diān Xié's 顛頡 spine
and displayed it to the people,
to show the reliability of the law.
After that, the people were all afraid and said:
"The ruler valued Diān Xié 顛頡 so highly,
yet the ruler still enforced the law on him,
what more can we expect?"
Duke Wén 文公 saw that the people were ready to fight,
and so he then raised an army to attack Yuán 原,
and conquered it.
He attacked Wèi 衛,
shifted their field boundaries eastward, and took Wǔ Lù 五鹿.
He attacked Yáng 陽. He conquered Guó 虢.
He attacked Cáo 曹.
He surrounded Zhèng 鄭 in the south,
and returned their city walls.
He lifted the siege of Sòng 宋.
He returned and fought the Jīng 荊 people at Chéng Pú 城濮,
greatly defeating the Jīng 荊 people,
and returned to form the alliance at Jiàn Tǔ 踐土,
and thus established the righteousness of Héng Yōng 衡雍.
With one move, he had eight accomplishments.
The reason for this
is nothing other than following the plans of Hú Yǎn 狐偃
and sacrificing the spine of Diān Xié 顛頡.
The pain of a boil
is such that if one does not pierce the bone marrow,
the vexation of the heart cannot be endured.
If it were not like that,
one could not make a person use a half-inch whetstone to flick it away.
The same is true for the ruler of men in governing:
it is not that they do not know that there is ease after suffering.
To govern one's country,
if it is not like that,
one cannot listen to wise counsel and punish rebellious ministers.
Rebellious ministers are certainly those who are highly regarded.
Those who are highly regarded are certainly those who are greatly loved by the ruler of men.
Those who are greatly loved by the ruler of men
are like those who share the same standards of hardness and whiteness.
To use the resources of a commoner
to separate the hardness and whiteness, the loved ones of the ruler of men,
is like trying to detach the left thigh by describing the right thigh.
One's body will certainly die
and the argument will not succeed.
Jīng One:
If rewards and punishments are shared,
then prohibitions and orders will not be carried out.
How can this be clarified?
Clarify it with Zàofù and Wū Qī.
Zǐhǎn arranged for a pig to appear,
Tián Héng provided gardens and ponds,
therefore the Sòng ruler and Jiǎn Gōng were assassinated.
The trouble lies in Wáng Liáng and Zàofù sharing a chariot,
Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào sharing a zither.
Jīng Two:
Good governance and strength arise from law,
weakness and chaos arise from favoritism.
If the ruler is clear about this,
then he will justly reward and punish
and not be benevolent to those below.
Rank and emolument arise from merit,
punishment and execution arise from crime.
If the ministers are clear about this,
then they will exhaust their strength
and not be loyal to the ruler.
If the ruler understands unbenevolence
and the ministers understand disloyalty,
then the state can achieve hegemony.
Zhāo Xiāng knew the ruler's feelings but did not open the five parks;
Tián Wěi knew the minister's feelings, so he taught Tián Zhāng,
and Gōng Yí resigned from his fish.
Jīng Three:
An enlightened ruler
observes outwardly,
and external affairs cannot but be accomplished,
therefore Sū Dài criticized the Qí King.
A ruler observes those above,
and those in office will be neither uncomfortable nor obscure,
therefore Pān Shòu spoke of Yǔ's feelings.
If a ruler has no awareness,
then I will understand it,
therefore, be wary of those with the same clothes and clan,
how much more so of those who borrow power!
Wú Zhāng knew this,
therefore he spoke with pretense,
how much more so than speaking with sincerity!
The Zhào King disliked fierce eyes and dammed them up.
The way
of an enlightened ruler
is like the Zhōu emissary turning away the Wèi Marquis.
Jīng Four:
A ruler
maintains the law and demands results
in order to establish achievements.
I have heard of officials who, though causing disorder,
have people who are uniquely good,
but I have not heard of disorderly people
having officials who are uniquely good at governing,
therefore an enlightened ruler governs officials, not the people.
The explanation lies in shaking the root of the tree
and pulling the rope of the net.
Therefore, the miserly man who loses a fire
cannot but be judged.
To put out a fire,
an official carrying a pot runs to the fire,
which is the use of one person.
Wielding a whip and using people
is to employ ten thousand men.
Therefore, encountering a skilled technique
is like Zàofù encountering a startled horse.
Pulling the horse and pushing the cart will not advance it,
but replacing the driver, holding the reins and whip
will make the horses gallop.
Therefore, the explanation lies in hammering and leveling,
using boards and straightening frames.
Otherwise,
failure lies in Nào Chǐ using Qí to slaughter Mǐn Wáng,
and Lǐ Duì using Zhào to starve Zhǔ Fù.
Jīng Five:
Follow the principles of things,
and it can be accomplished without labor.
Therefore, Zī Zhèng sat on the shafts of the cart and sang
to ascend Gāo Liáng.
The trouble lies in Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ asking the tax official about light and heavy taxes;
Bó Yí's statement that "the state is full,"
made Jiǎnzhǔ happy, but the treasury was empty,
the people were starving, and the corrupt officials were rich.
Therefore, Huán Gōng inspected the people
and Guǎn Zhòng examined spoiled wealth and resentful women.
Otherwise,
it is like Yánlíng riding a horse and being unable to advance,
and Zàofù passing by and weeping for him.
Shuō One:
Zàofù drove four horses,
galloping and circling
and indulging his desires with the horses.
Indulging his desires with the horses
meant controlling the reins and whip.
However, the horses were startled by the appearance of a pig,
and Zàofù could not restrain them,
not because the strictness of the reins and whip was insufficient,
but because the authority was divided by the appearance of the pig.
Prince Wū Qī was an assistant driver,
not using the reins and whip
but choosing to indulge the horses' desires,
controlling the benefits of fodder and water.
However, the horses passing by the gardens and ponds
caused the assistant driver to fail,
not because the benefits of fodder and water were insufficient,
but because virtue was divided by the gardens and ponds.
Therefore, Wáng Liáng and Zàofù
were the best drivers in the world,
but if Wáng Liáng held the left rein and shouted,
and Zàofù held the right rein and whipped,
the horses would not be able to travel ten *lǐ*,
because they were sharing authority.
Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào
were the best zither players in the world,
but if Tián Lián played the upper strings
and Chéng Qiào plucked the lower strings
they would not be able to complete a melody,
also because they were sharing authority.
With the skill of Wáng Liáng and Zàofù,
sharing the reins and driving cannot control the horses,
how can a ruler
share power with his ministers to govern?
With the skill of Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào,
sharing a zither cannot complete a melody,
how can a ruler
share authority with his ministers to achieve success?
One account says:
Zàofù was an assistant driver for the Qí King,
taming horses with thirst,
demonstrating the driving in a garden.
Thirsty horses saw the gardens and ponds,
abandoned the chariot and ran to the ponds,
and the driving failed.
Prince Wū Qī was asked by Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ to take a path
to compete for a thousand-*lǐ* marker.
At the beginning of the journey,
a pig was hiding in a ditch.
Prince Wū Qī aligned the reins and whip and advanced,
the pig suddenly jumped out of the ditch,
the horses were startled, and the driving failed.
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said to the Sòng Ruler:
"Rewards and gifts
are what the people like,
Your Lordship should do them yourself;
killing and punishing
are what the people dislike,
allow your minister to take responsibility for them."
The Sòng Ruler said:
"Agreed."
Therefore, he issued decrees with authority
and executed senior ministers.
The ruler said:
"Ask Zǐhǎn."
Therefore, the senior ministers feared him,
and the common people turned to him.
After a year,
Zǐhǎn killed the Sòng Ruler and seized power.
Therefore, Zǐhǎn arranged for a pig to appear
to seize his lord's state.
Jiǎn Gōng, while in power,
had heavy punishments and strict executions,
heavy taxation
and slaughtered the people.
Tián Chéng Héng established kindness and love,
showing leniency and generosity.
Jiǎn Gōng treated the Qí people like thirsty horses,
not adding kindness to the people;
while Tián Chéng Héng treated them with gardens and ponds of benevolence and generosity.
One account says:
Zàofù was an assistant driver for the Qí King,
taming horses with thirst,
and the taming was completed in a hundred days.
When the taming was completed,
he requested to demonstrate the driving to the Qí King.
The King said:
"Demonstrate the driving in the garden."
Zàofù drove the chariot into the garden,
the horses saw the gardens and ponds and ran,
Zào Fǔ could not stop them.
Zào Fǔ had long trained horses to obey hunger and thirst.
Now, the horses see a pond,
become wild and run,
even Zào Fǔ cannot control them.
Now, Jiǎn Gōng has long used laws to restrain his people,
but Tián Chéng constantly benefits them.
This is like Tián Chéng opening the garden pond
and showing it to thirsty people.
One account says:
Wángzǐ Yúqī served the Sòng ruler and was pursuing someone over a thousand *lǐ*.
Having harnessed the horses,
he observed the marks on their mouths and nostrils.
As he was about to set off,
urging them forward,
the wheels hit the ropes in the road;
when pulling them back,
the horses covered their tracks.
Patting them and releasing them,
a pig escaped from its pen.
The horse retreated backward,
the whip could not drive it forward;
the horse became wild and ran,
the reins could not correct it.
One account says:
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said to the Sòng ruler,
"Celebrations, rewards, and gifts
are what the people love;
Your Lordship should do them yourself.
Punishments, executions, and killings
are what the people hate;
let your subject be responsible for them."
Thereupon, he executed petty people and punished great ministers.
The ruler said,
"Discuss it with Zǐhǎn."
After a year,
the people knew that the power of life and death was controlled by Zǐhǎn,
so the entire country turned to him.
Therefore, Zǐhǎn kidnapped the Sòng ruler
and seized his government;
the law could not stop him.
Therefore, it is said:
"Zǐhǎn was like releasing the pig,
and Tián Chéng was constantly like the garden pond."
Now, if Wáng Liáng and
Zào Fǔ share a chariot,
with each person holding one side of the reins
and going out the gate,
the driving will surely fail and
the road will not be reached.
If Tián Lián and
Chéng Qiào share a *qín* (zither),
with each person plucking and waving at one string,
the sound will surely be ruined,
and the melody will not be completed.
Discourses Two:
King Zhāo of Qín was ill,
and the common people in the neighborhoods bought oxen
and each family prayed for the king.
Gōngsūn Shù went out and saw this,
and entered to congratulate the king, saying,
"The common people are all buying oxen by the neighborhood
to pray for the king."
The king sent someone to inquire about it,
and indeed it was so.
The king said,
"Fine the people two sets of armor.
To pray without being ordered is to love me, the lonely one.
To love me, the lonely one,
would lead me also to change the law
and to have my heart follow them,
and that would mean the law would not be established.
If the law is not established,
it is the way to chaos and ruin.
It is better to fine each person two sets of armor
and then continue to govern them."
One account says:
King Xiāng of Qín was ill,
and the people prayed for him;
when he recovered,
they slaughtered an ox to thank the spirits.
Lángzhōng Yán È and
Gōngsūn Yǎn went out
and saw this,
and said:
"It is not the time for the community sacrifice or the winter sacrifice,
why are you killing oxen
and sacrificing to the spirits?"
They were puzzled and asked about it.
The people said:
"When the ruler is ill,
we pray for him;
now that he has recovered,
we slaughter an ox to thank the spirits."
Yán È and
Gōngsūn Yǎn were pleased
and met with the king,
bowing and congratulating him, saying:
"You surpass Yáo and
Shùn."
The king was surprised and said:
"What do you mean?"
They replied:
"Yáo and
Shùn's
people did not go so far as to pray for them.
Now, when Your Majesty is ill,
the people pray with oxen;
when you recover,
they slaughter an ox to thank the spirits.
Therefore, your subjects secretly believe that Your Majesty surpasses Yáo and Shùn."
The king then sent someone to inquire, 〓#
and found out which neighborhood had done it, 〓#
and fined the neighborhood head, the head of the five-family unit, and the head of the village two sets of armor.
Yán È and Gōngsūn Yǎn were ashamed and dared not speak.
After several months,
the king was drinking wine and enjoying himself,
and Yán È and
Gōngsūn Yǎn said to the king:
"Previously, your subjects secretly believed that Your Majesty surpassed Yáo and
Shùn,
and were not just trying to flatter you.
When Yáo and Shùn were ill,
their people did not go so far as to pray for them.
Your Majesty then sent someone to inquire,
and found out which neighborhood had done it,
Now, when Your Majesty is ill, the people pray with oxen,
when you recover,
they slaughter an ox to thank the spirits.
Yet now you fine the neighborhood head, the head of the five-family unit, and the head of the village two sets of armor,
your subjects secretly find this strange."
The king said:
"Why do you not understand this?
The reason why these people serve me
is not because they love me,
but because they fear my power.
If I relinquish my power and become equal to the people,
then,
I would not be loved,
and the people would not serve me,
thus I would cut off the path of love."
There was a great famine in Qín.
Yìng Hóu requested, saying:
"The grass and plants in the five gardens:
vegetables,
acorns,
dates, and chestnuts,
are enough to sustain the people.
Please release them."
King Zhāo of Qín said:
"Our law in Qín
is that those who perform meritorious service receive rewards,
and those who commit crimes receive punishment.
Now, releasing the vegetables and grasses from the five gardens
would mean that those with merit and those without merit would both be rewarded.
To reward both those with merit and those without merit
is the way to chaos.
To release from the five gardens and cause chaos
is worse than abandoning the dates and vegetables and maintaining order."
One account says:
"If you order the release of the gourds,
vegetables, dates, and
chestnuts from the five gardens,
it would be enough to sustain the people,
but it would cause those with merit and those without merit to compete for them.
To live in chaos
is worse than to die and maintain order,
gentlemen, please abandon this idea."
Tián Wěi taught his son Tián Zhāng, saying:
"If you want to benefit yourself,
first benefit your ruler;
if you want to enrich your family,
first enrich your country."
One account says:
Tián Wěi taught his son Tián Zhāng, saying:
"The ruler sells official positions and titles,
the subjects sell their wisdom and strength.
Therefore, rely on yourself and do not rely on others."
Gōngyí Xiū was the chancellor of Lǔ and had a fondness for fish;
the whole country competed to buy fish and present them to him,
but Gōngyí Zǐ did not accept them.
His younger brother admonished him, saying:
"The master has a fondness for fish but does not accept them;
why is that?"
He replied:
"Precisely because I have a fondness for fish,
I do not accept them.
If I were to accept fish,
I would inevitably show a subservient manner;
with a subservient manner,
I would violate the law;
if I violate the law,
I would be dismissed from my position as chancellor.
Though I have a fondness for fish,
this would not necessarily result in them bringing me fish,
and I would also not be able to provide myself with fish.
If I do not accept fish and am not dismissed from my position as chancellor,
then, though I have a fondness for fish,
I will be able to provide myself with fish for a long time."
This clarifies that relying on others is not as good as relying on oneself,
and that being done for by others
is not as good as doing for oneself.
Discourses Three:
Zǐ Zhī was the chancellor of Yān,
esteemed and with the power of decision.
Sū Dài was sent by Qí as an envoy to Yān;
the king asked him, saying:
"What kind of ruler is the king of Qí?"
He replied:
"He will certainly not become a hegemon."
The king of Yān said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"In the past, when Duke Huán became a hegemon,
he entrusted internal affairs to Bào Shū,
and external affairs to Guǎn Zhòng;
Duke Huán would let his hair down and frolic with the women,
spending his days playing in the market.
Now, the king of Qí does not trust his great ministers."
Thereupon, the king of Yān greatly increased his trust in Zǐ Zhī.
Zǐ Zhī heard of this
and sent someone to give Sū Dài a hundred yì of gold,
and listened to his commands.
Another account:
Sū Dài was sent by Qí as an envoy to Yān;
seeing that not benefiting Zǐ Zhī,
he would certainly not be able to complete his mission and return,
and that tribute would also not be given,
he then met with the king of Yān
and praised the king of Qí.
The king of Yān said:
"Why is the king of Qí so worthy?
Will he then certainly become king?"
Sū Dài said:
"He is preoccupied with rescuing his state from decline;
how could he become king?"
The king of Yān said:
"Why is that?"
He said:
"His appointments of those he loves are not impartial."
The king of Yān said:
"Why will he perish?"
He said:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí loved Guǎn Zhòng,
placing him as his second father,
internal affairs were managed by him,
and external affairs decided by him,
the whole country submitting to him,
and therefore he rectified the world once
and convened the feudal lords nine times.
Now, Qí's appointments of those he loves are not impartial;
this is why I know it will perish."
The king of Yān said:
"Now I have appointed Zǐ Zhī,
has the world not heard of it?"
Thereupon, the next day he held court
and listened to Zǐ Zhī.
Pān Shòu said to the king of Yān:
"Your Majesty might as well cede the state to Zǐ Zhī.
The reason people call Yáo worthy
is because he ceded the world to Xǔ Yóu;
Xǔ Yóu would certainly not accept it,
and thus Yáo had the reputation of ceding to Xǔ Yóu,
but in reality did not lose the world.
Now, Your Majesty cedes the state to Zǐ Zhī;
Zǐ Zhī will certainly not accept it,
and thus Your Majesty will have the reputation of ceding to Zǐ Zhī,
and will act like Yáo."
Thereupon, the king of Yān ceded control of the state to
Zǐ Zhī, and Zǐ Zhī became greatly important.
Another account:
Pān Shòu
was a recluse.
Yān sent people to invite him.
Pān Shòu met with the king of Yān and said:
"I fear that Zǐ Zhī will be like Yì."
The king said:
"What was Yì like?"
He replied:
"In ancient times, when Yǔ died,
he was going to transmit the world to Yì;
the people of Qǐ then joined together to attack Yì and established Qǐ.
Now, Your Majesty trusts and loves Zǐ Zhī,
and is going to transmit the state to Zǐ Zhī;
the people of the heir apparent all hold official seals,
and there is not a single person who is of Zǐ Zhī's party
in the court.
If Your Majesty unfortunately abandons your ministers,
then Zǐ Zhī will also be like Yì."
The king then collected the seals of office,
and those of three hundred shí and above all gave them to Zǐ Zhī,
and Zǐ Zhī became greatly important.
The means by which a ruler reflects himself
are the retainers of the feudal lords;
now the retainers of the feudal lords
are all partisans of private households.
The means by which a ruler keeps himself from being obscured
are the scholars of remote
caves;
now the scholars of remote caves
are all the personal attendants of private households.
Why is this?
The resources of deprivation and bestowal are with Zǐ Zhī.
Therefore, Wú Zhāng said:
"A ruler should not feign love or hatred for people.
If he feigns love for people,
he cannot hate them again;
if he feigns hatred for people,
he cannot love them again."
Another account:
The king of Yān wanted to transmit the state to Zǐ Zhī,
and asked Pān Shòu about it.
He replied:
"Yǔ loved Yì and entrusted the world to Yì,
but then made the people of Qǐ officials.
When he was old,
he thought that Qǐ was not sufficient to be entrusted with the world,
so he transmitted the world to Yì,
but the power and influence were all with Qǐ.
Afterwards, Qǐ and his clique attacked Yì and seized the world from him;
thus Yǔ nominally transmitted the world to Yì,
but in reality caused Qǐ to take it for himself.
This shows that Yǔ was not as clear-sighted as Yáo and
Shùn.
Now, Your Majesty wants to transmit [the state] to Zǐ Zhī,
but the officials are all people of the heir apparent;
this is nominally transmitting it but in reality causing the heir apparent to take it for himself."
The king of Yān then collected the seals of office,
and those of three hundred shí and above all gave them to Zǐ Zhī,
and Zǐ Zhī then became important.
Fāng Wúzǐ said:
"I have heard of the ancient rites:
one should not ride in the same carriage with those who wear the same clothes,
nor share a household with those of the same clan,
let alone a ruler
who would lend his authority and alienate his power!"
Wú Zhāng said to King Xuān of Hán:
"A ruler must not feign love for people;
he cannot hate them again even for a single day;
he must not feign hatred for people;
he cannot love them again even for a single day.
Therefore, if the signs of feigned hatred or feigned love are seen,
then sycophants will take advantage of this to praise or disparage people.
Even if there is an enlightened ruler,
he will not be able to recover [from this situation],
let alone one who sincerely lends his authority to others!"
The King of Zhào (趙) was strolling in a garden,
when attendants stopped because of a hare and a tiger,
their eyes wide and staring around.
The King said,
"How detestable are
the eyes of a tiger!"
The attendants said,
"The eyes of Píngyáng Jūn (平陽君) are even more detestable than these.
Seeing these causes no harm,
but if one sees the eyes of Píngyáng Jūn like this,
then one will surely die!"
The next day,
Píngyáng Jūn heard of this,
and had someone kill the speaker,
but the King did not punish him.
The ruler of Wèi (衛) entered the court of Zhōu (周) to pay respects.
The Zhōu emissary asked his title,
and he replied,
"A duke avoiding strength (bì qiáng, 辟彊)."
The Zhōu emissary rejected this, saying,
"Dukes may not have the same title as the Son of Heaven."
The ruler of Wèi then changed his title to,
"A duke destroying (huǐ, 燬)."
And then he was let in.
Zhòng Ní (仲尼) heard of this and said,
"How far removed is coercion!
An empty name is not lent to others,
how much less an actual thing?"
Persuasion Four:
One who shakes a tree
must individually pluck each leaf;
this is laborious and incomplete.
Instead, if one strokes the base,
all the leaves will shake.
If one shakes a tree by a deep pool,
the birds will be startled and fly high,
and the fish will be frightened and dive down.
One skilled at spreading nets pulls the main rope.
If one had to pluck each of the myriad holes before catching anything,
that would be laborious and difficult;
pulling the main rope,
the fish are already in the bag.
Thus, officials
are the root of the people,
and the main rope.
Therefore, the sage governs officials, not the people.
One who puts out a fire
orders officials to carry pots and jars to run toward the fire;
this is the use of one person.
Wielding a whip and baton to point and direct people,
one controls ten thousand men.
Therefore, the sage does not personally involve himself with the common people,
and the enlightened ruler does not attend to petty matters.
Zàofù (造父) was hoeing in the fields,
when a father and son passed by in a carriage.
The horses were startled and would not move.
The son got out of the carriage to pull the horses,
and the father and son pushed the carriage.
They asked Zàofù to help them push the carriage.
Zàofù then put away his tools,
stopped hoeing and stowed them in the carriage.
He helped the son into the carriage,
and then took hold of the reins and whip.
He had not even used them,
and the horses were already galloping.
If Zàofù could not drive,
even if he exhausted himself
helping them push the carriage,
the horses would still not move.
Now he made himself comfortable,
and stowed his tools in the carriage,
being kind to the people,
because he had the skill to drive them.
Thus, the state
is the ruler's carriage;
power
is the ruler's horses.
Without the skill to drive them,
even if the ruler exhausts himself,
he will still not avoid disorder;
with the skill to drive them,
the ruler lives in comfort and pleasure,
and achieves the accomplishments of an emperor or king.
A hammer and anvil
are used to flatten what is uneven;
a straightening board
is used to correct what is not straight.
The law that the sage makes
is used to flatten what is uneven,
and to correct what is not straight.
When Nào Chǐ (淖齒) was employed by Qí (齊),
he pulled out the tendons of King Mǐn (閔王);
when Lǐ Duì (李兌) was employed by Zhào (趙),
he starved Zhǔ Fù (主父) to death.
These two rulers
were both unable to use their hammer, anvil and straightening board,
therefore they died by execution,
and became a laughingstock to the world.
It is said:
Entering Qí,
one only hears of Nào Chǐ, and not of the King of Qí;
entering Zhào,
one only hears of Lǐ Duì, and not of the King of Zhào.
Therefore it is said:
If a ruler does not wield authority,
then his power will be weak,
and his ministers will usurp his fame.
It is said:
King Wǔlíng (武靈王) had King Huìwén (惠文王) administer the government,
with Lǐ Duì as his prime minister.
King Wǔlíng did not personally control the power of life and death,
so he was kidnapped by Lǐ Duì.
It is said:
Tián Yīng (田嬰) was the prime minister of Qí.
Someone advised the king, saying,
"For the plans of the whole year,
if the king does not take a few days to listen to them himself,
then he will have no way of knowing the deception, evil deeds, gains and losses of the officials."
The king said,
"Good."
Tián Yīng heard of this,
and immediately requested the king to allow him to present the yearly plans.
The king was about to listen to them,
but Tián Yīng ordered the officials to prepare tally slips, measure stones, and three-tenths measures of grain.
The king listened to the plans himself,
but could not finish listening to them all.
After finishing his meal,
he sat down again,
but could no longer eat his evening meal.
Tián Yīng then said,
"The things that the assembled ministers dare not neglect day and night throughout the year,
if the king listens to them in one evening,
then the assembled ministers will be encouraged to exert themselves."
The king said,
"Okay."
Soon the king was already asleep.
The officials all pulled out their knives and whittled away at the tally slips and measures of grain.
The king listened to the plans himself,
and chaos began to arise.
Persuasion Five:
Zī Zhèng (茲鄭) was pulling a two-wheeled cart up a high embankment, but could not keep it from slipping.
Zī Zhèng sat on the shaft and sang;
those in front stopped,
and those in back hurried,
and the cart went up.
If Zī Zhèng had no skill to command people,
then even if he exhausted his strength to death,
the cart still would not have gone up.
Now, the cart went up without his personally suffering labor
because
he had the skill to command people.
When the Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ (趙簡主) sent out tax collectors,
the officials asked whether to collect lightly or heavily.
Jiǎnzhǔ said,
"Neither lightly nor heavily.
If heavy,
then the profit will enter the coffers above,
if light,
then the profit will revert to the people.
The officials will have no private gain, and will be upright."
Bó Yí (薄疑) said to Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ,
"The people in your state are full."
Jiǎnzhǔ was delighted and asked,
"How so?"
He replied,
"The treasuries above are empty,
and the common people below are hungry,
yet the corrupt officials are rich."
Qí Huán Gōng, dressed in plain clothes, went to inspect the homes of the common people.
Among them was a man who was old and supported himself.
Huán Gōng asked him the reason.
He replied:
"I have three sons,
but my family is poor and I cannot afford to marry them off.
The hired labor has not been repaid."
Huán Gōng returned
and told Guǎn Zhòng about it.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"If accumulated wealth is left to rot and be discarded,
then people will go hungry;
if there are resentful women in the palace,
then the common people will have no wives."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he selected women from the palace and married them off.
He issued an order to the people, saying:
"Men should marry at the age of twenty,
and women should marry at the age of fifteen."
Another account states:
Huán Gōng, dressed in plain clothes, was traveling among the common people when he encountered Lùmén Jì,
who was seventy years old and without a wife.
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng,
"Are there people who are old and without wives?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There is Lùmén Jì,
who is seventy years old and still without a wife."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What should be done to ensure he has a wife?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I have heard that
if those above accumulate wealth,
then the people below will surely be impoverished;
if there are resentful women in the palace,
then there will be old men without wives."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
He ordered within the palace
"to release unmarried women who have not been favored."
He then decreed that men should marry at the age of twenty
and women at the age of fifteen.
Thus, there would be no resentful women within
and no single men without.
Yánlíng Zhuō Zǐ was riding a carriage with blue dragons and embroidered decorations,
with hooks and ornaments in front
and embellished stops in the rear.
When the horse wanted to advance, the hooks and ornaments restrained it;
when it wanted to retreat, the embellished stops pierced it,
causing the horse to veer sideways.
Zàofù passed by and wept for it,
saying:
"The way people are governed today is similar.
Rewards are meant to encourage, yet destruction results;
punishments are meant to prohibit, yet praise is added.
The people are caught in the middle and do not know which way to turn.
This is what causes sages to weep."
Another account states:
Yánlíng Zhuō Zǐ was riding a carriage with blue dragons and embroidered decorations,
with inlaid ornaments in the front
and sharp stops in the rear.
When the horse moved forward, he pulled it back;
when it retreated, he urged it on.
The horse could not advance forward,
nor retreat backward,
so it evaded and fled,
whereupon he drew his knife and cut off its feet.
Zàofù saw this
and wept.
Another account states:
Yánlíng Zhuō Zǐ was riding a carriage with blue dragons and embroidered decorations,
with inlaid ornaments in the front
and sharp stops in the rear.
When the horse moved forward, he pulled it back;
when it retreated, he whipped it.
The horse could not advance forward,
nor retreat backward,
so it evaded and fled,
whereupon he drew his knife and cut off its feet.
Zàofù saw this and wept,
not eating all day.
He looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"The whip
is used to make it advance,
yet there are inlaid ornaments in front;
pulling back
is used to make it retreat,
yet there are sharp stops in the rear.
Nowadays, rulers promote those who are pure and upright,
and demote those who do not adapt to those around them;
they praise those who are just and impartial,
and dismiss those who do not obey.
The people are fearful,
caught in the middle and do not know which way to turn.
This is what causes sages to weep."
Jìn Wén Gōng was about to fight with the Chǔ people.
He summoned Jiù Fàn and asked him,
saying:
"I am about to fight with the Chǔ people;
they are many and we are few.
What should be done?"
Jiù Fàn said:
"I have heard that
gentlemen of elaborate ceremony are never tired of loyalty and trust;
on the battlefield,
one is never tired of deceit and falsehood.
Your Lordship should simply deceive them."
Wén Gōng dismissed Jiù Fàn
and then summoned Yōng Jì and asked him,
saying:
"I am about to fight with the Chǔ people;
they are many and we are few.
What should be done?"
Yōng Jì replied:
"If you burn the forest to hunt,
you may steal many animals,
but afterwards there will be no more animals;
if you treat the people with deceit,
you may steal a moment in time,
but afterwards there will be no more trust."
Wén Gōng said:
"Good."
He dismissed Yōng Jì and used Jiù Fàn's plan to fight the Chǔ people and defeat them.
Upon returning, he distributed rewards,
honoring Yōng Jì before Jiù Fàn.
The assembled officials said:
"In the affair at Chéngpú,
it was Jiù Fàn who devised the plan.
Is it proper
to use his words and yet rank him after?"
Wén Gōng said:
"This is not something you understand.
Jiù Fàn's words
are a temporary expedient;
Yōng Jì's words
are a benefit for all generations."
Zhòngní heard of this
and said:
"It is fitting that Wén Gōng became a hegemon!
He knew both the temporary expediency
and the benefit for all generations."
Someone said:
"Yōng Jì's response
was not appropriate to Wén Gōng's question.
When answering questions,
one should respond according to the size, urgency, and importance of the question.
If the question is lofty and significant,
but the response is petty and narrow,
then the wise ruler will not accept it.
Now Wén Gōng asked
'how to meet a large force with a small one,'
but Yōng Jì replied
'afterwards there will be no more.'
This is not an appropriate response.
Furthermore, Wén Gōng did not understand the temporary expedient
nor the benefit for all generations.
If he fights and wins,
then the state is secure and his position is stable,
the army is strong and his authority is established.
Even if there are future repercussions,
nothing is greater than this.
What worries could there be that the benefit for all generations
will not arrive?
If he fights and does not win,
then the state will perish and the army will be weak,
his body will die and his name will cease.
He will not even have time to avoid imminent death;
how can he wait for the benefit for all generations?
Waiting for the benefit for all generations
depends on victory today;
victory today
depends on deceiving the enemy."
Deceiving the enemy is a benefit for ten thousand generations.
It is said, therefore:
Thus it is said:
Yōng Jì's 雍季 answer
was not appropriate for Duke Wén's 文公 question.
Moreover, Duke Wén 文公 did not understand Jiù Fàn's 舅犯 words.
What Jiù Fàn 舅犯 meant by
"never be satisfied with deception and falsehood"
did not
mean deceiving his own people,
but deceiving his enemies.
The enemy
is the country to be attacked;
even if there is no more trust afterward,
what harm is there?
Why did Duke Wén 文公 prioritize Yōng Jì 雍季?
Was it because of his merit?
The one who achieved victory over Chǔ 楚 and broke the army
was Jiù Fàn's 舅犯 strategy;
was it because of his good words?
Yōng Jì 雍季 merely spoke of
"no trust afterward,"
which is hardly good advice.
This cannot be considered good advice.
Jiù Fàn 舅犯 combined both.
Jiù Fàn 舅犯 said that
"gentlemen with elaborate rituals
are never satisfied with loyalty and trustworthiness,"
for
loyalty
is how one loves one's subordinates,
and trustworthiness
is how one does not deceive one's people.
If one already loves and does not deceive,
what words are better than these?
However, the statement "coming from deception and falsehood"
refers to the strategies of war.
Jiù Fàn 舅犯 had good advice beforehand
and victory in battle afterward.
Therefore, Jiù Fàn 舅犯 was discussed only after he had achieved two merits,
while Yōng Jì 雍季 was rewarded before doing anything.
"Duke Wén's 文公 hegemony,
wasn't it appropriate?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 did not understand proper rewards.
The farmers of Mount Lì 歷山 encroached on boundaries.
Shùn 舜 went there to plow,
and within a year,
the furrows were straightened.
The fishermen of the Hé River 河濱 fought over sandbars.
Shùn 舜 went there to fish,
and within a year, they yielded to their elders.
The potters of the Eastern Yí 東夷 produced poor quality pottery.
Shùn 舜 went there to make pottery,
and within a year, the pottery was strong.
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 sighed and said:
"Plowing,
fishing, and pottery
were not Shùn's 舜 official duties,
but Shùn 舜 went to do them
to remedy the failures.
Shùn 舜 must have truly believed in benevolence!
He personally toiled in hardship,
and the people followed him.
Therefore, it is said:
The virtue of a sage transforms!"
Someone asked a Confucian:
"At this time,
where was Yáo 堯?"
The man said:
"Yáo 堯 was the Son of Heaven."
"In that case,
how does Zhòng Ní 仲尼 consider Yáo 堯 to be a sage?
If a sage's keen observation is in a high position,
he will ensure that there is no deceit in the world.
Now, if plowing and fishing are not contentious,
and pottery is not poor,
what virtue did Shùn 舜 have to transform?
If Shùn 舜 remedied the failures,
then Yáo 堯 must have been at fault.
Praising Shùn 舜 means
diminishing Yáo's 堯 keen observation;
praising Yáo 堯 as a sage
means diminishing Shùn's 舜 transformative virtue,
which cannot be both.
A man of Chǔ 楚 was selling shields and spears,
and he praised them, saying:
"My shields are so sturdy
that nothing can pierce them."
He also praised his spears, saying:
"My spears are so sharp
that they can pierce anything."
Someone asked:
"If you use your spears to pierce your shields,
what would happen?"
The man could not answer.
Shields that cannot be pierced
and spears that can pierce anything
cannot coexist in the world.
Now, the impossibility of praising both Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜
is like the story of the spear and shield.
This is the story of the spear and shield.
Moreover, if Shùn 舜 remedies a failure,
one year has already passed,
and three years have passed three times.
Shùn 舜 has his limits,
and life has its limits,
but the failures of the world are endless;
using the finite to pursue the infinite,
the chances of stopping are few.
Using rewards and punishments to ensure that the world follows orders,
issue a decree saying:
"Those who meet the standard will be rewarded,
and those who do not meet the standard will be punished."
If the decree changes from morning to evening,
and from evening to morning,
the whole world will be finished in ten days;
why wait a year?
Shùn 舜 still did not use this argument to make Yáo 堯 follow his orders,
but instead acted personally,
which isn't very skillful, is it?
Furthermore, for one to personally endure hardship
and then transform the people
is what Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜 found difficult;
to use one's position to correct one's subordinates
is what mediocre rulers find easy.
If one wants to govern the world,
abandoning what mediocre rulers find easy
and pursuing what Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜 found difficult
is not something to be done in politics."
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 became ill,
and Duke Huán 桓公 went to visit him,
saying:
"Zhòng Fù 仲父 is ill,
and if you unfortunately succumb to your fate,
what advice will you give to me?"
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 said:
"If you hadn't said anything,
I would have requested to see you anyway.
I hope you will get rid of Shù Diāo 豎刁,
eliminate Yì Yá 易牙,
and distance yourself from Wèi's 衛 Gōngzǐ Kāifāng 公子開方.
Yì Yá 易牙 was in charge of your tastes,
and since you had only never tasted human flesh,
Yì Yá 易牙 steamed his own son's head and presented it to you.
No one does not love their own son,
but now he does not love his own son,
how can he love you?
You are jealous and fond of the harem,
so Shù Diāo 豎刁 castrated himself to manage the harem.
No one does not love their own body,
but if he does not love his own body,
how can he love you?
Kāifāng 開方 has served you for fifteen years.
The distance between Qí 齊 and Wèi 衛 cannot be traveled in just a few days.
He abandoned his mother
and served in office for a long time without returning home.
If he does not love his mother,
how can he love you?
I have heard that
boasting about falsehoods will not last long,
and covering up emptiness will not last long.
I hope you will get rid of these three men."
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 died,
but Duke Huán 桓公 did not follow his advice.
When Duke Huán 桓公 died,
worms came out of his door, and he was not buried.
Someone said:
What Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 advised Duke Huán 桓公
was not the speech of someone with standards.
The reason for getting rid of Shù Diāo 豎刁 and
Yì Yá 易牙
is because they do not love their own bodies,
which caters to your desires.
Saying
"If they do not love their own bodies,
how can they love you?"
Then, for ministers who devote all their strength to serve their lord,
would Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 not use them?
It is said,
"If one does not cherish their life,
how can they cherish the ruler?"
This is wanting the ruler to get rid of loyal subjects.
Moreover, using not cherishing their own body
to surmise that they do not cherish the ruler,
is like using Guǎn Zhòng's inability to die for Gōngzǐ Jiū
to surmise that he would not die for Duke Huán,
in which case Guǎn Zhòng would also be among those to be removed.
The way of an enlightened ruler is not like this;
he establishes what the people desire in order to seek their service.
Therefore, he establishes ranks and emoluments to encourage them;
he establishes what the people dislike in order to prevent their villainy.
Therefore, he establishes punishments to awe them.
When rewards are trustworthy and punishments are certain,
the ruler attributes merit to the subjects,
and villainy cannot be used to influence the ruler.
Even with Shù Diāo,
what can he do to the ruler?
Moreover, subjects exhaust their strength
to bargain with the ruler,
and the ruler bestows ranks and emoluments
to bargain with the subjects.
The relationship between ruler and subject
is not the affection of father and son,
but comes from calculation.
When the ruler has the Way,
the subjects will exhaust their strength, and villainy will not arise;
without the Way,
the subjects will block the ruler's insight
and pursue their private interests below.
Guǎn Zhòng did not make these considerations
clear to Duke Huán;
he only wanted to remove Shù Diāo,
but another Shù Diāo would arrive.
This is not the way to eliminate villainy.
Moreover, Duke Huán's death
and the worms flowing out of the door unburied
were because the subjects were too powerful.
The reality of the subjects' power
was that they usurped the ruler's authority.
With subjects who usurp the ruler's authority,
the ruler's orders will not reach the lowest levels,
and the subjects' feelings will not reach the highest levels.
The power of one person can separate the ruler and the subjects,
causing good deeds and failures to be unheard,
and blessings and disasters to be unconnected.
Therefore, there was the calamity of not being buried.
The way of an enlightened ruler is this:
one person does not hold multiple offices,
and one office does not handle multiple affairs;
the lowly do not rely on the noble to advance,
and great ministers do not rely on attendants to be seen.
All officials communicate smoothly,
and all subjects converge like spokes on a wheel;
for those who deserve reward, the ruler sees their merit;
for those who deserve punishment, the ruler knows their crime.
When knowledge and perception are not contrary to what is before,
and rewards and punishments are not flawed in the aftermath,
how can there be the calamity of not being buried?
Guǎn Zhòng did not make these words clear to Duke Huán;
he only wanted to remove the three attendants.
Therefore, it is said:
Guǎn Zhòng was without principle.
Xiāng Zǐ was besieged in Jìnyáng,
and after breaking the siege,
he rewarded five people who had rendered meritorious service,
with Gāo Hè being the first to be rewarded.
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"In the matter of Jìnyáng,
Hè did not have great merit,
yet now he is the first to be rewarded,
why is this?"
Xiāng Zǐ said:
"In the matter of Jìnyáng,
this humble one's state was in danger,
and the altars of soil and grain were in peril.
None of my ministers did not have intentions of pride and disrespect,
only Hè Zǐ did not lose the proper rites between ruler and subject,
therefore, I put him first."
Zhòng Ní heard of this and said:
"A good reward,
Xiāng Zǐ!
Rewarding one person will make all those who serve as subjects under Heaven dare not lose the proper rites."
Someone said:
Zhòng Ní does not understand good rewards.
For those who are good at rewards and punishments,
all officials do not dare to encroach on their duties,
and all ministers do not dare to lose the proper rites.
The ruler establishes his laws,
and those below have no intention of treachery or deceit.
If this is the case,
then one can be said to be good at rewards and punishments.
If, when Xiāng Zǐ was in Jìnyáng,
orders were not carried out,
and prohibitions were not stopped,
then Xiāng Zǐ had no state,
and Jìnyáng had no ruler.
Who would defend it then?
Now, when Xiāng Zǐ was in Jìnyáng,
the Zhī clan flooded it,
and turtles grew in the stoves,
yet the people had no rebellious thoughts.
This is because the ruler and subjects were close.
If Xiāng Zǐ had the benefit of closeness between ruler and subjects,
and wielded the laws of orders being carried out and prohibitions being stopped,
and yet there were still ministers who were proud and disrespectful,
then Xiāng Zǐ had failed in punishment.
For those who serve as subjects,
if they take advantage of a situation and achieve merit, then they should be rewarded.
Now, Hè merely did not show pride or disrespect,
and Xiāng Zǐ rewarded him.
This is a failure of reward.
An enlightened ruler's rewards are not given to those without merit,
and punishments are not given to those without crime.
Now, Xiāng Zǐ did not punish the proud and disrespectful ministers,
but rewarded the unmeritorious Hè.
Wherein lies Xiāng Zǐ's good reward?
Therefore, it is said
"Zhòng Ní does not understand good rewards."
Duke Píng of Jìn was drinking with his ministers,
and when the drinking was in full swing,
he sighed and said:
"Nothing is more joyous than being a ruler,
because one's words are not disobeyed."
Shī Kuàng was attending him, sitting in front,
and he took the zither and struck him with it.
The Duke dodged, shifting his robe,
and the zither broke against the wall.
The Duke said:
"Grand Musician, whom did you strike?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Just now, there was a petty man speaking at my side,
so I struck him."
The Duke said:
"It was I."
Shī Kuàng said:
"Ah!
These are not the words of one who rules."
Those around him requested to punish him.
The Duke said:
"Release him,
so that he may be a warning to me."
Someone said:
Duke Píng lost the way of a ruler,
and Shī Kuàng lost the rites of a subject.
To punish someone for conduct that is not correct is the business of a ruler toward a subject;
if their conduct is not correct,
then present one's words,
and if good advice is not heeded,
then distance oneself.
This is the business of a subject toward a ruler.
Now, Shī Kuàng criticized Duke Píng's conduct,
but did not offer the advice of a subject.
Instead, he executed the punishment of a ruler,
raising a zither and striking his person.
This reverses the positions of superior and inferior,
and loses the rites of a subject.
