For those who serve as subjects,
if the ruler has faults, then they should advise him.
If the advice is not heeded,
then they should lightly regard rank and emolument and wait for him.
This is the proper rite of a subject.
Now, Shī Kuàng criticized Duke Píng's faults,
raising a zither and striking his person.
Even a strict father would not do this to his son,
yet Shī Kuàng did it to his ruler.
This is a method of great rebellion.
The subject committed a great rebellion,
and Duke Píng was pleased and listened to it.
This is losing the way of a ruler.
Therefore, Duke Píng's actions cannot be clarified,
for they cause rulers to err in listening
without realizing their mistakes.
Nor can Shī Kuàng's actions be clarified,
for they allow treacherous ministers to cloak extreme criticism
and adorn the way to assassinate the ruler.
It cannot be said that both were clear-sighted;
this was a double fault.
Therefore, it is said:
Píng Gōng lost the way of the ruler,
Shī Kuàng also lost the etiquette of the minister.
During the time of Qí Huán Gōng,
there was a recluse called Xiǎo Chén Jì.
Huán Gōng visited him three times but could not meet him.
Huán Gōng said:
"I have heard that a commoner
does not lightly value titles and emoluments,
and nothing can exchange him for the lord of ten thousand chariots;
the lord of ten thousand chariots,
if he does not value benevolence and righteousness,
cannot bring down the commoner."
Therefore, he visited him five times and finally met him.
Some say:
Huán Gōng did not understand benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness
are about worrying about the harm to the world,
hastening to the troubles of a single state,
and not avoiding baseness and humiliation;
this is called benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, Yī Yǐn considered Zhōngguó to be in a state of chaos
and
became the cook for Tāng;
Bǎi Lǐ Xī considered Qín to be in a state of chaos
and
became a captive for Mù Gōng.
All of them worried about the harm to the world,
hastened to the troubles of a single state,
and did not refuse baseness and humiliation;
therefore, they were called benevolent and righteous.
Now Huán Gōng, with the power of ten thousand chariots,
lowers himself to a commoner,
intending to worry about the state of Qí,
but Xiǎo Chén does not act,
showing Xiǎo Chén's forgetfulness of the people.
Forgetting the people cannot be called benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness
are about not losing the etiquette of a minister,
and not ruining the position of ruler and minister.
Therefore, within the four borders,
those who hold birds and attend court are called ministers,
and the officials who divide duties and receive tasks are called the populace.
Now Xiǎo Chén is among the multitude of the populace,
and opposes the wishes of the ruler,
therefore, he cannot be called benevolent and righteous.
Benevolence and righteousness are not present in him,
yet Huán Gōng still treats him with courtesy.
If Xiǎo Chén has intelligence but evades Huán Gōng,
it is concealment,
which deserves punishment;
if he has no intelligence
but arrogantly and falsely disdains Huán Gōng,
it is deceit,
which deserves execution.
The actions of Xiǎo Chén
deserve either punishment or execution.
Huán Gōng cannot understand the principles of ruler and minister,
and shows courtesy to those who deserve punishment or execution.
This is Huán Gōng teaching the custom of disrespecting superiors and insulting the ruler in the state of Qí,
which is not the way to govern.
Therefore, it is said:
Huán Gōng did not understand benevolence and righteousness.
During the Mí Jī military campaign,
Hán Xiànzǐ was about to execute someone.
Xiè Xiànzǐ heard of it
and drove his carriage to save him.
By the time he arrived,
the execution had already taken place.
Xiè Zǐ then said:
"Why not display the body?"
His servant said:
"Were you not intending to save him earlier?"
Xiè Zǐ said:
"How dare I not share the blame?"
Some say:
The words of Xiè Zǐ
must be carefully examined,
it is not about sharing the blame.
What Hán Zǐ executed,
if it was a criminal,
then he could not be saved;
saving a criminal
is why the law is ruined,
if the law is ruined, the country is in chaos.
If it was not a criminal,
then he should not be encouraged to display the body;
encouraging him to display the body
is to doubly wrong the innocent,
doubly wronging the innocent
is why the people harbor resentment,
if the people resent, the country is in danger.
The words of Xiè Zǐ,
if not dangerous, then chaotic,
must be carefully examined.
Moreover, if what Hán Zǐ executed was a criminal,
what blame does Xiè Zǐ share?
If what he executed was not a criminal,
then he has already been executed,
and Xiè Zǐ has only now arrived,
so Hán Zǐ's blame is already established,
and Xiè Zǐ has arrived late.
Furthermore, Xiè Zǐ says
"display the body,"
which is not enough to share the blame for executing the person,
and it creates the blame of executing the displayed body.
Is this man talking about sharing blame?
In the past, Zhòu created the burning pillar,
and Chóng Hóu and
È Lái also said
to cut off the shins of those crossing the river;
what blame did they share with Zhòu?
Moreover, the people's expectations of those above are very high;
if Hán Zǐ fails,
then they expect Xiè Zǐ to succeed;
now that Xiè Zǐ also fails,
then the people are completely hopeless about those above.
Therefore, it is said:
The words of Xiè Zǐ are not about sharing blame,
but increasing blame.
Moreover, Xiè Zǐ's going to save the criminal
is because he considered Hán Zǐ to be wrong,
but he did not speak of why he was wrong,
but encouraged him
to "display the body,"
which is to make Hán Zǐ unaware of his mistake.
Now that those below have no hope of those above,
and Hán Zǐ is also unaware of his mistake,
I have not understood how Xiè Zǐ is sharing the blame.
Huán Gōng released Guǎn Zhòng from his bonds and made him chancellor.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am favored,
but I am lowly."
The Duke said:
"I will make you stand above Gāo and
Guó."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am honored,
but I am poor."
The Duke said:
"I will give you the family with the three returns."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am rich,
but I am distant."
Thereupon he was established as Zhòng Fù.
Xiāo Lüè said:
"Guǎn Zhòng thought that being lowly was not suitable for governing the noble,
therefore he requested to be above Gāo and
Guó;
he thought that being poor was not suitable for governing the rich,
therefore he requested the three returns;
he thought that being distant was not suitable for governing relatives,
therefore he took the position of Zhòng Fù.
Guǎn Zhòng was not greedy,
but it was for the convenience of governance."
Some say:
Now, if a servant girl proclaims the ruler's orders to the ministers,
no one would dare not listen,
it is not that the ministers are lowly and the servant girl is honored,
but that the ruler's command is applied,
and no one dares not obey.
Now, if Guǎn Zhòng's governance
does not depend on Huán Gōng,
it is as if there is no ruler.
If a state has no ruler,
it cannot be governed.
If he relies on the authority of Huán Gōng
and issues Huán Gōng's orders,
it is the reason why the servant girl is believed,
why wait for the honor of Gāo,
Guó, and Zhòng Fù
before acting?
The officials of the current generation who carry out affairs,
even those below the level of Dū Chéng, who collect orders,
do not avoid the honored and noble,
and do not approach the humble and lowly.
Therefore, if actions are in accordance with the law,
even the lowest village official will be trusted more than ministers and counselors;
if actions are not in accordance with the law,
even high officials will yield to the common people.
Now, Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 does not strive to honor the ruler and clarify the law,
but instead seeks to increase favor and titles.
If this isn't Guǎn Zhòng's 管仲 greed for wealth and position,
then he must be foolish and unaware of statecraft.
Therefore, it is said:
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 had missteps,
Xiāo Lüè's 霄略 reputation is overblown.
Hán Xuānwáng 韓宣王 asked Jiū Liú 樛留:
"I want to jointly employ Gōng Zhòng 公仲 and
Gōng Shū 公叔,
is that permissible?"
Jiū Liú 樛留 replied:
"In the past, Wèi 魏 jointly employed Lóu 樓 and
Dí 翟,
and lost Xī Hé 西河;
Chǔ 楚 jointly employed Zhāo 昭 and
Jǐng 景,
and lost Yān 鄢 and
Yǐng 郢.
Now, if you jointly employ Gōng Zhòng 公仲 and
Gōng Shū 公叔,
they will surely compete for power and seek external gains,
then the state will certainly face trouble."
Someone said:
In the past, Qí Huángōng 齊桓公 jointly employed Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 and
Bào Shū 鮑叔,
Tāng 湯 jointly employed Yī Yǐn 伊尹 and
Zhòng Huǐ 仲虺.
If jointly employing ministers is a source of worry for the state,
then Huángōng 桓公 would not have become a hegemon,
and Tāng 湯 would not have become a king.
Mǐn Wáng 湣王 solely employed Nào Chǐ 淖齒,
and died in the Eastern Temple;
Zhǔ Fù 主父 solely employed Lǐ Duì 李兌,
and starved to death.
If the ruler has methods,
joint employment is not a cause for concern;
if he has no methods,
joint employment will lead to competition for power and external gains,
and sole employment will lead to tyranny
and assassination.
Now, Liú 留 has no methods to advise his ruler,
causing his ruler to abandon joint employment for sole employment.
If there is no worry of losing Xī Hé 西河,
Yān 鄢, and Yǐng 郢,
then there will surely be the misfortune of dying by starvation.
Thus, Jiū Liú 樛留 does not have the ability to know what is good to say.
Jǐng Gōng 景公 visited Yàn Zǐ 晏子 and
said:
"Your house is small
and close to the market.
I would like to move your family to the Yùzhāng 豫章 Garden."
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 bowed twice and declined, saying:
"Moreover, my family is poor
and relies on the market for food.
I go there morning and evening,
so I cannot live far away."
Jǐng Gōng 景公 laughed and said:
"You are familiar with the market,
do you know the prices of goods?"
At this time, Jǐng Gōng 景公 was excessive in his use of punishments.
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 replied:
"Amputated feet are expensive, while shoes are cheap."
Jǐng Gōng 景公 said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"Because there are many punishments."
Jǐng Gōng 景公 suddenly changed his expression and said:
"Am I being cruel?"
Thereupon, he reduced punishments by five.
Someone said:
Yàn Zǐ's 晏子 claim that amputated feet were expensive
was not sincere;
he wanted to use convenient words
to stop the excessive punishments.
This is a failure to examine governance.
Punishments should not be too many,
but they should not be too few.
It is wrong to not understand what is appropriate,
and to argue based on excessiveness
is a failure of statecraft.
The punishment of defeated armies is in the thousands,
yet they still do not stop fleeing;
the implementation of punishments for governing disorder
is as if one fears not being able to overcome it,
yet evildoers are still not eliminated.
Now, Yàn Zǐ 晏子 does not examine whether the punishments are appropriate,
but argues based on their excessiveness;
is that not absurd?
Those who pity weeds harm the rice plants,
and those who show leniency to thieves harm the good people.
Now, to ease punishments
and practice leniency
is to benefit the wicked and harm the good.
This is not the way to govern.
Qí Huángōng 齊桓公, drunk from drinking wine,
lost his hat,
felt ashamed of it,
and did not hold court for three days.
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 said:
"This is a disgrace to the state.
Why does Your Excellency not erase it with governance?"
The Duke said:
"Good indeed!"
Thereupon, he opened the granaries
and gave to the poor,
reviewed the prisons,
and released those with minor offenses.
After three days, the people sang:
"Why does Your Excellency not lose your hat again!"
Someone said:
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 erased Huángōng's 桓公 disgrace among the common people,
but created a disgrace for Huángōng 桓公 among gentlemen.
If Huángōng 桓公 opened the granaries
and gave to the poor,
reviewed the prisons
and released those with minor offenses,
it is not righteous,
and cannot erase the disgrace;
if doing so is righteous,
and Huángōng 桓公 harbored righteousness,
must he wait until he loses his hat to do it?
Then Huángōng's 桓公 actions were righteous,
not because of losing his hat?
Thus, although he erased the disgrace of losing his hat among the common people,
he also created the disgrace of abandoning righteousness among gentlemen.
Moreover, opening the granaries and giving to the poor
is rewarding those without merit;
reviewing the prisons and releasing those with minor offenses
is failing to punish wrongdoings.
Rewarding those without merit
causes the people to rely on luck and hope from above;
failing to punish wrongdoings
causes the people to not learn from their mistakes and easily commit wrongdoings.
This is the root of disorder;
how can it erase disgrace?
In the past, Wén Wáng 文王 invaded Méng 盂,
conquered Jǔ 莒,
and seized Fēng 酆.
After three military actions, Zhòu 紂 resented him.
Wén Wáng 文王 then became afraid
and offered to cede the land west of the Luò 洛 River
and the red soil country
of a thousand *lǐ* 方千里,
to request the abolishment of the *páoluò* 炮烙 punishment.
All under Heaven rejoiced.
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 heard of this
and said:
"How benevolent,
Wén Wáng 文王!
He values a thousand *lǐ* 千里之國 of land lightly
in order to request the abolishment of the *páoluò* 炮烙 punishment.
How wise,
Wén Wáng 文王!
He gave up a thousand *lǐ* 千里之地 of land
and gained the hearts of all under Heaven."
Someone said:
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 considered Wén Wáng 文王 to be wise,
is that not an overstatement?
The wise are those
who recognize dangerous places and avoid them,
so that their bodies do not suffer misfortune.
If the reason Wén Wáng 文王 was resented by Zhòu 紂 was
because he did not have the people's hearts,
then it would be acceptable to seek the people's hearts
in order to resolve the resentment.
If Zhòu 紂 resented him because he greatly gained the people's hearts,
Already, to lightly treat the land
in order to win the people's hearts,
is to be heavily suspected;
it was certainly the reason why he was fettered and imprisoned at Yǒulǐ.
Elder Zhèng had a saying:
"To embody the Dao,
is to be without action and without visibility."
This is most suitable for Wén Wáng,
so as not to cause people to suspect him.
Zhòng Ní considered Wén Wáng wise,
but did not reach this argument.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shū Xiàng, saying:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí nine times united the feudal lords,
once rectified the world.
I do not know if it was the strength of his ministers,
or the strength of the ruler?"
Shū Xiàng replied, saying:
"Guǎn Zhòng was good at designing the cut,
Bīn Xū Wú was good at trimming the seams,
Xí Péng was good at edging;
when the garment was completed,
the ruler lifted it and wore it.
It was also the strength of the ministers;
what strength did the ruler have?"
Shī Kuàng lowered his qín and laughed.
The Duke said:
"Grand Music Master, why do you laugh?"
Shī Kuàng replied, saying:
"I laugh at Shū Xiàng's response to the ruler.
All those who are ministers
are like cooks who blend the five flavors and present them to the ruler;
if the ruler does not eat them,
who dares to force him?
Allow me to make an analogy:
the ruler is
the soil;
the ministers are
the plants and trees.
It must be that the soil is good,
then the plants and trees will be large and strong.
It is also the strength of the ruler;
what strength do the ministers have?"
Someone said:
"The responses of Shū Xiàng and
Shī Kuàng
are both one-sided arguments.
To rectify the world once,
to unite the feudal lords nine times,
is a great thing of beauty;
it is not solely the strength of the ruler,
nor is it solely the strength of the ministers.
In the past, Gōng Zhī Qí was in Yú,
and Xī Fù Jī was in Cáo;
the wisdom of these two ministers
spoke correctly of events,
and their actions achieved success,
yet Yú and Cáo both perished;
why?
This is because they had ministers but did not have a ruler.
Moreover, Jiǎn Shū resided in Gàn, and Gàn perished;
he resided in Qín, and Qín became dominant;
it was not that Jiǎn Shū was foolish in Gàn
but wise in Qín,
it was that there was a ruler or no ruler.
Xiàng's saying
'It is the strength of the ministers' ,
is not so.
In the past, Duke Huán had two markets within the palace,
two hundred women's quarters,
with disheveled hair, managing the women.
Having Guǎn Zhòng,
he became the leader of the Five Hegemons;
losing Guǎn Zhòng,
and gaining Shù Diāo,
he died,
with maggots flowing out the door unburied.
To think it was not the strength of the ministers
and to not credit Guǎn Zhòng for hegemony;
to think it was the strength of the ruler
and to not blame Shù Diāo for the chaos.
In the past,
Duke Wén of Jìn was enamored with a Qí woman
and forgot to return home;
Jiù Fàn remonstrated to the extreme,
therefore he was able to return to the state of Jìn.
Therefore, Duke Huán united with Guǎn Zhòng,
and Duke Wén achieved hegemony with Jiù Fàn.
And Shī Kuàng said
'It is the strength of the ruler,'
again, this is not so.
All of the Five Hegemons who were able to achieve success and fame in the world,
certainly had both ruler and ministers contributing strength.
Therefore, it is said:
the responses of Shū Xiàng and
Shī Kuàng
are both one-sided arguments.
In the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
a guest from Jìn arrived,
and the officials requested the rites.
Duke Huán said
"Inform Zhòngfù"
three times.
And the actor laughed, saying:
"How easy it is,
to be a ruler!
Once you say Zhòngfù,
twice you say Zhòngfù."
Duke Huán said:
"I have heard
'A ruler is weary in seeking men,
but at ease in employing men.'
It was difficult for me to obtain Zhòngfù;
after obtaining Zhòngfù,
why would it not be easy?"
Someone said:
Duke Huán's response to the actor
is not the saying of a ruler of men.
Duke Huán considered being a ruler to be weary in seeking men;
why is seeking men wearying?
Yī Yǐn considered himself to be a cook managing Tāng,
Bǎi Lǐ Xī considered himself a captive managing Duke Mù.
"Captive" is what is disgraceful;
"cook" is what is shameful.
To endure shame and disgrace and attend to the ruler,
is the urgency with which the worthy worry about the world.
In that case, a ruler of men should simply not go against the worthy;
seeking the worthy is not difficult for a lord of men.
Moreover, official positions
are for entrusting the worthy;
ranks and emoluments
are for rewarding merit.
Establish official positions,
display ranks and emoluments,
and the scholars will come of their own accord;
why should a ruler of men be weary?
Employing men is also not what is easy.
Although a ruler of men employs men,
he must measure them with standards and scales,
and compare them with laws and names;
if an affair meets the law, then it proceeds;
if it does not meet the law, then it stops;
if merit matches the words, then it is rewarded;
if it does not match, then it is punished.
Using laws and names to control ministers,
and using standards and scales to measure subordinates,
this cannot be relinquished;
where is the ease for a ruler of men?
Seeking men is not wearying,
employing men is not easy,
and Duke Huán's saying that
"seeking men is wearying,
employing men is easy"
is
not so.
Moreover, it was not difficult for Duke Huán to obtain Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng did not die for his ruler but returned to Duke Huán;
Bào Shū lightly regarded office and yielded talent
and entrusted it to him;
it was not difficult for Duke Huán to obtain Guǎn Zhòng;
this is clear.
After already obtaining Guǎn Zhòng,
why would it suddenly be easy?
Guǎn Zhòng is not the Duke of Zhōu.
The Duke of Zhōu nominally acted as the Son of Heaven for seven years;
when King Chéng grew up,
he handed over the government to him;
this was not for the sake of the world,
but for the sake of his duty.
He who does not usurp from his son in order to govern the world
will certainly not betray his dead ruler to serve his enemy;
he who betrays his dead ruler to serve his enemy
will certainly not hesitate to usurp from his son in order to govern the world;
he who does not hesitate to usurp from his son in order to govern the world
will certainly not hesitate to usurp his ruler's state.
Guǎn Zhòng
was a minister of Gōngzǐ Jiū,
plotted to kill Duke Huán but was unable to;
his ruler died, and he became a minister of Duke Huán.
Guǎn Zhòng’s selections and rejections were not those of Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
this is knowable.
If Guǎn Zhòng was a great worthy,
he would be like Tāng
and Wǔ.
Tāng and
Wǔ were ministers of Jié
and Zhòu;
Jié and Zhòu created disorder,
and Tāng and Wǔ seized power from them.
Now, Duke Huán easily resides above them,
thereby placing the conduct of Jié
and Zhòu
above Tāng
and Wǔ,
Duke Huán is in danger.
If Guǎn Zhòng was a wicked person,
he would be like Tián Cháng.
Tián Cháng
was a minister of Duke Jiǎn,
yet he murdered his lord.
Now, Duke Huán easily resides above them,
thereby placing the ease of Duke Jiǎn
above Tián Cháng,
Duke Huán is again in danger.
It is clear that Guǎn Zhòng is not Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
but whether he will be like Tāng
and Wǔ, or Tián Cháng,
is not yet knowable.
Being like Tāng
and Wǔ
carries the danger of Jié
and Zhòu;
being like Tián Cháng
carries the disorder of Duke Jiǎn.
Having already obtained the position of Second Father,
why is Duke Huán so quick to change?
If Duke Huán trusts Guǎn Zhòng's appointment,
he must know that he does not deceive him,
which means he knows a minister who does not deceive his lord.
Yet, although he knows a minister who does not deceive his lord,
now Duke Huán relies so completely on Guǎn Zhòng's appointment,
and trusts Shù Diāo
and Yì Yá,
leaving maggots flowing out of the door unburied,
it is already clear that Duke Huán does not know whether his ministers deceive him
or not,
yet he trusts his ministers so completely,
therefore it is said that Duke Huán is a benighted lord.
Lǐ Kè governed Zhōngshān,
and the magistrate of Kǔ Xíng reported accounts, yielding high revenues.
Lǐ Kè said:
"Eloquent speech,
pleasing to the ear, but not measured by righteousness,
is called 'seductive words.'
High revenues without the benefit of mountains, forests, marshes, and valleys,
is called 'seductive wealth.'
A gentleman does not listen to seductive words,
nor accept seductive wealth.
You may be dismissed for now."
Someone said:
"Master Lǐ’s words were:
'Eloquent speech,
pleasing to the ear,
but not measured by righteousness,
is called "seductive words."'
Eloquence lies in the speaker,
and pleasing lies in the listener;
speech is not the listener.
What is meant by 'not measured by righteousness'
does not refer to the listener,
but must refer to what is heard.
The listener
is either a petty person
or a gentleman.
A petty person has no righteousness
and is certainly unable to measure it;
a gentleman who measures it with righteousness
would certainly not be pleased.
Thus, saying
'eloquent speech,
pleasing to the ear,
but not measured by righteousness'
means
the words are certainly insincere.
High revenues being 'seductive wealth'
cannot be carried out far."
Master Lǐ did not prohibit the deceit early on,
and waited until the accounting,
thus condoning the transgression.
Without methods to know why revenues are high,
high revenues
are like abundant harvests.
Even if revenues are doubled,
what can be done?
Undertaking affairs cautiously in accordance with the harmony of yin and yang,
planting and cultivating in accordance with the suitability of the four seasons,
without errors of earliness or lateness,
and without calamities of cold or warmth,
will lead to high revenues.
Not hindering great tasks with small efforts,
not harming public affairs with private desires,
with men exerting themselves fully in farming,
and women exerting themselves in weaving,
will lead to high revenues.
Diligence in the principles of animal husbandry,
and discernment of the suitability of the land,
so that the six domestic animals thrive
and the five grains flourish,
will lead to high revenues.
Clarity in strategic planning,
and careful consideration of the advantages of terrain,
boats, carts,
and machinery,
expending little effort
to achieve great results,
will lead to high revenues.
Facilitating the operation of commerce at markets, passes, and bridges,
being able to use what one has to obtain what one lacks,
attracting traveling merchants to return,
and retaining foreign goods,
frugality in the use of wealth,
moderation in clothing and food,
and ensuring that palaces and instruments are sufficient for use,
without indulging in luxuries,
will lead to high revenues.
High revenues
are all due to human effort.
If it is a matter of Heaven,
with timely wind and rain,
and suitable warmth and cold,
without increasing the size of the land,
yet achieving the results of a bountiful year,
then high revenues will result.
Human effort
and heavenly contributions,
these two things both contribute to high revenues,
not the benefits of mountains, forests, marshes, and valleys.
To call high revenues without the benefits of mountains, forests, marshes, and valleys
"seductive wealth"
is an expression of incompetence.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ besieged the outer walls of Wèi,
with rhinoceros-hide shields and towers,
erected where arrows and stones could not reach,
but when he drummed, the soldiers did not rise.
Jiǎnzǐ threw down the drumstick and said:
"Alas!
My soldiers are repeatedly failing."
The messenger Zhú Guò, removing his helmet, replied:
"I have heard it said:
It is also possible that it is a matter of the ruler's inability,
the soldiers have not failed.
In the past, my former lord Duke Xiàn annexed seventeen states,
subjugated thirty-eight states,
and won twelve battles;
this was the use of these people.
After Duke Xiàn died,
Duke Huì ascended the throne,
indulging in extravagance and disorder,
delighting in jade-like women,
and the people of Qín freely invaded,
reaching within seventeen *lǐ* of Jiàng;
this was also the use of these people.
After Duke Huì died,
Duke Wén took over.
He besieged Wèi,
seized Yè,
fought the battle of Chéngpú,
defeated the Jīng people five times,
and gained a respected name throughout the world;
this was also the use of these people.
It can also be a matter of the ruler's inability,
the soldiers have not failed."
Jiǎnzǐ then removed the shields and towers,
positioned them where arrows and stones could reach,
and when he drummed, the soldiers mounted them,
and won a great victory.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Gaining a thousand leather chariots is not as good
as hearing one word from the messenger Zhú Guò."
Someone said:
“The envoy has not yet persuasively explained it.
He says that Duke Hùi (Huì Gōng) was defeated because of this man,
and Duke Wén (Wén Gōng) achieved hegemony because of this man,
but I don't see how he employed people.
Jiǎnzi (Jiǎn Zǐ) should not hastily remove shields
and large shields.
When a strict parent is in danger,
lightly braving arrows and stones
is how a filial son loves his parent.
A filial son loving his parent
is one in a hundred.
Now, to assume that when one's own life is in danger,
people can still fight,
is to assume that the sons of all clans above
are like filial sons loving their parents.
This is the envoy's deception.
Liking profit and disliking harm
is what everyone has.
If rewards are generous and trustworthy,
people will take the enemy lightly;
if punishments are severe and certain,
people will not retreat.
Those who persevere in serving their superiors,
numbering hundreds, are not even one;
loving profit and fearing punishment
is the same for everyone.
A leader of the masses does not go beyond what is common to everyone,
yet he talks about the actions of one in a hundred.
The envoy does not know the way to use the masses.”
Duke Mù of Lǔ (Lǔ Mù Gōng) asked Zǐ Sī (子思):
“I heard that the son of Pánggōng (龐𥼴氏) is unfilial.
What is his behavior like?”
Zǐ Sī (子思) replied:
“A gentleman respects the worthy to elevate virtue
and promotes the good to observe the people.
As for excessive behavior,
that is what petty people recognize;
I do not know.”
Zǐ Sī (子思) left,
and Zǐfú Lìbó (子服厲伯) entered to see the Duke.
He asked about the son of Pánggōng (龐𥼴氏),
and Zǐfú Lìbó (子服厲伯) replied:
“He has three faults,
all of which you have never heard.”
From then on,
the Duke valued Zǐ Sī (子思)
and despised Zǐfú Lìbó (子服厲伯).
Someone said:
“The ducal house of Lǔ (魯),
for three generations has been threatened by the Jì (季) family;
is this not fitting?
A wise ruler seeks the good and rewards it,
seeks out the wicked and punishes them,
and achieves this.
Therefore, those who are known for their goodness
are those who speak of goodness in accordance with the ruler;
those who are known for their wickedness
are those who speak of wickedness in accordance with the ruler;
these are the ones who deserve rewards and praise.
Not reporting wickedness
is being different from the ruler and colluding with the wicked below;
these are the ones who deserve censure and punishment.
Now, Zǐ Sī (子思) was not known for reporting faults, yet Duke Mù (穆公) valued him;
Lìbó (厲伯) was known for reporting wickedness, yet Duke Mù (穆公) despised him.
People all like to be valued
and dislike being despised,
so the Jì (季) family's rebellion succeeded
and was not reported to the ruler.
This is why the ruler of Lǔ (魯) was threatened.
Moreover, this is the custom of a state heading for ruin,
taking what the people of Lǔ (魯) use to glorify themselves,
and Duke Mù (穆公) alone valued it;
is this not upside down?”
When Duke Wén (Wén Gōng) fled into exile,
Duke Xiàn (獻公) sent the eunuch Pī (披) to attack him at Púchéng (蒲城).
Pī (披) cut off his sleeve,
and Duke Wén (文公) fled to the Dí (翟) people.
When Duke Hùi (惠公) ascended the throne,
he again sent him to attack him at Huìdòu (惠竇),
but he failed.
When Duke Wén (文公) returned to the state,
Pī (披) sought an audience.
The Duke said:
“In the campaign at Púchéng (蒲城),
the ruler ordered one night,
and you arrived immediately;
in the difficulty at Huìdòu (惠竇),
the ruler ordered three nights,
and you arrived in one night.
Why were you so fast?”
Pī (披) replied:
“The ruler's order is not to be doubted.
Removing the ruler's enemies is what I fear I cannot do enough of.
The people of Pú (蒲),
the people of Dí (翟),
what do I care about them?
Now that you have ascended the throne,
is there no Pú (蒲) or Dí (翟) to be concerned about?
Furthermore, Duke Huán (桓公) appointed Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) as his minister despite Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) attempt to shoot him with a hook.”
The Duke then granted him an audience.
Someone said:
“Qí (齊) and Jìn (晉) lost their sacrifices;
is this not fitting?
Duke Huán (桓公) was able to use Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) merits
and forget the resentment of the attempt to shoot him with a hook;
Duke Wén (文公) was able to listen to the eunuch's words
and disregard the crime of cutting off his sleeve.
Duke Huán (桓公)
and Duke Wén (文公) were able to tolerate these two men.
Later generations of rulers
are not as insightful as these two dukes;
later generations of ministers
are not as virtuous as these two men.
Disloyal ministers serve rulers who are not discerning.
If the ruler does not know,
then there will be thieves like Yān Cāo (燕操),
Zǐ Hǎn (子罕),
and Tián Cháng (田常);
if he knows,
they will use Guǎn Zhòng (管仲)
and the eunuch to excuse themselves.
The ruler will certainly not punish them
and will think that he has the virtue of Duke Huán (桓)
and Duke Wén (文).
This is to have enemies as ministers, and one's insight cannot illuminate the situation,
relying heavily on deception
and thinking oneself virtuous without being cautious.
Then, even without descendants,
is that not fitting?
Moreover, the eunuch's words
directly embellish the ruler's orders without deviating;
this is being loyal to the ruler.
Dying for the ruler and then being resurrected,
only then is one not ashamed and can be considered loyal.
Now, Duke Hùi (惠公) died in the morning, and by evening, he served Duke Wén (文公).
What kind of non-deviation is the eunuch's?”
Someone posed a riddle about Duke Huán (桓公),
saying:
“One difficulty,
two difficulties,
three difficulties,
what are they?”
Duke Huán (桓公) could not answer
and told Guǎn Zhòng (管仲).
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) replied:
“One difficulty is
keeping entertainers close and distancing scholars.
The second difficulty is
leaving his state and counting the seas.
The third difficulty is
the ruler being old and establishing the crown prince late.”
Duke Huán (桓公) said:
“Good.”
Without choosing a day, he performed the ancestral temple ritual for the crown prince.
Someone said:
“Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) riddle about the hidden is not accurate.
The use of scholars does not depend on closeness or distance,
and actors and dwarfs
are certainly what the ruler associates with for entertainment.
Therefore, keeping entertainers close and distancing scholars
and thinking that this is governing well
is not the real difficulty.
Being in a position
and not being able to use what one has
and acting contrary to those who have not left the state
is using the strength of one person to restrain a state.
Using the strength of one person to restrain a state
rarely succeeds.
Being able to see distant treachery
and perceive hidden deceit,
and carrying out orders that must be followed,
even if one is far away at sea,
there will certainly be no changes within.
Therefore, leaving the state to go to sea
without being ambushed and killed
is not the real difficulty.”
Chǔ Chéng Wáng installed Shāng Chén as his heir apparent,
but then desired to install Gōngzǐ Zhí.
Shāng Chén created trouble,
and subsequently murdered Chéng Wáng.
Gōngzǐ Zǎi
was the Zhōu heir apparent.
Gōngzǐ Gēn was favored,
and consequently rebelled in Dōngzhōu,
dividing it into two states.
These are not the troubles caused by appointing an heir apparent late.
If authority is undivided,
secondary sons are insignificant,
favoritism has no basis,
and even if one is a great minister,
appointing an heir apparent late is permissible.
Therefore, if one appoints an heir apparent late,
and secondary sons do not cause chaos,
it is still not a difficult thing.
What is called difficult
must rely on others to gain power
and prevent them from harming oneself;
this can be called one difficulty.
Not allowing a favored concubine to become a second queen is
the second difficulty.
Not allowing a beloved son to endanger the rightful heir,
and exclusively listening to one minister
who dares not deceive the ruler—
this can be called the third difficulty.
Yè Gōng Zǐ Gāo asked Zhòngní about government,
and Zhòngní said,
"Government lies in pleasing those nearby
so as to attract those from afar."
Āi Gōng asked Zhòngní about government,
and Zhòngní said,
"Government lies in selecting the worthy."
Qí Jǐng Gōng asked Zhòngní about government,
and Zhòngní said,
"Government lies in economizing on wealth."
After the three dukes left,
Zǐgòng asked,
"The three dukes asked you about the same thing, government,
but you answered them differently.
Why is that?"
Zhòngní said,
"Yè is a large city but the state is small,
and the people have rebellious hearts,
therefore I said,
'Government lies in pleasing those nearby so as to attract those from afar.'
Lǔ Āi Gōng has three great ministers
who outwardly block the lords of the various states
and neighboring scholars,
and inwardly collude to fool their ruler,
causing the ancestral temples to be unswept
and the altars of the soil and grain to lack blood offerings.
These must be the three ministers,
therefore I said,
'Government lies in selecting the worthy.'
Qí Jǐng Gōng is building the Yōng Gate
and constructing a grand bedchamber,
and in one morning, he gave estates of three hundred chariots to three people,
therefore I said,
'Government lies in economizing on wealth.'"
Someone said,
"Zhòngní's answers
are words that lead to the destruction of states.
The people of Yè have rebellious hearts,
and to advise him
to 'please those nearby so as to attract those from afar'
is to teach the people to expect favors.
When favors are used in government,
those without merit receive rewards,
and those with crimes are pardoned.
This is why laws are ruined.
When laws are ruined and government is chaotic,
using chaotic government to rule defeated people
is unlikely to work.
Moreover, if the people have rebellious hearts,
it is because the ruler's insight does not reach everywhere.
If one does not emulate Yè Gōng's insight
but instead tries to please those nearby and attract those from afar,
it is abandoning the power that we can use to restrain
and instead using favors to compete with the people,
which is not the way to maintain power.
Yáo's virtue
was the crown of the six kings.
When Shùn moved once and formed a settlement,
Yáo lost the empire.
For someone to lack the methods to restrain those below,
yet rely on being Shùn and not lose his people,
is that not lacking in method?"
An enlightened ruler sees small treachery in its infancy,
therefore the people have no grand schemes;
he carries out small punishments for minor offenses,
therefore the people have no major rebellions.
This is what is meant by
"dealing with difficulties when they are easy,
and accomplishing great things when they are small."
Now, if those with merit are always rewarded,
the rewarded do not owe it to the ruler,
but to their own efforts;
if those with crimes are always punished,
the punished do not resent the ruler,
but their own crimes.
When the people know that rewards and punishments all originate from themselves,
they eagerly pursue merit and profit in their occupations
and do not accept gifts from the ruler.
"The highest
is when the people are barely aware of their ruler."
This saying means that under the highest
there are no praises from the people,
so where would there be people who expect favors?
The people of a supreme ruler have neither benefit nor harm,
and to instruct him to "please those nearby and attract those from afar"
is also permissible to discard.
Āi Gōng has ministers who outwardly block and inwardly collude
to fool their ruler,
and to instruct him to "select the worthy"
is not a discussion of merit and accomplishment,
but selecting those whom he personally considers worthy.
If Āi Gōng knew that the three ministers were outwardly blocking and inwardly colluding,
then the three ministers would not remain in their positions for a single day.
Āi Gōng does not know how to select the worthy,
but selects those whom he personally considers worthy,
therefore the three ministers are able to take charge of affairs.
Yān Zǐ Kuài esteemed Zǐ Zhī
but not Sūn Qīng,
so he died and was disgraced;
Fūchāi considered Tài Zǎi Pǐ wise
but considered Zǐxū foolish,
so he was destroyed by Yuè.
The ruler of Lǔ need not necessarily know the worthy,
but to instruct him to select the worthy
is to put Āi Gōng
in the same danger as Fūchāi
and Yān Kuài.
An enlightened ruler does not personally promote ministers;
ministers recommend each other.
He does not personally praise them;
their accomplishments recommend themselves.
He evaluates them based on their responsibilities,
tests them through their actions,
and assesses them based on their achievements.
Therefore, the ministers govern impartially and without personal interest,
not concealing the worthy
and not promoting the unworthy.
In that case, why should the ruler bother selecting the worthy?
Jǐng Gōng gives away estates of a hundred chariots,
and to instruct him to
"economize on wealth"
is to cause Jǐng Gōng to lack the means
to know the extravagance of wealth,
and to be frugal only on the surface,
which will not prevent poverty.
If a ruler uses a thousand *lǐ* to feed his own mouth and stomach,
then even Jié
and Zhòu would not be extravagant.
The state of Qí is three thousand *lǐ* square,
and yet Duke Huán used half of it to feed himself,
which is more extravagant than Jié
and Zhòu;
however, he was able to become the leader of the Five Hegemons
because he knew the places where extravagance and thrift were appropriate.
If a ruler cannot restrain those below
but restrains himself, that is called being robbed.
If he cannot adorn those below
but adorns himself, that is called chaos.
If he does not regulate those below
but regulates himself, that is called poverty.
An enlightened ruler makes the people selfless;
those who deceive for food are forbidden.
Those who exhaust their strength in service and attribute benefits to their superiors will surely be heard of,
and those heard of will surely be rewarded; those who engage in corrupt practices for personal gain will surely be known,
and those known will surely be punished.
If this is so, then loyal ministers will exhaust their loyalty to the public,
the common people will exert their strength for their families,
and the officials will be meticulous and demanding towards their superiors.
Even if it leads to extravagance exceeding that of Jǐng Gōng,
it will not be a national calamity.
Therefore, to persuade them with frugality is not the most pressing matter.
Indeed, to speak one word to the three highest ministers such that
the three highest ministers need have no worries,
this is what it means to understand those below.
When understanding of those below is clear,
then wrongdoing is prevented at its inception;
when wrongdoing is prevented at its inception,
then villainy does not accumulate;
when villainy does not accumulate,
then there are no collusions;
when there are no collusions,
then the public and private are distinct;
when the public and private are distinct,
then factions are dispersed;
when factions are dispersed,
then there is no worry of external obstruction or internal collusion.
When understanding of those below is clear,
then discernment is keen and thorough;
when discernment is keen and thorough,
then rewards and punishments are clear;
when rewards and punishments are clear,
then the state is not impoverished.
Therefore, it is said:
"One word to the three highest ministers such that they need have no worries"
is what it means to understand those below.
Zhèng Zǐchǎn went out early in the morning,
passing by the lane of an eastern artisan,
and heard a woman's weeping.
He held the hand of his driver and listened to it.
After a while,
he sent an official to arrest and question her,
and it turned out that she had strangled her husband.
Another day,
his driver asked, saying:
"How did you know that, Master?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"Her voice was fearful.
Generally, when people are close and affectionate,
they worry when someone starts to get sick,
they fear when someone is about to die,
and they grieve when someone has died.
Now, she weeps for the dead,
not grieving but fearful,
so I knew there was foul play."
Some say:
Zǐchǎn's governance,
isn't it too meddlesome?
If villainy must await the reach of one's ears and eyes
before being known,
then the number of villains caught in the state of Zhèng would be few.
To not employ officials in charge of standards,
to not examine the policies of mutual responsibility,
to not clarify measures,
to rely on exhausting one's intelligence,
to labor one's thoughts,
and thereby to know villainy,
isn't this lacking in method?
Moreover, things are numerous, and wisdom is limited;
the limited cannot overcome the numerous.
Wisdom is insufficient to know all things,
therefore, use things to manage things.
Those below are numerous, and those above are few;
the few cannot overcome the numerous.
What is said is that the ruler is insufficient to know all his ministers,
therefore, use people to know people.
Thus, the body is not labored, and affairs are governed;
thoughts are not used, and villainy is discovered.
Therefore, a person from Sòng said:
"If a single sparrow flies past Yì,
Yì will surely catch it,
then Yì would be deceitful.
If the whole world is used as a net for it,
then no sparrow will be missed."
Knowing villainy also has a great net,
not missing a single one is all that is needed.
To not follow its principles,
and to use one's own heart and observation as bow and arrow for it,
then Zǐchǎn would be deceitful.
Lǎozǐ said:
"To govern a state with cleverness
is the ruin of the state."
This is what he was referring to regarding Zǐchǎn.
Qín Zhāowáng asked his attendants, saying:
"In the present time, which is stronger, Hán
or Wèi, compared to their initial state?"
The attendants replied, saying:
"Weaker than their initial state."
"In the present time, which are better, Rú'ěr
and Wèi Qí,
compared to the former Mèngcháng
and Máng Mǎo?"
They replied, saying:
"Not as good."
The king said:
"Mèngcháng
and Máng Mǎo led the strong Hán and Wèi,
yet they could do nothing to me."
The attendants replied, saying:
"Very true."
Zhōng Qī pushed aside his zither and replied, saying:
"Your Majesty's assessment of the world is mistaken.
In the time of the Six Jìn,
the Zhī clan was the strongest,
destroying the Fàn
and Zhōngháng clans
and using the soldiers of Hán and Wèi
to attack Zhào,
flooding it with the waters of the Jìn River,
with only three boards remaining above the city that had not been submerged.
Zhī Bó went out,
Wèi Xuānzǐ drove the chariot,
and Hán Kāngzǐ was the lancer on the side.
Zhī Bó said:
'At first, I did not know that water could destroy a state,
but now I know it.
The Fén River can flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River can flood Píngyáng.'
Wèi Xuānzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
and Kāngzǐ stepped on Xuānzǐ's foot,
elbow and foot connecting on the chariot,
and the Zhī clan was divided below Jìnyáng.
Now, although Your Majesty is strong,
you are not as strong as the Zhī clan;
although Hán and Wèi are weak,
they have not reached the state of being below Jìnyáng.
This is a time when the world is using elbows and feet,
I hope Your Majesty does not dismiss this."
Some say:
Zhāowáng's question was flawed,
and the replies of his attendants and Zhōng Qī were excessive.
Generally, the enlightened ruler's governance of the state
relies on its strategic advantage.
If the strategic advantage cannot be harmed,
then even if the whole world is strong, it can do nothing to you,
and moreover, how could Mèngcháng,
Máng Mǎo,
Hán,
and Wèi do anything to me?
If its strategic advantage can be harmed,
then even those as unworthy as Rú'ěr
and Wèi Qí,
and Hán
and Wèi, can still harm it.
Therefore, whether one is harmed or not lies
solely in self-reliance;
why ask?
If one relies on one's invulnerability,
then what choice is there between strong and weak?
The error lies in not relying on oneself
and asking what to do;
it is only by luck that one is not harmed.
Shēn Zǐ said:
"To lose the method and seek to be trusted
is to be doubted."
This is what he was referring to regarding Zhāowáng.
Zhī Bó was immoderate,
following Hán Kāng
and Wèi Xuān
and plotting to flood and destroy their states with water.
This is why Zhī Bó's state was destroyed and he himself died,
his head becoming a drinking cup.
Now, if Zhāo Wáng were to ask whether he was stronger than at the beginning,
would he be worried about the calamities of the water people?
Even if he has attendants,
they are not like the two sons of Hán
and Wèi.
How could they be as close as elbows and feet?
Yet Zhōng Qī said
"Do not change."
This is empty talk.
Moreover, Zhōng Qī's official duty
is playing the qín and sè.
If the strings are not in tune
and the melody is unclear,
it is Zhōng Qī's responsibility.
This is how Zhōng Qī serves Zhāo Wáng.
If Zhōng Qī is good at fulfilling his duty
but still does not satisfy Zhāo Wáng,
and then speaks about what he does not know,
wouldn't that be absurd?
If the attendants answer,
"Weaker than at the beginning"
or
"Not as good,"
that would be acceptable,
but to say "Exactly so" is flattery.
Shēn Zǐ said:
"Governance should not exceed one's official duty;
even if one knows, one should not speak."
Now Zhōng Qī does not know but still speaks about it.
Therefore, it is said:
Zhāo Wáng's question was flawed,
and the attendants' and Zhōng Qī's answers were all mistakes.
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"See what is acceptable,
and explain it with evidence;
see what is unacceptable,
and express aversion with form.
If rewards and punishments are reliable in what is seen,
even in what is not seen,
who would dare to do it?
See what is acceptable,
and explain it without evidence;
see what is unacceptable,
and express aversion without form.
If rewards and punishments are unreliable in what is seen,
and one seeks beyond what is not seen,
it is impossible."
Some say:
The broad court and solemn residence
are where people are respectful.
The banquet room and solitary dwelling
are where Zēng and Shǐ were lax.
Observing where people are respectful
does not reveal their true feelings.
Moreover, the ruler
is adorned by his subjects.
If likes and dislikes are based on what is seen,
subjects will certainly use deceptive things to fool their ruler.
It is inevitable.
If one's discernment cannot illuminate distant deceptions
and see hidden subtleties,
and one relies on observing adorned behavior
to determine rewards and punishments,
wouldn't that be flawed?
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Speak in the room,
fill the room;
speak in the hall,
fill the hall;
this is called the King of All Under Heaven."
Some say:
What Guǎn Zhòng meant by
"speak in the room, fill the room;
speak in the hall, fill the hall"
does not only refer to words about amusement and food and drink;
it must refer to important matters.
The important matters of a ruler
are law and method.
Law
is the compiled and written documents
that are established in government offices
and proclaimed to the people.
Method
is what is stored in the heart,
used to manage all affairs
and secretly control the ministers.
Therefore, law should be obvious,
while method should not be revealed.
Thus, when an enlightened ruler speaks of law,
everyone, both high and low, within the territory will hear and know of it;
it does not only fill the hall.
When using method,
even close and trusted associates will not hear of it;
it cannot fill the room.
Yet Guǎn Zǐ still said:
"Speak in the room, fill the room;
speak in the hall, fill the hall."
This does not refer to the words of law and method.
Wèi Sūn Wén Zǐ was on a diplomatic visit to Lǔ,
and Duke Dēng also ascended.
Shū Sūn Mù Zǐ stepped forward and said:
"At the meetings of the feudal lords,
our lord has never been behind the lord of Wèi.
Now you are not one rank behind our lord;
our lord does not know what the fault is.
Please step down a bit."
Sūn Zǐ had no reply
and showed no sign of repentance.
Mù Zǐ retreated and told people,
"Sūn Zǐ will surely perish.
A minister who does not defer to his lord,
and does not repent his mistakes,
is the root of ruin."
Some say:
When the Son of Heaven loses the Way,
the feudal lords attack him;
thus there were Tāng
and Wǔ.
When a feudal lord loses the Way,
the grand officers attack him;
thus there were Qí
and Jìn.
If a subject who attacks his lord is destined to perish,
then Tāng
and Wǔ would not have become kings,
and Jìn and Qí would not have been established.
Sūn Zǐ was a lord in Wèi,
and then did not act as a subject in Lǔ;
he was his lord's subject.
The lord has faults,
therefore the subject has merits.
To predict ruin for a lord with faults
but also predict ruin for a subject with merits
is unwise.
Lǔ could not punish the grand officer of Wèi,
and the lord of Wèi's perspicacity
did not recognize the unrepentant minister.
Although Sūn Zǐ had these two flaws,
how could he perish because of them?
The reason for his ruin
is his fault, which is how he gained his lord's favor.
Some say:
The relationship between subject and ruler involves the distribution of power.
A subject who can usurp power from the ruler
does so by obtaining the right opportunities.
Therefore, taking what is not one's due
is what the masses will seize back;
relinquishing one's due and then taking it
is what the people will grant.
Thus, Jié demanded the women of Mount Mín,
and Zhòu sought Bǐ Gān's heart,
and the world turned away;
Tāng changed his identity,
and Wǔ willingly accepted abuse,
and all within the seas submitted.
Zhào Xuān fled to the mountains,
and the Tián clan served outside,
and Qí
and Jìn followed.
Therefore, the reason why Tāng
and Wǔ became kings,
and why Qí and Jìn were established,
was not necessarily because of their lords;
they obtained the power first and then used it to serve as lords.
Now, without having the means to obtain power,
to act as if one already has it
is to invert righteousness and defy virtue.
Inverting righteousness
leads to the failure of affairs;
defying virtue
leads to the accumulation of resentment.
How can one not be aware of the causes of failure and ruin?
Why?
Lǔ Yáng Hǔ wanted to attack the Three Huán families,
but failed and fled to Qí,
where Duke Jǐng treated him with courtesy.
Bào Wénzǐ advised,
"That's not acceptable.
Yáng Hǔ was favored by the Jì family but wanted to attack Jì Sūn,
because he coveted his wealth.
Now, you are wealthier than Jì Sūn,
and Qí is greater than Lǔ,
so Yáng Hǔ will use all his deceit."
Duke Jǐng then imprisoned Yáng Hǔ.
Some say:
"For a family with a thousand gold,
if their son is not benevolent,
people's eagerness for profit is extreme.
Duke Huán
was the foremost of the Five Hegemons,
yet he contended for the state and killed his elder brother.
His gain was great.
The relationship between subject and ruler
is not like the affection of brothers.
The merit of seizing power by killing
allows one to control ten thousand chariots and enjoy great benefit,
so which of the subjects is not a Yáng Hǔ?
Affairs are achieved through subtle skill,
and fail through obvious clumsiness.
The fact that the subjects have not yet started trouble
means that their preparations are not yet complete.
If all the subjects have the intentions of Yáng Hǔ,
but the ruler does not know,
this is subtle and skillful.
Yáng Hǔ's greed
is known throughout the land,
and he wants to attack his superior,
which is obvious and clumsy.
To not make Duke Jǐng further punish the skillful subjects of Qí,
but to make him punish the clumsy Hǔ,
is a reversal of Bào Wénzǐ's argument.
The loyalty or deceit of a subject
depends on what the ruler does.
If the ruler is wise and strict,
then the subjects are loyal;
if the ruler is weak and ignorant,
then the subjects are deceitful.
Knowing the subtle is called wisdom;
allowing no pardon or reprieve is called strictness.
Not knowing the skillful subjects of Qí
but punishing the one who caused chaos in Lǔ,
is that not absurd!
Some say:
"Benevolence and greed have different minds.
Therefore, Gōngzǐ Mù Yí resigned from Sòng,
while Chǔ Shāng Chén murdered his father;
Zhèng Qùjí gave the state to his younger brother,
while Lǔ Huán murdered his elder brother.
The Five Hegemons all annexed territory,
but to judge people by the standards of Duke Huán
would mean that none of them had integrity and honesty.
Moreover, if the ruler is wise and strict,
then the subjects are loyal.
Yáng Hǔ caused chaos in Lǔ,
failed, and fled.
Entering Qí and not being punished
is like condoning the chaos.
If the ruler is wise, he will punish;
knowing that Yáng Hǔ can accomplish chaos
shows the understanding of subtle situations."
The saying goes:
"The feudal lords treat the state as their kin."
If the ruler is strict, then Yáng Hǔ's crime cannot be overlooked;
this is the reality of no pardon or reprieve,
therefore punishing Yáng Hǔ
is the way to make the subjects loyal.
Not knowing the skillful subjects of Qí
but abandoning the punishment for obvious chaos,
blaming what has not yet happened,
and not punishing the obvious crime
is absurd.
Now, punishing the crime of causing chaos in Lǔ
to intimidate the subjects with treacherous intentions
can gain the support of Jì,
Mèng, and Shū Sūn.
How can Bào Wén's argument
be considered a reversal?
When Duke Zhèng was about to make Gāo Qúmí a minister,
Duke Zhāo detested him
and persistently advised against it, but was not listened to.
After Duke Zhāo ascended the throne,
he feared that he would be killed.
On the day of Xīn Mǎo,
he was murdered by Gāo Qúmí, who installed Zǐ Dǎn in his place.
The noble men said:
"Duke Zhāo knew what he hated."
Gōngzǐ Yǔ said:
"Gāo Bó will surely be executed,

Some say:
"The words of father and son Yǔ

The reason Duke Zhāo encountered disaster
was that his revenge for evil was too late.
But then the reason Gāo Bó's death was delayed
was that his revenge for evil was too extreme.
An enlightened ruler does not harbor anger.
If anger is harbored,
then guilty subjects will act lightly to carry out their plans,
and the ruler will be in danger.
Therefore, at the drinking at Língtái,
the Marquis of Wèi was angry but did not punish,
so Chǔ Shī created trouble.
When eating turtle soup,
the ruler of Zhèng was angry but did not punish,
so Zǐ Gōng killed the ruler.
The noble men's statement
"knowing what is hated"
is not about being extreme,
but rather saying: knowing it so clearly,
yet not carrying out punishment,

Therefore, "knowing what is hated"
shows his lack of authority.
A ruler not only lacks the ability to see trouble,
but also lacks the ability to make decisions.
Now, Duke Zhāo knew what was evil,
investigated the crime but did not punish,
allowing Qúmí to harbor hatred, fear death, and seek luck,
so he could not avoid being killed.
Thus, Duke Zhāo's revenge for evil was not extreme."
Some say:
"Revenge for evil being extreme
means punishing a minor crime with a severe punishment.
Punishing a minor crime with a severe punishment
is the extreme of imprisonment.
The trouble with imprisonment
is not in the way of punishment,
but in the multitude of enemies.
Therefore, Duke Lì of Jìn destroyed the Three Xiè families,
and Luán and
Zhōng Háng created trouble;
Zǐ Dōu of Zhèng killed Bó Xuān
and the cauldron of food caused disaster;
the King of Wú executed Zǐ Xū,
and Gōu Jiàn of Yuè achieved hegemony.
The expulsion of the Marquis of Wèi
and the murder of Líng of Zhèng
were not because Chǔ Shī was not killed or Gōng Fǔ was not punished,
but because they showed anger when they should not have,
and had the intention to punish when they should not have.
Being angry at the deserving,
and punishing without going against people's hearts,
what harm is there in harboring it?
If guilt has not yet been established,
and after ascending the throne,
the old crime is punished,
that is how Qí Hú was destroyed.
If a minister acts like a ruler,
there will still be future troubles,
let alone if a minister acts like a ruler for the ruler?
If the punishment is not appropriate
and the intention is to eliminate completely,
this is making an enemy of the world.
So even if one is killed,
is that not justifiable?
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Mí Zixiá was favored
and monopolized power in the state of Wèi.
A dwarf who had an audience with the duke said:
"My dream is shallow."
The duke said:
"What did you dream?"
"Dreaming of the stove
is like seeing you, my lord."
The duke was angry and said,
"I have heard that when one is about to meet a ruler, one dreams of the sun.
Why do you, upon seeing me, dream of a stove?"
The dwarf said,
"The sun shines on all under heaven,
and nothing can obstruct it.
A ruler shines on an entire state,
and no single person should be able to block it.
Therefore, when one is about to see a ruler, one dreams of the sun.
As for the stove,
if one person tends it,
then later people will have no way to see the fire.
Could it be that one person is tending the ruler?
If so, then my dreaming of the stove
is not inappropriate, is it?"
The duke said,
"Good."
Thereupon, he dismissed Yōng Chú,
sent away Mí Zixia,
and employed Sīkōng Gǒu.
Someone said,
"The dwarf cleverly used the dream
to point out the way of a ruler.
However, Líng Gōng did not understand the dwarf's words.
Dismissing Yōng Chú,
sending away Mí Zixia,
and employing Sīkōng Gǒu,
means discarding what was loved and employing what was considered worthy.
Zhèng Zidu considered Qìng Jiàn worthy and blocked him,
Yàn Zikuai considered Zǐ Zhī worthy and blocked him.
Discarding what is loved
and employing what is considered worthy
does not necessarily prevent one person from tending to the ruler.
An unworthy person tending the ruler is
not enough to obscure his vision;
but now, without increasing his knowledge,
to have a worthy person tend to himself
will surely be dangerous."
Someone said,
" Qū Dào was fond of *jì* water caltrop,
Wén Wáng was fond of sweet flag pickle;
these were not true flavors,
yet the two worthies esteemed them;
what is tasted is not necessarily good.
Jìn Línghóu delighted in Cān Wúxù,
Yàn Kuài considered Zǐ Zhī worthy;
these were not true gentlemen,
yet the two rulers honored them;
what is deemed worthy is not necessarily worthy.
To employ someone not worthy, believing them to be worthy,
is the same as employing someone out of affection.
If someone truly worthy is promoted because they are worthy,
it is different from employing someone out of affection.
Therefore, Chǔ Zhuāng promoted Sūn Shū'ao and became a hegemon,
Shāng Xīn employed Fèi Zhòng and was destroyed;
these both employed those they considered worthy,
yet the results were opposite.
Although Yàn Kuài promoted those he considered worthy,
it was the same as employing those he loved;
how could Wèi Xī be correct?
Thus, the dwarf's words are not yet clear.
The ruler is blocked but does not know he is blocked;
he knows he is blocked after he has been seen;
therefore, dismissing the blocking minister
is an increase in knowledge.
If it is said
'without increasing his knowledge,
to have a worthy person tend himself
will surely be dangerous,'
but now he has increased his knowledge,
then even if he is tended,
it will surely not be dangerous."
Shènzi said,
"A flying dragon rides the clouds,
a soaring snake wanders the mist;
when the clouds dissipate and the mist clears,
then the dragon and snake are the same as earthworms and ants;
they have lost what they rode on.
If a worthy person is humbled by an unworthy one,
it is because their authority is light and their position low;
if an unworthy person can be subjected to a worthy one,
it is because their authority is heavy and their position high.
Yáo, as a commoner,
could not govern three people;
but Jié, as the Son of Heaven,
could throw the world into chaos:
I know from this that power and position are reliable,
while worth and wisdom are not worth admiring.
If a crossbow is weak but the arrow flies high,
it is because it is propelled by the wind;
if a person is unworthy but their orders are carried out,
it is because they receive assistance from the masses.
When Yáo taught his subordinates, the people did not listen;
but when he faced south and ruled the world as king,
his orders were carried out,
and his prohibitions were obeyed.
From this, it can be seen that
worth and wisdom are not enough to subdue the masses,
while power and position are enough to humble the worthy."
Yīng Shènzi replied,
"A flying dragon rides the clouds,
a soaring snake wanders the mist;
I do not consider the dragon and snake to be
unrelated to the power of the clouds and mist.
However,
to abandon worth and rely solely on power,
is that enough to govern?
I have yet to see it.
That they have the power of clouds and mist and are able to ride and wander them
is because the dragon and snake have excellent abilities.
Now, if the clouds are dense but an earthworm cannot ride them,
if the mist is thick but an ant cannot wander it,
that they have the power of dense clouds and thick mist
but cannot ride and wander them
is because the earthworm and ant have meager abilities.
Now, Jié and Zhòu faced south and ruled the world,
taking the Son of Heaven's authority
as their clouds and mist,
yet the world could not escape great chaos;
this is because Jié and Zhòu had meager abilities.
Moreover, if those people had Yáo's power
to govern the world,
how would their power differ from Jié's power,
which threw the world into chaos?
Power
cannot necessarily ensure that worthy people will use it
and unworthy people will not.
When worthy people use it, the world is governed;
when unworthy people use it, the world is thrown into chaos.
Among human nature,
worthy people are few
while unworthy people are many;
and to use the benefits of power and authority
to aid the unworthy in a chaotic world
means that there are many who use power to throw the world into chaos,
and few who use power to govern the world.
Power is something that
facilitates governance but also benefits chaos.
Therefore, the *Zhou Shu* says,
"Do not add wings to a tiger;
it will fly into the city
and choose people to eat."
To place an unworthy person in a position of power
is to add wings to a tiger.
Jié and Zhòu built high terraces and deep pools
to exhaust the people's strength,
and created the *páo luò* (burning pillar)
to injure the people's nature.
That Jié and Zhòu were able to indulge themselves was
because the Son of Heaven's authority gave them wings.
If Jié and
Zhòu were commoners,
they would not have been able to carry out a single action
before their bodies were subjected to punishment.
Power is something that
nourishes the heart of tigers and wolves
and results in violent and chaotic affairs;
this is the great calamity of the world.
As for power's role in governance and chaos,
it originally has no fixed position;
and to speak exclusively of
power as being sufficient to govern the world
is to have a shallow understanding.
A good horse is harnessed to a sturdy cart;
if a slave drives it,
he will be laughed at;
if Wáng Liáng drives it,
he will travel a thousand *lǐ* in a day.
The cart and horse are no different;
whether it reaches a thousand *lǐ*
or is laughed at
depends on the great difference between skill and clumsiness.
Now, to take the position of the state as the cart,
power as the horse,
commands as the reins,
and punishments as the whip,
if Yáo and
Shùn drive it, the world will be governed;
if Jié and Zhòu drive it, the world will be thrown into chaos;
then the difference between the worthy and the unworthy is great indeed."
Now, wanting to pursue speed and achieve distance,
yet not knowing to employ Wáng Liáng 王良;
wanting to advance benefit and eliminate harm,
yet not knowing to employ the worthy and capable:
this is the affliction of not understanding categories.
Moreover, Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜 are also the Wáng Liáng 王良 of governing the people.
In response, he said:
"Those men rely on authority as sufficient to govern officials."
The guest said,
"If one must wait for the worthy to govern, "
then that is not so.
Authority,
its name is singular, but its variations are countless.
If authority must arise from nature,
then there is no need to speak of authority.
What I mean by speaking of authority
is speaking of that which is established by people.
Moreover, Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜 were born already in high positions;
even if there were ten Jié 桀 or
Zhòu 紂, they could not cause disorder;
this is governance by authority.
Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 were also born already in high positions;
even if there were ten Yáo 堯 or Shùn 舜, they still could not govern;
this is disorder by authority.
Therefore, it is said:
"Governance by authority cannot be disrupted,
while disorder by authority cannot be governed."
This is a natural authority,
not something that can be established by people.
What I am speaking of is only what can be established by people;
what use is there for the worthy?
What use is there for the worthy?
How can this be demonstrated?
The guest said:
"There was a man who sold spears and shields,
praising his shield's firmness:
'Nothing can penetrate it.'
After a while, he then praised his spear, saying:
'My spear is so sharp
that it penetrates everything.'
A man responded, saying:
'If you use your spear
to penetrate your shield,
what would happen?'
The man could not answer."
To consider a shield that cannot be penetrated
and a spear that penetrates everything
as names that cannot coexist.
The way of the worthy cannot be forbidden,
while the way of authority has nothing that cannot be forbidden.
Using the worthy, which cannot be forbidden,
with the authority that has nothing that cannot be forbidden,
this is the saying of the spear and shield.
That the worthy and authority are incompatible is also clear.
Moreover, Yáo 堯,
Shùn 舜, Jié 桀, and
Zhòu 紂
appear once every thousand generations; are they born shoulder to shoulder, heel to toe?
are they born shoulder to shoulder, heel to toe?
The governance of the world never ceases in the middle;
what I mean by speaking of authority
is the middle.
The middle
is above the reach of Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜,
and below it is not Jié 桀 or
Zhòu 紂.
Embracing the law and dwelling in authority
leads to order;
turning away from the law and abandoning authority
leads to chaos.
Now, abandoning authority and turning away from the law
while waiting for Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜—
if Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜 arrive, then there will be order—
this is a thousand generations of chaos
followed by one instance of order.
Embracing the law and dwelling in authority
while waiting for Jié 桀 and
Zhòu 紂—
if Jié 桀 and
Zhòu 紂 arrive, then there will be chaos—
this is a thousand generations of order
followed by one instance of chaos.
Moreover, order for a thousand generations and chaos for one,
compared to order for one generation and chaos for a thousand,
is like riding Jì 驥 or Ér 駬 and racing separately;
is like riding Jì 驥 or Ér 駬 and racing separately;
the distance between them is quite far.
Now, abandoning the method of the compass and square,
discarding the numbers of measurement and calculation,
and making Xī Zhòng 奚仲 build a carriage
will not result in a single wheel being made.
Without the encouragement of rewards and praise
and the awe of punishments and penalties,
releasing authority and entrusting to the law,
even if Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜 went door to door persuading and people debated it,
they could not govern three families.
That authority is sufficient for use is also clear,
and to say "one must wait for the worthy"
is also not so.
Moreover, to not eat for a hundred days while waiting for fine meat and grain
will leave the starving unable to live.
Now, waiting for the worthiness of Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜
to govern the people of the present age
is like the saying of waiting for fine meat and grain to save the starving.
To say
"a good horse and a sturdy carriage,
if a servant drives them, will be laughed at,
but if Wáng Liáng 王良 drives them,
then he will travel a thousand *lǐ* in a day,"
I do not think that is so.
Now, waiting for a Yuè 越 person who is good at swimming in the sea
to save a drowning person from the central states—
although the Yuè 越 person is good at swimming,
the drowning person will not be rescued.
Now, waiting for the ancient Wáng Liáng 王良
to drive the horses of today
is like the saying of the Yuè 越 person saving the drowning person;
that it is not possible is also clear.
Now, a good horse and a sturdy carriage,
with a relay every fifty *lǐ*,
if an average driver drives them,
pursuing speed and achieving distance,
it can be reached,
and a thousand *lǐ* can be achieved in a day;
why must one wait for the ancient Wáng Liáng 王良?
Moreover, in driving,
if it is not Wáng Liáng 王良 who drives,
then it must be a servant who ruins it;
in governing, if it is not Yáo 堯 and
Shùn 舜 who govern,
then it must be Jié 桀 and
Zhòu 紂 who cause chaos.
This taste is not like candy or honey;
it must be bitter *lái* 萊 or *tínglì* 亭歷.
it must be bitter *lái* 萊 or *tínglì* 亭歷.
This is accumulating arguments and piling up words,
departing from principle and losing technique,
a discussion of two extremes;
how can it be used to challenge the words of principle and reason?
The guest's discussion has not reached this point.
Someone asked:
"How does argument arise?"
He answered:
"It arises from the obscurity of the ruler."
The questioner said:
"The obscurity of the ruler thus gives rise to argument;
how so?"
He answered:
"In the state of an enlightened ruler,
decrees
are the most valued words;
laws
are the most appropriate matters.
Words have no double value,
laws do not fit two situations;
therefore, words and actions
that do not conform to laws and decrees
must be prohibited.
If there are no laws and decrees,
but there are those who can engage in deception,
respond to changes,
generate profit,
and assess matters,
the ruler must adopt their words
and demand their actual results.
If the words are correct,
then there is great benefit;
if they are not correct,
then there is severe punishment.
Therefore, the foolish fear punishment
and dare not speak,
while the wise have nothing to argue with.
This is why there is no debate.
In chaotic times, it is not so;
the ruler has decrees,
but the people use literary arguments to criticize them;
the government has laws,
but the people use private conduct to subvert them.
The ruler values those who gradually circumvent the laws and decrees
and honors the wisdom and conduct of scholars,
hence the abundance of literature in this era.
Words and deeds,
are aimed at achieving practical results.
If one sharpens arrows but shoots wildly,
the tip may sometimes hit a fine hair,
but one cannot be called a good archer,
for there is no constant target.
Set a five-inch target
at a distance of ten paces,
only Yì
and Páng Méng can be certain to hit it,
because there is a constant target.
Therefore, with a constant target,
Yì
and Páng Méng are skillful at hitting a five-inch target;
without a constant target,
hitting a fine hair with a wild shot is considered clumsy.
Now, listening to words and observing conduct,
if one does not aim for practical results,
even if the words are extremely insightful and the conduct extremely steadfast,
they are just like wild shots.
Therefore, in chaotic times, listening to words
means considering those difficult to understand as insightful,
and those with extensive learning as eloquent;
observing conduct
means regarding those who stand apart from the crowd as virtuous,
and those who defy their superiors as unyielding.
Rulers favor eloquent and insightful words,
and honor the conduct of the virtuous and unyielding,
therefore, those who create methods and techniques,
establish systems of selection and rejection,
and distinguish between arguments and contentions,
are not held accountable.
Thus, there are many who wear Confucian robes
and carry swords,
but few soldiers who till the land and fight;
empty and unsubstantial arguments flourish,
while the laws and decrees of the state are neglected.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the ruler is not clear-sighted,
debates arise."
Xú Qú asked Tián Jiū, saying:
"I have heard that wise scholars do not approach the ruler through lowly positions,
and sages do not gain access to superiors without demonstrating merit.
Now, Yáng Chéng Yìqú,
is a brilliant general,
yet he is placed in command of a small garrison;
Gōngsūn Dǎn Huí,
is a sagacious minister,
yet he is assigned to a local department.
Why is this?"
Tián Jiū said:
"There is no other reason for this,
it is because the ruler has standards and the superiors have methods.
Furthermore, have you not heard
that the Chǔ general Sòng Gū lost his government
and the Wèi minister Féng Lí lost his state?
These two rulers were swayed by fame and rhetoric,
dazzled by eloquent arguments,
and did not test them in small garrisons
or assign them to local departments,
hence they suffered the calamity of losing their government and state.
Judging from this,
the absence of trials in small garrisons
and assignments to local departments,
is truly the preparation of an enlightened ruler!"
Táng Xī Gōng said to Hán Feìzi:
"I have heard that adhering to rituals and practicing deference
is the art of self-preservation;
cultivating oneself and withdrawing from wisdom
is the path to success.
Now, you, sir, establish laws and techniques,
and set up standards and measures.
I humbly believe that this is dangerous to your person
and perilous to your body.
How can this be shown?
I have heard your teachings say:
'Chǔ did not use Wú Qǐ and fell into disorder,
Qín implemented Shāng Jūn and became wealthy and powerful.
The words of these two men were certainly correct,
yet Wú Qǐ was dismembered
and Shāng Jūn was torn apart by chariots,
because they did not encounter an era or ruler that suited them.'
Such encounters cannot be guaranteed,
and calamities cannot be warded off.
To abandon the path of self-preservation and success
and indulge in dangerous actions,
I humbly believe is not worthwhile for you, sir."
Hán Feìzi said:
"I understand your words.
The way to govern the world,
and the standards to regulate the people,
are indeed not easy to handle.
However, the reason why I abandon the teachings of the former kings
and practice what this humble servant believes is right,
is because I believe that establishing laws and techniques,
and setting up standards and measures,
is the way to benefit the people,
and bring convenience to the masses.
Therefore, to not fear the calamities caused by a disordered ruler or a benighted superior,
and to be committed to enriching the people,
is an act of benevolence and wisdom.
To fear the calamities caused by a disordered ruler or a benighted superior,
and to avoid the harm of death,
to be clear about one's own welfare
but not see the benefit to the people,
is the behavior of the greedy and base.
I cannot bear to lean towards the behavior of the greedy and base,
and dare not harm the act of benevolence and wisdom.
You, sir, have the intention of favoring me,
but in reality, you greatly harm me."
A questioner asked:
"Shēn Bùhài
and Gōngsūn Yāng,
which of these two's teachings is more urgent for the state?"
The response was:
"This cannot be measured.
If a person does not eat
for ten days, they will die;
in the height of severe cold,
if they do not wear clothes, they will also die.
To ask whether clothing or food is more urgent for a person,
is to misunderstand that one cannot do without either,
as they are both means of sustaining life.
Now, Shēn Bùhài speaks of techniques,
while Gōngsūn Yāng advocates laws.
Techniques
means assigning officials based on their abilities,
demanding results based on their titles,
holding the power of life and death,
and assessing the capabilities of the officials;
this is what the ruler holds onto.
Law
means that ordinances and decrees are made clear in the government,
punishments are impressed upon the hearts of the people,
rewards are given to those who carefully adhere to the law,
and punishments are applied to those who violate the decrees;
this is what the ministers follow.
If the ruler lacks techniques,
they will be blinded from above;
if the ministers lack laws,
there will be disorder below.
One cannot do without either,
as both are essential tools for emperors and kings."
The questioner asked:
"What is the problem with only having techniques without laws,
or only having laws without techniques?"
The reply was:
"Shēn Bùhài
was the assistant of Hán Zhāohóu.
Hán
was a separate state of Jìn.
The old laws of Jìn had not yet ceased,
and the new laws of Hán were already being created;
the decrees of the former ruler had not yet been retracted,
and the decrees of the later ruler were already being issued.
If Shēn Bùhài did not control his laws
and unify his ordinances and decrees,
then there would be much corruption.
Therefore, if there was a benefit in the old laws and former decrees,
they would follow them;
if there was a benefit in the new laws and later decrees,
they would follow them.
Benefits lie in the old and new being opposites,
the front and back opposing each other.
Therefore, even if Shēn Bùhài repeatedly made Zhāo Hóu
use strategy,
treacherous ministers would still find ways to twist his words.
Thus, the strength of Hàn, controlling ten thousand chariots for seventeen years,
did not lead to hegemony.
Though strategies were employed by the ruler,
the problem was that the law was not diligently enforced by the officials.
Gōngsūn Yāng's governance of Qín involved
establishing mutual accusation
and demanding verification of facts,
linking groups of ten and five
and sharing their punishments,
making rewards generous and trustworthy,
and punishments severe and certain.
As a result, its people toiled diligently without rest
