and pursued enemies bravely without retreating,
so the state became rich and the army strong.
However, lacking the art to detect treachery,
its wealth and strength
merely benefited its ministers.
After Xiào Gōng and
Shāng Jūn died,
Huì Wáng ascended the throne,
and though the laws of Qín had not yet deteriorated,
Zhāng Yí used Qín to appease Hán and
Wèi.
When Huì Wáng died
and Wǔ Wáng took the throne,
Gān Mào used Qín to appease Zhōu.
When Wǔ Wáng died
and Zhāo Xiāng Wáng ascended the throne,
Rǎng Hóu bypassed Hán and
Wèi to attack Qí to the east.
For five years, Qín did not gain an inch of land
but instead fortified his fief of Táo Yì.
Yīng Hóu attacked Hán for eight years,
establishing his fief in Rǔnán.
From then on,
those who served Qín were all like Yīng and
Rǎng.
Thus, if battles were won,
great ministers were honored;
if land was gained,
private fiefs were established;
the ruler lacked the art
to detect treachery.
Though Shāng Jūn meticulously ornamented his laws,
the ministers turned them to their own advantage.
Therefore, controlling the resources of a strong Qín for decades
did not lead to imperial rule;
though the law was diligently enforced by the officials,
the problem was that the ruler lacked the art at the top."
The questioner asked:
"Is it acceptable for the ruler to use Shēnzi's art
and the officials to implement Shāng Jūn's laws?"
The answer was:
"Shēnzi did not fully understand the art,
and Shāng Jūn did not fully understand the law.
Shēnzi said,
'Governance should not exceed the official's duty;
even if one knows, one should not speak.'
Governance not exceeding the official's duty
can be called adherence to one's post;
knowing but not speaking
cannot be considered a fault.
The ruler uses the eyes of the entire state to see,
so his vision is the clearest;
he uses the ears of the entire state to listen,
so his hearing is the sharpest.
Now, if one knows but does not speak,
on whom else should the ruler rely?"
Shāng Jūn's law said:
'Those who behead one enemy receive one rank of nobility;
those who wish to be officials will be given positions yielding fifty *shí*;
those who behead two enemies receive two ranks of nobility;
those who wish to be officials will be given positions yielding one hundred *shí*.'
The promotion of official rank should correspond to the merit of beheading enemies.
Now, if there were a law saying:
'Those who behead enemies should be made doctors or
craftsmen,'
then houses would not be built properly and illnesses would not be cured.
A craftsman's skill lies in his hands,
and a doctor's skill lies in preparing medicine,
but to assign them based on the merit of beheading enemies
would not match their abilities.
Now, governing officials requires
wisdom and ability,
while beheading enemies relies on
the application of courage and strength.
To use the application of courage and strength
to govern an office requiring wisdom and ability
is like using the merit of beheading enemies
to make doctors and craftsmen.
Therefore, it is said:
these two masters' understanding of law and art
was not entirely perfect."
The greatest aspect of governance
is not just that its rewards and punishments are appropriate.
To reward those without merit
and punish innocent people
is not what is meant by "enlightened."
To reward the meritorious
and punish the guilty
without missing the mark
depends on the people involved;
it does not create merit or prevent transgression.
Therefore, in the laws against treachery,
the highest form prevents it in the heart,
the next prevents it in speech,
and the next prevents it in action.
Nowadays, people all say:
"To honor the ruler and secure the state,
one must rely on benevolence, righteousness, and intelligence,"
but they do not realize that those who demean the ruler and endanger the state
also rely on benevolence, righteousness, and intelligence.
Therefore, enlightened rulers
distance themselves from benevolence and righteousness,
abandon intelligence,
and govern with law.
Thus, praise spreads and fame becomes awe-inspiring,
the people are governed well, and the state is secure—
because they understand the method of using the people.
In general, the art of governance
is what the ruler grasps;
the law
is what the officials follow.
However, to have a courtier hear the Way outside the court gates daily
or to have the law seen daily within the borders
is not the difficult part.
In the past, the Yǒu Hù clan lost its measure,
Huān Dōu had an unfilial son,
Sān Miáo had Chéng Jū,
Jié had Jiā Chǐ,
Zhòu had Chóng Hóu Hǔ,
and Jìn had Yōu Shī.
These six men
were ministers who ruined their states.
They spoke of right as if it were wrong,
and spoke of wrong as if it were right;
they were treacherous inside and harmful;
they were superficially cautious
to show their goodness;
they praised the past
to ruin good deeds;
they flattered their ruler
to accumulate subtle power;
they disrupted him with what he loved.
These are the types of courtiers and attendants.
Rulers of past generations
either obtained men who brought them peace and their states survival
or obtained men
who brought them danger and their states ruin.
The name "obtaining men" is the same,
but the benefits and harms differ by the thousands.
Therefore, the ruler must be cautious about those around him.
If a ruler can truly understand what his ministers are saying,
he can distinguish between the worthy and unworthy as easily as between black and white.
As for Xǔ Yóu,
Xù Yá,
Jìn Bóyáng,
Qín Diānxié,
Wèi Qiáorú,
Húbùjī,
Chóngmíng,
Dǒngbùshí,
Biàn Suí,
Wù Guāng,
Bó Yí, and
Shū Qí,
these twelve men
did not rejoice at seeing profit above,
did not fear facing difficulty below,
and some refused the empire when offered to them.
If they faced the shame of disgrace,
they would not enjoy the benefits of eating grain.
Now, if one sees profit but is not pleased,
even if the ruler bestows generous rewards,
it will not encourage him;
if one faces danger but is not afraid,
even if the ruler imposes severe punishments,
it will not intimidate him:
this is what is called a disobedient people.
These twelve types of people,
some would rather die hidden in caves,
some would rather wither away among plants and trees,
some would rather starve in mountain valleys,
some would rather drown in springs and streams.
If there are such people,
even the ancient sage kings could not make them their subjects;
in this current age,
what use would they be?
As for Guān Lóngpáng, Wángzǐ Bǐgān, Suí Jìliáng,
Chén Xièyě, Chǔ Shēnxū, and Wú Zǐxū,
these six people,
all vehemently contended and strongly remonstrated to overcome their rulers.
If their words were heeded and their actions implemented,
it would be like the relationship between teacher and disciple;
if one word was not heeded,
if one action was not implemented,
then they would confront their lord with words,
and await his response with their own lives,
even if it meant their own death and the destruction of their families,
their heads and necks separated,
their hands and feet in different places,
they would not hesitate to do it.
Such ministers,
even the ancient sage kings could not tolerate;
in this current age,
what use would they be?
As for Qí Tián Héng,
Sòng Zǐhǎn,
Lǔ Jìsūn Yìrú,
Jìn Qiáo Rú,
Wèi Zǐnán Jìng,
Zhèng Tàizǎi Xīn,
Chǔ Bái Gōng,
Zhōu Dān Tú,
and Yān Zizhī,
these nine people, as ministers,
all formed cliques and factions to serve their rulers,
concealing the correct way and practicing personal biases,
oppressing their ruler above and disrupting governance below,
invoking external forces to agitate internal affairs,
befriending subordinates to plot against superiors,
they would not hesitate to do it.
Such ministers,
only sage kings and wise rulers could restrain them,
but as for foolish and chaotic rulers,
could they even recognize them?
As for Hòu Jì,
Gāo Yáo,
Yī Yǐn,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
Tài Gōng Wàng,
Guǎn Zhòng,
Xí Péng,
Bǎi Lǐxī,
Jiǎn Shū,
Jiù Fàn,
Zhào Cuī,
Fàn Lǐ,
Dàfū Zhǒng,
Péng Tóng,
and Huá Dēng,
these fifteen people, as ministers,
all rose early and slept late,
humbled themselves and demeaned their bodies,
kept their hearts respectful and intentions pure;
clarified punishments,
managed official duties
to serve their rulers,
offered good advice,
expounded on righteous methods
but dared not boast of their own goodness,
had successful achievements
but dared not claim credit for their efforts.
They would not hesitate to ruin their families to benefit the state,
sacrifice themselves to secure the ruler,
considered their ruler as high and venerable as the heavens and Mount Tài,
and considered themselves as low as valleys and small streams;
if the ruler had a bright reputation and widespread praise in the state,
they would not hesitate to accept
the lowliness of valleys and small streams.
Such ministers,
even under foolish and chaotic rulers, they could still achieve merit,
much more so under enlightened rulers!
These are called the assistants of hegemons and kings.
As for Zhōu Huá Zhī,
Zhèng Wángsūn Shēn,
Chén Gōngsūn Níng,
Yí Xíngfù,
Jīng Yùyǐn,
Shēn Hài,
Suí Shàoshī,
Yuè Zhǒng Gàn,
Wú Wángsūn É,
Jìn Yáng Chéng Xiè,
Qí Shù Diāo,
and Yì Yá,
these twelve people, as ministers,
all thought of petty gains and forgot the principles of law and justice,
when advancing, they would conceal and obscure the virtuous
to darken their ruler,
when retreating, they would disrupt and confuse the hundred officials
and create disasters;
all flattered their rulers,
indulged their desires,
if they could gain a single word of approval from the ruler,
even if it meant destroying the state and killing the masses,
they would not hesitate to do it.
If there are such ministers,
even sage kings would fear losing them,
much more so for foolish and chaotic rulers,
how could they not make mistakes?
Ministers like these,
all end up dying and their states perishing,
becoming a laughingstock to the world.
Therefore, Zhōu Wēi Gōng was killed,
and his state was divided into two;
Zhèng Zǐyáng was killed,
and his state was divided into three;
Chén Líng Gōng died at the hands of Xià Zhēngshū;
Jīng Líng Wáng died on the banks of Gānxī;
Suí was destroyed by Jīng;
Wú was annexed by Yuè;
Zhī Bó was annihilated below Jìnyáng;
Huán Gōng's body was left unburied for seven days after his death.
Therefore, it is said:
flattering and sycophantic ministers,
only sage kings know them,
but chaotic rulers keep them close,
hence the result is death and the destruction of the state.
Sage kings and enlightened rulers are not like that;
in internal appointments, they do not avoid relatives,
in external appointments, they do not avoid enemies.
If ability resides in someone,
then they promote him accordingly;
if ability does not reside in someone,
then they punish him accordingly.
Therefore, the virtuous and capable advance, while the treacherous and wicked retreat,
thus one act of appointment is enough to subdue the feudal lords.
It is recorded that:
Yáo had Dānzhū,
and Shùn had Shāngjūn,
Qǐ had Wǔ Guān,
Shāng had Tàijiǎ,
and Wǔ Wáng had Guǎn and Cài.
Those whom these five kings punished
were all close relatives like fathers, brothers, and sons,
but what was the reason for killing and destroying their own families?
It was because they harmed the state, injured the people, and ruined the laws and customs.
Looking at those whom they promoted,
some were in the mountains, forests, marshes, and caves,
some were in prisons, bound by ropes and chains,
some were engaged in butchering, feeding livestock, and feeding cattle.
Yet enlightened rulers did not shame their own humble origins,
but because of their abilities,
believing that they could clarify the laws,
benefit the state and the people,
they promoted them accordingly,
bringing them security and honor.
Chaotic rulers are not like that;
they do not understand the intentions and conduct of their ministers,
yet they entrust them with the state,
so that in minor cases, their reputation is tarnished and their territory is reduced,
and in major cases, their state is destroyed and they themselves die,
because they are not discerning in their use of ministers.
Those who have no standards to measure their ministers
will inevitably judge them by the opinions of the masses.
What the masses praise,
they follow and are pleased with;
what the masses condemn,
they follow and detest.
Therefore, ministers who ruin their families and destroy their fortunes,
internally build factions,
externally connect with local clans to gain praise,
secretly make agreements to solidify their position,
and falsely promise ranks and emoluments to encourage each other.
They say:
"Those who side with me will benefit,
those who don't will suffer."
The masses, greedy for their benefit,
and intimidated by their power, say:
"If they are truly pleased,
they can benefit me;
if they are displeased and angry,
they can harm me."
The masses flock to them, and the people remain,
their praise fills the country,
and it reaches the ruler's ears.
The ruler, unable to discern the truth,
mistakenly believes them to be virtuous.
They also employ cunning and deceitful men,
who outwardly pretend to be favored envoys of the feudal lords,
provided with carriages and horses,
trusted with credentials,
appeased with eloquent words,
and supplied with silks and treasures,
to make the feudal lords
persuasively speak on their behalf to their rulers,
subtly incorporating private interests into public discussions.
Those who act as envoys
are rulers of foreign states;
those who engage in talks
are people close to the ruler.
The ruler delights in their words and admires their eloquence,
thinking these people are virtuous scholars of the world.
Internally and externally, those around the ruler,
their suggestions are consistent and their words are the same.
The great do not hesitate to humble themselves
and treat them with respect, despite their high positions;
the small use high ranks and generous rewards to benefit them.
When the ranks and emoluments of treacherous men are high
and their factions become more numerous,
and they also harbor treacherous intentions,
then treacherous ministers increasingly turn around and persuade them,
saying:
"The so-called sage rulers and enlightened kings of ancient times
did not ascend to the throne by age, hereditary succession, or order.
It was by building factions,
gathering local clans,
forcing their superiors, and assassinating their rulers
to seek their own benefit."
They say:
"How do you know this is true?"
Then they say:
"Shùn 舜 forced Yáo 堯,
Yǔ 禹 forced Shùn 舜,
Tāng 湯 exiled Jié 桀,
and Wǔwáng 武王 attacked Zhòu 紂.
These four kings
were ministers who assassinated their rulers,
yet the world praises them.
Examining the intentions of the four kings,
they were motivated by greed;
judging their actions,
they used violent and chaotic forces.
However, the four kings promoted themselves widely,
and the world called them great;
they made their names known,
and the world called them enlightened.
Their power was sufficient to dominate the world,
their benefits were sufficient to cover the age,
and the world followed them."
They also say:
"Based on what is heard today,
Tián Chéngzǐ 田成子 seized Qí 齊,
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn 司城子罕 seized Sòng 宋,
Tàizǎi Xīn 太宰欣 seized Zhèng 鄭,
Dānshì 單氏 seized Zhōu 周,
Yìyá 易牙 seized Wèi 衛,
and the three families of Hán 韓, Wèi 魏, and Zhào 趙 divided Jìn 晉.
These eight men
were ministers who assassinated their rulers."
When treacherous ministers hear this,
they are startled and prick up their ears, thinking it is right.
Therefore, they internally build factions,
externally extend local clans,
observe the timing and initiate actions,
seizing the state in one fell swoop.
Moreover, those who internally use factions to coerce and assassinate their rulers,
and externally use the power of the feudal lords
to change their state,
conceal the proper way,
hold onto private interests,
restrain the ruler above,
and disrupt the government below,
are too numerous to count.
Why is this?
It is because they are not clear about selecting ministers.
It is recorded:
"Since the time of King Xuān of Zhōu 周宣王,
dozens of states have been destroyed,
and many of their ministers have assassinated their rulers and seized their states."
Therefore, the origin of difficulties arises half from within, and half from external actors.
Those who can exhaust their people's strength
,destroy their state and kill themselves
,are all still virtuous rulers.
As for those who change their position easily
,preserve the multitudes and pass down the state
,this is the worst of their afflictions
For the one who is a ruler
,if he is truly clear about what his ministers are saying,
then even if he hunts with nets and arrows,
strikes the bells and dances with women,
his state will still exist;
if he is not clear about what his ministers are saying,
even if he is frugal and hardworking,
wears cloth and eats poorly,
his state will still perish.
The late Lord Jìng of Zhào 趙敬侯,
did not cultivate virtue and conduct,
but indulged in desires,
catering to the comfort of his body,
and the pleasures of his eyes and ears,
hunting with nets and arrows in winter,
and floating and reveling in summer,
making long nights,
without setting down the wine cup for several days,
forcing those who could not drink to drink through bamboo tubes,
and beheading those who were not respectful in their movements
or reverent in their responses before him.
Thus, his dwelling and diet were so unrestrained,
and his punishments and killings were so excessive,
yet Lord Jìng 敬侯 enjoyed the state for decades,
his troops were not defeated by enemy states,
his territory was not diminished by neighboring states,
there was no chaos among his ministers and officials internally,
and there was no trouble from the feudal lords and neighboring states externally,
because he was clear about how to employ his ministers.
Lord Kuài 噲 of Yān 燕,
a descendant of Shào Gōng Shì 召公奭,
possessed a territory of several thousand *lǐ* 里,
and commanded hundreds of thousands of soldiers,
yet he did not enjoy the pleasures of children,
nor did he listen to the sounds of bells and chimes,
internally he did not fill in the pools and build terraces and pavilions,
externally he did not hunt with nets and arrows,
and he even personally held the plow to cultivate the fields.
Lord Kuài's 噲 hardship and concern for the people
were so extreme,
that even the so-called sage kings and enlightened rulers of ancient times
were not more diligent and concerned for the world
than him.
However, Lord Kuài 噲 died and his state was destroyed,
seized by Zǐzhī 子之,
and the world laughed at him.
What was the reason for this?
It was because he was not clear about how to employ his ministers.
Therefore, it is said:
A minister has five kinds of treachery,
which the ruler does not know.
Among the ministers,
some extravagantly use wealth and bribes
to gain praise,
some busily bestow rewards and gifts
to sway the masses,
and some busily form parties, follow the wise, and honor scholars
to achieve their own desires.
Some are intent on achieving influence through amnesty, pardon, and prison release,
using these events to demonstrate authority;
others are intent on flattering inferiors with twisted truths,
strange words,
extravagant clothing,
and exaggerated praise,
to dazzle the ears and eyes of the people.
These five types,
are what an enlightened ruler doubts,
and what a sagacious sovereign prohibits.
Eliminate these five types,
and those who are noisy and deceitful will not dare to stand facing north and engage in idle talk;
those who use many flowery words
but perform few practical deeds
that do not accord with the law,
will not dare to falsely represent situations through eloquent speeches.
Thus, when officials are at home, they cultivate themselves;
when they are active, they exert their abilities;
without the sovereign's command,
they dare not rashly create hasty speech and fabricate events.
This is how a sagacious king governs his ministers and subordinates.
Those sagacious sovereigns and enlightened rulers do not employ objects of suspicion to spy on their ministers.
To see objects of suspicion and have no one rebel
is rare in the world.
Thus it is said:
"An illegitimate son who rivals the legitimate heir,
a concubine who rivals the wife,
a minister in court who rivals the prime minister,
and a subject whose favor rivals that of the ruler"—
these four are what endanger a state.
Thus it is said:
"Inner favor that rivals the queen,
outer favor that interferes with government,
a branch son who is matched with the heir,
and a great minister who rivals the ruler"—
these are the ways to chaos.
Thus the *Zhōu Jì* (周記) says:
"Do not honor concubines and demean wives,
do not favor illegitimate sons over legitimate heirs,
do not honor pet ministers and match them with high officials,
do not honor great ministers to rival their ruler."
If the four rivals are destroyed,
then the ruler will have no ulterior motives,
and the subordinates will have no strange behavior.
If the four rivals are not destroyed,
then one will fall and the state will be destroyed.
There are three things by which the sage governs:
the first is benefit (*lì* 利),
the second is authority (*wēi* 威),
the third is reputation (*míng* 名).
Benefit
is how one gains the people;
authority
is how one enforces orders;
reputation
is the path followed equally by superiors and inferiors.
Without these three,
even if one has, it's not urgent.
Now, it is not as if benefit does not exist,
yet the people are not transformed by the ruler;
it is not as if authority does not exist,
yet subordinates do not obey;
it is not as if the government has no laws,
yet governance does not match the name.
It is not as if these three do not exist,
so why is the world sometimes governed and sometimes in chaos?
It is because what the ruler values
is the opposite of what governs.
Establishing names and titles
is how to achieve honor;
but now, those who have lowly names and meager substance
are regarded by the world as noble.
Establishing ranks and positions
is how to create a foundation for lowliness and nobility;
but those who are disrespectful to their superiors and do not seek to be seen
are regarded by the world as virtuous.
Authority and benefit
are how to enforce orders;
but those who have no benefit and lightly exercise authority
are regarded by the world as important.
Laws and regulations
are how to govern;
but those who do not follow laws and regulations
and act out of personal kindness
are regarded by the world as loyal.
Official positions and titles
are how to encourage the people;
but those who love fame and righteousness and do not advance in officialdom
are regarded by the world as righteous scholars.
Punishments and penalties
are how to wield authority;
but those who disregard the law and do not avoid the crimes of punishment, execution, and death
are regarded by the world as brave men.
The people's eagerness for fame
exceeds their pursuit of benefit.
If this is the case,
then how can starving and destitute scholars
not dwell in caves and afflict themselves
to compete for fame in the world?
Thus, the reason why the world is not governed
is not the fault of the subordinates,
but that the superiors have lost their way.
They constantly value what causes chaos
and disdain what brings order;
therefore, what the subordinates desire
always contradicts what the superiors do to govern.
Now, for subordinates to listen to their superiors
is what the superiors urgently desire.
But those who are sincere, honest, and trustworthy,
careful in their thoughts and reserved in their speech,
are called miserly.
Those who uphold the law firmly
and listen to orders carefully
are called foolish.
Those who respect their superiors and fear punishment
are called timid.
Those who speak according to the times
and act appropriately
are called incompetent.
Those who have no ulterior motives or private learning
and listen to officials and follow instructions
are called ignorant.
Those who are difficult to persuade
are called upright.
Those who are difficult to give to
are called incorruptible.
Those who are difficult to restrain
are called disciplined.
Those who do not listen to orders
are called brave.
Those who are of no benefit to their superiors
are called well-meaning.
Those who have few desires,
are generous and kind,
and practice virtue
are called benevolent.
Those who are grave, dignified, and self-respecting
are called elders.
Those who form groups based on private learning
are called teachers and disciples.
Those who are quiet, peaceful, and live in seclusion
are called thoughtful.
Those who diminish benevolence and pursue profit
are called quick.
Those who are dangerous, rash, fickle, and rebellious
are called wise.
Those who act for others before acting for themselves,
resemble names and titles,
and speak of loving the world universally
are called sages.
Those who speak of grand principles,
which, when discussed, are impractical,
and, when practiced, are contrary to the world
are called great men.
Those who disdain rank and emolument
and do not yield to their superiors
are called outstanding.
When subordinates gradually behave in this way,
they will cause chaos among the people at home
and be useless abroad.
Superiors should prohibit their desires
and eliminate their traces,
but they do not stop;
instead, they honor them,
which teaches subordinates to cause chaos above as a way to govern.
In general, what superiors use to govern
are punishments and penalties;
but now, those who privately practice righteousness are honored.
What the state relies on to stand
is peace and quiet;
but those who are noisy, dangerous, slanderous, and flattering are given positions.
What the country relies on to be obeyed
is trustworthiness and virtue;
but those who are biased, knowledgeable, and subversive are employed.
That by which commands are carried out,
that by which authority is established,
is reverence, frugality, and listening to superiors;
yet those who dwell in caves and are not of this world are made prominent.
That by which the granaries are filled,
is the fundamental task of cultivating and farming;
yet those who make ornamental tassels and ribbons,
brocades and embroideries,
and intricate carvings
as secondary occupations become wealthy.
That by which reputation is achieved,
that by which city walls are expanded,
is warriors;
now the orphans of soldiers who died in battle are hungry and begging on the roads,
while actors who perform and laugh and drunkards ride in carriages and wear silk.
Rewards and emoluments
are the means by which to exhaust the people's strength and easily have them die for the state;
now those soldiers who are victorious in battle and capture territory
are toiling but do not receive rewards,
while those who divine by tortoise shells,
read palms,
or use fox-spirits and witchcraft
to utter flattering words to those in power receive daily gifts.
The ruler grasps measures and weights,
thereby holding the power of life and death;
now those officials who uphold standards and maintain measures
wish to win the ruler's favor with loyalty
but are not granted an audience,
while those who use clever and advantageous words
and practice treacherous schemes to steal a lucky life
are frequently employed.
To rely on the law and speak directly,
to make names and punishments correspond,
to follow the plumb line and ink marker,
and to execute wicked people
—this is how a ruler governs,
but it only leads to increasing alienation,
while flatterers who cater to desires and comply with wishes
are close to the ruler, endangering the state.
Collecting all taxes
and focusing the people's strength
is the means to prepare for disasters and fill the storehouses;
yet soldiers and commoners flee from service and hide,
relying on the doors of those with power
to avoid corvée labor and taxes,
and the ruler cannot find them, numbering in the tens of thousands.
To allocate good fields and profitable residences
is how to encourage warriors and soldiers;
yet those who are beheaded and have their bellies torn open,
scattering their bones on the plains and fields,
have no residence to live in,
and their fields are seized after their deaths;
while women and younger sisters who are beautiful,
and great ministers and attendants who have no merit,
choose residences to receive,
and choose fields to eat from.
Rewards and benefits should all come from the ruler,
so as to properly control subordinates;
yet soldiers who fight in armor do not get positions,
while scholars who live in seclusion are honored and prominent.
If the ruler uses this as instruction,
how can the ruler's name not be debased,
how can the ruler's position not be endangered?
For those whose names are debased and whose positions are endangered,
it must be because their subordinates do not follow laws and regulations
and harbor divided loyalties, pursuing private learning and rebelling against the world;
yet their actions are not forbidden,
their groups are not broken up to scatter their parties,
and they are even honored,
those who govern are at fault.
That by which the ruler establishes integrity and shame
is the means to encourage subordinates;
now scholar-officials are not ashamed of filth, mud, ugliness, and disgrace
but seek office,
and women and younger sisters of those connected to private interests
do not wait in line but seek office.
Rewards and gifts
are meant to be valued;
yet soldiers who have merit in battle are poor and lowly,
while flatterers and actors are promoted beyond their rank.
Names and titles must be genuine and trustworthy
to extend authority;
yet the ruler is obscured,
and close attendants and female petitioners act in concert,
with the hundred officials controlling appointments and promoting people,
those who govern are at fault.
If great ministers appoint officials
and conspire with subordinates in advance, forming factions,
even if they act unlawfully,
authority and benefit lie with subordinates,
then the ruler is debased and the great ministers are weighty.
To establish laws and regulations
is to abolish selfishness.
When laws and regulations are implemented,
selfish paths are abandoned.
Selfishness
is what disrupts the law;
yet scholars harbor divided loyalties and private learning,
dwelling in caves and remote paths,
relying on deep contemplation,
with the great ones criticizing the world,
and the lesser ones confusing subordinates;
if the ruler does not prohibit this
and even honors them with titles
and enriches them with substance,
it is to make the undeserving prominent
and the unlaborious wealthy.
If this is the case,
then how can scholars who harbor divided loyalties and private learning
not contemplate deeply,
striving to know deception
and slandering laws and regulations,
in order to seek that which is contrary to the world?
All who disrupt the ruler and rebel against the world
are ordinary scholars who harbor divided loyalties
and private learning.
Therefore, the *Běnyán* 本言 says:
"That by which to govern
is the law;
that by which to cause chaos
is selfishness.
If the law is established,
then no one can act selfishly."
Therefore, it is said:
to follow selfishness leads to chaos;
to follow the law leads to order.
If the ruler does not have the proper Way,
then the wise will have selfish words,
and the virtuous will have selfish intentions.
If the ruler has selfish favors,
then subordinates will have selfish desires.
Sage-like wisdom forms groups,
creating words and phrases
to present unlawful things to the ruler,
if the ruler does not prohibit and obstruct this,
but even honors them,
it is teaching subordinates not to listen to the ruler and not to follow the law.
Therefore, the virtuous are prominently displayed and reside in high positions,
while wicked people rely on rewards and become wealthy.
If the virtuous are prominently displayed and reside in high positions,
and wicked people rely on rewards and become wealthy,
then the ruler cannot overcome subordinates.
Those who fear death and avoid difficulty
are people who surrender and submit,
yet the world honors them by calling them "gentlemen who value life."
Those who study the Way and establish principles
are people who deviate from the law,
yet the world honors them by calling them "men of letters."
Those who travel about and live in luxury,
obtaining food for profit,
are people who seek to eat off of others, yet the world honors them by calling them "men of ability."
Those who speak in crooked ways and seek to know,
are people who are deceptive and fraudulent,
yet the world honors them by calling them
"men of eloquent wisdom."
Those who wield swords and attack and kill,
are violent and aggressive people,
yet the world honors them by calling them
"brave and valorous men."
Those who keep thieves alive and harbor evildoers,
are people who deserve to die,
yet the world honors them by calling them "men who uphold reputation."
These six types of people
are those whom the world praises.
Those who rush into danger and sacrifice themselves for loyalty,
are people who die for their principles,
yet the world belittles them by calling them
"people who miscalculate."
Those who hear little and follow commands,
are people who fully comply with the law,
yet the world belittles them by calling them
"simple and ignorant people."
Those who exert their strength to work and eat,
are people who create profit,
but the world considers them few and calls them
"people of little ability."
Those who are generous, honest, and pure,
and who prepare grain,
but the world considers them few and calls them
"foolish and dull people."
Those who value orders, fear trouble, and respect their superiors,
but the world considers them few and calls them "cowardly and fearful people."
Those who thwart bandits and stop treachery,
and are clear to their superiors,
but the world considers them few and calls them
"flattering and slandering people."
These six types of people,
are those whom the world denigrates.
The six types of people who are treacherous, deceitful, and useless,
are praised by the world as if they were good;
the six types of people who plow the fields and fight, and are beneficial,
are denigrated by the world in this way.
This is called the "Six Reversals."
Commoners follow their private interests to praise them,
rulers of the world listen to empty praise to treat them with propriety,
wherever propriety is shown, benefit is certainly added.
The common people follow their private harms to criticize them,
the rulers of the world are blocked by customs to despise them,
wherever contempt is, harm is certainly added.
Therefore, fame and rewards are given to the people who are privately evil and deserve punishment,
while destruction and harm fall on the officers who are publicly good and deserve rewards,
to seek the wealth and strength of the state,
is impossible.
In ancient times there was a saying:
"Governing is like bathing,
even if there is discarded hair, it must be done."
To begrudge the expense of discarded hair and forget the benefit of long hair,
is not knowing how to weigh things.
To lance a boil is painful,
to drink medicine is bitter,
if because of the bitterness and weariness
one does not lance boils or drink medicine,
then the body will not live, and the disease will not stop.
Now the connection between those above and those below,
does not have the kindness of father and son,
and if one wants to use righteousness to restrain those below,
then the interaction will certainly have gaps.
Moreover, when parents have a child,
they congratulate each other if a boy is born,
but kill the child if a girl is born.
These both come from the embrace of the parents,
yet the boy is congratulated and the girl is killed,
because of the consideration of future convenience and the calculation of long-term benefit.
Therefore, the parents' treatment of their children,
is still treating each other with calculating hearts,
and how much more so when there is no father-son kindness?
Now the scholars' advice to the rulers,
all rejects the heart of seeking benefit,
and advocates the way of loving each other,
this is seeking the ruler to be more intimate than parents,
this is not understanding the discussion of favor,
and is deceitful and false,
therefore a wise ruler will not accept it.
The governance of the sages,
is careful in laws and prohibitions,
if laws and prohibitions are clear and obvious,
then the officials govern well;
must be certain in rewards and punishments,
if rewards and punishments are not biased,
then the people are used.
If the people are used well and the officials govern well,
then the state is wealthy,
if the state is wealthy,
then the army is strong,
and the task of hegemony can be accomplished.
Hegemony,
is the great benefit of the ruler.
If the ruler holds great benefits to listen to governance,
then those whom he appoints as officials are capable,
and his rewards and punishments are without bias.
To make the officers and people clear about it,
to exert their strength and risk their lives,
then achievements can be established and rank and salary can be obtained,
if rank and salary are obtained, then the task of wealth and nobility can be accomplished.
Wealth and nobility, is the great benefit of the ministers.
If the ministers hold great benefits to work,
then their actions are dangerous and they risk death,
their strength is exhausted and they do not hope for reward.
This is called the ruler being unkind,
and the ministers being disloyal,
then hegemony can be achieved.
If evil is certainly known, then it is guarded against,
if it is certainly punished, then it stops;
if it is not known, then it is unrestrained,
if it is not punished, then it is done.
If light goods are displayed in a dark place,
even Zēng (Zēng Shēn 曾參) and Shǐ (Shǐ Yú 石碏) can be suspected;
if one hundred gold pieces are hung in the market,
even a great thief will not take them.
If it is not known,
then Zēng (Zēng Shēn 曾參) and Shǐ (Shǐ Yú 石碏) can be suspected in the darkness;
if it is certainly known,
then a great thief will not take the suspended gold in the market.
Therefore, the wise ruler's governing the state,
increases the number of guards and increases their punishment,
causing the people to be restrained by laws
and not stopped by integrity.
The mother's love for her son is double the father's,
but the father's orders are carried out to the son ten times more than the mother's;
the officers to the people have no love,
but their orders are carried out to the people ten thousand times more than the father's.
The mother accumulates love but her orders are exhausted,
the officer uses authority and the people obey,
the strategy of severity and love can also be decided.
Moreover, what parents seek from their children,
in actions
they want them to be safe and have benefit,
in conduct
they want them to be far from crime.
The ruler's treatment of the people,
in times of difficulty he uses their death,
in times of peace he uses their strength.
Parents use thick love to tie their children to safety and benefit
but are not listened to,
the ruler uses loveless benefit
to seek the people's life-risking strength but his orders are carried out.
The wise ruler knows this,
therefore he does not nurture a heart of love and kindness,
but increases the force of authority.
Therefore, where the mother thickly loves,
the sons are often defeated,
this is the result of love.
Where the father thinly loves and teaches with a whip,
the sons are often good,
this is the use of strictness.
Now, in the management of family property,
they endure hunger and cold together,
they force each other to toil,
even encountering the difficulties of military campaigns,
the disasters of famine,
those who have warm clothes and delicious food,
are certainly from this family.
They pity each other with clothing and food,
they favor each other with ease and pleasure,
in times of natural hunger and bad harvest,
those who marry off their wives and sell their children,
are certainly from this family.
Therefore, the way of law,
is bitter at the beginning but beneficial in the long run;
the way of benevolence,
is stealing pleasure but poor in the end.
The sage weighs their lightness and heaviness,
and chooses their great benefit,
therefore he uses the endurance of law,
and abandons the pity of benevolent people.
The words of scholars all say
"lenient punishment,"
this is the art of chaos and destruction.
All rewards and punishments that are certain,
are encouragement and prohibition.
If rewards are generous, then what is desired is obtained quickly,
if punishments are severe, then what is hated is prohibited urgently.
Those who desire benefit must hate harm,
harm,
is the opposite of benefit.
If it is the opposite of what is desired,
how can one not hate it?
Those who desire order must hate chaos,
chaos,
is the opposite of order.
Therefore, those who greatly desire order,
their rewards must be generous;
those who greatly hate chaos,
their punishments must be severe.
Now, those who take lenient punishments,
their hatred of chaos is not great,
their desire for order is also not great.
This is not only without skill, but also without conduct.
Therefore, the strategy of deciding whether someone is virtuous or not virtuous,
foolish or wise,
lies in the lightness and heaviness of rewards and punishments.
Moreover, harsh punishments are
not for the sake of the criminals.
The laws of an enlightened ruler are a standard.
Governing robbers
is not governing those already governed;
governing those already governed
is governing the dead.
Punishing thieves
is not punishing those already punished;
punishing those already punished
is punishing the conscripted laborers.
Therefore, it is said:
to heavily punish the crime of one villain
is to stop the wickedness within the borders;
this is the way to govern.
Heavy punishment is for
thieves and robbers,
but those who are fearful
are the good people.
Those who desire order, why hesitate to use heavy punishments?
As for generous rewards,
they are not only for rewarding merit,
but also for encouraging the entire nation.
Those who receive rewards gladly seek profit,
those who have not yet been rewarded admire achievements;
this is to repay the merit of one person
and encourage the masses within the borders.
Those who desire order, why hesitate to use generous rewards?
Now, those who do not understand governance all say:
"Heavy punishments harm the people;
light punishments can stop wickedness;
why must they be heavy?"
These are people who do not understand governance.
If wickedness can be stopped with heavy punishments,
it cannot necessarily be stopped with light punishments;
if wickedness can be stopped with light punishments,
it certainly can be stopped with heavy punishments.
Therefore, when the ruler imposes heavy punishments,
wickedness is completely stopped.
If wickedness is completely stopped,
then how does this harm the people?
What is meant by heavy punishments is that
the profit from wickedness is small,
but the punishment imposed by the ruler is great.
The people will not risk a great punishment for a small profit,
therefore wickedness will certainly be stopped.
What is meant by light punishments is that
the profit from wickedness is great,
but the punishment imposed by the ruler is small.
The people admire the profit and disregard the punishment,
therefore wickedness will not be stopped.
Therefore, the ancient sages had a proverb that said:
"One does not stumble on a mountain, but stumbles on an anthill."
Mountains are large,
so people respect them;
anthills are tiny,
so people disregard them.
If punishments are light,
the people will certainly disregard them.
To commit offenses without being punished
is to drive the state away and abandon it;
to commit offenses and be punished
is to set a trap for the people.
Therefore, light punishments
are the anthills of the people.
Thus, light punishments as a guide for the people,
if they do not disorder the state,
then they set a trap for the people;
this can be said to harm the people.
Now, scholars all recite the praiseful words in books and records,
but do not examine the real events of the present age,
saying:
"If the ruler does not love the people,
and levies taxes that are always heavy,
then resources will be insufficient
and the people will resent the ruler,
therefore the world will be in great disorder."
They believe that by making the resources sufficient and adding love,
even with light punishments,
the state can be governed.
This saying is not correct.
The reason why people incur heavy punishments
is certainly after their needs have been satisfied.
Even if resources are sufficient
and love is bestowed generously,
if punishments are light,
the state will still be in disorder.
When a wealthy family loves its son,
material goods are sufficient.
When material goods are sufficient,
they are used lightly,
and when used lightly,
there is extravagance and excess.
When parents love their son,
they cannot bear to be strict;
unable to be strict,
the son becomes arrogant and willful.
Extravagance
leads to poverty,
arrogance and willfulness
lead to violence.
This is the problem with light punishments, even when resources are sufficient and love is abundant.
Generally, when people are born,
sufficient resources cause them to slacken in their efforts;
a weak ruler
allows them to indulge in wrongdoing.
That resources are sufficient and yet one exerts effort is like
Shén Nóng;
that the ruler governs weakly and yet one cultivates oneself is like
Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiū.
It is clear that the people cannot all be like Shén Nóng, Zēng Shēn, and Shǐ Qiū.
Lǎo Dān had a saying:
"Knowing when to be content prevents disgrace,
knowing when to stop prevents danger."
Lǎo Dān
does not seek beyond what is sufficient because of the possibility of danger and disgrace.
To think that making the people content
is sufficient for governing
is to assume that all the people are like Lǎo Dān.
Therefore, Jié held the position of emperor
yet was not content with the honor,
possessed everything within the four seas
yet was not content with the treasure.
Even if a ruler makes the people content,
he cannot make them content with being emperor,
and Jié might not have thought being emperor was enough;
therefore, even if the people are content,
how can that be sufficient for governing?
Therefore, the enlightened ruler governs the state by
adjusting policies to the times to produce wealth,
discussing taxes to equalize wealth and poverty,
increasing ranks and stipends to utilize the wise and capable,
increasing punishments to prohibit wickedness,
allowing the people to become wealthy through labor,
achieve status through deeds,
receive punishment for offenses,
and achieve rewards for merit,
without relying on gifts of kindness and favor;
this is the government of emperors and kings.
When everyone is asleep,
the blind do not know;
when everyone is silent,
the mute do not know.
Awaken them and make them see,
ask them and make them answer,
then the mute and blind will be exposed.
If you do not listen to their words,
the unskilled will not be known;
if you do not employ their abilities,
the unworthy will not be known.
Listen to their words and seek what is appropriate,
employ their abilities and demand their achievements,
then the unskilled and unworthy will be exposed.
If you want to find a strongman
and listen to his self-praise,
you cannot distinguish between an ordinary person and Wū Huò;
but
if you give them a ding-cauldron and zǔ-stand,
then their strength will be revealed.
Therefore, official positions
are the ding-cauldron and zǔ-stand for capable people;
employ them with tasks, and the foolish and wise will be distinguished.
Therefore, the unskilled benefit from not being used,
the unworthy benefit from not being employed.
They are not used
yet embellish their words to appear eloquent,
their abilities are not employed yet they adorn themselves to appear superior;
the ruler is deceived by their eloquence,
overlooks their lack of ability, and honors them,
this is like determining clarity without needing to see,
determining eloquence without needing to listen;
the mute and blind cannot be exposed.
The enlightened ruler listens to their words
but demands their usefulness,
observes their actions
but seeks their achievements;
then the empty teachings of the past will not be discussed,
and boastful, false conduct will not be adorned.
Acting privately for an old friend
is called not abandoning them;
distributing public wealth to others
is called being benevolent;
valuing one's own well-being over official salary
is called being a *jūnzǐ*;
twisting the law to favor relatives
is called having integrity;
abandoning office to indulge in friendships
is called being chivalrous;
distancing oneself from the world to follow higher ideals
is called being aloof and arrogant;
arguing against orders
is called being strong-willed;
bestowing favors to gain popular support
is called winning the people.
He who does not abandon,
officials engage in corruption;
he who is benevolent,
public wealth is damaged;
he who is a *jūnzǐ*,
the people are hard to command;
he who has integrity,
laws and regulations are destroyed;
he who is chivalrous,
official positions are left vacant;
he who is aloof and arrogant,
the people do not serve;
he who is strong-willed,
orders are not carried out;
he who wins the people,
the ruler is isolated.
These eight,
are the private praises of common men,
and the great defeats of rulers.
The opposite of these eight,
are the private condemnations of common men,
and the public benefit of rulers.
If a ruler does not examine the benefits and harms to the state,
but uses the private praises of common men,
and expects the state to be without danger and chaos,
it is impossible.
Employing people in positions
is the mechanism of survival, destruction, order, and chaos.
If there is no method to employ people,
there will be nothing but failure.
Those whom the ruler employs
are either the articulate and intelligent or the virtuous and pure.
To employ people
is to grant them power.
The intelligent are not necessarily trustworthy,
because their intelligence is great,
it obscures their trustworthiness.
If the plans of an intelligent man,
are combined with the resources of a powerful position,
and used for his private needs,
then the ruler will surely be deceived.
Because the intelligent cannot be trusted,
the virtuous and pure are employed
to make judgements.
The virtuous and pure are not necessarily intelligent,
because of their pure character,
it obscures their intelligence.
If the ignorance of a foolish man,
is combined with a position of authority,
and used to confirm his own beliefs,
then affairs will surely be in chaos.
Therefore, without a method to employ people,
employing the intelligent leads to the ruler being deceived,
employing the virtuous leads to the ruler's affairs being in chaos,
this is the trouble of having no method.
The way of the enlightened ruler,
the low can discuss with the high,
inferiors can confront superiors,
decisions are made with sincerity and consultation,
and listening is without prejudice,
therefore the intelligent cannot deceive.
Rewarding based on merit,
assigning tasks based on ability,
observing the beginnings and looking for mistakes,
punishing those with faults,
rewarding those with ability,
therefore the foolish are not given positions.
The intelligent do not dare to deceive,
the foolish cannot make decisions,
then there will be no mistakes.
A discerning man can understand,
but cannot be a standard for orders,
because the people are not all discerning.
A virtuous man can perform,
but cannot be a standard for laws,
because the people are not all virtuous.
Yáng Zhū,
Mò Dí,
were the most discerning in the world,
they encountered a chaotic world but could not decide,
though discerning
they could not be the standard for official orders.
Bào Jiāo,
Huá Jiǎo,
were the most virtuous in the world,
Bào Jiāo embraced a withered tree,
Huá Jiǎo drowned himself in the river,
though virtuous
they could not be soldiers for farming and war.
Therefore, what the ruler examines,
intelligent men will exhaust their arguments;
what the ruler respects,
capable men will exhaust their performance.
If today's rulers examine useless arguments,
and respect deeds that are far from practical,
and expect the state to be rich and strong,
it is impossible.
Having broad learning and clever arguments like Kǒng
and Mò,
if Kǒng
and Mò do not plow and weed,
then how will the state benefit?
Cultivating filial piety and few desires like Zēng and Shǐ,
if Zēng and Shǐ do not fight and attack,
then how will the state benefit?
Common men have private benefits,
rulers have public benefits.
To have ample provisions without working,
and to have a distinguished name without serving,
these are private benefits;
to end literature and clarify laws and standards,
to block private benefits and unify labor,
these are public benefits.
It is to establish laws to guide the people,
but to also value literature,
then what the people learn and follow will be in doubt;
it is to reward merit to encourage the people,
but to also respect virtuous conduct,
then the people will become lazy in producing benefits.
To value literature and doubt the laws,
to respect virtuous conduct and divide the labor,
expecting the state to be rich and strong,
is impossible.
Holding court tablets and shields,
cannot match having sharp iron weapons;
ascending, descending, and circling,
cannot compare to presenting hundreds of reports by midday;
shooting at a target with *líshǒu*,
cannot match firing a powerful crossbow;
using city walls to resist a siege,
is not as effective as blocking tunnels with explosives.
The ancients valued virtue,
the middle ages pursued wisdom,
and today we compete with strength.
The ancients had few affairs and simple equipment,
rustic and incomplete,
therefore there were those who used clam shells
to push carts.
The ancients had few people and were close to each other,
there were many things and they lightly valued benefits and easily yielded,
therefore there were those who yielded the empire through courteous gestures.
Then, practicing yielding,
valuing compassion and kindness,
and guiding with benevolence and generosity,
are all pushing the cart politically.
To live in a time of many affairs,
and use the tools of few affairs,
is not the preparation of the wise;
to live in an age of great conflict,
and follow the path of yielding,
is not the governance of the sage.
Therefore, the wise do not ride in carts pushed by others,
and the sages do not push the cart politically.
Laws are used to control affairs,
affairs are used to establish merit.
Laws have what is easy to establish and what is difficult,
weigh the difficulty and if the matter can be completed,
then establish it;
if completing the matter has harm,
weigh the harm and if the merit is greater,
then do it.
A method without difficulty,
an achievement without harm—
such things do not exist in the world.
Therefore, when someone captures a city with walls a thousand *zhàng* high,
defeats an army of a hundred thousand,
has casualties amounting to a fraction of the army,
breaks and blunts weapons and armor,
and suffers deaths and injuries among the soldiers,
but is congratulated for winning the battle and gaining territory,
it is because they are focusing on the greater good and not the minor harm.
When bathing, one sheds hair;
when removing a growth, one injures flesh and blood.
If someone, seeing the difficulty,
abandons the task,
he is an unskilled person.
The former sages had a saying:
"A compass has wear,
and water has ripples;
I want to correct them,
but what can I do?"
This is speaking of understanding contingencies.
Therefore, some theories are well-established
but remote from reality,
and some words are clumsily phrased
but urgently needed.
Therefore, the sage does not seek harmless words,
but strives for things that are not easily done.
People do not use balances and weights,
not because they are honest and far from profit,
but because the stone cannot add or subtract for people,
the balance cannot make things lighter or heavier for people,
and seeking them is futile;
therefore, people do not use them.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
officials dare not bend the law,
and clerks dare not pursue private gain;
bribes do not circulate.
Thus, affairs within the borders
are as accurate as a balance and weights.
Therefore, if his ministers are treacherous, he will surely know it;
and those he knows, he will surely punish.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler
does not seek flawless officials,
but strives for techniques that ensure he knows the truth.
A loving mother's care for her weak child
cannot be surpassed.
However, if the weak child behaves perversely,
she makes him follow a teacher;
if he has a serious illness,
she makes him seek a doctor.
If he does not follow a teacher, he will fall into punishment;
if he does not seek a doctor, he will be close to death.
Although the loving mother loves him,
it is useless for avoiding punishment and saving him from death.
Therefore, preserving the child is not (merely) love.
The nature of mother and child
is love;
the power of ruler and minister
is strategy.
If a mother cannot preserve her family with love,
how can a ruler maintain his state with love?
An enlightened ruler, by understanding wealth and power,
can then attain his desires.
Therefore, diligently attending to governance
is the method for wealth and power.
Clarify laws and prohibitions,
examine plans and schemes.
If the laws are clear, there will be no internal troubles;
if the plans are successful, there will be no external disasters of being captured.
Therefore, what preserves a state
is not benevolence and righteousness.
A benevolent person
is kind and generous with wealth;
a violent person
is resolute and quick to punish.
Being kind
means being unwilling (to punish);
being generous with wealth
means being fond of giving.
Being resolute
means hatred is shown to subordinates;
being quick to punish
means random killings are inflicted on people.
Being unwilling (to punish)
means penalties are often pardoned;
being fond of giving
means rewards are often given without merit.
If hatred is shown,
subordinates will resent their superiors;
if killings are random, the people will rebel.
Therefore, when a benevolent person is in a high position,
subordinates are unrestrained
and easily violate prohibitions,
stealing and hoping from above;
when a violent person is in a high position,
the laws are reckless and the ruler and ministers are at odds,
the people resent him and rebellious thoughts arise.
Therefore, it is said:
"Both the benevolent and the violent
are destroyers of states."
Being unable to prepare fine food and encourage a hungry person to eat
does not make one capable of saving the starving;
being unable to clear land and grow grain
and instead encouraging loans and gifts
does not make one capable of enriching the people.
The words of scholars today
do not focus on fundamental tasks but instead favor superficial matters,
knowing empty sagehood
to persuade the people.
This is like the theory of "encouraging eating".
The theory of "encouraging eating"
is not accepted by an enlightened ruler.
If books are concise, disciples will dispute;
if laws are simple, lawsuits among the people will be frequent.
Therefore, the books of sages must include detailed arguments,
and the laws of enlightened rulers must be thoroughly detailed.
Exhausting thought
to weigh gains and losses
is difficult for the wise;
without thought or consideration,
taking previous words and demanding later results
is easy for the foolish.
An enlightened ruler considers what is easy for the foolish
and does not demand what is difficult for the wise;
therefore, intellectual labor is not used,
yet the state is well-governed.
If sour, sweet, salty, and bland flavors
are not judged by the mouth
but decided by the chief steward,
then the cook will slight the ruler
and value the chief steward.
If high and low pitches,
pure and turbid sounds
are not judged by the ear
but decided by the music master,
then the blind musicians will slight the ruler
and value the music master.
If right and wrong in governing the state
are not judged by method
but decided by favorites,
then ministers and subjects will slight the ruler
and value the favorites.
If the ruler does not personally observe and listen,
but judgments are made by subordinates,
he is someone who relies on the state for food.
If you make people not feel hunger when not clothed or fed,
and not feel cold,
and also not fear death,
then they will have no intention of serving their superiors.
If intentions are not controlled by the ruler,
then they cannot be used.
Now, if the power of life and death
is in the hands of great ministers,
and the ruler's orders can still be carried out,
that has never happened.
A tiger or leopard will certainly not abandon its claws and teeth
to have the same authority as a shrew;
a family with ten thousand in gold will certainly not abandon its wealth
to have the same resources as a gatekeeper.
A ruler with territory,
if he cannot benefit those he likes,
and cannot harm those he dislikes,
yet demands that people fear and respect him,
that is impossible.
When ministers freely express their desires,
it is called "chivalry" (*xiá*);
when rulers freely express their desires,
it is called "chaos" (*luàn*).
When ministers look down on their superiors, it is called "arrogance" (*jiāo*);
when rulers look down on their subordinates, it is called "tyranny" (*bào*).
Actions that are logically consistent
bring praise to subordinates
but blame to superiors.
Great gains for ministers
mean great losses for the ruler.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
there are esteemed officials,
but no powerful officials.
Esteemed officials are those
whose ranks are high and offices are great;
powerful officials are those
whose words are heeded and whose influence is extensive.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
officials are promoted gradually, rank by rank,
and offices and titles are bestowed based on merit;
therefore, there are esteemed officials.
Words that do not align with actions and those containing falsehoods
are invariably punished;
therefore, there are no powerful officials.
48.1 Relying on Emotions
In governing the world,
one must rely on human emotions.
Human emotions
involve likes and dislikes;
therefore, rewards and punishments can be employed.
If rewards and punishments can be employed,
then laws and prohibitions can be established,
and the tools of governance are complete.
The ruler holds the levers of power and occupies a position of authority;
therefore, orders are carried out and prohibitions are enforced.
The levers of power are the means of life and death;
a position of authority is the means of overcoming the multitude.
Indiscriminate granting or withholding of appointments diminishes authority,
and rewards and punishments shared with subordinates divide power.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not listen with affection
and does not make plans by dwelling on opinions.
Thus, if one listens to opinions without verification,
then power is shared with the treacherous;
if intelligence and abilities are not utilized,
then the ruler is made destitute by his ministers.
Therefore, the actions and regulations of an enlightened ruler are like Heaven,
and his use of men is like ghosts.
Being like Heaven, he makes no mistakes;
being like ghosts, he is not stymied.
Authority is exercised and education is strict,
so opposition does not lead to defiance,
and praise and criticism are unified and not debated.
Therefore, rewarding the virtuous and punishing the violent
is the ultimate way to promote goodness;
rewarding the violent and punishing the virtuous
is the ultimate way to promote evil.
This is called rewarding conformity and punishing dissent.
No reward is better than generosity,
which benefits the people;
no praise is better than excellence,
which honors the people;
no punishment is better than severity,
which makes the people fear;
no condemnation is better than vilification,
which shames the people.
Then, one uniformly implements the law,
prohibits private punishment within families,
and does not undermine merit or crime.
Rewards and punishments must be known;
when they are known,
the Way is exhausted.
48.2 The Way of the Ruler
Strength cannot contend with the multitude,
and wisdom cannot encompass all things.
Rather than employing one person,
it is better to employ an entire state;
therefore, intelligence and strength are matched,
and the multitude overcomes.
Calculating correctly leads to private labor,
and calculating incorrectly leads to blame.
An inferior ruler exhausts his own abilities;
a middling ruler exhausts the abilities of others;
a superior ruler exhausts the wisdom of others.
Therefore, when matters arise, wisdom is gathered,
and opinions are heard publicly and jointly.
If opinions are not unified,
then later actions contradict earlier ones;
if later actions contradict earlier ones,
then the foolish and the wise are not distinguished.
If opinions are not heard publicly and jointly,
then there is hesitation and indecision;
if there is indecision, then affairs are delayed.
Relying on oneself alone
avoids the burden of falling into a pit.
Therefore, one makes them offer suggestions;
suggestions are finalized, and then one becomes angry.
Therefore, on the day that opinions are presented,
there must be written records.
Gathering wisdom means that events are revealed and verified;
gathering abilities means that
achievements are seen and plans are successful or unsuccessful.
If success or failure is evident,
rewards and punishments follow accordingly.
If affairs are successful, then the ruler takes the credit;
if plans fail, then the minister bears the blame.
A ruler joins tallies together but does not do it personally,
much less exert physical force!
Affairs of wisdom are not done personally,
much less left in suspense!
Therefore, his use of men does not involve seeking agreement;
if there is agreement, then the ruler is angered.
Making men use each other makes the ruler divine;
if the ruler is divine, then subordinates exhaust their abilities.
If subordinates exhaust their abilities,
then ministers do not depend on the ruler,
and the Way of the Ruler is complete.
48.3 Inciting Chaos
He who knows the different interests of ministers and the ruler is a king;
he who thinks they are the same is robbed;
he who shares affairs with them is killed.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler examines the division between public and private
and scrutinizes the territory of benefit and harm;
then, treachery has no opportunity to take hold.
There are six sources of chaos:
the ruler's mother,
the queen and consorts,
sons and relatives,
brothers,
great ministers,
and the conspicuously virtuous.
Entrusting duties to officials and holding ministers accountable means that the ruler's mother does not act presumptuously;
applying different rites to different ranks means that the queen and consorts are not suspicious;
dividing power and not allowing it to be duplicated means that legitimate and illegitimate heirs do not contend;
not relinquishing power and authority means that brothers do not encroach;
not allowing subordinates to form cliques means that great ministers do not amass influence;
ensuring that rewards and punishments are carried out means that the conspicuously virtuous do not cause chaos.
Ministers have two supports,
which are called external and internal.
The external support is called fear,
and the internal support is called love.
Obtaining what is feared
and having what is loved listened to are what treacherous ministers rely upon.
For those placed among the officials from foreign states,
cutting off close ties, punishing intimacy, and imposing heavy taxes
means that external support is not built.
Bestowing ranks and emoluments based on merit,
and punishing those who make requests,
means that internal support is not relied upon.
If external support is not built
and internal support is not relied upon,
then treachery and deceit are blocked.
Advancing officials gradually based on their performance,
until they reach positions of great responsibility,
demonstrates wisdom.
For those whose positions reach the highest level and whose responsibilities are greatest,
they are controlled with three constraints:
they are called pledges (zhì),
safeguards (zhèn),
and fortifications (gù).
Relatives and children are pledges;
generous and assured ranks and emoluments are safeguards;
mutual oversight and shared accountability are fortifications.
The virtuous are stopped by pledges,
the greedy are transformed by safeguards,
and the treacherous are exhausted by fortifications.
If forbearance is not controlled, then subordinates become superiors;
if small evils are not eliminated, then there will be great punishments,
and if names and realities match, then take the direct path.
If someone causes harm to affairs
or damages reputation in death,
then give him food and drink;
otherwise,
make him an enemy to his foe;
this is called eliminating hidden treachery.
Concealment is called guǐ;
guǐ is called yì.
Rewarding achievement when it is seen
and punishing offenses when they are seen
will stop guǐ.
Failing to prevent disclosure of right and wrong,
failing to make remonstrances accepted,
and changes cannot be implemented.
Dismissing virtuous and capable elder family members, saying,
“They invite disaster,”
the danger is that neighboring enemies will be greatly strengthened.
Treating people fit for humiliation and disgrace as close associates, saying,
“They are intimate with traitors,”
the danger
is that resentment and suspicion of humiliation will arise.
Concealing anger and holding onto offenses without expressing them,
saying, "It increases chaos,"
the danger is that those who seek fortune through reckless actions will emerge.
Great ministers, with both weights balanced and not tilting,
saying, "It accumulates disaster,"
the danger is that the difficulty of family prosperity leading to
robbery and murder will arise.
Being overly lenient and failing to be discerning,
saying, "It diminishes authority,"
the danger is that the chaos of treacherous husbands using poison will arise.
These five dangers
are due to the ruler's lack of understanding,
which leads to events of robbery and murder.
Matters of dismissal and appointment,
arising internally lead to order,
arising externally lead to chaos.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler assesses based on merit internally,
and provides resources for profit externally,
so his state is ordered while the enemy is in chaos.
The way to chaos is this:
if ministers are hated,
then external troubles arise as if dazed;
if ministers are loved,
then internal troubles arise as if poisoned.
48.4 Establishing the Way
The way of 參伍 (sān wǔ, three and five):
employ "three" to seek plentiful planning,
evaluate "five" to demand responsibility for mistakes.
Employing "three" must involve splitting,
evaluating "five" must involve anger.
Not splitting leads to disrespect of superiors,
not being angry leads to collusion.
The evidence of splitting
is sufficient to know the amount,
the anger in advance prevents it from reaching the masses.
The method of observation and listening,
its evidence lies in forming cliques
while rewarding differences,
punishing without seeking permission
while the crimes are the same.
When words gather various viewpoints,
certainly measure them by territory (dì),
plan them by timing (tiān),
verify them with matters (wù),
and compare them with people (rén).
When these four tests align,
then it is possible to observe.
Cross-examine words to know their sincerity,
subtly observe to correct their appearance,
hold onto observations to gain the extraordinary.
Use favor to keep close to attendants,
repeat words to intimidate distant envoys.
Bring up the past to understand their history,
draw near to know their inner thoughts,
casually place to know their external relations.
Hold onto clarity to ask about what is obscure,
use deceitful envoys to cut off corruption and leakage.
Reverse words to test suspicions,
discuss opposition to discover hidden treachery.
Set up remonstrances to manage acting alone,
observe actions to see treacherous movements.
Clearly speak to induce avoidance of mistakes,
humbly accommodate to observe the upright and flattering.
Widely proclaim to understand the unseen,
create conflict to scatter factions.
Deeply unify to warn the crowd's minds,
leak differences to change their considerations.
If they seem similar, combine their "three,"
present errors to clarify their resolve.
Knowing crimes and avoiding crimes stops power,
secretly employ occasional inspections
to examine
sincerity,
gradually change to separate alliances.
The lower ranks make agreements to encroach upon their superiors,
the prime minister (xiàng shì)
makes agreements with his court officials,
the court officials
make agreements with their subordinates,
military officers
make agreements with their soldiers,
sending envoys
to make agreements with their travelling messengers,
the county magistrate (xiàn lìng)
makes agreements with his appointed officials,
the court gentleman (láng zhōng)
makes agreements with his attendants,
the queen (hòu jī)
makes agreements with her palace women.
This is called the way of controlled communication,
if words are communicated and matters are leaked,
then the method will not work.
48.5 Cross-Examination
An enlightened ruler,
his task lies in being thorough and meticulous,
therefore, joy shown
means virtue is rewarded,
anger shown means authority is divided.
Therefore, the words of an enlightened ruler
are separated and not communicated,
thorough and meticulous and not seen.
Therefore, to gain ten from one is
the way of the inferior,
to gain one from ten is
the way of the superior.
An enlightened ruler carries out both the upper and lower ways,
therefore, treachery has nowhere to escape.
Groups of five (wǔ), neighborhoods (lǘ),
linked, counties (xiàn), and districts as neighbors,
reporting errors receives reward,
failing to report errors receives punishment.
The superior towards the inferior,
and the inferior towards the superior is also the same.
Therefore, superiors and inferiors, nobles and commoners fear each other through law,
and teach each other through profit.
The nature of the people
has the reality of life,
and the reputation of life.
For the ruler,
there is the reputation of virtue and wisdom,
and the reality of rewards and punishments.
When both reputation and reality arrive together,
then good fortune and goodness will certainly be heard of.
48.6 Listening to the Law
Listening without cross-examination
means there is no way to hold subordinates accountable;
if words are not examined for their use,
then heretical words will be esteemed.
The nature of words is that they are believed more when they are many;
if it is not that way,
if ten people say there is doubt,
will a hundred people agree?
A thousand people cannot be understood!
A hesitant person's words are doubtful,
an eloquent person's words are believable.
The way treachery feeds on the ruler
is by taking resources from the crowd,
borrowing credibility from eloquence,
and using categories to adorn their private affairs.
If the ruler does not suppress anger and awaits combined cross-examination,
the situation is that he relies on subordinates.
An enlightened ruler who listens to words
examines their use,
assesses their merits,
with merit assessed, rewards and punishments arise,
therefore, useless eloquence does not remain in the court.
If those in charge of affairs know they are insufficient to manage their positions,
then the office is taken back.
If the arguments are grand and exaggerated, then their limits are reached,
therefore, treachery is discovered and anger arises.
Groundless statements that are inappropriate are slander,
and slander punishes ministers.
Words must have a response,
arguments must be held accountable for their use,
therefore, the words of factions will not be heard.
The way of listening is this:
ministers use loyal arguments to report treachery,
broadly discuss to internally unify;
if the ruler is not wise,
then treachery gains resources.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
If he likes something,
he seeks out the reasons it was accepted;
if he is angry about something,
he investigates the reasons it was formed;
discussing it after it has already changed,
in order to obtain evidence of praise, blame, public and private matters.
Many offer advice to demonstrate their intelligence,
causing the ruler to choose one for himself to avoid blame.
Therefore, the advice of the many is defeated,
and the selection of the ruler is too.
Do not have subordinates speak in agreement before you
to establish what is about to happen;
let the correctness of words be verified afterwards
to know whether they are deceptive or sincere.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
a minister must not offer two pieces of advice,
but must be entrusted with one word;
he must not act alone,
but must align with his peers,
therefore, wicked people have no way to advance.
48.7 Categories of power
without laws result;
when laws are not enforced,
the ruler is ignorant.
If the ruler is ignorant and without measure,
then officials act according to their own will;
if officials act according to their own will,
then the benefits they receive are unprecedentedly great;
if the benefits they receive are unprecedentedly great,
then taxes are numerous;
numerous taxes cause wealth.
The wealth of officials is what
gives rise to chaotic achievements.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
selection based on ability,
excellence in office,
rewards based on merit.
If speech is in accordance,
the ruler rejoices,
and both will surely benefit;
if it is not appropriate,
the ruler becomes angry,
and both will surely suffer harm;
in that case, people will not favor their fathers and brothers
but recommend their enemies.
If authority is sufficient to enforce the law,
if compensation is sufficient to provide for affairs,
then private gain will have no place to arise,
therefore, the people will labor diligently and respect officials.
In employing people, do not give them multiple responsibilities,
ensuring that their favor is tied to their rank;
those holding office must not be partial,
ensuring that their benefits are tied to their salary,
therefore, the people will respect rank and value salary.
Rank and salary
are for the purpose of reward;
if the people value what is used for reward,
then the state is well-governed.
If punishments are troublesome,
then the names are confused.
If rewards and praise are inappropriate, then the people will be in doubt,
for the people value names and rewards equally.
If those who are rewarded are slandered,
it will not be enough to encourage;
if those who are punished are praised,
it will not be enough to deter.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
rewards must come from public benefit,
and reputation must rest on service to the ruler.
Rewards and praise follow the same path,
punishments and executions proceed together.
In this way, the people will not find glory outside of rewards.
Those who receive severe punishments will inevitably have a bad reputation,
therefore the people will be in awe.
Punishment
is for the purpose of deterrence;
if the people fear what is used to deter,
then the state will be well-governed.
48.8 Ruler's Authority
If righteousness is practiced and favors are shown, then the ruler’s authority will be divided;
if kindness and benevolence are heeded, then laws and institutions will be destroyed.
If the people use regulations to inspire awe in their superiors,
