and superiors use their power to humble their inferiors,
then inferiors will be unbridled and insolent, taking pride in customs that disrespect the ruler,
and the ruler’s authority will be divided.
If the people use the law to make it difficult to offend their superiors,
and superiors use the law to distort kindness and benevolence,
then inferiors will openly love favors
and strive for a government of bribery and acceptance,
and therefore, laws and ordinances will be ruined.
Honoring private conduct weakens the ruler’s authority,
practicing bribery and acceptance casts doubt on the law.
Listening to them leads to chaotic governance,
not listening to them leads to slandering the ruler,
therefore, the ruler's position is demeaned
and the law is in chaos within the government,
this is called a state without constancy.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
a minister must not achieve glory through righteous conduct,
nor must he achieve merit through family benefit.
The source of merit and fame
must come from official laws.
Outside of what the law allows,
even if there are difficult tasks,
they must not be made conspicuous,
therefore the people will have no way to gain private fame.
Establish laws and measures to regulate the people,
be trustworthy in rewards and punishments to fully utilize the people's abilities,
make clear criticisms and praises to encourage and deter.
Titles, rewards, punishments, and laws and ordinances are three corners.
Therefore, if high officials act correctly,
they will honor the ruler;
if the common people have merit, they will benefit the ruler;
this is called a state with the Way.
In the ancient times,
the population was small and the number of birds and beasts was great,
and the people could not overcome the birds, beasts, insects, and snakes.
There was a sage who arose,
building wooden nests
to avoid the harm of the masses,
and the people were pleased with him,
making him ruler of the world,
and he was called Yǒucháo Shì (有巢氏).
The people ate fruits, melons, clams, and shellfish,
which were rancid, foul-smelling,
and harmed their stomachs,
and the people suffered many illnesses.
There was a sage who arose,
drilling wood to make fire
to transform the rancid and foul-smelling food,
and the people were pleased with him,
making him ruler of the world,
and he was called Suìrén Shì (燧人氏).
In the medieval times,
there was a great flood in the world,
and Gǔn (鯀) and
Yǔ (禹) dredged the waterways.
In recent ancient times,
Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂) were tyrannical and violent,
and Tāng (湯) and
Wǔ (武) launched punitive expeditions.
If someone were to build wooden nests and drill for fire
in the time of the Xiàhòu (夏后) clan,
they would surely be laughed at by Gǔn (鯀) and
Yǔ (禹);
if someone were to dredge waterways
in the time of the Yīn (殷) and Zhōu (周) dynasties,
they would surely be laughed at by Tāng (湯) and
Wǔ (武).
Therefore, if someone were to praise the ways of Yáo (堯), Shùn (舜), Tāng (湯), Wǔ (武), and Yǔ (禹)
in the present age,
they would surely be laughed at by the new sages.
Therefore, the sage does not seek to imitate the past,
nor does he model himself on what is constantly applicable,
but deliberates on the affairs of the age
and prepares accordingly.
There was a farmer from Sòng (宋) who was plowing his field,
and there was a stump in the middle of the field,
a rabbit ran into the stump,
broke its neck and died,
so he abandoned his plow and guarded the stump,
hoping to get another rabbit,
but the rabbit could not be obtained again,
and he became a laughingstock in the state of Sòng (宋).
Now, to try to govern the people of the present age
with the policies of the former kings
is just like guarding the stump.
In ancient times, men did not plow the fields,
because the fruits of plants and trees were enough to eat;
women did not weave,
because the skins of birds and beasts were enough to wear.
Without exerting effort, they had enough to eat,
the population was small and there was a surplus of wealth,
therefore the people did not contend.
Therefore, generous rewards were not practiced,
severe punishments were not used,
and the people governed themselves.
Nowadays, having five sons is not considered many;
each son then has five sons;
before the grandfather dies, he has twenty-five grandsons.
Thus, the population is large while wealth is scarce,
labor is arduous while support is meager,
hence the people contend.
Even doubling rewards and heaping up punishments
cannot prevent disorder.
When Yáo 堯 ruled the world,
the thatch on his roof was not trimmed,
the rafters were not planed;
he ate coarse millet,
and had soup of goosefoot greens;
in winter he wore deerskin robes,
and in summer, clothing of coarse cloth.
Even the attire and sustenance of a gatekeeper
were no less than this.
When Yǔ 禹 ruled the world,
he personally held the plow and hoe, taking the lead among the people,
his thighs had no down,
and his shins grew no hair.
Even the labor of slaves and prisoners
was no more arduous than this.
From this, it can be said that
those in ancient times who relinquished the throne
were abandoning the sustenance of a gatekeeper
and departing from the toil of slaves and prisoners;
in ancient times, passing on the world was not considered much.
Today's county magistrate,
should he die in office for even a single day,
his descendants will, for generations, maintain their carriages,
hence people value it greatly.
Therefore, in regard to abdication,
people lightly reject the ancient Son of Heaven,
but find it difficult to relinquish the county magistrate's post today,
because the reality of the substantiality is different.
Those who live in the mountains and draw water from the valleys
exchange water with each other during the *lóulà* 膢臘 festivals;
those who live in the marshes and suffer from bitter water
hire laborers to dredge waterways.
Therefore, in the spring of famine years,
even younger brothers are not fed;
in the autumn of bountiful years,
even distant guests are certainly fed.
It is not that they are estranged from their own flesh and blood
and love passing strangers more,
but that the reality of plenty and scarcity is different.
Therefore, in ancient times, the easy relinquishment of wealth
was not due to benevolence,
but because wealth was abundant;
today's contentiousness and grasping
are not due to baseness,
but because wealth is scarce.
Lightly resigning from being the Son of Heaven
is not due to loftiness,
but because the position held little power;
contending for an officer's stipend
is not due to lowness,
but because the power is significant.
Therefore, the sage deliberates on plenty and scarcity,
and discusses meagerness and substantiality,
in order to govern well.
Thus, light punishment is not considered merciful,
and strict execution is not considered tyrannical;
one acts in accordance with prevailing customs.
Therefore, affairs depend on the times,
and preparations are adapted to the circumstances.
In ancient times,
Wén Wáng 文王 resided between Fēng 豐 and Hào 鎬,
in a territory of one hundred square *lǐ* 里.
He practiced benevolence and righteousness
and won the allegiance of the western Róng 戎 tribes,
and eventually became king over all under Heaven.
Xú Yǎn Wáng 徐偃王 resided east of the Hàn 漢 River,
in a territory of five hundred square *lǐ* 里.
He practiced benevolence and righteousness,
and thirty-six states ceded territory and paid homage to him.
Jīng Wén Wáng 荊文王 feared that he would be a threat to him,
so he raised an army to attack Xú 徐,
and eventually destroyed it.
Therefore, Wén Wáng 文王 practiced benevolence and righteousness
and became king over all under Heaven,
while Yǎn Wáng 偃王 practiced benevolence and righteousness
and lost his state.
This shows that benevolence and righteousness were useful in ancient times
but are not useful today.
Thus, it is said:
when the times change, affairs change.
During the time of Shùn 舜,
the Miáo 有苗 tribes did not submit,
and Yǔ 禹 was about to attack them.
Shùn 舜 said:
“No.
To not cultivate virtue deeply and yet resort to military force
is not the Way.”
So he cultivated education for three years,
and performed dances holding shields and battleaxes,
and the Miáo 有苗 tribes then submitted.
In the battles of Gòng Gōng 共工,
those with short iron halberds reached the enemy,
and those with weak armor were wounded.
This shows that shields and battleaxes were useful in ancient times
but are not useful today.
Thus, it is said:
when affairs change, preparations change.
In high antiquity, people competed in morality;
in the middle ages, they pursued intelligence and strategy;
today, they contend in physical strength.
When Qí 齊 was about to attack Lǔ 魯,
Lǔ 魯 sent Zǐ Gòng 子貢 to persuade them.
The people of Qí 齊 said:
“What you say is not without eloquence,
but what we desire is land,
not what these words speak of.”
So they raised an army and attacked Lǔ 魯,
taking ten *lǐ* 里 from the city gates to serve as the boundary.
Therefore, Yǎn Wáng 偃王's benevolence and righteousness led to the demise of Xú 徐,
and Zǐ Gòng 子貢's eloquence and wisdom led to the decline of Lǔ 魯.
From this, it can be said that
benevolence, righteousness, eloquence, and wisdom
are not the means to maintain a state.
If one were to discard Yǎn Wáng 偃王's benevolence
and suppress Zǐ Gòng 子貢's wisdom,
and instead followed Xú 徐
and Lǔ 魯's strength
to confront an enemy with ten thousand chariots,
then the desires of Qí 齊 and Jīng 荊 could not be carried out against these two states.
Ancient and modern customs are different,
and new and old preparations are different.
If one desires to use lenient governance
to govern the people of a turbulent age,
it is like driving a wild horse without reins or whip—
this is the calamity of ignorance.
Today, both the Ru 儒 (Confucians) and Mò 墨 (Mohists) all praise the former kings
for universally loving all under Heaven,
and for regarding the people as their parents.
How do they demonstrate that this is so?
They say:
“When the Minister of Justice carries out punishments,
the ruler refrains from enjoying music;
upon hearing reports of the death penalty,
the ruler sheds tears.”
This is what they cite regarding the former kings.
If the relationship between ruler and subjects were like that of father and son,
then there would necessarily be good governance;
extending this reasoning,
then there would be no disorder among fathers and sons.
The human sentiment is most pronounced with one's parents;
everyone is loved, yet there is not necessarily good governance.
Even with deep love,
how could it not easily lead to disorder?
Now, the former kings' love for the people
did not exceed the love of parents for their children.
If children do not necessarily avoid disorder,
then how can the people necessarily be well-governed?
Furthermore, to carry out punishments according to the law
while the ruler sheds tears
is to demonstrate benevolence,
not to establish governance.
To weep and be reluctant to inflict punishment
is benevolence;
however, what cannot be avoided is punishment,
which is the law.
The former kings prioritized the law,
not listening to their weeping,
then it is clear that benevolence cannot be used for governance.
Moreover, the people are inherently obedient to power
and few are those who embrace righteousness.
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 (Confucius)
was a sage of the world.
He cultivated his conduct and clarified the Way
to travel within the seas.
The world admired his benevolence
and praised his righteousness,
but only seventy people served him.
It is clear that those who value benevolence are few,
and those who can practice righteousness are rare.
Therefore, with the vastness of the world,
those serving as laborers numbered seventy,
while those practicing rén yì (仁義) were but one.
Lǔ Āi Gōng (魯哀公),
was an inferior ruler.
Facing south, he ruled the state;
within its borders, none dared to disobey him.
The people are inherently submissive to power,
and power is indeed easy to use to subdue people.
Thus, Zhòng Ní (仲尼) instead became a subject,
while Āi Gōng (哀公) remained the ruler.
Zhòng Ní (仲尼) did not embrace righteousness,
but submitted to his power.
Therefore, in terms of yì (義),
Zhòng Ní (仲尼) would not submit to Āi Gōng (哀公),
but leveraging power,
Āi Gōng (哀公) would make Zhòng Ní (仲尼) his subject.
Now, when scholars persuade rulers,
they do not rely on a position of assured victory,
but insist that practicing rén yì (仁義)
will lead to hegemony.
This is to expect the ruler to necessarily match Zhòng Ní (仲尼),
and to presume that all commoners are like the disciples,
which is surely a recipe for failure.
Now, suppose there is an incompetent son;
his parents scold him, but he does not change;
the villagers rebuke him, but he remains unmoved;
the teachers instruct him, but he does not transform.
With the love of parents,
the conduct of villagers,
and the wisdom of teachers,
these three good influences combined
yet he remains unmoved,
not even a hair on his legs changes.
But when the officials of the prefecture and county,
wielding official weapons,
enforcing public law,
seek out and arrest criminals,
then he becomes fearful,
alters his behavior,
and changes his ways.
Therefore, parental love is insufficient to educate a child;
it must await the strict punishments of the prefecture and county,
for the people are inherently spoiled by love
and heedful of authority.
Thus, a ten-rèn (仞) wall,
Lóu Jì (樓季) could not scale it because
it was steep;
a thousand-rèn (仞) mountain,
a lame ewe can easily graze because
it is level.
Therefore, a wise ruler makes his laws steep and his punishments severe.
A piece of cloth, even of small value,
an ordinary person will not discard;
but a hundred yì (溢) of molten gold,
even Dào Zhí (盜跖) would not pick up.
If there is no necessary harm,
they will not discard the ordinary,
but if it is certain to harm the hand,
they will not pick up the hundred yì (溢);
therefore, a wise ruler makes his punishments certain.
Thus, no reward is as good as being generous and trustworthy,
making the people benefit from it;
no punishment is as good as being severe and certain,
making the people fear it;
no law is as good as being uniform and fixed,
making the people know it.
Thus, a ruler who bestows rewards without changing,
executes punishments without pardon,
praise accompanies his rewards,
and disgrace follows his punishments,
then both the worthy
and the unworthy will exert their full efforts.
But now it is not so:
those who have merit are given titles,
but their official positions are low;
those who cultivate the land are rewarded,
but their family estates are small;
those who do not gather wealth are ostracized,
but those who disregard the world are esteemed;
those who violate prohibitions are punished,
but their courage is admired.
The application of praise, blame, reward, and punishment
are mutually contradictory,
therefore, the laws and prohibitions are broken, and the people become more chaotic.
Now, if a brother is invaded,
one who certainly attacks is considered
lián (廉);
if a close friend is insulted,
one who follows to seek revenge is considered
zhēn (貞).
When acts of lián zhēn (廉貞) are established,
the laws of the ruler are violated.
If the ruler honors acts of zhēn lián (貞廉)
but forgets the crimes of violating prohibitions,
then the people strive for courage,
and the officials cannot control them.
Those who do not engage in labor but still have clothes and food are called capable;
those who do not achieve merit in battle but are still honored are called virtuous.
When acts of virtue and capability are established,
the army becomes weak and the land becomes barren.
If the ruler appreciates acts of virtue and capability
but forgets the disasters of a weak army
and barren land,
then private conduct is established
and public benefit is destroyed.
The Rú (儒) use literature to disrupt the law,
and the xiá (俠) use martial arts to violate prohibitions,
yet the ruler bestows favor on both;
this is the reason for disorder.
Those who deviate from the law are punished,
but the various teachers are chosen for their literary skills;
those who violate prohibitions are executed,
but the groups of xiá (俠) are supported with private swords.
Therefore, what the law rejects
is what the ruler selects;
what the officials punish
is what the ruler supports.
Law, interest, superior, inferior
are all contrary,
and without any fixed standard,
even if there were ten Huáng Dì (黃帝)s,
they could not govern.
Therefore, those who practice rén yì (仁義) should not be praised,
for praising them harms merit;
those skilled in literature should not be employed,
for employing them disrupts the law.
In Chǔ (楚) there was Zhí Gōng (直躬),
whose father stole a sheep,
and he reported him to the authorities.
The Lìng Jūn (令君) said:
"Execute him!"
considering him to be upright towards the ruler but disloyal to his father,
so he reported him and punished him.
From this perspective,
the ruler's upright subject
is the father's cruel son.
A man of Lǔ (魯) followed the ruler into battle
and retreated three times in three battles.
Zhòng Ní (仲尼) asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"I have an old father,
and if I die, there will be no one to care for him."
Zhòng Ní (仲尼) considered him filial
and promoted him.
From this perspective,
the father's filial son
is the ruler's disloyal subject.
Therefore, when the Lìng Yǐn (令尹) punishes,
crimes in Chǔ (楚) are not reported;
when Zhòng Ní (仲尼) rewards, the people of Lǔ (魯) easily surrender and retreat.
The benefits to superiors and inferiors
are so different,
yet the ruler indiscriminately promotes the conduct of commoners
and seeks to achieve the prosperity of the state;
this is surely impossible.
In ancient times, when Cāng Jié (蒼頡) created writing,
that which encircled inwards was called sī (私) "private",
and that which turned away from private was called gōng (公) "public".
The mutual opposition of public and private
was something Cāng Jié (蒼頡) knew well.
To now regard them as mutually beneficial
is the calamity of not observing carefully.
Then, to plan for oneself,
nothing is better than cultivating virtuous conduct and practicing literature.
If rén yì (仁義) is cultivated, one gains trust;
if one gains trust, one receives appointments;
if one practices literature, one becomes a renowned teacher;
if one becomes a renowned teacher, one achieves glory:
this is the excellence of a commoner.
But to receive appointments without merit
and to achieve glory without rank,
if the government is conducted in this way,
then the state will surely be in chaos and the ruler will surely be in danger.
Therefore, things that are incompatible
cannot coexist.
Rewarding those who slay enemies while praising the conduct of gāo cí huì;
bestowing ranks and emoluments upon those who capture cities while extolling the principles of xìn lián ài;
strengthening armor and sharpening weapons to prepare for difficulties while admiring the finery of *jiàn shēn*;
enriching the state through agriculture, relying on soldiers to repel enemies, while esteeming men of letters;
abolishing people who respect superiors and fear the law while supporting bands of wandering swordsmen.
Conducting affairs in this way makes it impossible to achieve order and strength.
A state at peace supports scholars and knights-errant, but in times of trouble relies on armed soldiers.
What is benefited is not what is used; what is used is not what is benefited.
Therefore, those engaged in practical occupations become few, while wandering scholars increase daily. This is why the world is in disorder.
Moreover, what the world calls worthy is the conduct of zhēn xìn;
what is called wise is subtle speech.
Subtle speech is difficult even for the most intelligent to understand.
Now, laws are made for the multitude, but are based on what is difficult for even the most intelligent to understand, so the people have no way of knowing them.
Therefore, those who are not full on chaff and husks do not aspire to fine rice and meat, and those whose short coats are not whole
do not wait for embroidered silk.
The affairs of governing a state, if what is urgent cannot be obtained,
then what is less urgent is not what should be pursued.
Now, in the government and affairs being managed, what the people, men and women, clearly understand is not used,
while theories that only superiors understand are admired, which is contrary to good governance.
Therefore, subtle speech is not what the people should be concerned with.
As for worthy and faithful conduct, one must value those who do not deceive;
those who do not deceive also have no art of not deceiving.
When commoners associate with each other, there is no wealth to benefit each other,
and no power to intimidate each other,
so they seek those who do not deceive.
Now, the ruler occupies a position of controlling others,
has the resources of an entire state,
has heavy rewards and severe punishments,
and is able to grasp the handle of power.
By cultivating what is illuminated by clear laws, even if there are ministers like Tián Cháng and Zǐ Hǎn,
they would not dare to deceive.
Why wait for those who do not deceive?
Now, honest and trustworthy men do not amount to ten,
while the number of officials within the borders is in the hundreds.
If trustworthy men must be appointed,
then there will not be enough men for the offices.
If there are not enough men for the offices,
then those who govern will be few, and those who create disorder will be many.
Therefore, the way of a wise ruler is to unify the laws and not seek wisdom, to solidify techniques and not admire trustworthiness,
so the laws are not broken,
and the officials have no fraud or deception.
Now, rulers in their speech, delight in their eloquence but do not seek whether it is appropriate;
in their use of actions, they praise the reputation but do not demand results.
Therefore, among the masses of the world, those who talk strive to be eloquent
but are not thorough in practical use,
so those who cite the words of the former kings on benevolence and righteousness fill the court,
but the government cannot avoid disorder;
those who conduct themselves compete to be lofty
but do not align with merit,
so wise men retreat to caves and mountains,
return their stipends and refuse to accept them,
but the military cannot avoid weakness.
If the military cannot avoid weakness,
and the government cannot avoid disorder,
what is the reason for this?
What the people praise and what superiors honor are the techniques of a state in disorder.
Now, the people within the borders all speak of governance;
those who possess the laws of Shāng and Guǎn
can be found in every household,
but the state becomes poorer and poorer,
and while many speak of farming, few hold a plow.
Within the borders, all speak of military affairs;
those who possess the books of Sūn and Wú
can be found in every household,
but the military becomes weaker and weaker,
and while many speak of war, few wear armor.
Therefore, a wise ruler uses their strength and does not listen to their words;
rewards their merits and prohibits what is useless,
so the people exhaust their strength
to follow their superiors.
Farming is strenuous labor, but the people do it,
saying, "It can bring wealth."
War is a dangerous undertaking, but the people do it,
saying, "It can bring nobility."
Now, if cultivating literature and practicing speech
can bring the reality of wealth without the labor of farming, and the honor of nobility without the danger of war,
then who would not do it?
Therefore, a hundred people engage in wisdom
while one person exerts strength.
When many engage in wisdom,
the laws are broken;
when few exert strength,
the state becomes poor.
This is why the world is in disorder.
Therefore, in the state of a wise ruler, there are no writings on bamboo and silk, using the law as teaching;
there are no sayings of the former kings, using officials as teachers;
there is no defense with private swords, using beheading as courage.
Thus, the people within the borders, their words must conform to the law, their actions must lead to merit, and their courage must be exhausted in the military.
Therefore, in times of peace, the state is rich;
in times of war, the military is strong.
This is called the resources of a king.
Having accumulated the resources of a king
and taking advantage of the enemy states' weaknesses,
surpassing the Five Emperors and matching the Three Kings,
this method is essential.
Now, it is not so;
the officials and people are unrestrained internally,
and those who speak gain power externally.
Internal and external affairs are both bad,
waiting for a strong enemy;
is this not dangerous?
Therefore, the words of the assembled ministers on foreign affairs,
are either part of the alliance of Vertical and Horizontal,
or loyal out of enmity,
and borrow the strength of the state.
The Vertical alliance is uniting the weak to attack the strong;
the Horizontal alliance is serving the strong to attack the weak;
neither is a way to maintain the state.
Now, the ministers who speak of the Horizontal alliance all say, "If we do not serve the great power,
we will encounter enemies and suffer disaster."
Serving the great power
may not have substance, so they hand over the map and entrust the seal, and offer tribute and request soldiers.
Offering the map diminishes the territory,
entrusting the seal lowers the name,
diminishing the territory reduces the map,
and lowering the name throws the government into disorder.
Serving the great power as a Horizontal alliance, I have not seen its benefit,
but it results in losing territory and disrupting the government.
Those ministers who advocate for yielding always say:
"If we don't rescue the small and attack the large,
we will lose the world.
If we lose the world, the state will be in danger.
If the state is in danger, the ruler will be debased."
Rescuing the small may not actually be effective,
and thus we raise troops to oppose the large.
Rescuing the small may not ensure its survival,
while attacking the large
may inevitably reveal weaknesses,
and revealing weaknesses will allow us to be controlled by strong states.
If we send out troops, the army will be defeated.
If we retreat to defend, the cities will be captured.
Rescuing the small seems virtuous,
but I have yet to see its benefits,
only the loss of territory and defeat of armies.
Therefore, serving the strong
allows one to use external power to become an official internally.
Rescuing the small
allows one to use internal importance to seek benefits externally.
The state's interests are not yet established,
but the fiefs and generous salaries have already arrived.
Although the ruler is debased,
the ministers are honored.
Although the state's territory is diminished,
private families are enriched.
If things succeed,
one's power will grow and importance increase.
If things fail,
one can retire comfortably with wealth.
When a ruler listens to his ministers,
before matters are accomplished, their ranks and emoluments are already honored.
If they are not punished for failure,
then what persuaders
would not use the talk of *zēng jiǎo* (pointed arrows)
to gamble for success?
Therefore, states are destroyed and rulers perish
by listening to the specious words of orators.
What is the reason for this?
It is that the ruler does not understand the benefits of public versus private,
does not examine the appropriateness of words,
and does not necessarily punish failures afterward.
They all say:
"In external affairs,
success can lead to hegemony,
and small victories can bring peace."
A hegemon
is one who can attack others,
but peace
means being unassailable.
Strength
is what allows one to attack others,
but order
means being unassailable.
Order and strength cannot be demanded from the outside;
they are the result of internal governance.
Now, if we do not implement laws and methods internally
and instead rely on wisdom externally,
we will not achieve order and strength.
A common saying goes:
"Long sleeves are good for dancing,
and much money is good for trading."
This saying means that abundant resources make it easy to be skillful.
Therefore, order and strength make it easy to strategize,
while weakness and chaos make it difficult to plan.
Thus, when used in Qín (秦),
ten changes
in strategy rarely lead to failure.
When used in Yān (燕), one change
rarely leads to success.
It is not that those used in Qín (秦) are necessarily wise
or those used in Yān (燕) are necessarily foolish,
but rather that the resources for order and chaos are different.
Therefore, Zhōu (周) abandoned Qín (秦) for alliance (從, *cóng*),
and was overthrown in a year.
Wèi (衛) left Wèi (魏) for counter-alliance (衡, *héng*),
and perished in half a year.
This shows that Zhōu (周) was destroyed by alliance,
and Wèi (衛) perished by counter-alliance.
If Zhōu (周) and Wèi (衛)
had delayed their alliance strategies
and focused on improving their internal governance,
clarifying their laws and prohibitions,
ensuring their rewards and punishments,
exhausting their land's resources to increase their reserves,
and encouraging their people to die for the defense of their cities,
then if the world obtained their land,
the benefit would be small,
and attacking their state would cause great harm.
No state with ten thousand chariots
would dare exhaust itself beneath their fortified walls
and allow a strong enemy to exploit its weaknesses.
This is the art of certain survival.
Abandoning the art of certain survival
and pursuing actions that inevitably lead to destruction
is the fault of those who govern states.
When wisdom is exhausted externally and governance is chaotic internally,
destruction cannot be averted.
The people's plans and calculations
all tend towards safety and profit,
just as they avoid danger and poverty.
Now, if we engage them in attacks and battles,
advancing means death at the hands of the enemy,
and retreating means death by punishment,
then they are in danger.
If they abandon their private affairs
and are required to toil in battle,
their families will be impoverished, and the ruler will not consider it,
then they are in poverty.
Poverty and danger are what the people
cannot avoid.
Therefore, serving private interests
and fortifying their homes
allows them to avoid distant battles,
and avoiding distant battles brings peace.
Bribing those in power
allows one to obtain what one seeks,
and obtaining what one seeks brings private security,
and private security is where profit lies,
so how can they not pursue it?
Therefore, there are few public-minded citizens
and many self-interested individuals.
The policy of an enlightened ruler governing the state
is to minimize the number and lower the status of merchants, artisans, and those who live off others' labor,
in order to reduce those pursuing secondary occupations
and encourage those engaging in essential tasks.
Nowadays, when the requests of close associates are granted,
official positions and titles can be bought.
If official positions and titles can be bought,
then merchants and artisans are no longer base.
If merchants who deal in fraudulent goods and wealth are employed in the markets,
then there will be no shortage of merchants.
If collecting wealth is valued more than farming
and leads to higher status than those who cultivate the land and fight in battles,
then there will be few upright men
and many merchants.
Therefore, in the customs of a chaotic state,
the scholars
invoke the ways of the former kings to establish reputations for integrity,
wear elaborate clothing and adorn eloquent speeches,
to cast doubt on the laws of the present era,
and divide the ruler's heart.
The orators
create false pretenses,
borrow from external powers,
to achieve their private gains,
and forsake the interests of the state.
Those who carry swords
gather followers,
establish principles,
to display their fame,
and violate the prohibitions of the government.
Those seeking exemption from service
accumulate wealth privately,
exhaust their goods in bribery,
and use the influence of powerful men to avoid service,
and evade the labor of battle.
The merchants and artisans
repair shoddy tools,
amass extravagant wealth,
accumulate and wait for the opportune moment,
and strive for the same profit as farmers.
These five are the parasites of the state.
If the ruler does not eliminate these five types of parasites,
and does not nurture upright men,
then even if there are states within the realm that are destroyed,
and dynasties that are extinguished,
it should not be surprising.
The prominent schools of thought in the world are those of
the Rú (Confucians) and the Mò (Mohists).
The origin of the Rú lies with
Kǒng Qiū (Confucius).
The origin of the Mò lies with
Mò Dí (Mozi).
After the death of Kǒngzǐ,
there arose the Rú of Zǐzhāng,
the Rú of Zǐsī,
the Rú of the Yán lineage,
the Rú of the Mèng lineage,
the Rú of the Qīdiāo lineage,
the Rú of the Zhòngliáng lineage,
the Rú of the Sūn lineage,
the Rú of the Yuèzhèng lineage.
After the death of Mòzǐ,
there arose the Mò of the Xiānglǐ lineage,
the Mò of the Xiāngfū lineage,
the Mò of the Dèngl陵 lineage.
Thus, after Kǒng
and Mò,
the Rú split into eight,
and the Mò diverged into three.
Their adoptions and rejections were contradictory and different,
yet each claimed to be the true Kǒng and Mò.
Kǒng
and Mò cannot be revived;
who then can be made to settle the learning of the world?
Kǒngzǐ
and Mòzǐ both spoke of Yáo
and Shùn,
yet their adoptions and rejections differed,
and each claimed to be the true Yáo
and Shùn.
Yáo
and Shùn cannot be revived;
who then can be made to determine the sincerity of the Rú and
Mò?
The Yīn and Zhōu dynasties lasted for over seven hundred years,
the Yú and Xià dynasties for over two thousand years,
yet they could not determine the truth of the Rú and
Mò.
Now, to try to examine the Way of Yáo
and Shùn
from three thousand years ago—
is it not likely to be uncertain?
To insist on something without comparison or verification is
foolish;
to assert something that cannot be confirmed is
false.
Therefore, those who clearly base themselves on the former kings
and definitively decide on Yáo and Shùn
are either foolish or false.
Foolish and false learning,
confused and contradictory actions—
enlightened rulers do not accept them.
The Mò, in their funerals,
wear winter clothing in winter
and summer clothing in summer,
use a three-inch thick paulownia coffin,
and observe mourning for three months.
The rulers of the world consider this frugal and honor them.
The Rú, in their funerals, bankrupt their families,
observe mourning for three years,
engage in extreme self-mortification, and use walking sticks.
The rulers of the world consider this filial and honor them.
But is the frugality of Mòzǐ
not the extravagance of Kǒngzǐ? Is the filial piety of Kǒngzǐ
not the contrariness of Mòzǐ?
Now filial piety, contrariness, extravagance, and frugality
are all found in the Rú and Mò,
yet the rulers honor them both.
The arguments of Qīdiāo
do not bend to expression,
nor do they avert the eyes;
to act according to the rules is to violate the customs of servants,
to act uprightly is to anger the feudal lords.
The rulers of the world consider this incorruptible and honor him.
The arguments of Sòng Róngzǐ
are such that he does not incite strife,
he does not seek revenge when wronged,
he is not ashamed of imprisonment,
and he does not feel disgraced when insulted.
The rulers of the world consider this tolerant and honor him.
But is the incorruptibility of Qīdiāo
not the forbearance of Sòng Róng?
Is the tolerance of Sòng Róng
not the violence of Qīdiāo?
Now tolerance,
incorruptibility, forbearance,
and violence
are all found in these two men,
yet the rulers honor them both.
Because foolish and false learning
and confused and contradictory arguments are contended,
and the rulers listen to them all,
therefore the scholars within the seas
have no fixed doctrines,
and their actions have no constant principles.
Ice and charcoal cannot stay long in the same container,
and cold and heat do not arrive at the same time.
Confused and contradictory learning cannot coexist and govern.
Now, to listen to diverse learning and wrongly practice
words of similarity and difference,
how can there be no chaos?
If listening and actions are like this,
it is bound to be the same in governing people.
Now, the scholars of the world who speak of governance
often say:
"Give to poor lands to supplement those without resources."
Now, if people are all the same,
and there is no extra profit from a good harvest,
yet one alone is able to be self-sufficient,
it must be through diligence or frugality.
If people are all the same,
and there are no disasters of famine,
sickness,
or misfortune and crime,
yet one alone is poor,
it must be through extravagance or laziness.
Those who are extravagant and lazy are poor,
while those who are diligent and frugal are rich.
Now, if the ruler levies taxes from the rich
to distribute to the poor,
he is taking from the diligent and frugal
to give to the extravagant and lazy,
and wanting to demand that the people work hard and be economical,
it cannot be done.
Now, if there is a person here who
will not enter a dangerous city out of righteousness,
will not serve in the military,
and will not exchange a single hair on his shin for all the benefits in the world,
the ruler of the world will certainly follow and honor him,
valuing his wisdom and esteeming his conduct,
considering him
to be a scholar who values life over material things.
But the reason why the ruler displays fine fields and large houses
and establishes ranks and salaries
is to induce the people to risk their lives.
Now, if the ruler respects and values scholars who value life over material things,
and demands that the people risk death
and place importance on dying for the ruler's affairs,
it cannot be done.
Those who store books,
practice argumentation,
gather disciples and servants,
adorn themselves with literature, and engage in debate,
the rulers of the world will certainly follow and honor them,
saying:
"Respecting worthy scholars
is the way of the former kings."
But those whom the officials tax are
the farmers,
while those whom the ruler supports are
the scholars.
The farmers are heavily taxed,
while the scholars are richly rewarded.
And demanding that the people work hard and speak less,
it cannot be done.
Those who establish principles and clearly discern,
uphold integrity and are unyielding,
and when words of resentment pass their ears,
immediately follow them with a sword,
the rulers of the world will certainly follow and honor them,
considering them to be scholars who cherish themselves.
But if the labor of beheading enemies is not rewarded,
while the bravery of fighting in one's own home is revered and made prominent,
and demanding that the people fight fiercely against the enemy
and not engage in private feuds,
it cannot be done.
When the state is at peace,
it supports scholars and chivalrous men;
when difficulty arrives,
it employs armored soldiers.
Those who are supported are not those who are employed,
and those who are employed are not those who are supported—
this is why there is chaos.
Moreover, when the ruler of men listens and learns,
if the words are correct,
he should assign the speaker to an office and employ his person;
if the words are incorrect,
he should dismiss the person and stop the source [of such words].
Now, if he deems the words correct,
yet does not assign him to an office;
if he deems them incorrect,
yet does not stop the source [of such words],
to deem them correct but not employ [the speaker],
to deem them incorrect but not stop [the source],
is the way to chaos and ruin.
Tán Tái Zǐyǔ,
had the appearance of a *jūnzǐ*;
Zhòng Ní nearly chose him,
but after associating with him for a long time,
his actions did not match his appearance.
The words of Zǎi Yǔ
were refined and eloquent;
Zhòng Ní nearly chose him,
but after associating with him for a long time,
his wisdom did not match his eloquence.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ said:
"If I judged people by their appearance,
I would have misjudged Zǐyǔ;
if I judged people by their words,
I would have misjudged Zǎi Yǔ."
Therefore, even with the wisdom of Zhòng Ní,
there was the reputation of misjudging talent.
Now, new debaters are more unrestrained than Zǎi Yǔ,
and the rulers of the world are more dazzled than Zhòng Ní.
If they are pleased by their words
and consequently entrust them with office,
how can they avoid making mistakes?
Therefore, Wèi entrusted Mèng Mǎo with his eloquence,
and suffered the calamity of Huá Xià;
Zhào entrusted Mǎ Fú with his eloquence,
and suffered the disaster of Chángpíng.
These two cases
are examples of the mistakes of entrusting eloquence.
To examine forged tin and seek green and yellow,
Qū Yě cannot guarantee a good sword;
if [a sword] can strike down swans and geese in water,
and sever foals and horses on land,
then even a servant would not doubt its sharpness.
To assess teeth, lips, and facial features,
Bólè cannot guarantee a good horse;
if [a horse] is put in a carriage and driven,
and one observes its performance on the road,
then even a servant would not doubt its worthiness.
Observing appearance and dress,
listening to words and speeches,
Zhòng Ní could not guarantee a good official;
if one tests them in official positions,
and assesses their accomplishments and achievements,
then even an ordinary person would not doubt their intelligence and wisdom.
Therefore, the officials of an enlightened ruler:
the chief ministers must rise from the provinces and departments,
the brave generals must emerge from the ranks of soldiers.
If those with merit are invariably rewarded,
then ranks and emoluments will be substantial
and encourage greater effort;
if one advances in office and inherits ranks,
then official duties will be grand
and governance will become better.
If ranks and emoluments are grand
and official duties are well-managed,
this is the way to become king.
A huge rock of a thousand *lǐ* is
cannot be called wealth;
a million statues of people
cannot be called strength.
The rock is not small,
the number is not few,
yet they cannot be called wealth and strength
because the rock does not produce grain,
and the statue-people cannot be deployed to resist enemies.
Now, merchants and artisans
also eat without tilling the land,
so if the land is not tilled,
it is the same as having huge rocks.
If scholars and knights-errant do not endure military labor
yet become prominent and honored,
then the people will not be employed,
which is the same as having statue-people.
To know the harm of huge rocks and statue-people,
but not to know the harm of merchants, officials, scholars, and knights-errant
who are like untilled land,
and unemployable people,
is to not understand the nature of things.
Therefore, even if the ruler of an enemy state
praises my righteousness,
I will not accept his tribute and become his subject;
even if the lords within the pass
criticize my actions,
I will compel them to bring tribute and attend court.
Therefore, if one has great strength,
others will come to court;
if one has little strength,
one will attend court to others.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler strives for strength.
Strict families do not have violent members,
but indulgent mothers have delinquent sons.
From this I know that power and authority can restrain violence,
but great virtue is not enough to stop disorder.
The sage's governance of the state
does not rely on people doing good,
but uses [methods] to ensure they cannot do wrong.
If one relies on people doing good,
the territory will not even increase tenfold;
if one uses [methods] to ensure people cannot do wrong,
the entire state can be made uniform.
Those who govern
employ the many and discard the few,
therefore, they do not strive for virtue
but strive for law.
If one insists on arrows that are straight by themselves,
there will be no arrows for a hundred generations;
if one insists on wood that is round by itself,
there will be no wheels for a thousand generations.
Arrows that are straight by themselves,
wood that is round by itself,
are not found in one out of a hundred generations,
yet the world is full of people riding in carriages and shooting birds.
Why?
Because the methods of straightening and rounding are employed.
Even if there are arrows that are straight by themselves
without relying on straightening,
or wood that is round by itself,
good artisans do not value them.
Why?
Because those who ride in carriages are not one person,
and those who shoot arrows do not shoot once.
If one does not rely on rewards and punishments
but relies on people being good by themselves,
an enlightened ruler does not value it.
Why?
Because the state's laws cannot be lost,
and those who are governed are not one person.
Therefore, a ruler with methods
does not follow occasional goodness,
but implements a reliable way.
Now, if someone were to say to a person:
"I will make you certain to be wise and live long,"
the world would surely consider him mad.
Wisdom
is innate;
longevity
is destiny.
Innate nature and destiny
are not things learned from others,
and to persuade people with what people cannot do,
is why the world calls him mad.
To say that he cannot do it
is to instruct him;
to instruct him about his innate nature.
To teach people with benevolence and righteousness
is to persuade them with wisdom and longevity;
a ruler with standards will not accept it.
Therefore, admiring the beauty of Máo Qiǎng
and Xī Shī
does not improve my face;
but using rouge and powder
doubles its original beauty.
Speaking of the benevolence and righteousness of the former kings
does not improve governance;
making my laws and standards clear,
and ensuring my rewards and punishments are certain,
is the rouge and powder of the state.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler values its assistance
and deemphasizes its praise,
and thus does not advocate benevolence and righteousness.
Now, when shamans and priests bless people, they say,
"May you live for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years!"
The sound of "a thousand autumns and ten thousand years" fills the ears,
but not a single day is added to the person's lifespan.
This is why people disregard shamans and priests.
Now, the scholars of the present age advise rulers,
not improving the current methods of governance,
but speaking of the merits of past governance;
not understanding the matters of official law,
nor investigating the nature of treachery and evil,
but all praising
the transmitted reputations of ancient times,
and the achievements of the former kings.
Scholars embellish their words, saying,
"Listen to my words,
and you can achieve hegemony and kingship!"
These advisors are like shamans and priests,
and rulers with standards do not accept them.
Therefore, enlightened rulers value practical matters,
discarding the useless,
not speaking of the past precedents of rén 仁 (benevolence) and yì 義 (righteousness),
and not listening to the words of scholars.
Now, those who do not understand governance invariably say,
"Win the hearts of the people."
If one could govern simply by winning the hearts of the people,
then there would be no need for Yī Yǐn 伊尹
and Guǎn Zhòng 管仲;
one would simply listen to the people.
The wisdom of the people is not to be relied upon,
just like the mind of an infant.
If an infant's head is not shaved, he will have abdominal pain;
if a boil is not lanced, it will worsen.
Shaving the head
and lancing the boil
require someone to hold the infant,
while a loving mother treats him,
yet he still cries incessantly.
The infant does not understand that by enduring a small pain,
he achieves a great benefit.
Now, when the ruler urgently encourages plowing fields and clearing wasteland
to increase the people's wealth,
the people regard him as cruel;
when he establishes strict punishments and heavy penalties to prevent evil,
the people regard him as harsh;
when he collects taxes and grain to fill the granaries,
and to relieve famine
and prepare for military campaigns,
the people regard him as greedy;
when the people within the borders are required to know military affairs
and have no private exemptions,
and to exert their strength in battle
to capture the enemy,
the people regard him as violent.
These four things
are the means to achieve peace and stability,
but the people do not find them pleasing.
Seeking scholars with sagely understanding
to be teachers is insufficient to guide the people.
In the past, Yǔ 禹 dredged the rivers,
but the people gathered tiles and stones to obstruct him;
Zǐchǎn 子產 opened up fields and planted mulberry trees,
but the people of Zhèng 鄭 criticized him.
Yǔ 禹 benefited the world,
and Zǐchǎn 子產 preserved the people of Zhèng 鄭,
yet both were subjected to slander.
The unreliability of the people's wisdom is thus clear.
Therefore, promoting officials based on seeking the wise and intelligent,
and governing with the aim of pleasing the people,
are both sources of chaos
and cannot be relied upon for governance.
The world all considers the principles of filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and obedience
to be correct,
but no one knows how to examine
the principles of filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and obedience
and carefully implement them,
which is why the world is in chaos.
Everyone considers the ways of Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜 to be correct
and emulates them,
which is why there are cases of regicide
and injustice towards fathers.
Yáo 堯, Shùn 舜, Tāng 湯, and Wǔ 武 sometimes violated the principles of ruler and subject,
corrupting the teachings for later generations.
Yáo 堯, as a ruler, treated his ministers as rulers treat their subjects;
Shùn 舜, as a minister, acted as if he ruled his ruler;
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武, as ministers,
killed their lords and executed their corpses,
yet the world praises them.
This is why the world remains ungoverned to this day.
The so-called enlightened ruler
is one who can employ his ministers;
the so-called wise minister
is one who can clarify laws and regulations
and manage official duties to support his ruler.
Now, Yáo 堯 considered himself enlightened
but could not employ Shùn 舜;
Shùn 舜 considered himself wise
but could not support Yáo 堯;
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 considered themselves righteous
but killed their rulers and superiors.
This is because enlightened rulers are ordinary,
and wise ministers are always seeking to seize power.
Therefore, to this day, there are sons who seize their fathers' families
and ministers who seize their rulers' states.
For a father to yield to his son
and a ruler to yield to his minister
is not the way to establish a fixed order and consistent teachings.
What I have heard is this:
"Ministers serve their rulers,
sons serve their fathers,
and wives serve their husbands.
When these three relationships are harmonious, the world is well-governed;
when they are reversed,
the world is in chaos.
This is the constant way of the world."
If an enlightened ruler and a wise minister do not change this,
then even if the ruler is incompetent,
the minister will not dare to usurp power.
Now, the current practice of valuing the wise and entrusting the intelligent without any fixed standard
is a reversal of the proper way,
yet the world constantly considers it good governance.
Therefore, the Tián 田 family seized the Lǚ 呂 family's state of Qí 齊,
and the Dài 戴 family seized the Zǐ 子 family's state of Sòng 宋.
Were these men not wise and intelligent?
Were they foolish and incompetent?
Therefore, abandoning constant principles to value the wise leads to chaos;
abandoning law to rely on intelligence leads to danger.
Thus it is said,
“Uphold the law and not the worthy.”
The Record says,
"When Shùn 舜 saw Gǔsǒu 瞽瞍 (his blind father),
his expression was strained."
Confucius said,
"At that time, how precarious it was!
The world was in a perilous state!
For those who possess the Dao,
the father certainly cannot control the son,
and the ruler certainly cannot control the minister."
I say,
Confucius fundamentally did not understand
the principles of filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and obedience.
In that case, do those who possess the Dào 道 not advance to serve as ministers
or retreat to be sons?
The reason why a father desires to have a virtuous son
is that if the family is poor, he will enrich it;
if the father suffers, he will bring him joy.
The reason why a ruler desires to have a virtuous minister
is that if the state is in chaos, he will govern it;
if the ruler is weak, he will honor him.
Now, if one has a virtuous son who does not benefit his father,
then the father's life in the family will be miserable;
if one has a virtuous minister who does not benefit his ruler,
then the ruler's position will be precarious.
In that case, fathers with virtuous sons
and rulers with virtuous ministers are merely inviting harm,
so how could they gain any benefit?
The so-called loyal minister does not endanger his ruler;
the filial son does not criticize his parents.
Now, Shùn 舜 seized his ruler's state through his virtue,
and Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武, in the name of righteousness, exiled and killed their rulers.
All of these are cases of endangering the ruler through virtue,
yet the world praises them for their virtue.
The heroic men of old did not serve their rulers when they advanced
and did not care for their families when they retreated.
Thus, they criticized their rulers when they advanced
and criticized their parents when they retreated.
Moreover, advancing and not serving the ruler,
retreating and not managing the household,
is the way to extinction in a chaotic world.
Therefore, to praise Xián Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ
and to admire martyrs
is a technique for creating chaos in the world.
Gǔsǒu was Shùn's father, yet Shùn exiled him;
Xiàng was Shùn's brother, yet he planned to kill him.
Exiling one's father and killing one's brother cannot be called benevolence;
marrying the two daughters of the emperor and seizing the empire
cannot be called righteousness.
Without benevolence and righteousness,
one cannot be called enlightened.
The *Shī* says:
"Under the broad heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's;
on the shores of the entire land,
there is no one who is not the king's subject."
If one truly believes the words of the *Shī*,
then when Shùn goes out, he is a subject of his ruler;
when he enters, he is a subject of his father;
he takes his mother as a concubine and marries the emperor's daughters.
Therefore, a martyr does not manage his household internally,
leading to extinction in a chaotic world;
externally, he defies his ruler,
his decaying bones and rotten flesh
scattered on the land,
flowing into rivers and valleys,
not avoiding treading on water and fire.
If the world follows and emulates him,
then the world will die everywhere
and desire premature death.
All of this is abandoning the world
and not governing.
What the world considers martyrs
are those who depart from the masses and act alone,
seeking to be different from others,
pursuing the learning of tranquility
and discussing obscure words.
I believe that tranquility
is useless teaching;
obscurity
is a word without law.
Words that come from lawlessness
and teaching that comes from uselessness
are what the world calls discerning.
I believe that a person
must serve the ruler and nourish his parents;
serving the ruler and nourishing one's parents
cannot be done with tranquility;
governing people
must be done with words of loyalty and trustworthiness, laws and techniques;
words of loyalty and trustworthiness, laws and techniques
cannot be done with obscurity.
Obscure words
and the learning of tranquility
are techniques for confusing the world.
A filial son serving his father
does not compete to seize his father's household;
a loyal subject serving his ruler
does not compete to seize his ruler's state.
If someone, being a son,
constantly praises another person's parents, saying:
"So-and-so's parents
sleep late and rise early,
striving to generate wealth
to support their children, grandchildren, subjects, and concubines,"
he is slandering his own parents.
If someone, being a subject, constantly praises the virtues of the former kings
and yearns for them,
he is slandering his own ruler.
Those who are not his parents know that this is unfilial,
but those who are not his ruler
are considered virtuous by the world,
and this is the reason for chaos.
Therefore, a subject should not praise the virtue of Yáo and Shùn,
should not admire Tāng and Wǔ's conquests,
and should not speak of the loftiness of martyrs;
dedicating all his strength to upholding the law
and focusing his heart on serving his lord is what makes a loyal subject.
In ancient times, the common people were ignorant and simple,
so they could be won over with empty names.
Now the people are clever and inquisitive,
want to use their own judgment,
and do not listen to their superiors.
Superiors must first encourage them with rewards
before they will advance;
and also frighten them with punishments
before they dare not retreat.
But the world all says:
"Xǔ Yóu declined the empire,
rewards are not enough to encourage him;
Dào Zhí violated the law and rushed into danger,
punishments are not enough to deter him."
I say:
Having no empire
and not regarding the empire as important is what Xǔ Yóu did;
Xǔ Yóu is an example of this;
having an empire and not regarding the empire as important is what Yáo and Shùn did;
Yáo and Shùn are examples of this;
sacrificing integrity for wealth,
violating the law to pursue profit,
forgetting the death of one's own body
is what Dào Zhí did;
Dào Zhí is an example of this.
These two are aberrant things.
The way to govern the state and use the people
does not measure by these two.
Governing means
governing what is constant;
the Dao means guiding what is constant.
Aberrant things and subtle words
are the harm of governing.
The highest-level scholars in the world
cannot be encouraged with rewards;
the lowest-level people in the world
cannot be deterred by punishments.
However, if rewards are not established for the highest-level scholars
and punishments are not established for the lowest-level people,
then the way to govern the state and use the people is lost.
Therefore, many people in the world do not speak of state law
but speak of alliances and oppositions.
Those dukes who speak of alliances say:
"Success in alliances will surely lead to hegemony."
And those who speak of oppositions say:
"Success in oppositions will surely lead to kingship."
The Shandong people's talk of alliances and oppositions
has never stopped for a single day,
yet success and fame are not achieved
and hegemony and kingship are not established,
because empty words are not the means to achieve governance.
The king acts alone and is called king;
therefore, the Three Kings did not strive for separation and unity
but for correctness,
and the Five Hegemons did not rely on alliances and oppositions
but on careful observation,
governing internally to control the external.
The reason why rulers face personal danger and states perish
is that high ministers are too powerful
and those at their sides are too influential.
Those who are called powerful
act arbitrarily without law,
seizing the state's power and using it for private gain.
Those who are called influential
wield authority and manipulate its importance.
These two
cannot but be carefully observed.
The reason why horses can bear heavy loads
and pull carts to distant roads
is their muscle strength.
The ruler of ten thousand chariots
and the lord of a thousand chariots,
who control the world and conquer the dukes,
do so with their power and authority.
Power and authority are the muscle strength of the ruler.
Now, if high ministers gain authority
and those at their sides wield influence,
then the ruler loses strength;
of the rulers who lose strength and are still able to maintain their state,
there is not one in a thousand.
The reason why tigers and leopards can overcome people
and control all beasts
is their claws and teeth;
if tigers and leopards lose their claws and teeth,
then people will surely control them.
Now, those who wield great influence
are the ruler's claws and teeth,
a ruler who loses his claws and teeth
is like a tiger or leopard.
The Sòng ruler lost his claws and teeth to Zǐ Hǎn,
Duke Jiǎn lost his claws and teeth to Tián Cháng,
and because they did not seize them back early,
they died and their states perished.
Now, rulers without techniques
all clearly know the mistakes of Sòng
and Jiǎn,
but they do not realize their own losses
and do not observe similar cases.
Moreover, men of law and arts
and ministers currently in power
are incompatible.
How can this be shown?
If the ruler has men of arts,
then the great ministers cannot control affairs,
and close attendants dare not sell their influence for profit;
when the power of the great ministers and close attendants is reduced,
then the way of the ruler becomes clear.
But now it is not so;
the ministers currently in power gain influence and monopolize affairs
to enrich their own private interests,
and the close attendants form cliques and factions
to control those who are distant.
In that case, when can men of law and arts be employed,
and when can the ruler make judgments?
Therefore, having arts does not necessarily lead to employment,
and power cannot be shared;
how can men of law and arts not be in danger?
Therefore, if a ruler is not able to reject the advice of great ministers
and turn his back on the slanders of close attendants,
but only agrees with what is said to be the right way,
then how can men of law and arts
dare to risk death
and offer their advice?
This is why the world is not well governed.
An enlightened ruler
promotes and rewards according to merit,
and assigns offices according to ability;
those he promotes must be virtuous,
and those he employs must be capable.
When virtuous and capable men advance,
then private requests will cease.
If those with merit receive high rewards,
and those with ability hold high office,
then how can warriors devoted to private causes
not abandon their private courage
and eagerly confront the enemy,
and how can traveling officials
not refrain from private solicitations
and strive for integrity?
This is how to gather virtuous and capable men
and disperse the followers of private interests.
Now, close attendants are not necessarily wise;
when a ruler considers a person,
he may know something and listen to him,
but then discusses his words with close attendants,
listening to the close attendants without considering their wisdom;
this is discussing wisdom with fools.
Those currently in power are not necessarily virtuous;
when a ruler considers a person,
he may admire his virtue and treat him with respect,
but then discusses his conduct with those currently in power,
listening to their words and not employing the virtuous;
this is discussing virtue with the unworthy.
Therefore, if the wise make decisions based on the opinions of fools,
and virtuous men are judged by the standards of the unworthy,
then when can virtuous and wise men be employed,
and the ruler's discernment will be blocked.
In the past, Guān Lóngféng 關龍逄 advised Jié 桀 and was injured in his limbs,
Wángzǐ Bǐgān 王子比干 remonstrated with Zhòu 紂 and had his heart cut out,
and Zǐxū 子胥 was loyal and upright to Fūchāi 夫差 but was killed at Shǔlóu 屬鏤.
These three men,
as ministers, were not disloyal,
and their advice was not inappropriate,
but they could not avoid the calamity of death
because the ruler did not examine the words of the virtuous and wise
but was blinded by the folly of the unworthy.
Now, if a ruler
is unwilling to use men of law and arts
and listens to foolish and unworthy ministers,
then which virtuous and wise man
would dare to face the danger of the three men
and offer his intelligence and ability?
This is why the world is in chaos.
If orders are strictly enforced,
then the law will not be changed;
if the law is impartial,
then officials will have no opportunity for corruption.
Once the law is established,
do not harm it with fine words.
If merit is valued,
then the people will speak less;
if goodness is valued,
then the people will speak more.
Enforce the law decisively;
a state that decides cases decisively within five *lǐ* 里 will become a kingdom,
a state that decides cases decisively within nine *lǐ* 里 will become strong,
and a state that postpones decisions will be weakened.
Govern with punishments,
fight with rewards,
and use high salaries to employ those with skills.
If the regulations of the capital are transgressed,
then there will be no illicit markets in the capital.
If manufactured goods are abundant and the merchant class is large,
and if agriculture is neglected and corruption prevails,
then the state will certainly be weakened.
If the people have surplus food,
use grain to confer ranks;
it must be according to their labor,
then the farmers will not be lazy.
If a three-inch pipe is not capped,
it cannot be filled.
If granting official positions and offering benefits and rewards are not based on merit,
it is like an uncapped pipe.
If the state grants official positions and ranks according to merit,
this is called using achievement to devise strategies
and using courage to fight bravely;
such a state will have no enemies.
If the state grants official positions and ranks according to merit,
then governance will be simplified
and words will be suppressed;
this is called using order to eliminate disorder,
and using silence to eliminate chatter;
it is rewarding merit with ranks.
Therefore, the state will be strong,
and no one in the world will be able to invade it.
When its troops go out, they will certainly take what they seek,
and what they take they will certainly be able to hold;
if it rests its troops and does not attack, it will certainly be rich.
In matters of the court,
small faults should not be censured.
Evaluate merit to grant official positions and ranks;
even if there are critical words in the court,
they must not interfere with this;
this is called governing with numbers.
To attack with force is to gain ten for every one expended;
to attack with words is to lose a hundred for every ten expended.
If the state values force,
this is called attacking with difficulty;
if the state values words,
this is called attacking with ease.
If one
can overcome his own harms,
lighten his own burdens,
and channel his remaining strength to the state,
then no one will fail to fulfill his responsibilities to the ruler.
If there are no hidden resentments within,
so that the intelligent do not interfere with each other,
then there will be no lawsuits;
if officials do not hold multiple positions,
then their skills will be specialized;
if people do not share the same tasks,
then there will be no disputes.
This is called being easily attacked.
Heavy punishments and few rewards mean
the ruler loves the people,
and the people will die for rewards;
many rewards and light punishments mean
the ruler does not love the people,
and the people will not die for rewards.
If benefits come from one source,
that state will be invincible;
if benefits come from two sources,
its troops will be only half effective;
if benefits come from ten sources,
the people will not defend it.
Severe punishments enlighten the people,
and strict regulations direct the people;
then the ruler will benefit.
In administering punishments,
if you punish the minor offenses severely,
minor offenses will not occur,
and major offenses will not arise;
this is called using punishments to eliminate punishments.
If crimes are serious but punishments are light,
and if punishments are light, then troubles will arise;
this is called using punishments to invite punishments,
and that state will surely be weakened.
The sage ruler governs the people
by considering the fundamentals,
not by following their desires,
but only by aiming to benefit them.
Therefore, his inflicting of punishments
is not because he dislikes the people,
but is the foundation of his love for them.
When punishments prevail, the people are peaceful;
when rewards are abundant, corruption arises.
Therefore, for those who govern the people,
severe punishments
are the foundation of governance;
numerous rewards
are the root of chaos.
The nature of the people is to rejoice in disorder and not be close to the law.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler's way of governing a state is this:
with clear rewards,
the people are encouraged to contribute;
with strict punishments,
the people are close to the law.
When contributions are encouraged,
public affairs are not violated;
when people are close to the law,
treachery has no place to sprout.
Therefore, those who govern the people
must prohibit treachery before it sprouts;
and those who employ troops
must ensure obedience to battle resides in the hearts of the people.
Prohibiting before its inception is the basis of order;
battles fought in the hearts of the people are victories.
The sage's governance of the people
means that prioritizing order leads to strength,
and prioritizing battle leads to victory.
The affairs of state must prioritize
unifying the hearts of the people,
focusing solely on public matters
and preventing private interests from prevailing,
rewarding those who report wrongdoing so that treachery does not arise,
and clarifying the law so that governance is not cumbersome.
Being able to utilize these four strengthens,
not being able to utilize these four weakens.
That which strengthens a state
is governance;
that which exalts the ruler
is authority.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler possesses both authority and governance,
while a chaotic ruler also possesses both authority and governance;
yet their accumulations differ,
which is why their establishments diverge.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler wields authority and is esteemed above,
and with unified governance, the state is ordered.
Therefore, law
is the foundation of kingship;
punishment
is the origin of love.
The nature of the people
is to dislike labor and enjoy leisure.
Leisure leads to neglect;
neglect leads to disorder;
disorder leads to chaos;
and rewards and punishments, not practiced throughout the land,
will inevitably be blocked.
Therefore, desiring to accomplish great achievements
but finding it difficult to obtain the necessary strength
means that great achievements cannot be attained with any hope of success;
desiring to govern through law
but finding it difficult to change established customs
means that the disorder of the people cannot be governed with any hope of success.
Therefore, governance of the people has no constant;
only law serves as governance.
When law changes with the times, order prevails;
when governance suits the era, there is achievement.
Therefore, when the people are simple and prohibitions are enforced with clarity,
order prevails;
when the age is characterized by knowledge and restraints are maintained with punishments,
they will comply.
When times change but governance does not adapt, there is disorder;
when capabilities are plentiful but prohibitions remain unchanged,
there is decline.
Therefore, the sage's governance of the people
means that law changes with the times
and prohibitions adapt with abilities.
Those who can surpass their strength on the land become wealthy;
those who can rouse their strength against the enemy become strong;
those whose strength cannot be contained become kings.
Therefore, the way of kings lies in what is opened
and what is closed;
closing off treachery ensures kingship.
Therefore, the art of kingship does not rely on the absence of external disorder,
but relies on its own inability to be thrown into disorder.
Relying on the absence of external disorder
to establish order leads to decline;
relying on one's own inability to be thrown into disorder
to implement the law leads to prosperity.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler's governance of the state
is suited to the art of preventing disorder.
When noble ranks are valued,
the ruler is esteemed above;
therefore, when rewards are based on merit and ranks are assigned accordingly,
evil has no avenue to interfere.
Those who value strength have noble ranks;
when ranks are noble,
the ruler is honored;
when the ruler is honored,
kingship is assured.
When a state does not value strength but relies on private learning,
its ranks are low;
when ranks are low,
the ruler is debased;
when the ruler is debased, decline is inevitable.
Therefore, the way to establish a state and employ the people
is to be able to close off the external, block private interests,
and rely on oneself above;
then kingship can be achieved.
Truly, broad territories and esteemed rulers
have never been achieved without strict laws, thus enabling commands to be executed and prohibitions enforced throughout the land.
Therefore, those who rule others must divide ranks and regulate stipends,
and the law must be strictly and heavily enforced.
When the state is ordered, the people are secure;
when affairs are chaotic, the state is endangered.
Enforcing the law strictly captures the people's feelings;
making prohibitions lenient loses sight of reality.
Furthermore, the willingness to die for a cause
is what the people possess;
their feelings compel them to exert their utmost efforts
to achieve what they desire;
and what they like and dislike
is what is determined by those above;
the people like profit and rewards
and dislike punishments and penalties.
When those above control likes and dislikes
to direct the people's efforts,
the reality of the situation should not be lost;
yet if prohibitions are lenient and the reality is lost,
it means that punishments and rewards are misapplied.
To govern the people without upholding the law as good
is like this:
it is as if there is no law.
Therefore, regarding the principles of order and chaos,
it is appropriate to prioritize clearly distinguishing punishments and rewards as a matter of urgency;
those who govern a state all have laws,
yet some survive and some perish.
Those that perish
are those whose systems of punishment and reward
are not clearly distinguished.
For those who govern a state,
there must be clear distinctions in punishment and reward.
Having conflicting opinions and calling it distinction
cannot be called distinction.
As for the distinctions made by a discerning ruler,
they are uniquely distinct.
Therefore, his people value the law and fear prohibitions,
desiring not to incur punishment and daring not to collude in seeking rewards.
Hence it is said:
the people engage in affairs
without awaiting punishments and rewards.
Therefore, in a state of perfect order,
the focus is on being adept at stopping treachery;
why is this so?
Its laws are aligned with human nature
and are concerned with governance.
In that case, what is the way to eliminate minor treachery?
It is to diligently ensure that they regulate each other's emotions.
Then how can they be made to spy on each other?
It is said:
The principle is to implicate each other.
When prohibitions still have connections to oneself,
one cannot but spy on each other,
fearing only that one will not be able to avoid punishment.
Those with treacherous intentions are not allowed to forget,
and those who spy are numerous.
In this way,
one is cautious about oneself and spies on others,
revealing the secrets of treachery.
Those who report transgressions are exempted from punishment
and receive rewards;
those who fail to report treachery will be punished
and subjected to collective punishment.
In this way,
all types of treachery will be exposed.
Treachery cannot be tolerated in its minute forms;
this is due to the imposition of joint responsibility for private reports.
Now, the clearest principle of governance is to
rely on standards and not on individuals.
Therefore, in a state that has methods,
if one is not recommended, then one should not be employed;
the territory will certainly be well-governed,
because it relies on standards.
A state that is destroyed allows troops to publicly march across its land,
yet is unable to defend against or prohibit them,
because it relies on individuals and lacks standards.
Attacking oneself is human,
attacking others relies on standards.
Therefore, a state that has methods
abandons words and relies on law.
Generally, extraordinary achievements that conform to regulations are difficult to recognize,
and transgressions of law that are based on words are difficult to perceive,
therefore, rewards and punishments are confused and inconsistent.
The so-called conforming to regulations being difficult to recognize
refers to treacherous achievements;
the difficulty in perceiving ministers' transgressions
lies in losing the root.
Following principles without seeing false achievements,
and measuring sentiments while being deceived by treacherous roots,
then how can these two avoid both losses?
Therefore, empty scholars establish reputations internally,
and orators devise strategies externally,
so foolishness, cowardice, courage, and wisdom are connected,
and by empty principles, they appeal to customs
and are tolerated by the world.
Therefore, their laws are not used,
and punishments are not applied to the despicable.
If this is the case,
how can rewards and punishments avoid accommodating both?
Authenticity, therefore, reaches a certain point,
and principles lose their measure.
The loss of measure
is not caused by the law,
but by the law being fixed and relying on wisdom.
Abandoning the law and relying on wisdom,
then how can those who receive affairs obtain their duties?
If duties and affairs do not align,
then how can the law avoid being lost,
and how can punishments avoid being troublesome?
Therefore, rewards and punishments are chaotic,
and the state's path is erroneous,
because rewards and punishments are not clearly distinguished.
